lessons.plain: The software development lifecycle, usually shortened to SDLC, is the path a piece of software travels from an idea to running in front of users and then keeps being changed. Think of a kitchen producing meals: someone decides what to cook, plans the recipe, prepares ingredients, tastes before serving, serves, and then watches how customers react. Different teams arrange these steps differently. Some finish each step fully before starting the next, while others loop through small rounds again and again. Knowing the phases and the shape of the model a team uses tells you where mistakes get caught, how fast changes reach users, and where automation can take over the repetitive parts.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team finishes all of its design and testing before writing any code, then writes everything, and only tests at the end. Compared with a team that ships a small working change every two weeks, what is the biggest risk of the first approach, and why?
lessons.teach:
Definition. The software development lifecycle (SDLC) is the set of phases a change goes through: plan (decide what to build and why), design (decide how the pieces fit together), build (write the code and package it into a versioned artifact, meaning a stored, labelled bundle that can be deployed), test (check that it behaves correctly and is safe), release (put it into an environment users can reach), and operate (run it, monitor it, and feed what you learn back into planning). A model is the rule a team follows for moving through those phases. In a waterfall model each phase finishes before the next starts. In an iterative or agile model, such as Scrum, the team passes through the phases in short cycles, each producing a working increment. In continuous delivery, the release step is automated so that every change passing the tests can reach production on its own.

Why it works. Defects found early are cheap to fix. A bug caught by a unit test minutes after a commit costs far less than one a customer finds after a six-month release. Short cycles shrink how much change is at risk at once, so when something breaks, the cause is easier to find. Automation lets a machine repeat the checks every time, which people tend to skip under pressure.

Worked example. A team changes a fare calculation. Plan: the change is scoped to one function. Build: the code is compiled and packaged as artifact version 42. Test: a unit test fails because a rounding rule was changed by accident. The pipeline stops, and the artifact never reaches release. Without that test phase, the wrong fare would have reached riders the same afternoon.

Common mistake. Treating the phases as a one-way sequence where testing is a final gate. Defects are then found late, when fixing them is expensive and the release is already overdue.

Consequence. In a running system, a release that batches many changes together is hard to roll back, because you cannot tell which change caused the fault. Small, frequent releases keep each change traceable, so the fastest safe fix is usually to revert one small change.

questions.prompt: A clinic's booking team changes the wording of appointment reminder texts. Plan: the change is limited to the reminder message only. Build: the code is packaged as artifact version 8, a stored and labelled bundle that can be deployed. Test: a check confirms the clinic's phone number still appears in the text, and that check passes. Missing step: the pipeline now hands artifact version 8 to the release phase because every test passed. Which choice correctly describes what the release phase does with it?
choices: It rebuilds the code from source, creating version 9, and discards version 8 so the labels stay unique.
It moves version 8 directly to the operate phase, skipping release, since the change has already been tested.
It puts artifact version 8 where users can reach it, and in continuous delivery this happens without a person having to approve it.
It waits for a manual design review, because a passing test is never enough to allow release.
questions.why: Under continuous delivery the release phase is automated, so an artifact that passes all tests is placed in an environment users can reach without a further human step.

questions.prompt: Which term describes a stored, labelled bundle of code that can be deployed to an environment?
choices: An artifact
A model
An operate phase
A sprint backlog
questions.why: The teaching text defines an artifact as a stored, labelled bundle that can be deployed, produced in the build phase.

questions.prompt: A ticket-booking company batches 14 changes into one release. A fault appears after release and the team cannot tell which change caused it. Based on the SDLC teaching text, what would most help them in future?
choices: Batching more changes per release so that fewer releases need to be checked
Keeping releases small and frequent so each change stays traceable and can be reverted alone
Rolling back the whole release every time, since reverting one change is never useful
Removing the test phase so that the cause is easier to spot during operation
questions.why: Small, frequent releases keep each change traceable, so the fastest safe fix is usually to revert a single small change.

questions.prompt: A team runs its tests only once, after all development is finished, and treats that run as the last checkpoint before release. What common mistake does this show?
choices: Working in short cycles that each produce a working increment, which the teaching text warns against
Automating the release step so that every change can reach production on its own
Attaching version labels to artifacts, which makes the build phase slower
Treating the phases as a one-way sequence where testing is a final gate, so defects are found late when they are expensive to fix
questions.why: The teaching text names treating testing as a final gate in a one-way sequence as the common mistake, because late-found defects cost more to fix and delay the release.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate asks why we do not just write the whole feature and test it at the end, like we used to. Explain in your own words the lifecycle phases that matter for this question, which model you would recommend and where it is weakest, and name one limit of your recommendation.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would explain the lifecycle as a loop of plan, design, build, test, release and operate, with what we learn from operating feeding back into planning. Testing only at the end is the weak point: defects found there are expensive to fix, and a large batch makes it hard to know which change broke things. I would recommend short iterative cycles with automated tests run on every commit, so each change is checked while the author still remembers it. The limit is that small cycles only work with reliable test automation and a safe way to release; without those, frequent releases just mean frequent breakage. Some work, such as a regulated sign-off or a large data migration, also has a fixed sequence and cannot be split into daily releases, so the model should match the risk of the work rather than being applied as a slogan.
rubricPoints: Names the lifecycle phases (plan, design, build, test, release, operate) and the feedback from operating into planning.
Explains that defects found late cost more and that large batched changes are hard to trace or roll back.
Recommends short iterative cycles with automated tests on every commit, and says why they help.
States a real limit, such as needing test automation and safe release, or work that cannot be split.

suggested.rationale: That mission has the learner work through an iterative model in practice, covering the model half of this objective, while the phase vocabulary is only read here.

lessons.plain: A deployment pattern is the set of choices that decide how code moves from a developer's commit to the place users run it, and where those places live. In a single-account setup, one set of cloud resources holds the pipeline and every environment, which is simple but means a mistake in one place can reach everything. In a multi-account setup, each environment such as development, test or production sits in its own isolated account, and a central pipeline account reaches into them through narrow permissions. The idea is like keeping separate rooms for separate jobs: when one room floods, the others stay dry. You are learning which layout to choose and why.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose a build pipeline and the production system share one cloud account, and a deploy script has a bug that deletes resources. What is the worst thing it could reach, and what would change if production lived in its own separate account?
lessons.teach:
A pipeline is an ordered series of stages that takes a commit through build, test and deploy steps. A stage is one step in that series, and an environment is a place where the software runs, such as development, test or production. An AWS account is a boundary for resources and permissions: a role, a bucket or a server in one account is invisible to another unless you grant access explicitly. Single-account deployment keeps the pipeline and every environment inside one account. It is simple to set up, but permissions are shared, so a broken or over-privileged deploy step can reach production directly. Multi-account deployment places each environment in its own account, and usually a separate tooling account runs the pipeline. The pipeline reaches each target by assuming a cross-account role, which is a role defined in the target account that trusts the tooling account and grants only deploy actions for a short session.

Worked example. A commit lands on the main branch. Step 1: the build stage runs in the tooling account and writes a versioned artifact to an artifact store. Step 2: the test stage runs against that same artifact. Step 3: the deploy-to-test stage assumes the test account's deploy role and releases the artifact there. Step 4: a manual approval gate pauses the flow. Step 5: the deploy-to-production stage assumes the production role and releases the same artifact, not a rebuilt one. Each hop is an explicit grant, so a compromised test account cannot quietly write into production.

Common mistake: giving the tooling account administrator rights in production so deploys never fail on permissions. This removes the boundary the layout was built to create. Another frequent failure is forgetting that the artifact's encryption key must also allow the target accounts to decrypt it, which produces an access-denied error only at the deploy stage.

In a running system, the layout decides blast radius: a bad deploy in a multi-account setup can break the account it targets, while the others keep serving traffic.

questions.prompt: A furniture retailer runs its pipeline in a tooling account (111). Its staging account is 222 and its live store account is 333. A commit lands on the release branch and the flow runs as follows. Step 1: the build stage runs in account 111 and writes artifact sales-api-3.2.0 to the artifact store. Step 2: the test stage runs against that exact artifact. Step 3: the deploy-to-staging stage assumes the staging deploy role in account 222 and releases sales-api-3.2.0 there. Step 4: [MISSING STEP]. Step 5: the deploy-to-live stage assumes the live deploy role in account 333 and releases the same sales-api-3.2.0 artifact. Which choice correctly fills in Step 4?
choices: The tooling account's administrator role is granted write access in account 333 so the live deploy cannot be blocked by permissions.
Account 222 is granted the live deploy role so it can copy the artifact into account 333 without a second assumption.
A manual approval gate pauses the flow until a reviewer approves the release to live.
The live deploy stage rebuilds the code from the release branch so it picks up the latest commits before deploying.
questions.why: The layout places a manual approval gate between the staging and live deploys, so the flow pauses there until a person approves, while the live stage still releases the same artifact rather than a rebuilt one.

questions.prompt: A logistics company keeps its pipeline in account 500 and its production workloads in account 600. Which arrangement matches the multi-account pattern described in the teaching model?
choices: Account 600 runs its own copy of the pipeline and pulls code from account 500 on a schedule.
The pipeline in account 500 holds a long-lived access key for account 600 stored in its build configuration file.
The pipeline in account 500 assumes a role defined in account 600 that trusts account 500 and grants only deploy actions for a short session.
Both accounts share one administrator role so that deploy steps never fail on permissions.
questions.why: In the multi-account pattern the target account defines a cross-account role that trusts the tooling account and grants only deploy actions for a short session, which is what the first choice describes.

questions.prompt: A media company's pipeline builds an artifact in its tooling account and passes it to a production account. The build and test stages pass, but the production deploy stage fails with an access-denied error, and the production account cannot read the artifact at all. The deploy role itself has the correct permissions. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The encryption key protecting the artifact does not allow the production account to decrypt it.
The test stage ran too early and the artifact was not yet finished uploading.
The production deploy role is trusted by the wrong branch name in the source repository.
The artifact was built with a different version number than the one the test stage expected.
questions.why: A key that does not grant the target account decrypt permission causes an access-denied error only at the deploy stage, even when the deploy role itself is correctly permitted.

questions.prompt: A bank has three workload accounts, A, B and C, each deployed by the same pipeline layout. A bad release is deployed to account C only. What is the expected effect on accounts A and B?
choices: Both A and B stop serving traffic too, because the pipeline shares one set of permissions across accounts.
A and B keep running, but they must rebuild their artifacts before they can serve traffic again.
Neither A nor B is affected in its traffic, because the bad deploy only reaches the account it targeted.
Both A and B roll back automatically, because the pipeline treats all accounts as a single environment.
questions.why: Because each environment sits in its own account and the bad deploy only reached account C, the blast radius is limited to C while A and B keep serving traffic.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why a multi-account deployment layout is worth its extra setup cost, and name one limit or tradeoff it introduces.
lessons.modelAnswer: Separate accounts give each environment its own permission boundary, so a bad deploy or a leaked credential in one environment cannot directly change another. The pipeline lives in a tooling account and reaches each target through a narrow cross-account role that only allows deploy actions. Production is also protected from test-stage mistakes because the same artifact is promoted rather than rebuilt. The tradeoff is real setup cost: you manage more roles, trust policies and encryption key policies, and a missing grant shows up as an access-denied failure at the deploy stage rather than in the code. For a small team with one application, a single account with clear approval gates may be the better starting point, and the extra accounts earn their keep as blast radius and audit needs grow.
rubricPoints: Separate accounts create permission boundaries that limit blast radius between environments
The pipeline reaches targets through narrow cross-account roles rather than shared admin rights
Promoting the same versioned artifact keeps production matched to what was tested
Tradeoff: more roles, trust and key policies to manage, and failures appear at the deploy stage

suggested.rationale: A planned deployment-strategies engine would let the learner trace promotion across environments and watch where a missing cross-account grant stops a release.

lessons.plain: An artifact is the packaged thing a build produces, such as a library, a container image, or a zip of compiled code. An artifact repository is the shelf where those packages are stored, labelled with versions, and handed out to the pipeline stages that need them. Instead of rebuilding code every time something needs it, the pipeline builds once, stores the result, and every later stage pulls that same stored copy. Configuring a repository means deciding what it holds, who may read or write it, and how long old copies are kept.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your build produces a container image on Monday, and the deploy job pulls the tag 'latest' on Friday. Without looking anything up, what could go wrong, and what would you change so the deploy always gets the exact image that was tested?
lessons.teach:
An artifact is any file a build produces that later stages consume. A repository is managed storage for those files. Three kinds matter here. A package repository, such as AWS CodeArtifact, holds language packages like Python or Java libraries, and can act as a single trusted source that build tools query. A container image registry, such as Amazon Elastic Container Registry (ECR), holds container images, which are packaged filesystems plus start-up instructions. Object storage, such as Amazon S3, holds any other file, such as zip bundles, test reports, or deployment packages.

The reason to use a repository is that it lets the pipeline build once. The build stage stores an artifact under an immutable version, such as the commit hash. Every later stage (tests, staging, production) pulls that exact copy, so what was tested is what ships. Access is controlled by identity policies: the build role may push, deploy roles may only pull, and humans do not push to production by hand. Lifecycle rules expire old or untagged copies so storage does not grow forever, but they must keep any version that is still deployed or that a rollback might need.

Worked example. A build for commit a1f3 creates the image app:a1f3 and pushes it to ECR. The test stage pulls app:a1f3 and runs integration tests. The deploy stage pulls the same image, by its digest, which is a fixed fingerprint of the content. A lifecycle rule keeps the last 30 images, so app:a1f3 and the previous release are still there if a rollback is needed.

Common mistake: deploying a mutable tag such as latest. If the tag is overwritten, the bits in production differ from the bits that were tested, and two instances can run different code under the same name.

In a running system this shows up during scaling or recovery. A replacement instance that pulls latest may start a build nobody tested, and a lifecycle rule that expired the previous image can make an incident rollback impossible at the moment you need it.

questions.prompt: A team building a payments service runs this pipeline. Step 1: the build for commit 4b7e pushes a container image to a registry under the tag payments:4b7e, and the registry reports the image's digest, a fixed fingerprint of its exact contents. Step 2: the integration test stage pulls payments:4b7e and the tests pass. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: the production deploy stage pulls the image by that digest and starts it. What completes step 3?
choices: The build stage rebuilds the image from the commit again just before deploy so the copy is fresh.
The registry is told to overwrite the tag payments:4b7e with each new build so the tag always points to the newest image.
The pipeline carries the digest recorded in step 1 forward with the release record so the deploy stage receives that exact fingerprint rather than a tag.
A developer downloads the image to a laptop and pushes it to production by hand after the tests pass.
questions.why: Passing the recorded digest forward guarantees that the deploy stage ships the same bytes that the tests ran against, which is the purpose of building once and storing an immutable artifact.

questions.prompt: In artifact storage, what does it mean for a version to be immutable?
choices: The version is automatically deleted after a fixed number of days.
The version is copied to every region so that any region can serve it.
Once stored under that version name, the contents can never be replaced or changed, so the name always means the same bytes.
The version can be renamed later without changing its contents.
questions.why: Immutability means the stored bytes behind a version name cannot be altered, so pulling that name always yields what was originally tested.

questions.prompt: A team keeps only the last 10 images in its registry using a lifecycle rule. Production is running an image from 8 builds ago that has no other copy. A new build succeeds and the rule runs. What is the most serious risk?
choices: The new build will fail its tests because the older image is missing.
The registry will refuse to accept the new build until the old image is deleted by hand.
Deployments will become faster but less secure because fewer images are stored.
The production image may be expired by the rule, so a later restart or rollback cannot pull the version that is running and known to work.
questions.why: Lifecycle rules must keep any version still deployed or needed for rollback, and expiring the running image removes the ability to recover to it.

questions.prompt: Two instances in an auto scaling group both start from the mutable tag stable. The tag was overwritten between their launches, so they run different code under the same name. Which practice prevents this?
choices: Add more instances so the group averages out the differences between versions.
Ask each engineer to confirm the tag manually before every launch.
Pin each deployment to the image digest, a fixed fingerprint of the content, instead of the mutable tag.
Schedule the tag to be overwritten only at midnight each day.
questions.why: A digest identifies exact contents and cannot be silently changed, so every instance launched from it runs identical code regardless of later tag overwrites.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why the pipeline should build one immutable artifact, store it in a repository, and have every later stage pull that exact copy, instead of rebuilding from source in each stage. Name one limit or tradeoff of this approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: Building once and storing the result under a fixed version means every stage tests and deploys the same bytes. If each stage rebuilt from source, dependencies or base images could have changed between stages, so a test could pass on one build and production could run a different one. The repository is the record of what exists and who may use it, so access rules can limit who pushes and who only pulls. The tradeoff is storage and governance: artifacts accumulate, so lifecycle rules are needed, and a rule that deletes too aggressively can remove the version a rollback depends on. A second tradeoff is that a stored artifact can be stale if it bakes in a vulnerable library, so it needs rebuilding and rescanning on a schedule, not just trust.
rubricPoints: Build once and promote the same immutable artifact so tested bits equal deployed bits.
Repositories enforce access: build roles push, deploy roles pull, no manual production pushes.
Lifecycle rules control storage growth but must keep deployed and rollback versions.
Mutable tags such as latest break traceability and can cause untested code to run.

suggested.rationale: This objective is mostly repository facts, access settings, and console configuration that are best learned by reading and then checking the explanation.

lessons.plain: Version control is a shared history of every change to your code, where each change gets a permanent label and can be compared, reviewed and undone. Connecting a pipeline to it means the automated delivery line starts from a specific saved change, not from someone's laptop. Each environment, meaning a place where a copy of the app runs such as test, staging or production, is linked to a branch or a tag, which is a named pointer into that history. When a change lands on that pointer, the pipeline builds it and moves it toward the matching environment. The result is that you can always answer which exact code is running where, and return to a known earlier state.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your team merges a fix into the branch that deploys to staging and it passes tests there. What should production receive, and how could you prove production is running the same code that was tested?
lessons.teach:
Version control is a system that stores every change to a project as an ordered history of commits. A commit is a saved snapshot of changes, identified by a long unique ID called a hash. A branch is a movable name that points at a commit, and a tag is a fixed name for one commit. An environment is one place the application runs, such as test, staging or production. Integrating a pipeline with environments means connecting these pieces: each environment is tied to a branch or tag, and a change arriving there starts the pipeline.

Why it works: the commit hash is a precise, unchanging identity for the code. If the pipeline records the hash it built from, every later stage can show it is handling the same code, and an audit can state exactly what is in production.

Worked example: a team maps the branch release to production and develop to staging. Step 1: a developer merges a fix into develop at commit abc123. Step 2: the push triggers the pipeline, which records abc123. Step 3: it builds one artifact labelled abc123 and deploys it to staging. Step 4: tests pass, and the team merges develop into release at the same commit. Step 5: the pipeline sees the release change, reuses the stored artifact labelled abc123 rather than rebuilding, and deploys it to production. Production now runs exactly what staging tested.

Common mistake: rebuilding from the branch name in each environment. Two builds from the same branch can differ if a dependency changed in between, so production may run code that was never tested. Another mistake is hard-coding environment settings into the branch, which forces code edits every time code is promoted.

Consequence: if production breaks, the team can point the release branch at the previous known-good commit and redeploy the artifact already stored for it. That is faster and safer than rebuilding under pressure.

questions.prompt: Tidewater Parcels runs two environments. The branch named live is tied to production and the branch named qa is tied to staging. Production has started failing after commit 4c1a was pushed to live. The last commit production ran successfully was 77d2, and the pipeline stored an artifact labelled 77d2 when that commit was first built. The team wants to roll back. Step 1: the team moves the live branch so it points at commit 77d2. Step 2: the push triggers the pipeline, which sees a change on live and records that the change is commit 77d2. Step 3: the pipeline looks up the artifact already stored under the label 77d2. Step 4: [missing step to be completed by the learner]. Which action completes step 4?
choices: The team edits the production settings inside the live branch to point at an older release number, then rebuilds.
The pipeline rebuilds the code from the live branch name so production gets a fresh build of 77d2 with current dependencies.
The pipeline deploys the stored artifact labelled 77d2 to production without rebuilding it.
The pipeline deploys the artifact labelled 4c1a again, because that is the one production most recently received.
questions.why: The stored artifact for commit 77d2 is the exact build that ran successfully before, so deploying it reproduces that known-good state without a rebuild that could introduce different code.

questions.prompt: What does a commit hash give a pipeline that a branch name does not?
choices: A movable pointer that automatically follows the newest change added to the branch.
A setting that tells the environment which database to connect to.
A list of every environment the application has ever been deployed to.
A permanent identity for one exact snapshot of the code, so later stages can confirm they are handling the same code.
questions.why: A hash is a precise, unchanging identifier for one commit, whereas a branch name points at whichever commit is current and can move.

questions.prompt: A team deploys to production by having the pipeline rebuild from the branch name each time, instead of reusing the artifact that was tested in staging. A week later production misbehaves but staging passed. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The developers forgot to write any tests for the new feature.
The commit hash was too long, so the pipeline truncated it and deployed the wrong file.
Production was built from the branch later, and a dependency may have changed between the staging build and the production build, so production ran code that was never tested.
The production servers have too little memory to run the application.
questions.why: Rebuilding from a branch name can produce a different result if anything it depends on changed in between, which means production can run untested code.

questions.prompt: An auditor asks exactly which code is running in production right now. Which record answers this most directly, given how the pipeline is integrated with environments?
choices: The commit hash the pipeline recorded when it deployed to production.
The number of commits made to the branch in the last month.
The name of the production environment written on the server's label.
The name of the developer who most recently pushed to the release branch.
questions.why: Because the pipeline records the hash it built from and carries it through each stage, the hash recorded at production deployment states exactly what is in production.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a release branch should be linked to the production environment in your pipeline, and name one limit or tradeoff of tying environments to branches.
lessons.modelAnswer: Each environment points at a branch or tag in version control, and a push to that pointer starts the pipeline. The key is that the pipeline records the exact commit it used, builds one artifact labelled with that commit, and promotes that same artifact through the environments instead of rebuilding for each one. That way production runs the bytes that were tested. The tradeoff is that branch-per-environment models get heavy: long-lived branches drift apart, and a hotfix made on the production branch has to be merged back into the development line or it gets lost. Many teams keep one main line and use tags or an approval step for production instead. The trigger also needs careful scoping, because a stray push to a shared branch could otherwise deploy straight to production.
rubricPoints: Each environment is tied to a specific branch or tag that starts the pipeline
The pipeline records the exact commit and promotes one built artifact rather than rebuilding per environment
Production runs the same tested artifact, which makes rollback and audit possible
A tradeoff such as branch drift, hotfix merge-back, or accidental triggers on shared branches

suggested.rationale: Repairing a broken CI pipeline makes the learner trace how triggers, branches and build steps connect, which is the core of this objective.

lessons.plain: A build is the step that turns source code into something you can run or ship: it compiles, packages, and runs checks. AWS CodeBuild is Amazon's managed build service, which means you do not keep your own build servers running. You describe the steps in a file, CodeBuild starts a fresh, temporary environment, runs those steps on your source, saves the outputs, and then throws the environment away. Think of it as hiring a clean kitchen for each meal instead of cooking in a shared one where yesterday's leftovers could change today's dish. Setting it up well means deciding where the source comes from, what the environment contains, what the steps are, and where the results go.
lessons.guessPrompt: Why might a team want every build to start from a brand-new, empty environment instead of reusing the machine that ran the previous build?
lessons.teach: A build project is the saved configuration for one kind of build in CodeBuild. It names four things: the source (where the code comes from, such as a repository or a bucket), the build environment (a container image with the tools installed, plus a compute size), the buildspec (a YAML file in your repository that lists the steps), and the artifacts (the outputs to keep and where to store them). The project also has a service role, an identity with permissions that the build borrows to write logs, read secrets, or push images. Each build runs in a fresh environment, so anything not in the source or the image is missing. That is why builds are repeatable: the same commit and the same image should produce the same result. The buildspec is organised into phases. install prepares tools, pre_build runs checks such as linting, build does the main work, and post_build finishes. A worked example: a Python service has a buildspec whose install phase installs its dependencies, whose build phase runs the unit tests and then creates a package in a folder called dist, and whose artifacts section names that folder. When a build starts, CodeBuild fetches the commit, runs install, then build. If the tests exit with a nonzero code, the build is marked failed and no artifact is published. A common mistake is writing a secret, such as a password, directly into the buildspec, where anyone with read access to the repository can see it; the buildspec should reference a secret store instead. The consequence in a running system is that a pipeline can pass today only because of files left over from an earlier build, then fail on a clean run tomorrow.

questions.prompt: A team builds a Go API with a buildspec that has these steps. Step 1: CodeBuild fetches the commit from the repository. Step 2: the install phase runs nothing, because the container image already contains Go 1.22. Step 3: the pre_build phase runs a formatting check that exits with code 1 if any file is unformatted. Step 4 is missing and is what you must supply. Step 5: the artifacts section keeps only the file bin/api, and only from a successful build. Which completion correctly fills step 4?
choices: The build phase compiles the binary into bin/api, and post_build then publishes it even though pre_build failed.
The build phase runs first, because pre_build only prints warnings and cannot change the result of the build.
CodeBuild retries the pre_build phase three times and then runs the build phase anyway, so the artifact is published.
Because pre_build exited nonzero, the build is marked failed, the build phase does not run, and no artifact is published.
questions.why: A nonzero exit in an earlier phase marks the whole build failed, so the later build phase is skipped and nothing is published, which matches the rule that a failing check stops the artifact from being kept.

questions.prompt: A build project is configured with a service role. Which statement best describes what that role is?
choices: An identity with permissions that the build borrows to do things like write logs, read secrets, or push images.
The username the team uses to log into the CodeBuild console and edit the project.
The compute size chosen for the build container, which controls how many CPU cores it gets.
A list of the commands in the build phase, stored separately from the buildspec file.
questions.why: The service role is the identity the build assumes to get permissions for its work, not a login, a command list, or a hardware setting.

questions.prompt: A team puts the database password for its integration tests directly in the buildspec, so the tests can connect during the build phase. A colleague with read-only access to the repository can see the password. What is the best correction?
choices: Have the buildspec reference the password from a secret store, so the file holds only a reference and not the value.
Rename the buildspec file to a hidden name so that repository readers cannot find it.
Move the password into the install phase, because install runs before the tests and the password is then hidden.
Keep the password in the buildspec but add a comment warning people not to share it.
questions.why: A secret written in the buildspec is visible to anyone who can read the repository, so the buildspec should point to a secret store instead; the other fixes only move or hide the text.

questions.prompt: A build passes on a team's own machine, which still has packages installed from an earlier experiment. The same commit fails in CodeBuild on a clean run. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The service role lacks permission to write logs, so the build always fails regardless of the code.
The build depends on a file that existed only in the earlier local environment and is not in the source or the container image.
The artifacts section names the wrong folder, which causes the tests to fail before they run.
CodeBuild does not support Python packages, so every build with them fails by default.
questions.why: Each CodeBuild build starts in a fresh environment, so anything not in the source or the container image is missing, which is why a build can pass only because of leftover files.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what a CodeBuild build project needs in order to run a build, and name one limit or tradeoff of using a managed build service compared with running your own build server.
lessons.modelAnswer: A CodeBuild build project tells the service where the source code is, which container image and compute size to use for the build environment, which buildspec file holds the steps, which outputs to keep as artifacts and where to store them, and which service role grants the permissions the build needs, such as writing logs or reading a secret. Each build runs in a fresh environment, so nothing from a previous build is available unless it is in the source, the image, or an explicit cache. The tradeoff of the managed service is that you get no permanent machine to customise or inspect. Anything that needs special software, a long-lived cache, or a particular network position has to be built into the image or configured explicitly. You also depend on the service's limits on build time and compute size, so very long or very heavy builds may need to be split up.
rubricPoints: Names the core parts of a build project: source, environment, buildspec, artifacts, and service role
Explains that each build starts fresh, so repeatability depends on what is explicitly provided
Describes at least one real limit or tradeoff of a managed build service, such as no persistent machine or build time and size limits

suggested.rationale: Repairing a broken CI pipeline makes the learner read build steps, failing commands and their effect on the outcome, which is the core of this objective.

lessons.plain: A build or deployment often needs passwords, API keys, and database credentials. If these are typed into code or config files, anyone who can read the repository can use them, and they tend to spread into logs and old copies. This topic is about keeping those values out of the code and handing them to the pipeline only when it needs them. AWS offers two managed places for this: a secret store built for sensitive values that can rotate them, and a configuration store that holds plain settings and can also hold encrypted values. The skill is choosing where a value lives, letting the pipeline fetch it at run time under its own narrow identity, and never printing it. Think of a locked key cabinet that the build may open briefly, not a note taped to the door.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your pipeline needs a database password to run a migration. Where would you put it so that someone reading the repository never sees it, and what could still go wrong even then?
lessons.teach:
A secret is any value that grants access, such as a password, an API key, or a signing token. A configuration value is everything else the pipeline needs, such as a region name or a feature flag. Keeping the two apart matters because secrets need stricter handling. The core rule is that secrets are never written into source code, build scripts, container images, or log output. Instead, the pipeline asks a managed store for the value at run time.

AWS Secrets Manager is a managed secret store. It encrypts stored values, controls which identities may read them, can record who read them, and can rotate a value on a schedule, meaning it generates a new password, updates the database, and retires the old one. AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store is a managed configuration store that holds named values in a hierarchy. A parameter can be plain text, or a SecureString that is encrypted. Parameter Store suits settings and simpler secrets; Secrets Manager suits credentials that need rotation.

The reason this works is that the pipeline runs under an identity, usually a role with a narrow permission such as reading one named secret. The secret never appears in the repository, and revoking that permission cuts access without changing any code.

Worked example: a deploy job needs a database password stored under the name prod/orders/db. Step one, the password is stored once in Secrets Manager, encrypted. Step two, the pipeline's role is granted read access to that one secret only. Step three, at run time the job requests the value, uses it to connect, and keeps it in memory only for that step. Step four, when the password is rotated, the next run fetches the new value with no code change.

Common mistake: echoing the value to debug a failed step, or passing it as a command-line argument, where it can show up in process lists and build logs. Consequence: a leaked deploy credential can let someone reach production data until the value is rotated, so narrow permissions and rotation are the real safety net.

questions.prompt: A mobile team at another company keeps a signing token for its test-store uploads. Their setup, traced in order: (1) the token is saved once as a SecureString parameter, which is a Parameter Store value that is encrypted at rest, at the path /mobile/android/upload-token; (2) the build role, the identity the pipeline runs under, gets read access to that one parameter path only; (4) after the token is changed, the next run picks up the new value with no edit to the build file. Step 3 is missing. What must the job do at run time to complete the flow?
choices: Print the parameter to the build log at the start of the job so the value can be checked by eye.
Bake the token into the container image so that it is present on every run without a lookup.
Request the parameter at run time with decryption on and use the value in memory for that step only.
Write the token into the Gradle build file so the build can read it even when offline.
questions.why: Step 3 is the run-time fetch: the job asks the store for the value when it needs it and keeps it in memory, which is what lets rotation and revocation work without code changes.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a configuration value rather than a secret, as the teaching text uses those words?
choices: A database password for a reporting service.
An API key that lets a script post to a chat tool.
A signing token used to sign release packages.
A region name such as eu-west-2 that the deploy step reads.
questions.why: A region name grants no access, so under the teaching text's definition it is configuration, while the other three all grant access and are therefore secrets.

questions.prompt: A deploy script receives a token as a command-line argument so it can call a service. A reviewer says the repository is clean because the token is never committed. What is the remaining risk?
choices: The script will fail at start-up because the secret store rejects tokens passed as arguments.
The shell encrypts arguments automatically, so the value cannot be read by anyone else on the machine.
The value can appear in process listings and build logs, so it can leak even though it was never committed.
The risk only exists if the repository is public, so a private repository is fully safe.
questions.why: Arguments are visible to other processes and often end up in logs, which is the common mistake the teaching text warns about, even when the source code is clean.

questions.prompt: A pipeline's role currently reads a database password from a secret store. The security team wants that access cut off right away, and no code may change. Which action does this?
choices: Turn on verbose logging for the build so that any misuse is recorded.
Remove the role's read permission on that one secret.
Edit the pipeline definition file to point at a different secret name.
Delete the secret's old commits from the repository history.
questions.why: Because the pipeline reaches the secret through its role, removing that narrow permission revokes access without touching code, while the other choices either change code or do not stop reads.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why a pipeline should fetch a database password from a managed store at run time instead of reading it from a config file in the repository, and name one limit or tradeoff of that approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: The repository is read by many people and copied into forks, backups, and build logs, so a password committed there is effectively visible to everyone with access. Fetching it at run time means the pipeline's own role is granted read access to that one secret, the value never sits in code, and rotating it needs no commit. The tradeoff is dependency and availability: if the store is unreachable or the role's permission is wrong, the deploy fails at the moment it needs the secret, so the team has to monitor that path and make the failure loud rather than silent. There is also added latency and more permissions to manage. Secrets Manager adds rotation, while Parameter Store is simpler and cheaper for plain settings, so the choice depends on what the value needs.
rubricPoints: Secrets in a repository are exposed to everyone who can read or copy it, so they must live outside the code.
The pipeline fetches the value at run time under a narrow role with read access to only that secret.
Rotation or revocation happens without a code change or commit.
A named limit: the store becomes a runtime dependency, so outages or wrong permissions fail deploys.

suggested.rationale: This mission makes the learner wire a deploy's secret through a managed store without leaking it, which is the objective's core skill.

lessons.plain: A deployment strategy is the plan for how a new version of software replaces the old one on the machines or containers that run it. Instead of switching everything at once and hoping, you pick a pattern: replace servers in place a few at a time, stand up a parallel copy and move traffic over to it, or send a small share of users to the new version first and widen only if it behaves. AWS CodeDeploy is the managed service that carries out these patterns for EC2 servers, on-premises machines, Lambda functions, and ECS services. It can pause or roll back when health checks or alarms show a problem. Choosing a strategy means balancing speed, cost, risk, and how quickly you can undo a bad release.
lessons.guessPrompt: You have ten identical web servers behind a load balancer and a new release that you are not fully sure about. Would you update all ten at once, or update them in smaller groups, and why?
lessons.teach:
A deployment group is the set of target machines or resources that a CodeDeploy deployment acts on. A deployment configuration is the rule that says how many targets may be changed at a time, or what share of traffic moves first. For EC2 and on-premises machines, the built-in choices are AllAtOnce, HalfAtATime and OneAtATime, and you can define your own minimum-healthy-host rule. For Lambda and ECS, the choices are shaped as Canary (a small slice first, then the rest after a wait), Linear (equal steps over time) and AllAtOnce. A blue/green deployment does not touch the running machines; it creates a second, replacement set (blue is current, green is new), then shifts traffic and keeps the old set around so you can switch back. The agent is the small program on each machine that receives the instructions. The appspec file is the instruction file in your bundle that names the lifecycle hooks, such as stopping the old version, copying files and running a validation script. Alarms and health checks are the signals that trigger an automatic stop and rollback.

Worked example: ten EC2 instances in a fleet, deployed in place with HalfAtATime. Step one, CodeDeploy takes five instances out of the load balancer. Step two, it runs the hooks on those five and installs the new version. Step three, a validation hook calls the health endpoint and it passes. Step four, the five return to service. Step five, the other five repeat the same steps. If the validation fails on the first group, the deployment stops before the second group is touched.

Common mistake: believing an in-place rollback is instant. Rolling back means deploying the old version again, which takes as long as the original deployment. For this reason, a blue/green setup is the better choice when fast reversal matters most.

Consequence: during an in-place rollout, old and new versions run side by side for a while, so any database or API change must work with both. A strategy that looks safe on paper can still cause errors if this overlap is ignored.

questions.prompt: A team runs a fleet of 12 EC2 instances behind a load balancer and deploys in place with the OneAtATime setting, so only one instance is changed at a time. Step one: instance 4 is taken out of the load balancer. Step two: the lifecycle hooks run on instance 4 and the new version is installed. Step three: the validation hook on instance 4 calls the health endpoint and it passes. Step four is missing from this list. Which step comes next, before the deployment moves on to instance 5?
choices: Instance 4 is replaced by a new instance from a second, separate fleet
Instance 4 is registered back with the load balancer so it serves traffic again
All 12 instances are switched to the new version at the same time
Instance 4 is restored from a snapshot, which counts as the rollback
questions.why: With OneAtATime, each instance must return to the load balancer after it passes validation before the next instance is processed.

questions.prompt: In CodeDeploy, what is a deployment group?
choices: The instruction file in the bundle that names the lifecycle hooks
The set of target machines or resources that a deployment acts on
The small program on each machine that receives instructions
The rule that sets how many targets may change at a time
questions.why: A deployment group is defined in the teaching text as the set of targets a CodeDeploy deployment acts on, while the other options describe the deployment configuration, the appspec file and the agent.

questions.prompt: A team with 20 EC2 instances deploys in place using AllAtOnce. Fifteen minutes in, they find a serious bug in the new version. What is the most accurate description of how they get back to the old version?
choices: They flip traffic back to the old set, which is kept running, within seconds
They deploy the old version again, which takes about as long as the original deployment
Nothing is needed, because AllAtOnce keeps a copy of the old version on every machine
The agent automatically reverts each instance the moment the bug appears
questions.why: In-place rollback means redeploying the old version, which takes as long as the original deployment, because it is not an instant switch.

questions.prompt: During an in-place rollout across a fleet, some machines run the old version while others already run the new one. A developer renames a database column in the same release. Why is this risky, and what keeps it safe?
choices: It is risky because both versions run side by side, so the change must work with both during the overlap
It is safe because the agent pauses all traffic until every machine finishes
It is safe as long as the old version is deleted before the rollout starts
It is risky only if the rollout uses blue/green, not in-place
questions.why: In an in-place rollout old and new versions overlap for a while, so a schema or API change must be compatible with both, which is why an apparently safe strategy can still cause errors.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between in-place and blue/green deployment for a customer-facing service on CodeDeploy, naming at least one limit or tradeoff of the option you would not choose.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would pick in-place with a partial configuration like HalfAtATime or OneAtATime when capacity is tight and I can tolerate a slower rollout, because it avoids paying for a second full set of machines. The tradeoff is that old and new versions run together during the rollout, so the release must stay compatible with the previous version, and rolling back means redeploying, which takes real time. I would choose blue/green when a fast, clean switch back matters more than cost, since traffic can move back to the untouched old set at once. The cost is running roughly double capacity during the cutover, and the new set must be provisioned and warmed before traffic moves. Either way I would tie CodeDeploy to alarms so a bad error rate stops or reverses the deployment automatically.
rubricPoints: Explains in-place versus blue/green in terms of capacity cost and rollback speed
Names the compatibility risk of old and new versions running side by side during in-place rollout
Mentions that a partial configuration limits how many targets fail at once
Connects automatic rollback to health checks or alarms

suggested.rationale: That mission makes the learner roll back a bad release quickly and then fix forward, which is the core judgement this objective tests.

lessons.plain: A test is an automatic check that a piece of software does what it should. Tests come in layers, and each layer catches a different kind of mistake. Some check one small function on its own, like a calculator step that must return 4 for 2 plus 2. Others check that several parts work together, such as a service actually reading from its database. Some check the software from the user's point of view, and some look for security weaknesses like known vulnerable libraries. The skill is knowing which layer to run and when, so that quick checks catch problems early and slow checks run only on changes that have already passed the quick ones.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your team's pipeline takes 50 minutes because every commit runs a full end-to-end browser test suite before anything else. Which kinds of test would you run on every commit, which would you save for later stages, and why?
lessons.teach: A unit test checks one small piece of code, such as a single function, in isolation. Anything it depends on, like a database or a network call, is replaced with a stand-in called a test double. Unit tests are fast, usually milliseconds each, so they run on every commit. An integration test checks that two or more real components work together, for example that your service can write a row to a real database and read it back. These are slower because they start real dependencies, so they usually run after unit tests pass. An acceptance test checks behaviour against what the business asked for, written as a scenario such as 'a dispatcher can cancel a pending order'. A user interface test drives the screen through a browser and checks what appears. Both are slow and brittle, so keep them few and run them against a staging environment after deployment. A security scan inspects code, dependencies or built images for known weaknesses, and can run at build time, especially whenever a new dependency is added. Worked example: a commit changes a price rounding function. Step 1, build, compiles the code and succeeds. Step 2, unit tests run in seconds and one fails because 0.5 rounds the wrong way. The pipeline stops, so the slower stages never run, and the fix takes minutes. Without that unit test, the bug would reach integration testing or production. Common mistake: putting every test type into one slow stage at the end, so a simple arithmetic error costs an hour and a half of waiting. Consequence in a running system: a missed unit test can ship wrong charges to customers, and a missed security scan can ship a library with a known exploit. Pipelines should fail fast, running the cheapest and most frequent checks first and gating each promotion to the next environment on passing results.

questions.prompt: A team runs a pipeline for a ticketing API. Step 1: a commit adds a new JSON parsing library, and the build compiles the container image successfully. Step 2: unit tests run in 40 seconds and all pass. Step 3: [missing step]. Step 4: an integration test starts a real test database, saves a ticket row and reads it back, and it passes. Which choice correctly fills Step 3?
choices: The pipeline skips unit tests from now on because the new library ships with its own test suite.
A user interface test drives the ticket screen in a browser against the staging site.
The pipeline deploys the image to production so that integration tests can use live ticket data.
A security scan inspects the new library and the built image for known weaknesses; it reports none, so the pipeline continues.
questions.why: A new dependency arrives at build time, so a security scan belongs right after the build and unit tests, before the slower integration stage, and the pipeline only moves on when it passes.

questions.prompt: A team's test replaces the shipping-rate web service with a stand-in and checks only the function that adds a weight surcharge to a parcel. Which test type is this?
choices: An integration test, because it calls a real function in the codebase.
A user interface test, because the surcharge eventually appears on a customer's screen.
An acceptance test, because the surcharge rule was written by the business.
A unit test, because one small function is checked with its dependency replaced by a stand-in.
questions.why: A unit test checks one small piece of code in isolation, with its dependencies swapped for test doubles, which is exactly what the description shows.

questions.prompt: A pipeline runs every test type in one 90-minute stage at the very end. A developer's wrong sort order in a single function is only discovered after the full 90 minutes. Which change best addresses this?
choices: Add more runners so the one stage finishes sooner.
Remove the unit tests, because integration tests exercise the same function.
Run unit tests in their own early stage and gate the later stages on them passing.
Run the browser tests first, since they cover the most visible behaviour.
questions.why: Running the fast, frequent checks first lets a simple error stop the pipeline in minutes instead of after the slow stages have run.

questions.prompt: Which statement about security scans is correct?
choices: They replace slow dependencies with stand-ins so that each function can be run alone.
They drive the screen through a browser and check what a user sees on the page after deployment.
They inspect code, dependencies or built images for known weaknesses, and can run at build time.
They confirm that two live services can exchange a message in production traffic.
questions.why: Security scans look for known weaknesses in code, dependencies or built images and can run at build time, especially when a new dependency is added.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who is new to testing why we run unit tests on every commit but run user interface tests only after deployment to a staging environment. Name one limit or tradeoff of each.
lessons.modelAnswer: Unit tests check one small piece of code with its dependencies replaced by stand-ins, so they finish in seconds and tell you exactly which function broke. That speed makes it practical to run them on every commit, which gives feedback before anyone reviews the change. Their limit is that they cannot prove the parts fit together, so a passing unit suite can still hide a wrong database query. User interface tests drive a real browser through the whole system, which is the closest check to what a user experiences. But they take minutes, are fragile when a button moves, and need a running environment with realistic data. So they run after deployment to staging, once the cheap checks have already passed. Their tradeoff is slow, sometimes flaky feedback, which is why we keep them few.
rubricPoints: Unit tests are fast and isolated, so they run on every commit.
UI tests need a running environment and are slow and brittle, so they run later, such as after deployment to staging.
Each test type has a limit: unit tests miss problems between components, UI tests give slow, fragile feedback.
Stages are ordered cheapest first so a failure stops the pipeline early.

suggested.rationale: Repairing a broken CI pipeline makes the learner decide which stage a failing check belongs in.

lessons.plain: When a team member proposes a change, the team wants an automatic checker to examine it before anyone trusts it. A pull request is a request to merge a proposed change into the shared code, and a merge is the moment that change joins the shared line. Running builds and tests on a pull request means that, as soon as the proposal exists, an automatic system packages the change and runs the checks. The goal is to catch problems within minutes, while the change is still small and its author still remembers it, before the change reaches customers. Think of it as a checkpoint at a factory door that every part must pass through.
lessons.guessPrompt: A developer's change passes every test on their own laptop, but the automated check fails it as soon as they open a pull request. Name two differences between the laptop and the automated check that could explain this, and say which one you would investigate first.
lessons.teach:
A pull request is a proposal to merge one branch of code into another, usually the shared main line, and a merge is the act of accepting that proposal. Continuous integration, often shortened to CI, is the practice of running an automated build and test process every time a change is proposed or accepted. A build turns source code into something runnable or packageable, such as compiled output or a container image. A test is an automated check that runs the code and confirms that expected behaviour still holds.

The approach works because of isolation and repetition. The automated runner starts from a clean, known environment, so the code cannot quietly depend on a file that exists only on one developer's machine. Because the process runs on every proposal, problems surface while the change is small. The outcome is reported back to the pull request as a status check, and branch protection rules can refuse a merge until the required checks pass.

Worked example. Priya opens a pull request that adds a new rate limit. Step one: a trigger fires when the pull request is opened and again whenever she pushes new commits to its branch. Step two: the runner checks out her branch and combines it with the current main line, so it tests what would really exist after merging. Step three: it installs dependencies from a pinned lock file, which records exact versions. Step four: it builds the package. Step five: it runs the unit tests, and one fails because it still expects the old limit. Step six: the check turns red, and the merge button stays blocked until Priya fixes the test.

Common mistake: treating a green run on the author's branch as proof about main. Other changes merged since the branch was created can conflict with it, so the check should run on the combined result, and it should run again on main after the merge.

Consequence: if a team lets red changes merge, main stops building, every teammate's next pull request inherits the failure, and the team loses time working out which change broke what. A gate that stays closed on failure keeps the main line releasable.

questions.prompt: Harbor Tiles runs a small shop-floor scheduling service. Kofi opens a pull request that changes how overtime hours are rounded. Step one: a trigger fires when the pull request is opened and again on each new push to its branch. Step two: the runner checks out Kofi's branch and merges the current main line into it, so the tests see what would exist after merging. Step three: [MISSING]. Step four: the runner builds the package. Step five: the overtime rounding test fails, so the status check is set to failed and the merge button stays blocked. Which action completes step three?
choices: Merge the pull request into main first, so the build runs on the final code
Install dependencies from the pinned lock file so the exact versions are used on a clean runner
Post a passing status to the pull request before any tests run so teammates are not delayed
Skip installing dependencies and reuse whatever was left on Kofi's laptop to save time
questions.why: A clean runner must install the exact pinned dependency versions before it can build and test, which is what the lock file exists to guarantee; the other options either merge before the gate, depend on a laptop the runner cannot see, or fake a result.

questions.prompt: In the context of pull request CI, what is a status check?
choices: The outcome of an automated run, reported back to the pull request, which branch protection rules can use to block a merge
A copy of the build output stored next to the source code so it can be downloaded later
A manual review sign-off that a senior engineer records in the repository settings
A nightly report that summarises how many commits landed on main during the week
questions.why: The teaching text defines a status check as the reported outcome of the automated run on the pull request, and says branch protection can refuse a merge until required checks pass.

questions.prompt: Ruth's branch passed CI three weeks ago, but main has since received several merged changes. She wants to merge now and says the old green result is still valid. What is the best response based on the CI idea of testing the combined result?
choices: The old green result is valid because the code on her branch has not changed
Merge immediately, since main is always tested separately by its own nightly job
Only the pull request's own commits need retesting; the rest of main is already trusted
Run the checks again on the combined result, and again on main after the merge, because the earlier run did not include the newer changes
questions.why: A green run on the author's branch does not prove anything about main once other changes have landed, so the checks must run on the combined result and again after merging.

questions.prompt: A team at Lantern Books sets a branch protection rule that requires their build-and-test check to pass before any merge into main. A developer's change fails that check because a config file it needs exists only on his workstation and was never committed. Why did the check fail, and what does the gate do?
choices: The runner is broken and the gate should be turned off until the file is copied to the server
The developer should merge first and fix the missing file afterwards, since the check only runs on main
The gate is designed to ignore missing files so that only code logic is tested
The runner is a clean, known environment, so the missing local file exposes a hidden dependency and the gate keeps the failing change out of main
questions.why: Because the runner starts from a clean environment with only committed content, a file present only on one machine causes a failure, and the closed gate prevents that change from merging into the main line.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what happens between opening a pull request and merging it. Cover what a build and a test each contribute, and name one limit or tradeoff of running these checks on every change.
lessons.modelAnswer: When someone opens a pull request, the automated system starts a fresh environment, combines the proposed branch with the current main line, installs pinned dependencies, builds the package, and runs the tests. The build shows the code can be turned into a working package. The tests show that the behaviour we care about still holds. Each result is posted back as a status check, and our branch rule refuses the merge until the required checks are green. The same process runs again on main after merging, because the combined result is what we ship. One tradeoff is speed: a test suite that takes an hour would slow every proposal, so we keep the pull request checks fast and move slow integration runs to later stages. Another limit is that a passing check only covers what the tests check. A flaky test that fails at random teaches people to ignore red results, which is worse than having no test at all.
rubricPoints: Explains a pull request as a proposal to merge, with a trigger that starts the checks on open and on new commits.
States that the build and tests run in a clean environment against the combined result, not only the author's branch.
Describes the gate: status checks and branch protection block a merge when required checks fail.
Names a tradeoff, such as fast feedback versus full coverage, or flaky tests eroding trust in results.

suggested.rationale: Repairing a broken CI pipeline makes the learner run and read the build and test checks that gate a change, which is the core of this objective.

lessons.plain: Load and stress testing means deliberately sending a system the kind of work it will face, and sometimes more, before real users do. A load test asks whether the system stays fast and error-free at the traffic you expect. A stress test keeps raising the pressure to find where it breaks and whether it recovers afterward. Performance benchmarking means measuring the same scenario the same way every time, so you can tell whether a new release made the system slower or faster. Doing this at scale means generating the traffic from many machines at once, because one test computer cannot pretend to be thousands of customers.
lessons.guessPrompt: A new version of an API passes all its functional tests, but on launch day it responds slowly once 2,000 requests per second arrive. Which single measurement would have warned you before launch, and how would you have produced that load?
lessons.teach:
Load testing applies a planned amount of traffic to a system, usually the peak you expect, and checks whether it meets its targets. Stress testing keeps increasing the traffic past that point to find the breaking point and to see how the system fails and recovers. Soak testing runs a moderate load for hours to expose slow leaks such as memory growth or exhausted connection pools. Benchmarking runs the same scripted scenario under the same conditions on each build, so the numbers can be compared across versions.

Why this works: a system's behavior under load is not a straight line. Response time often stays flat until a resource such as CPU, a database connection pool or a thread pool becomes saturated, meaning it is full and cannot take more work. Then response time climbs sharply. Only sending realistic load reveals that point. The measurements that matter are latency at percentiles (p95 is the time that 95 percent of requests beat), throughput in requests per second, error rate, and the saturation of key resources.

Worked example: the target is 500 requests per second with p95 latency under 300 milliseconds and an error rate under 0.1 percent. Step one, ramp from 0 to 500 requests per second over ten minutes so autoscaling and caches have time to act. Step two, hold that rate for 30 minutes and record the percentiles. Step three, p95 comes back at 420 milliseconds, so the gate fails. The team finds the database connection pool at its maximum, adjusts it, and re-runs the same script to confirm.

Common mistake: reporting only the average latency. An average of 150 milliseconds can hide a p99 of four seconds, which is what the slowest one percent of customers feel. Another mistake is generating the load from a single machine, which can saturate the test client before the system under test is stressed.

In a pipeline, a load test run against a staging environment after deployment can block promotion to production when a percentile threshold is breached, so a slow release never reaches customers.

questions.prompt: A ticketing service for a regional rail operator is load tested before a holiday sale. The target is 1,200 requests per second, p95 latency under 750 milliseconds (p95 is the response time that 95 percent of requests beat), and an error rate under 0.05 percent. Step one: ramp from 0 to 1,200 requests per second over 15 minutes. Step two: hold that rate for 45 minutes and record the results, which show p95 at 910 milliseconds and an error rate of 0.02 percent. Step three is missing. Which step completes the gate decision?
choices: Report the 240 millisecond average as the result, since averages are the standard summary and it is well under target
Pass the gate, because the error rate of 0.02 percent is under the 0.05 percent limit and that is the only threshold that counts
Compare the p95 of 910 milliseconds with the 750 millisecond target, mark the latency check as failed, and block promotion to production
Raise the load to 2,000 requests per second and re-run, since a higher load test will show whether the service is healthy
questions.why: A load test gate fails if any threshold is breached, and the p95 of 910 milliseconds exceeds the 750 millisecond limit, so the release must be held even though the error rate passes.

questions.prompt: A mobile game backend is held at a steady 300 requests per second for six hours. The team wants to know whether memory use keeps climbing over that time, which would suggest a slow leak. Which kind of test fits this goal?
choices: Soak testing
Benchmarking
Stress testing
Load testing
questions.why: Soak testing runs a moderate load for a long period specifically to expose slow leaks such as growing memory use.

questions.prompt: A team runs its load script from one developer laptop against a cloud service. The laptop reports a p95 latency (the response time that 95 percent of requests beat) of 180 milliseconds, but the laptop's CPU is pegged at 100 percent while the service's CPU sits at 35 percent. What is the most likely problem with this result?
choices: The load generator is the bottleneck, so the measured latency does not reflect what the service can actually handle
The p95 figure is accurate and the team can promote the release with confidence
The service has plenty of headroom and should be sent more traffic from the same laptop
The service needs a larger database connection pool before any test result can be trusted
questions.why: When the machine generating load is saturated, it limits the traffic it sends, so the numbers say more about the client than about the system under test.

questions.prompt: A payments API team runs the same scripted scenario against build 41 and build 42 on identical hardware with identical test data. The p95 latency rises from 210 to 260 milliseconds. What does this comparison most directly show?
choices: The difference is meaningless, because benchmarks only matter for average latency
The test conditions were held constant, so the change is a signal worth investigating as a possible regression
The two builds should be compared by error rate alone, and latency can be ignored
Build 42 is faster, because the scenario was identical and the number went up
questions.why: Benchmarking keeps the scenario and conditions fixed so that a change in the numbers between builds can be attributed to the code, which makes it a possible regression to investigate.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between a load test, a stress test and a benchmark, and name one limit or tradeoff of running these tests against a staging environment instead of production.
lessons.modelAnswer: A load test sends the traffic you expect, such as peak, and checks that the system meets its latency and error targets at that level. A stress test keeps raising the load past that until something breaks, so you learn the breaking point, which resource saturates first, and whether the system recovers when the pressure drops. A benchmark is a fixed, repeatable scenario run the same way on each build, so you can compare numbers between releases and spot a regression. The tradeoff of staging is that it is rarely identical to production: instance sizes, data volume, cache state and third-party rate limits differ. A pass therefore shows relative behavior and a rough capacity estimate, not a guarantee. Results should be read as trends with a stated margin, and tests should never be aimed at production in a way that could harm real customers.
rubricPoints: A load test checks expected peak traffic against latency and error targets.
A stress test pushes past the peak to find the breaking point and recovery behavior.
A benchmark repeats the same scenario so builds can be compared fairly.
Staging differs from production, so results are relative and carry a margin of uncertainty.

suggested.rationale: Choosing the right test type and the right metric for a realistic situation is reasoning practice, and no listed mission covers load testing directly.

lessons.plain: When a program finishes, it hands a small whole number back to whatever started it. By convention, zero means it went fine and any other number means something went wrong. Automation tools read that number rather than the program's printed text, so a simple check can report healthy or unhealthy in a form a machine can act on. This objective is about using those numbers to judge whether an application is working, and about noticing when a number misleads you. You will meet it in build steps, deployment hooks and post-release checks. The core idea is that one number decides whether the pipeline keeps going, stops, or rolls back.
lessons.guessPrompt: A deploy script runs a health check that prints 'service down' in red, but the script's last line is a command that succeeds. What does an automated deployment tool most likely conclude, and why?
lessons.teach:
An exit code is the number a program returns when it finishes. Zero means success. Any non-zero value, usually between 1 and 255, means failure, and the author can choose meanings for different numbers. A health check is a small program or script whose only job is to answer whether an application is working, and it reports that answer through its exit code. Automation such as a build pipeline or a deployment tool does not read the words the script printed. It reads the number and decides what to do: continue, stop, or roll back.

Why it works: the number is simple, universal and easy to act on. Almost any language can produce it, and almost any orchestrator can check it.
