The scanner role retries the publish using its long-lived access key, which bypasses the deny
The resource policy's explicit deny also matches the publish action, and an explicit deny overrides any allow
Because an allow matched, the request is permitted and the deny is only logged as a warning
questions.why: An explicit deny that matches the request overrides any matching allow, so the publish is refused even though the identity policy allows it.

questions.prompt: In a permission check for an artifact repository, what is a principal?
choices: The document containing allow and deny statements attached to a repository
The specific repository or package that an action targets
The named operation, such as publishing a new version or deleting an image
The identity, usually a role that a build job or person temporarily assumes, that asks to perform an action
questions.why: A principal is the identity making the request, usually a temporarily assumed role, as the teaching text defines it.

questions.prompt: A release role has an allow for read actions on the repository billing-artifacts and no other statement mentions that role. The role tries to upload a new package version to billing-artifacts. What is the outcome, and why?
choices: The upload is refused by implicit deny, because no statement allows publishing for that role
The upload succeeds only after the repository owner approves it manually
The upload succeeds, because the role can already reach the repository
The upload is refused because read and publish rights must be granted in the same statement
questions.why: With no allow matching the publish action, the request falls through to the default refusal called implicit deny.

questions.prompt: A publish credential for a team's package repository is leaked. Which set of controls best limits the damage an attacker can do with it?
choices: Narrow the publish rights to the one repository needed, avoid long-lived keys, and protect how new version numbers are accepted
Rotate the repository name every week so the attacker cannot find it
Remove the deny statements so that the attacker's requests are logged more clearly
Grant the publish role every action on every repository so that future deploys never fail
questions.why: Scoping publish rights to one repository, using expiring credentials, and protecting version handling contain what a stolen publish role can push and how far downstream builds will pick it up.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would set up permissions so a build job can publish packages to a shared repository while a production server can only download them. Name one limit or tradeoff of your approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would give the build job its own role, with publish actions allowed only on the one repository it feeds, and give the production servers a separate role with read actions only on that same repository. Nothing else gets write access, and no person holds a standing key that the pipeline uses. Both roles receive temporary credentials that expire, so a leaked token goes stale quickly. The tradeoff is ongoing maintenance: every new repository or new consumer needs a policy change, so the team has to keep the role list small and reviewed. A policy that is too tight shows up as a failed deploy, and someone must diagnose it before the deploy works again.
rubricPoints: Separates publish rights from read rights using distinct roles.
Scopes each role to a specific repository and only the actions it needs.
Uses temporary credentials rather than long-lived shared keys.
Names a tradeoff such as policy maintenance overhead or over-tight rules blocking deploys.

suggested.rationale: Evaluating allow and deny statements against a request is the core skill here, and the planned authorization policy evaluator would let the learner test who can publish and who is refused.

lessons.plain: A deployment agent is a small helper program that runs on a server and does the actual installing work when a new release is pushed. Think of a delivery driver who checks the depot regularly for parcels rather than waiting for the shop to phone each house. Setting one up means installing the helper on each machine, giving it permission to read the release package and report back, and telling it which group of machines it belongs to. Once that is right, a pipeline can ship a new version to a whole fleet without anyone logging in by hand. This lesson covers what the helper does, what it needs in order to work, and how it reports success or failure.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose a release has to be copied to twenty servers and a script run on each. Would you rather have one central controller reach into each server over a network connection, or a small program on each server that periodically asks the controller whether it has work? Which one keeps working better when servers are added, replaced or hidden behind a firewall, and why?
lessons.teach: A deployment agent is a program installed on each server, often called an instance, that receives deployment instructions and carries them out locally. The CodeDeploy agent is the AWS version of this for virtual machines and on-premises servers. It does not run on container or serverless platforms, which use their own deployment mechanisms. The agent works by polling, meaning it repeatedly asks the deployment service whether there is work for it, rather than waiting for the service to connect in. That is why it works behind firewalls and why a new server can join simply by starting up. A deployment group is the named set of servers that a deployment targets. Each server must prove its identity, usually through an attached instance role, which is a set of permissions granted to the machine. The role must allow reading the release bundle and reporting results. The bundle contains an application specification file that lists where files go and which lifecycle event scripts to run, such as stopping the old version, installing the new one, and running a health check. Worked example: a release goes to three web servers. The agent on server A polls, receives a revision, downloads the bundle, runs the stop script, copies the files, runs the start script, and reports success. If the health-check script exits with a non-zero code, which signals failure, the agent reports failure and the deployment stops or rolls back according to its settings. Common mistake: installing the agent but giving the instance no role, so polling fails with access errors and the deployment sits pending with no obvious cause. Consequence: a server that never reports is one that quietly keeps running an old version, so fleet status must be checked rather than assumed.

questions.prompt: A ticketing company releases revision 12 to its worker group tickets-workers, which holds four Linux virtual machines. Worker W3 has the agent installed and an instance role that lets it read the release bundle. Here is the sequence on W3. The agent polls the deployment service and is offered revision 12. It downloads the bundle. It runs the stop script for the old worker process. It copies the new files into place. It runs the start script. The health-check script then runs and exits with code 2. The one step not stated is what the agent does next, and that step is the missing one to supply.
choices: The agent writes the exit code to W3's local log file and waits for someone to read it.
The agent reports the failed health-check result to the deployment service, which marks W3 as failed and applies the group's stop or rollback setting.
The agent deletes the bundle and polls again, so the service retries the same revision automatically.
The agent reports success as soon as the files are copied, so the health check is only a log entry.
questions.why: The agent reports results back to the deployment service, and a non-zero health-check exit code is reported as a failure that triggers the deployment's configured stop or rollback behaviour.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes how the CodeDeploy agent receives work?
choices: The agent runs on container and serverless platforms and receives work through their built-in mechanisms.
The agent repeatedly asks the deployment service whether there is work for it, which is called polling.
The deployment service opens a connection into each server and pushes files over it.
The agent is started by an administrator for each individual release and stops when the release ends.
questions.why: The agent polls, meaning it repeatedly asks the service for work, and this is why it can operate behind firewalls and why new servers can join by simply starting up.

questions.prompt: A team at a logistics firm launches a new virtual machine from a template that already has the agent installed, but the machine was created without an instance role. The machine is placed in the correct deployment group. What is the most likely result?
choices: The group automatically removes the machine and deploys to the remaining servers without any warning.
The deployment finishes immediately because the agent does not need permissions to run.
The agent is not allowed to poll or download the bundle, so the deployment sits pending and the cause is not obvious from the deployment status alone.
The service pushes the release over a direct connection and the machine receives it normally.
questions.why: Each server proves its identity through an attached instance role, and without that role the agent's polling and bundle download fail with access errors, leaving the deployment pending.

questions.prompt: A deployment to ten servers reports success on nine. The tenth server never reported a result. Which conclusion is correct?
choices: The tenth server is still running the old version quietly, so the fleet status must be checked directly rather than assumed to be correct.
The silent server has been removed from the deployment group, which means it no longer needs checking.
The service has already rolled back all ten servers, so no server is running anything new.
The deployment is complete and the silent server is running the new version because the other nine succeeded.
questions.why: A server that never reports keeps running whatever version it had before, so the status of every server in the group needs to be verified rather than inferred from the others.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what the deployment agent does on each server, how it finds out about work, how it proves it is allowed to do that work, and one limit or tradeoff of relying on an agent running on every machine.
lessons.modelAnswer: The agent is a program on each server that does the installing locally. It polls the deployment service on a schedule, asking whether there is a new revision for its deployment group, instead of having the service connect in. When work arrives, it downloads the bundle, runs the lifecycle scripts named in the application specification file in order, and reports success or failure for each step. To do this it needs an instance role with permission to read the bundle and report status; without that, it cannot authenticate and the deployment hangs. The tradeoff is that every server now runs an extra process that must be installed, kept updated and kept permitted, so a fleet can quietly drift when some machines are missing the agent or its role. Checking per-instance status is therefore part of the job, not an afterthought.
rubricPoints: The agent runs on each server and performs the install work locally
It polls the service for work rather than being contacted from outside
It needs an instance role or equivalent identity with permission to read the bundle and report results
Lifecycle scripts and the application specification file define what happens during a deployment
A missing or misconfigured agent or role leaves servers stuck or running old versions, so status must be verified

suggested.rationale: Getting a deploy process to authenticate from a machine without leaking credentials is the closest hands-on match to giving an agent the right identity and permissions.

lessons.plain: A blue/green deployment keeps two matching copies of a production environment: the one users currently reach (blue) and an identical idle one (green). You install the new version on the idle copy, test it there, then switch all traffic over at once. If something breaks, you switch back. A canary deployment is more cautious: you send a small slice of real traffic, such as one percent, to the new version, watch how it behaves, and only then grow the slice until it takes everything. Both methods limit how many users a bad release can hurt, and both depend on a traffic router, the component that decides which version each request reaches, which is what makes the switch cheap to reverse.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your app runs on five servers behind a router, and you want to release version 2 without taking the site down. Before reading on, what would you do with the servers and the router, and how would you undo the change if version 2 misbehaved?
lessons.teach:
An environment is a complete set of servers and supporting parts that serves users. A traffic router is the component (a load balancer, or a DNS or service setting) that decides which environment or version each request reaches. A health check is an automatic probe that asks a server whether it is working. A rollback is returning to the previous known-good version.

Blue/green: you run two identical environments. Blue serves live traffic on version 1. You deploy version 2 to green, which receives no real users, and you test it there. When it passes, you point the router at green in one step. Blue stays running and untouched, so rollback means pointing the router back at blue.

Canary: you send version 2 a small share of real requests, such as 5 percent, while the rest still go to version 1. You compare the new version's error rate and latency with the old one's. If the numbers stay healthy over a set period, you raise the share in steps (5, 25, 50, 100). If they get worse, you send all traffic back to version 1.

Worked example: 100 requests arrive per second and the router splits them 95 to version 1 and 5 to version 2. Version 2 returns 2 errors out of its 5 requests, a 40 percent error rate, against 0.1 percent for version 1. The pipeline's gate sees the threshold breached, sets the split back to 100 percent on version 1, and the 95 other users never saw the bug.

Common mistake: teams assume blue/green is safe because the old environment still exists, then change the database schema in a way version 1 cannot read. Rolling back the router works, but the old code now fails against the new data. Both versions must be able to read and write shared data during the switch.

Consequence in a running system: rollback speed depends on how quickly the router changes and how long in-flight requests take to finish, so keep the old environment alive until the new one has proven itself. A release strategy is only as safe as the health signals that trigger it.

questions.prompt: A logistics company runs a canary for its parcel-tracking API. Step 1: the router sends 10 percent of 800 requests per minute to version 2, so 80 requests go to the new version and 720 stay on version 1. Step 2: in that minute version 2 returns 6 errors out of its 80 requests, a 7.5 percent error rate, while version 1 runs at 0.3 percent. Step 3: the pipeline's gate compares the two rates and flags that the new version breached the threshold. Step 4: [missing step]. Result: all 800 requests per minute are served by version 1 only, and version 2 receives no further real traffic.
choices: The gate raises the canary share to 20 percent so that it collects a larger sample before deciding.
The gate deletes version 2 so that its error counts stop appearing in the dashboards.
The gate sets the router so that 100 percent of requests go to version 1.
The gate waits 24 hours before changing the router, so that a short spike is not treated as a real problem.
questions.why: A canary that breaches its health threshold is rolled back by moving the whole traffic split back onto the version that is still healthy, which here is version 1.

questions.prompt: In a blue/green deployment, why is the old environment kept running after traffic has moved to the new one?
choices: Because the router cannot point at an environment that was created more than one release ago.
So that the health check has two servers to compare, which is required before any traffic can move.
So that the old environment can be used to store the new version's logs for later review.
So that rollback is a router change back to the old environment, which is fast because nothing has to be rebuilt.
questions.why: The old environment stays untouched and running, so pointing the router back at it restores the previous known-good version without a rebuild.

questions.prompt: A team runs a canary for a notification service. They send 2 percent of traffic to the new version, which handles 4 requests in its first 10 minutes. All 4 succeed, and the team declares the canary healthy and moves to 100 percent. What is the main flaw in this decision?
choices: A canary should never send more than 1 percent of traffic, so the 2 percent share was itself the error.
The new version was never checked by a health check, so its success count means nothing.
Four requests is too small a sample to show that the error rate is healthy, so the signal is not yet reliable enough to trigger promotion.
The router should have been switched to blue/green instead, because canaries cannot be used for services that send notifications.
questions.why: A canary's promotion decision depends on comparing error rates and latency over enough real requests and time, and four requests cannot distinguish a healthy version from a broken one.

questions.prompt: A reporting service is moving from version 1 to version 2 using blue/green. Version 2 changes the layout of the messages it writes to a shared queue that version 1 still reads from during the switch. What must be true for the switch to be safe?
choices: The queue must be cleared of all messages before the router is changed, so neither version reads old data.
The health check must be disabled on version 1, so the router does not treat its failed reads as a reason to roll back.
Version 1 must be deleted from the queue's configuration before green receives traffic, so there is only one reader.
Both versions must be able to read the shared message format during the switch, because rolling back the router does not undo data that version 2 has already written.
questions.why: Rolling back the router only changes which environment receives requests; messages already written in the new format remain in the shared queue and must still be readable by the old version.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between blue/green and canary deployments, and name one limit or tradeoff of each that would affect which one you pick for a service that writes to a shared database.
lessons.modelAnswer: Blue/green keeps two full environments and flips all traffic at once, so rollback is fast and simple: point the router back at the old environment. The costs are running double capacity during the switch and the risk that every user hits a bad release the moment you flip. Canary sends a small share of real traffic to the new version first, so a bad release harms few users and gives real evidence before a full rollout. Its limit is that you need good health metrics and enough traffic for a small slice to reveal problems in a reasonable time, and the rollout takes longer. For a service writing to a shared database, either method needs schema changes that both versions can read and write, because during the transition two versions of the code touch the same data.
rubricPoints: Blue/green runs two full environments and switches all traffic at once, making rollback a router change.
Canary sends a small share of real traffic first and widens it only when health signals stay good.
Blue/green costs double capacity during the switch and exposes all users at the flip.
Canary needs reliable metrics and enough traffic, and it takes longer to complete.
Both methods need database changes that old and new versions can share during the transition.

suggested.rationale: The planned deploy-shift engine would let a learner practise shifting traffic between blue and green or canary splits and watching the rollback path.

lessons.plain: Troubleshooting a deployment issue means working out why a new version of software behaved badly after it went live, and getting users back to a working state. Think of a restaurant that sends out a new dish and starts getting complaints: first it stops serving the bad dish, then it checks the recipe and ingredients to find what changed. Good troubleshooting separates two questions: what do I do right now to stop the harm, and what caused it so it does not happen again. The skill is reading the evidence the delivery process leaves behind, such as logs, version numbers, and health checks, in the right order.
lessons.guessPrompt: A new version of an app goes live at 09:00 and the error rate jumps at 09:02. Before you know anything else about the system, what is the first thing you would do, and why would you do it before finding the root cause?
lessons.teach: A deployment is the act of putting a specific built version of your software onto the machines or services that serve users. A release is the same event seen from the product side. When a deployment goes wrong, limit the harm first and understand the cause second. Several terms matter here. An artifact is the packaged, versioned output of a build, such as a container image or a zip file, and it should never change once created. A rollback returns the system to the previous known-good artifact. A forward fix leaves the new version in place and ships a corrected one. A health check is an automatic probe that asks a running instance whether it responds correctly. Rollback comes first because it is fast and uses something you already built and tested, while diagnosing a broken version while users see errors costs trust every minute. Health checks and error-rate comparisons before and after the change then tell you whether the deployment caused the problem. Worked example: version 42 deploys at 09:00. Step one, two of four instances fail their health checks and the error rate rises from 0.1 percent to 6 percent. Step two, identify the change: version 42 replaced version 41. Step three, roll back to the artifact tagged 41 and confirm the error rate returns to baseline. Step four, only then read the logs from version 42 to find the cause, such as a missing environment variable. Common mistake: rolling back without checking whether version 42 already changed the database schema in a way version 41 cannot read. The rollback then causes new errors. In a running system, a bad deploy left in place keeps failing requests for every minute of diagnosis, and a rollback that ignores data changes can turn one failure into two.

questions.prompt: Larkspur Health runs its appointment API on five containers. At 14:00, build 118 replaces build 117. Two of the five containers fail their health checks, and the error rate climbs from 0.3 percent to 9 percent. The team confirms that build 118 is the change. Step three is missing. Step four: they roll back to the artifact tagged 117 and confirm the error rate returns near 0.3 percent. Which step three completes the procedure safely?
choices: Redeploy build 118 to all five containers to see whether the failures repeat.
Change the health check threshold so the two failing containers appear healthy on the dashboard.
Read the logs from build 118 to find the root cause before doing anything else.
Check whether build 118 changed the database schema in a way build 117 cannot read, and only then roll back.
questions.why: Rollback comes first, but a rollback that ignores data changes can cause new errors, so the schema check must happen before step four.

questions.prompt: In deployment terms, what is an artifact?
choices: A live server that is updated in place with each new release.
A probe that asks a running instance whether it responds correctly.
A decision to keep a broken version running while a fix is written.
The packaged, versioned output of a build that should not change once it is created.
questions.why: An artifact is the packaged, versioned build output, and it must stay unchanged so that rollbacks return to a known version.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm ships build 9.4 of its parcel tracking service, and the error rate jumps sharply within minutes. Which first action best limits the harm?
choices: Ship build 9.5 immediately with a guessed fix for the error.
Roll back to the previous tagged artifact after checking for data changes, then read the build 9.4 logs.
Turn off the health checks so the errors stop appearing on the monitoring dashboard.
Spend an hour reading the logs of build 9.4 before changing anything else.
questions.why: Rolling back to a previously built and tested artifact is the fastest way to stop the harm, and diagnosis comes after that.

questions.prompt: A team rolls back a service from version 5 to version 4, but errors continue. Version 5 had added a column and written rows that version 4 rejects. Which mistake caused the continuing errors?
choices: Choosing a forward fix instead of a rollback, which is always slower to ship.
Running health checks on version 4 before routing any traffic to it.
Rolling back without checking whether version 5 changed data in a way version 4 cannot read.
Keeping version 4 as an artifact that the team edits when they need to.
questions.why: A rollback that ignores data changes made by the newer version can leave the older version unable to read the data, creating new failures.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would handle a deployment that has just raised the error rate, in the order you would act, and name one limit of rolling back.
lessons.modelAnswer: First I would stop the damage. I would check whether the error rate and failed health checks began right after the deploy, and if they did, I would roll back to the last known-good artifact, the previously built and versioned package, rather than debugging the new one while users are hit. I would confirm the metrics return to baseline before doing anything else. Then I would compare the two versions: what changed in code, configuration, and secrets, and I would read the logs from the failing instances to find a specific error. The limit of rollback is that it only undoes the code. If the new version changed a database schema or wrote data the old version cannot read, rolling back can fail or corrupt results, so I would check compatibility first. In that case a forward fix may be safer, applied through the same pipeline so it is built and tested like any other change.
rubricPoints: Mitigate first by restoring the last known-good version, then diagnose the cause.
Confirm the deploy is the cause by comparing error rates and health checks against the deploy time.
Name the limit: rollback does not undo data or schema changes made by the new version.
Use logs and the differences between versions to find the specific failing change.

suggested.rationale: That mission has you roll back a bad release quickly and then fix it forward, which is the core skill of this objective.

lessons.plain: Infrastructure as code means describing the resources you need, such as queues, databases, networks and permission roles, in text files instead of clicking through a web console. A tool then makes the real environment match those files. Because the files are text, they can be stored in version control, reviewed like any other code, and applied again to build the same setup in another account or region. AWS offers several ways to do this: its native CloudFormation templates, the CDK, which lets you write infrastructure in a general programming language, SAM for serverless applications, and third-party tools such as Terraform. Choosing among them mostly depends on who writes the code, how it is reviewed, and where it must run.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your team must build the same set of resources in a test account and a production account, and a colleague suggests writing them down as text files instead of clicking through the console twice. What main benefit would you expect from that, and what new risk would you watch for?
lessons.teach:
Infrastructure as code (IaC) means you describe the resources you want, such as a queue, a database, a network and a permission role, in a file, and a tool makes the real environment match that file. The file is the source of truth. Because it is text, it can be kept in version control, reviewed like any other code, and applied again to build an identical copy somewhere else.

There are two broad styles. Declarative tools let you state the end result, and the tool works out which create, update or delete steps are needed. Imperative tools run a sequence of steps you wrote in order. Most AWS IaC tools are declarative underneath, even when you write them in a programming language, because the code ultimately produces a declarative template.

The main options for AWS are AWS CloudFormation, the native service that reads JSON or YAML templates and manages a group of related resources as one stack; the AWS Cloud Development Kit (CDK), which lets you write infrastructure in a language such as TypeScript or Python and then generates a CloudFormation template from that code; AWS Serverless Application Model (SAM), an extension of CloudFormation with shorter syntax for serverless functions and APIs; and third-party tools such as Terraform, which use their own language and call the AWS API. Configuration tools such as Ansible or Chef manage what runs inside machines. They are not a substitute for creating the resources in the first place.

Worked example: a team wants a queue and a function that reads from it. In one CloudFormation template they declare both resources and the link between them. They deploy the stack. The service creates the queue, then the function, then the link, and records the stack's state. Later the team changes the queue's settings in the template and creates a change set first, which previews what will be modified or replaced before anything happens.

Common mistake: editing a resource by hand in the console after a stack created it. The stack's record now disagrees with reality, which is called drift. The next deploy may silently overwrite the manual change or fail, and nobody remembers why.

In a running system this matters because a drifted stack can no longer be trusted to rebuild production exactly as it is.

questions.prompt: Brightwater Clinics writes its database and private network in TypeScript using the AWS CDK, following four steps. Step 1: a developer writes TypeScript that declares a private network and a database inside it. Step 2: they run the CDK synth command, which generates a CloudFormation template file from that code. Step 3 is missing. Step 4: CloudFormation creates the network and database and records the stack's state. What belongs in Step 3?
choices: Deploy the generated template as a CloudFormation stack, so the service applies it and records the state
Hand the TypeScript straight to the AWS API one call at a time, skipping the template
Run an Ansible playbook against the database to install the schema before any stack exists
Edit the database's instance size in the RDS console so it matches the TypeScript, then continue
questions.why: The generated template must be deployed as a stack so CloudFormation applies it and keeps the state record that Step 4 depends on.

questions.prompt: A team proposes using Ansible to create the VPC, subnets and EC2 instances for a new reporting service, since Ansible already handles their server setup. Which statement is most accurate?
choices: Ansible is suitable for this because any tool that runs commands on a server can also create cloud resources as a stack
Ansible configures software inside machines, so an IaC tool should create the network and instances, and Ansible then configures what runs on them
Ansible can replace an infrastructure as code tool entirely here, since its playbooks are plain text files a team can keep in version control and review like code
The team should create the VPC by hand first, then let Ansible record its settings so they become the source of truth
questions.why: Configuration tools manage what runs inside machines and are not a substitute for creating the resources in the first place.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm's script runs these commands in order: create a table, add an index, then insert 50 rows. A colleague instead writes a template that states a table with an index must exist. Which statement is true?
choices: The template is declarative: it states the end result and the tool works out which steps are needed
The script is declarative because it names the table and index explicitly
Both are imperative because both end up creating the same table
The template is declarative with a list of steps the tool must follow in order
questions.why: A declarative definition describes the wanted end state and leaves the create, update or delete steps to the tool, while the script is an ordered sequence of steps and so imperative.

questions.prompt: A media company's stack creates an S3 bucket. A separate team adds a Terraform configuration that also declares the same bucket, and both run on the same schedule. What is the most likely consequence?
choices: Nothing, because the bucket is created only once and both tools skip whatever already exists
Each tool keeps its own record of the bucket, so later updates can conflict or undo each other's changes
The bucket becomes read-only until one of the tools is removed from the account
The bucket is copied to a second region automatically to keep the two records in sync
questions.why: Each IaC tool keeps its own state record of what it created, so two sources of truth for one resource can drift apart and overwrite each other on the next apply.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says we should use the CDK for everything because it is the newest option. Explain to them, in your own words, how the CDK relates to CloudFormation, and name one limit or tradeoff of choosing it over writing templates directly or using Terraform.
lessons.modelAnswer: The CDK is a way of writing infrastructure in a general programming language. When you run it, it produces a CloudFormation template, and CloudFormation still does the actual deploying, so stacks, change sets and drift behaviour are CloudFormation's. That means the CDK does not remove CloudFormation's limits. One tradeoff is that the generated template can be long and hard to read when something fails, so the team must learn to read the synthesized output, not only the code. Another is that a code library adds a dependency whose upgrades can change what gets generated. If the team already runs Terraform across several clouds, adopting the CDK means maintaining two IaC styles. So I would choose based on team skills, existing tooling and whether the work spans clouds, not on what is newest.
rubricPoints: Explains that the CDK generates CloudFormation templates, which then do the deploying
Names a concrete tradeoff such as hard-to-read generated output or library upgrade risk
Mentions the cost of running two IaC tools if Terraform is already in use
Recommends choosing based on team skills and existing tooling rather than novelty

suggested.rationale: Choosing among IaC tools is mostly product facts and comparisons, and no listed mission or planned engine covers provisioning tools.

lessons.plain: Infrastructure as code means describing the cloud resources you want, such as servers, storage and permissions, in a text file rather than clicking them together in a web console. That file is a template. A tool reads it and builds the resources, and it can build the same setup again in another account or Region. This objective covers writing those templates in three styles: plain declarative templates, a shorthand layer for serverless applications, and a general-purpose programming approach that produces templates. Knowing which style fits which job, and how a deployment moves from file to running resources, is what makes environments repeatable.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you run the same template twice in two different AWS accounts, what do you expect to be the same afterward, and what do you expect to differ?
lessons.teach:
A template is a text file, written in YAML or JSON, that declares resources and their settings. CloudFormation is the managed service that reads a template and creates those resources as a stack, a single named group that is tracked as one unit. Each resource has a logical ID, the name used inside the template, which is separate from the physical name the cloud assigns. Parameters are inputs supplied at deploy time, and outputs are values the stack reports back, such as a bucket name. Intrinsic functions are built-in template operations; Ref returns a resource's identifier, and Fn::GetAtt reads one of its attributes.

Why it works: the template describes the desired state. A deployment compares it with what already exists and creates, updates or replaces only what differs. A change set previews those differences before anything changes. If an update fails, the stack rolls back to its last good state.

SAM (Serverless Application Model) is a shorthand layer. A template that declares a Transform line naming the SAM version lets you write a short function or API definition, and the transform expands it into full CloudFormation resources at deploy time. The sam build and sam deploy commands package and submit the result.

The CDK (Cloud Development Kit) lets you write infrastructure in a general-purpose language such as TypeScript or Python, using constructs, which are reusable building blocks. Running cdk synth produces a CloudFormation template, and cdk deploy submits it, so CloudFormation still performs the work.

Worked example: a template declares a bucket with logical ID Logs. Renaming that ID to LogsBucket looks harmless, but CloudFormation treats it as a new resource. It creates a new bucket and deletes the old one, losing the data unless a retain policy is set.

Common mistake: changing resources in the console. The live stack then differs from the template, which is called drift. The next deploy may silently undo the manual fix.

Consequence: a production stack with drift, or an accidental replacement, can cause an outage or data loss, which is why change sets are reviewed before every deploy. The template file is the source of truth.

questions.prompt: A payments team at a travel firm runs a stack with an SQS queue whose logical ID is Retries. The template sets its visibility timeout to 30 seconds. An engineer changes the live queue to 90 seconds in the console to fix a slow consumer and does not touch the template. Later, the team runs a deploy from the unchanged template. Step 1: the live queue now differs from the template, which is drift. Step 2: the deploy compares the template with what exists and finds the timeout differs. Step 3 is missing. Choose the step that completes the sequence and states the queue's timeout after the deploy.
choices: Step 3: the deploy keeps 90 seconds, because the live value takes priority over the template.
Step 3: the deploy updates the timeout back to the template value of 30 seconds, undoing the manual change.
Step 3: the deploy stops with an error and rolls the whole stack back to its state before the console change.
Step 3: the deploy creates a second queue under a new logical ID and leaves Retries at 90 seconds.
questions.why: A deploy makes the live resources match the template, so the timeout returns to 30 seconds and the manual change is overwritten.

questions.prompt: A template declares a notification topic with logical ID AlertTopic. Which statement describes the logical ID?
choices: It is the name used inside the template, kept separate from the physical name the cloud assigns.
It is the value the stack reports back in its outputs when the deploy finishes.
It is the Amazon Resource Name the cloud assigns to the topic after it is created.
It is a value supplied at deploy time by the person running the deploy command.
questions.why: The logical ID is the template-internal name, which is distinct from the physical name the cloud assigns to the resource.

questions.prompt: A clinic's engineers write a short definition for a serverless function and its API, and the template begins with a Transform line naming the SAM version. What happens to the short definition at deploy time?
choices: It runs locally on the engineer's laptop during sam build and is never sent to the cloud.
It is ignored, and the stack is created only from the resources written out in full.
It is converted by sam deploy into the cloud's own console settings after the stack exists.
It is expanded into full CloudFormation resources by the transform before the stack is created.
questions.why: The Transform line tells CloudFormation to expand the SAM shorthand into full resource definitions when the template is processed.

questions.prompt: An engineer at an insurance firm runs a deploy and a change set shows that a database resource will be replaced rather than updated. The engineer did not expect this. What is the safest first response?
choices: Edit the live database in the console so it matches the template before running the deploy again.
Delete the whole stack and redeploy it from scratch so that no unexpected changes remain.
Execute the change set, since the template is the source of truth and a replacement is always harmless.
Pause and do not execute; find which property forces the replacement and confirm the data is protected before approving.
questions.why: Change sets preview differences before anything changes, so an unexpected replacement should be investigated and its data risk checked before the change is executed.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how CloudFormation, SAM and the CDK relate to each other, and name one limit or risk of renaming a logical ID or editing resources by hand.
lessons.modelAnswer: CloudFormation is the engine. It reads a template and creates or updates a stack from it. SAM is a shorthand on top of that: you write a few lines describing a serverless function or API, and the SAM transform expands them into full CloudFormation resources before deploy. The CDK is a different front end. You write the infrastructure in a programming language, and cdk synth turns it into a CloudFormation template, which then deploys the same way. So all three end up as CloudFormation stacks. The main limit is that the logical ID is how CloudFormation tracks a resource. If you rename it, CloudFormation may replace the resource, which can delete stateful data. Editing resources by hand in the console creates drift, so the next deploy may undo the change or fail unexpectedly. The fix is to change the template and review a change set first.
rubricPoints: CloudFormation is the underlying service that turns a template into a stack.
SAM is a shorthand that expands into CloudFormation resources at deploy time.
The CDK is a programming layer that synthesizes a CloudFormation template.
Renaming a logical ID can cause replacement and data loss, and manual console edits cause drift.

suggested.rationale: Choosing between SAM, CloudFormation and the CDK for a scenario, and predicting the effect of a change, is best practised by reasoning through an exam-style situation.

lessons.plain: Imagine the same set of safety settings must be switched on in a dozen separate offices, and you want to do it from one desk instead of visiting each office. That is the idea behind pushing one infrastructure template into many separate cloud accounts and many geographic regions at once, from a single managing account. Each copy that lands in one account and one region is a separate piece you can check, update, or remove, and the whole group stays consistent. You will learn when this saves real effort, and how it can spread a mistake faster than anyone notices.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose one template creates a read-only audit role, and you need it in 10 accounts across 3 regions. Before any teaching, how would you keep the 30 copies identical, and how would you find out which copies failed?
lessons.teach:
A CloudFormation stack is a group of cloud resources created together from one template, which is a text file describing those resources. A stack set is a single template definition kept by a managing account and used to create matching stacks elsewhere. Each individual stack created from it, in one target account and one Region, is called a stack instance. The managing account is the administrator account, and the accounts that receive instances are target accounts.

The stack set holds the one true version of the template. When you change it and roll it out, the service applies the change to every stack instance and reports the status of each one. Permissions work in one of two ways. With self-managed permissions, you build the trust roles yourself in each target account. With service-managed permissions, AWS Organizations creates those roles and can deploy automatically to accounts placed in chosen organizational units, including accounts created later.

Worked example. You deploy the audit role to accounts A, B and C in Regions X and Y. That is 3 times 2, so 6 stack instances. You set the rollout to touch at most two accounts at a time and to stop if more than one account fails. Accounts A and B succeed in Region X, but account C fails because a role with that name already exists there. One failure is within your tolerance, so the rest continue, and you can see exactly which instance needs fixing.

Common mistake. Hard-coding values that must differ by account or Region, such as a name that is already taken somewhere else, and then assuming a clean rollout means the change worked everywhere.

Consequence. A stack set operation can leave the estate partly updated. The per-instance status report, not the template, tells you the true state, and removing instances needs as much planning as creating them.

questions.prompt: A retail firm keeps one stack set for an encryption-key policy template. It targets 4 accounts (north, south, east, west) across 2 Regions. Step 1: count the instances, which is 4 times 2, so 8. Step 2: set the rollout to touch one account at a time with a failure tolerance of 0. Step 3 is missing. Step 4: the rollout halts after the east account fails in Region 2 because a key alias with that name already exists there, leaving 3 of the 8 instances unchanged. Which choice correctly fills the missing Step 3?
choices: Change the failure tolerance to 4 so the remaining accounts are still attempted after the failure
Assume the rollout succeeded because it ended without a visible error message in the console
Delete the stack set so that no stale instances remain before the next attempt
Run the rollout and check the per-instance status report to see which instances succeeded or failed
questions.why: The per-instance status report is the only reliable record of which instances are complete, failed or unchanged, which is why it must be read during the rollout rather than the template or the absence of an error being trusted.

questions.prompt: What is a stack instance in the context of a stack set?
choices: A template file stored in the administrator account that holds the one true definition
The trust role that AWS Organizations creates in each target account automatically
The whole group of target accounts that receive the template during a rollout
One stack created from the set in one target account and one Region
questions.why: A stack instance is the single stack produced from the stack set's template in one specific target account and one specific Region.

questions.prompt: A company has 5 target accounts and 3 Regions and uses one stack set for a logging template. How many stack instances exist once the set is fully deployed, and what setting limits how many accounts change at the same time?
choices: 5 instances, one per account, because the Region count does not change the number
15 instances, but the cap on simultaneous change is the number of Regions
8 instances, capped by the failure tolerance setting alone
15 instances, capped by the maximum number of accounts updated at a time
questions.why: Instances equal accounts times Regions, which is 5 times 3 for 15, and the maximum concurrent accounts setting controls how many accounts are changed at once.

questions.prompt: A team writes a bucket name tied to one Region directly into the stack set template. The rollout finishes without halting, and the team concludes the change is correct in every account and Region. What is the flaw in that conclusion?
choices: Templates cannot contain bucket names at all, so the rollout should have failed outright on the first account
Nothing is wrong, since a rollout that never halts means every instance has been checked and confirmed correct by the service
The rollout must be run one Region at a time, which this team skipped, so the instances in the other Region are now unreliable
Values that differ by account or Region belong in per-instance inputs, and the per-instance status report must be checked because a finished rollout does not prove each instance is right
questions.why: Hard-coding account- or Region-specific values causes errors that a clean-looking rollout can hide, so the per-instance status report, not the completion of the rollout, shows the true state.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has only deployed single stacks what a stack set adds, and name one limit or tradeoff you would watch for when rolling one out to many accounts and Regions.
lessons.modelAnswer: A stack set is one template definition that the administrator account uses to create a matching stack in each target account and Region, so a change is made once and pushed out. Each copy is a stack instance, and the stack set reports status for every instance separately. The main tradeoff is blast radius. A bad template or a bad parameter reaches every instance you target, so you limit it with a maximum number of accounts updated at once and a failure tolerance, and you roll out to a small set first. Permissions also need planning. With self-managed permissions you build the trust roles yourself in each account. With service-managed permissions through AWS Organizations, new accounts in the chosen organizational units can receive the stack automatically, which is convenient but means a mistake also spreads to future accounts. Always check the per-instance results rather than assuming success.
rubricPoints: A stack set is one template pushed to many account and Region targets, and each copy is a stack instance.
The blast-radius tradeoff is limited by concurrency and failure tolerance settings, with a small first rollout.
Self-managed permissions require you to build trust roles, while service-managed permissions can auto-deploy to new accounts.
Per-instance status should be verified rather than assuming a rollout succeeded everywhere.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine covers multi-account template rollout, so an exam-style scenario about choosing rollout settings adds the most.

lessons.plain: Change management for infrastructure as code is the set of rules that decides how a change to your cloud setup gets proposed, checked, approved, and released. Your infrastructure is described in text files, so a change is an edit to a file. That lets you apply the same discipline used for software: the change is written down, another person reads it, a tool shows what it will do before it does it, approvals are recorded, and you can return to a known good version if something goes wrong. The goal is that nobody changes production by hand in a hurry, and every change can be explained afterward.
lessons.guessPrompt: A teammate edits a template that controls your production database, merges it straight to the main branch with no review, and then runs the deploy. What could go wrong, and what two checks would you add before anything reaches production?
lessons.teach:
Infrastructure as code (IaC) means describing servers, networks, databases, and permissions in files, so that a tool can create or change them. A change request becomes a change to those files. Change management is the process around that edit. A preview, sometimes called a change set or plan, is a tool's statement of what it would add, modify, or delete if you applied the files. Drift is the gap that appears when the real resources no longer match the files, usually because someone edited something by hand in the console. A promotion is moving the same tested change through stages such as development, staging, and production. An approval gate is a required human sign-off before the next stage runs. Rollback means reapplying the last known good version of the files.

It works because the files become the record of truth. Review catches mistakes before they run, the preview shows effects before they happen, and promoting the same change through stages means what was tested is what ships.

Worked example: you add a rule that opens port 443 on a load balancer's security group. Step 1: you commit the change to a branch and open a review. Step 2: the pipeline validates the syntax and produces a preview showing one modified security group rule and no replacements. Step 3: a reviewer reads the preview and approves. Step 4: the change deploys to staging, and automated checks pass. Step 5: after a second approval gate, the same change is promoted to production.

Common mistake: deploying from a laptop with uncommitted local edits, so the running system matches no reviewed version. Another is approving without reading the preview. If a preview says a resource will be replaced, a database could be deleted and recreated, so that line needs its own review.

In a running system, drift and out-of-band edits are dangerous because the next deploy can silently undo a hand fix or fail in a surprising way. Strict change control keeps the files, the preview, and the live system in agreement.

questions.prompt: Harbor Dental's platform team keeps its backup volumes described in files and promotes changes from staging to production. An engineer changes the encryption key on one backup volume. Step 1: the engineer commits the change to a branch and opens a review. Step 2: the pipeline produces a preview showing one volume marked for replacement and zero modified. Step 3: this step is missing and must be filled in. Step 4: after staging checks pass, a second approval gate is cleared and the same change is promoted to production. Which choice completes step 3?
choices: The reviewer approves at once, since the pipeline's syntax check already passed.
The reviewer treats the replacement line as a separate risk, confirms a recent backup exists, and only then approves.
The team skips staging and applies the change straight to production to save time.
The team reapplies the previous version of the files to clear the preview.
questions.why: A replacement can destroy and recreate the volume, so that line needs its own review before anyone approves the change.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what does drift mean in an infrastructure-as-code platform?
choices: Moving the same tested change from development to production.
A required human sign-off before the next stage runs.
The gap when real resources stop matching the files, often after a console edit.
A planned change that a tool applies automatically on a schedule.
questions.why: The teaching text defines drift as the gap between real resources and the files, usually caused by a hand edit in the console.

questions.prompt: A team's pipeline reapplies its files every night. During an incident yesterday, an engineer opened a port in the console and did not update the files. What is the most likely result?
choices: Nothing changes, because console edits only affect newly created resources.
The next run may silently remove the port opening, because the files no longer describe the live system.
The console change is written into the files automatically, so nothing is lost.
The pipeline stops working until someone deletes the console change by hand.
questions.why: Because the files are the record of truth, a nightly apply can undo an out-of-band fix without warning, which is the danger the teaching text describes.

questions.prompt: A team tests a build in staging. On release day, production is built fresh from the repository, and a dependency changed in between, so production differs from what was tested. Which principle has been broken?
choices: Rollback is missing, because each release needs its own fresh rollback plan.
What was tested must be what ships, so the tested change itself should be promoted.
Drift is acceptable because it means the system is updating itself.
Approval gates should be removed so that releases move faster.
questions.why: Promotion means moving the same tested change through stages; rebuilding it for production breaks the link between what was tested and what ships.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a change to our infrastructure code should travel from a proposal to production. Name one limit or tradeoff of the process you describe.
lessons.modelAnswer: A change starts as a commit on a branch, with a review request that describes what we want and why. The pipeline then checks the files and produces a preview of what would be added, changed, or deleted. A reviewer reads that preview, paying special attention to any resource marked for replacement, because replacement can destroy data. Once approved, the same artifact goes to staging first, where automated tests run. Production requires a second approval gate. Every step is recorded, so we can roll back to the last good version if needed. The tradeoff is speed: each gate adds waiting time, and a real emergency may tempt someone to bypass the process. We keep a documented, audited emergency path, and afterward we bring the change back into the files so drift does not build up.
rubricPoints: Describes the steps from proposal through review, preview, staging, and production
Explains why the preview and reading replacement lines matter
Notes that the same tested artifact is promoted through stages
Names a real tradeoff such as delay or pressure to bypass gates, and a way to handle it

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through an exam-style change scenario, with a risky preview and an approval decision, adds the most to this process-based objective.

lessons.plain: When a company runs many servers and applications on AWS, someone has to decide how their settings get applied, checked, and kept consistent over time. Amazon Web Services offers four tools that sound similar but do different jobs. Think of them as four specialists: one watches and records what things look like, one carries out instructions across many machines, one keeps machines in an agreed shape, and one changes live application settings in careful steps. Choosing the right one starts with asking what problem you are solving, not which name sounds most familiar.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your team must change a timeout on live services, make sure servers stay compliant with a security rule, and apply a patch every month. Which of these four tools would you guess handles each part, and why might no single tool cover all three?
lessons.teach:
AWS Config records how your resources are configured over time and checks them against rules you choose, so you can spot non-compliance and drift, meaning a live setting that no longer matches what you intended. AWS Systems Manager is a toolbox for operating many machines: it runs commands across a fleet, patches operating systems, stores parameters, and offers State Manager, which repeatedly re-applies a declared state such as agent installed and running. AWS AppConfig delivers application settings like feature flags (on/off switches for features) and timeouts to running software without a redeploy, validating changes and rolling them out in stages with alarms that trigger a rollback. AWS OpsWorks is a managed home for Chef or Puppet, configuration tools that describe a desired state as code; AWS has been retiring older OpsWorks offerings, so check current status first.

Why it works: each service sits at a different layer. Config observes, Systems Manager acts on machines, AppConfig changes application values safely, and OpsWorks hosts existing Chef or Puppet code.

Worked example: a team has three needs. To keep the monitoring agent running on every server, create a State Manager association, which re-checks and reinstalls the agent on a schedule. To find any security group open to the world, enable Config with a rule that flags it. To roll a new retry timeout to 200 running instances, store it in AppConfig, validate it, and deploy in 10 percent steps with an alarm that rolls back. Three problems, three services.

Common mistake: treating Config as a fixer. Config reports that a resource is non-compliant; it changes nothing unless you attach a remediation, an automatic fix usually run as a Systems Manager automation. Teams that expect repairs from Config leave violations open.

Consequence: editing a timeout file on every server at once gives no staged rollout or automatic rollback, so one bad value can fail the whole fleet together.

Pick the service by the question you are asking: observe, act on machines, change application settings, or manage existing Chef or Puppet code.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm runs 40 batch servers and 6 storage buckets in its own AWS account. Its three needs are handled as follows. Step 1: the log-shipping agent must stay installed and running on all 40 servers, so the team creates a State Manager association, which re-checks that state on a schedule and reinstalls the agent if it is missing. Step 2: a storage bucket that allows public read access must be found, so the team enables AWS Config with a rule that flags public buckets, and the rule reports bucket-7 as non-compliant. Step 3 is missing: the team also wants bucket-7 made private automatically, without someone opening the console. Which should the team add to the Config rule?
choices: A remediation that runs a Systems Manager automation document to change the bucket setting
A Chef recipe hosted in AWS OpsWorks that runs on a schedule against the buckets
An AWS AppConfig deployment that sets a bucket-privacy flag in small steps
A second AWS Config rule that checks the same bucket setting every hour
questions.why: AWS Config only reports non-compliance, so an automatic fix must be attached as a remediation, which is usually a Systems Manager automation that acts on the resource.

questions.prompt: Which service records how resources are configured over time and checks those records against rules you choose, without changing the resources itself?
choices: AWS Systems Manager Run Command
AWS OpsWorks
AWS AppConfig
AWS Config
questions.why: AWS Config observes configuration history and evaluates rules; it does not act on machines or change settings unless a remediation is attached.

questions.prompt: A mobile backend runs on 500 servers. The team must switch off a feature flag across all of them within minutes, roll the change out in stages, and roll back automatically if an error-rate alarm fires. Which service fits?
choices: An AWS Config conformance pack
AWS Systems Manager Patch Manager
AWS AppConfig
AWS OpsWorks with a Puppet server
questions.why: AppConfig delivers application settings such as feature flags to running software, validates them, and rolls them out in stages with alarm-triggered rollback.

questions.prompt: A team expects Systems Manager State Manager to flag any security group that is open to the whole internet. Why will State Manager not do this by itself?
choices: State Manager re-applies a declared machine state on a schedule, so it does not evaluate resource rules the way AWS Config does
State Manager reports only after a rollback, so it cannot detect open groups in time
State Manager only works on Windows machines and cannot read firewall rules
State Manager is designed to hold application feature flags, not machine state
questions.why: State Manager keeps a declared state such as agent installed in place; checking resources against chosen rules and reporting non-compliance is the job of AWS Config.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between AWS Config, Systems Manager and AppConfig for a given change, and name one limit or tradeoff of the choice you would make.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start by asking what the change needs to do. If we need to know whether something drifted or broke a rule, I use Config, which records and evaluates but does not fix anything by itself. If we need to run something on many machines or keep them in a declared state, I use Systems Manager, such as a State Manager association that re-applies the agent on a schedule. If we need to change a live setting like a timeout, I use AppConfig, because it validates the value and rolls it out in stages with alarms. The tradeoff is that using AppConfig adds a dependency: the application has to read its settings through the AppConfig mechanism, so it is more work than editing a file. Also, Config alone leaves violations open until someone attaches a remediation, so I always pair the rule with a fix.
rubricPoints: Config observes and evaluates compliance but does not change resources by itself
Systems Manager acts on machines and maintains a desired state through State Manager
AppConfig safely delivers and rolls back application settings without a redeploy
A named limit or tradeoff, such as the integration effort or the need for a remediation

suggested.rationale: Choosing among four similar services is best practised by reasoning through a mixed scenario that needs more than one tool.

lessons.plain: Think of a company that builds houses from a catalogue of approved floor plans. Instead of an architect redrawing the kitchen for every new house, the plans already include the wiring, smoke alarms and locks that the building code requires. A new house is built by picking a plan and filling in a few choices, such as the number of bedrooms. This objective is about writing those plans for cloud accounts: reusable blueprints for servers, networks and storage, with the required safety rules built in, so every new environment starts compliant without someone setting it up by hand in the console.
lessons.guessPrompt: If ten teams each need a database set up the same secure way, what would go wrong if each team wrote its own setup by hand, and what would a single approved, reusable version prevent?
lessons.teach:
A template is a text file that describes a set of cloud resources, such as a database, a network and the permissions around them, so the whole set can be created the same way every time. CloudFormation is the AWS service that reads a template and creates those resources as one unit called a stack. Updating or deleting the template updates or deletes the stack. A module is a reusable piece of a template with its own inputs and outputs, which other templates can include. The AWS CDK (Cloud Development Kit) lets you write the same kind of definition in a general-purpose programming language. Its reusable pieces are called constructs, and it turns them into CloudFormation templates before deploying. AWS Service Catalog publishes approved templates as products inside portfolios. A portfolio is a collection that specific teams or accounts may launch from, often with constraints such as allowed sizes or a required naming pattern. A guardrail is a rule that prevents or detects a non-compliant setting, such as forcing encryption on storage.

Why it works: the approved version is written once and reviewed once. Every launch then inherits the same security settings, so compliance comes from the template rather than from memory.

Worked example: a team needs a private storage bucket. Step 1: the platform team writes a module that creates a bucket with public access blocked and encryption switched on. Step 2: they publish a Service Catalog product that wraps the module and constrains the input so the bucket name must follow a naming rule. Step 3: a team launches the product from their portfolio and fills in only the name. Step 4: the resulting stack has the required settings, and a later fix to the module reaches new launches.

Common mistake: treating a template as a one-time script, then letting people edit resources by hand in the console. This creates drift, where the live resource no longer matches the template. The next stack update may overwrite the manual change or fail because of it.

Consequence: a drifted resource can look compliant on paper while not being compliant. Reviewers then trust the template when they should be checking the live system. The approved template is the single source of truth for the pattern, so keeping live resources in step with it is part of the job.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm wants every new message queue to keep its messages encrypted. Step 1: the platform team writes a CloudFormation module that creates a queue with encryption switched on. Step 2: they publish that module as a Service Catalog product in a portfolio shared with two product teams. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: a team in one of those accounts launches the product and gets a stack whose queue is encrypted, without changing any setting by hand. Which action fills the missing step 3?
choices: The team launches the product from the shared portfolio, supplying only the allowed inputs such as the queue name.
The platform team deletes the portfolio so that every team creates queues from scratch.
The team opens the console and turns on encryption for the queue after the stack is created.
The team copies the module source into its own template so it can change settings freely.
questions.why: The launch from the portfolio is the step that makes the approved, encrypted template produce the stack, while the other choices bypass or edit around the approved source.

questions.prompt: In this course's sense, what is an AWS Service Catalog portfolio?
choices: A collection of approved products that specific teams or accounts may launch, often with constraints on their inputs.
A single template file that only its original author is allowed to deploy.
A rule that blocks a non-compliant setting before the resource is created.
A live list of every resource running in an account, refreshed automatically.
questions.why: A portfolio is the collection that holds approved products and controls which teams or accounts may launch them, which matches the teaching text's definition.

questions.prompt: A team needs a different encryption setting on one storage bucket. Which approach keeps the approved template as the single source of truth?
choices: Edit the live bucket in the console and leave the template unchanged.
Delete the stack, create the bucket by hand, and keep the old template for records.
Ask a reviewer to approve the console change so the template can be ignored.
Change the approved module through review, then launch from it so the live resource matches the template.
questions.why: Changing the module and launching from it keeps the live resource in step with the template, whereas any hand edit or manual rebuild creates drift.

questions.prompt: A storage bucket was edited by hand in the console so public access is now on, but its template still says public access is blocked. Why is a reviewer who trusts the template wrong about this bucket?
choices: The stack will be rejected at the next launch, so the bucket is never really created.
Console edits are recorded automatically in the template, so the template is already up to date.
Templates cannot describe public access settings, so the template is silent on the matter.
The live bucket has drifted from the template, so the template no longer describes what is actually running.
questions.why: Drift means the live resource no longer matches the template, so the template looks compliant on paper while the running bucket is not.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would give a dev team a secure, reusable way to create a database. Choose between a Service Catalog product, a CloudFormation module and a CDK construct, and name one limit or tradeoff of the approach you pick.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would write the database pattern once, as a CloudFormation template or a CDK construct, with encryption, backups and private networking already set. The choice between them depends on who maintains it. A CDK construct suits a team that wants to write in a programming language and test it, because it still compiles down to a CloudFormation template. A plain CloudFormation module suits teams that want straightforward template reuse. Then I would publish the approved version as a Service Catalog product in a portfolio that only the dev team's accounts can see, and limit the inputs they can change, such as instance size or name prefix. The tradeoff is that the platform team now owns the pattern. Every change needs review and a version, and teams stuck on an old version will not get fixes until they relaunch or upgrade. Drift is also still possible if people edit the resource by hand, so I would check for it.
rubricPoints: Names a reusable template, module or construct as the place where security settings are fixed once.
Explains Service Catalog as a way to publish approved products and limit who can launch them and with which inputs.
Notes the tradeoff of central ownership, versioning and slow adoption of fixes by teams on old versions.
Mentions drift from manual changes and how it undermines the approved pattern.

suggested.rationale: Choosing between a catalogue product, a module and a CDK construct for a scenario is best practised by reasoning through an exam-style situation, since no listed mission or planned engine covers templates.

lessons.plain: An AWS account is a separate, fenced-off workspace in Amazon's cloud where a company's servers, databases and bills live. An account structure is how a company arranges many of these workspaces, often grouped into folders so that rules can be applied to a whole group at once. The practical reasons are simple: one team's mistake, a stolen password or a runaway bill stays inside its own fence instead of spreading across the whole company. Good practice is to create each new account through automation, not by hand, so every account starts already set up with the same logging, security rules and tags.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company runs its test environment and its live customer system inside one shared account, and a developer's test script accidentally deletes a database that customers depend on. Would splitting those two environments into separate accounts have made this kind of accident less likely to reach customers, and why?
lessons.teach:
An AWS account is a separate container for cloud resources. It has its own bill, its own service limits, and its own identities and permissions. An account structure is the way a company arranges many such accounts. Accounts are usually grouped into organizational units, which are folders that hold accounts and can have shared rules applied to them. AWS Organizations is the service that creates and holds these accounts under one management account, the root of the tree. The management account pays the combined bill and should run nothing except governance tooling. AWS Control Tower is a service that builds a landing zone, which is a prepared baseline with standard accounts such as a log archive and an audit account, plus guardrails. A guardrail is a rule applied across accounts that either blocks an action or detects a violation.

Why it works: an account is a hard boundary. A mistake, a compromised credential or an exhausted quota in one account generally cannot reach resources in another unless someone deliberately builds a trust between them.

Worked example. A company has a production workload, a staging workload and a security team. Step 1: it creates a Workloads organizational unit with two child units, Prod and NonProd, and a Security unit holding a log archive account and an audit account. Step 2: a new payments service is requested, so an account-vending pipeline creates a member account in NonProd from a template, with tags for owner and cost center. Step 3: baseline logging and guardrails are applied automatically. Step 4: the team deploys only into that account.

Common mistake: running workloads in the management account. If that happens, one compromise or one billing problem touches the whole organization.

Consequence: if a staging load test exhausts a service quota, only that account's quota is hit, and production keeps running. Account structure is a deliberate design decision, and the practice is to create every account through automation so it is governed from its first minute.

questions.prompt: Harbor Retail runs a nightly reporting job from its management account because that was the quickest setup years ago. The team decides to move it into a new account. Step 1: they ask for a new account under the Workloads organizational unit, which is a folder that groups accounts and can carry shared rules. Step 2: the account-vending pipeline creates the account from a template with owner and cost-center tags. Step 3: baseline logging and guardrails are applied automatically before anyone deploys. Step 4 is missing. Which step completes the move?
choices: Copy the management account's identities into the new account so both can run the same job.
Give the reporting team administrator rights in the management account so the job can keep its old access.
Delete the audit account in the Security unit to reduce the bill for the new account.
Stop the job in the management account, point its deployment at the new account, and confirm the management account runs only governance tooling.
questions.why: The management account should run nothing except governance tooling, so the job must be stopped there and redeployed into the new account, with the management account then checked to be clear of workloads.

questions.prompt: A company wants a single place to group several accounts so that one shared rule can be applied to all of them. Which structure is designed for this?
choices: An organizational unit, which is a folder that holds accounts and can have rules applied to it
A member account, which is the container for one set of resources and its own bill
A guardrail, which is the rule itself and does not hold accounts
A landing zone, which is a prepared baseline holding standard accounts such as a log archive
questions.why: An organizational unit is the folder that groups accounts and carries shared rules, while the other options either describe a baseline, a rule, or a single account.

questions.prompt: A data team's load test in its staging account used up a service quota, which is a cap on how much of a resource the account may use. Which outcome does the account boundary predict for the company's production account?
choices: Production's quota is reduced to match staging so both stay balanced.
