Production stops until the management account approves a quota reset.
Production keeps running, because the quota belongs to the staging account and does not reach other accounts without a deliberate trust.
Production is throttled at the same moment because quotas are shared across the organization.
questions.why: An account is a hard boundary, so an exhausted quota in one account generally cannot affect resources in another unless someone builds a trust between them on purpose.

questions.prompt: A security lead wants a rule that stops any account in the organization from creating resources in regions the company has not approved. Which description best fits what that rule is?
choices: An organizational unit, meaning the folder that holds the accounts and their billing
A landing zone, meaning the prepared baseline that holds the log archive and audit accounts
A guardrail, meaning a rule applied across accounts that blocks an action or detects a violation
A management account, meaning the root account that pays the combined bill
questions.why: A rule applied across accounts that blocks or detects a violation is a guardrail, while the other three describe a structure, a baseline, or the root account.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why we use several AWS accounts instead of one for a company, and name one limit or tradeoff of splitting them up.
lessons.modelAnswer: We split workloads into several accounts because an account is a hard boundary. Production, staging and the security logging account each get their own, so a bad deploy, a compromised key or a runaway quota in staging cannot reach live customers. Each account has its own bill, which makes cost easy to attribute to a team, and its own service limits, so one busy team does not starve the others. The main tradeoff is overhead. Every account needs its own baseline setup, its own access paths and its own monitoring, and cross-account access has to be designed on purpose. The structure only pays off if we create accounts through automation and apply the same guardrails to each one. Without that, the number of accounts grows faster than anyone can govern them.
rubricPoints: An account is a hard boundary that limits how far a mistake or compromise can spread.
Separate accounts give separate bills and service limits, which helps cost attribution and isolation.
A tradeoff is the operational overhead of more accounts, including baseline setup, access, and cross-account links.
Accounts should be created through automation with the same guardrails so the structure stays governed.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine covers account structure directly, so reasoning through an exam-style scenario about splitting accounts is the most useful practice.

lessons.plain: When a company creates a new cloud account for a team, it should not depend on someone remembering a checklist. Standardizing account provisioning means every new account is created from one approved recipe: it lands in the right group, gets the same security rules, the same logging, and the same patching schedule, and any drift from that recipe gets noticed. Automating it means a request turns into a finished account by machine rather than by hand in a web console. Think of a factory that stamps out identical, pre-inspected boxes instead of someone packing each one from scratch.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team asks for a new cloud account today. If five different people each set up accounts by hand over a year, what differences would you expect to find between those accounts, and which of those differences would hurt you most during an incident?
lessons.teach:
An account is an isolated container for cloud resources, with its own billing and its own permission boundary. An organization is a group of accounts managed together, and an organizational unit (OU) is a folder inside that organization that groups accounts sharing the same rules. A guardrail is a rule applied at the organization level, either preventive (it blocks an action, such as turning off audit logging) or detective (it reports when something is wrong). A baseline is the standard set of resources and settings every account receives on day one, such as audit logging, a read-only audit role, and a budget alarm. Account vending means creating accounts from a template through an automated request, and drift is what happens when a real resource no longer matches the template that created it.

Why it works: the template is the single source of truth. Creating accounts through it gives every account the same starting state, and guardrails stop anyone from quietly removing that state later.

Worked example: a team requests a new non-production account. The request names the Non-production OU. The vending process creates the account inside that OU, then pushes the baseline: logging is switched on, the audit role is created, and a spending alarm is set. A guardrail on the OU now denies any attempt to disable the logging. Weeks later a detective check reports that one bucket has public access, and that drift is visible and fixable.

Common mistake: treating the baseline as a one-time setup and letting people create accounts outside the pipeline. Those accounts skip every control.

Consequence: an account without logging cannot be reconstructed after an incident, so the investigation stalls.

Standardized provisioning means no account is born without its controls, and drift is caught rather than assumed away.

questions.prompt: Lumen Health is creating a new analytics account for its Data OU, a folder for accounts that share the same rules. The vending process creates the account inside the Data OU. Next, the baseline is pushed: audit logging is switched on, a read-only audit role is created, and a budget alarm of 500 per month is set. The next step is missing and must be filled in: the team needs to ensure that nobody can quietly switch audit logging off later. Which action completes the process?
choices: Add a detective report that flags whenever audit logging is disabled, with no blocking rule
Ask the account owner to re-enable audit logging whenever they happen to notice it is off
Attach a preventive guardrail to the Data OU that denies any attempt to disable audit logging
Move the new account to the root of the organization for a week so it inherits no rules
questions.why: A preventive guardrail on the OU blocks the disabling action before it happens, whereas a detective check only reports the problem after it has already occurred.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes a baseline in account provisioning?
choices: A rule at the organization level that blocks a specific action in every account
A copy of a live account's resources taken after months of changes
The standard set of resources and settings every new account receives on its first day
A single alarm that tells the team when spending passes a set limit
questions.why: A baseline is the standard starting set of resources and settings that every account gets on day one, such as audit logging, an audit role, and a budget alarm.

questions.prompt: A developer creates a new account by hand in the console, outside the vending pipeline, and later audit logging in that account is found to be off. What is the most accurate consequence?
choices: The account is still fully governed because the organization applies baselines to any account automatically
The organization will move the account into the Non-production OU, which restores logging automatically
Nothing is affected until the next billing cycle closes, because logging only matters for cost reports
The account skipped the baseline and its controls, so an incident there may be hard or impossible to reconstruct
questions.why: Accounts created outside the pipeline skip the baseline and guardrails, and an account without logging cannot be reconstructed after an incident, so the investigation stalls.

questions.prompt: A template defines a storage bucket as private. Someone changes the bucket's policy by hand so it is publicly readable, and nothing else changes. What is this situation called, and how is it caught?
choices: A guardrail violation, because the template itself has become invalid and must be deleted and recreated
Normal operation, because only the account owner decides what a private bucket may contain after creation
Drift, because the live resource no longer matches the template that created it, and a detective check can report it
A baseline failure, because the account was missing its day-one resources, so vending must be rerun
questions.why: Drift is the gap between a live resource and the template that created it, and a detective check is the mechanism that reports it, so it can be fixed.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would make sure every new account starts with the same security and logging setup, and name one limit or tradeoff of your approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would stop treating accounts as hand-built. Every new account would be requested through one automated process that places it in a specific organizational unit and then applies the baseline: audit logging, a read-only audit role, and a spending alarm, all defined in templates kept in version control. Guardrails on the organizational unit would block actions that weaken those controls, such as turning off logging. Detective rules would report any resource that later drifts from the template. The tradeoff is that the baseline becomes a shared dependency: a bad template change can affect every account at once, so changes need review and staged rollout. Another limit is that the controls only cover accounts created through the pipeline, so I would also check for accounts created outside it.
rubricPoints: Accounts are created from one automated, template-driven process rather than by hand
A baseline of logging, roles and alarms is applied to every new account
Guardrails at the organizational unit level prevent weakening of controls
Detective checks and drift detection find resources that later differ from the template
A stated tradeoff, such as shared-template blast radius or accounts created outside the process

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through a provisioning scenario with drift and guardrails adds the most, and no listed mission or planned engine covers account provisioning directly.

lessons.plain: Think of a company's cloud accounts as separate apartments in one building. AWS Organizations is the building manager: it lets you create new apartments, group them into floors, and receive one combined bill for the whole building. AWS Control Tower is the set of house rules and a standard floor plan: it builds a well-set-up starting layout with logging and security checks, and gives you a repeatable way to hand out new accounts that already follow those rules. The goal is that a new account is governed from the day it is born, without someone setting it up by hand in the console.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company has ten separate cloud accounts, each set up by a different person in a different way. Before any teaching, what would you expect to go wrong over time, and what single change would make all ten behave the same?
lessons.teach:
An AWS account is a container that holds resources and acts as a boundary for billing, permissions, and limits. AWS Organizations is the service that links many accounts under one management account. The management account is the one that created the organization; it pays the combined bill and controls the structure. Member accounts are the other accounts that join it. Organizational units, or OUs, are named groups you place accounts into, such as Production or Sandbox, so that a rule can apply to a whole group at once. Service control policies are organization-wide limits on what member accounts are allowed to do, applied through the OU tree.

Why it works: an account is the strongest isolation boundary AWS offers, and Organizations lets you create new accounts through an API instead of signing up one at a time. Control Tower sits on top. It sets up a landing zone, which is a prepared baseline that includes a dedicated logging account and a dedicated security audit account. It also provides guardrails, which are ready-made rules: preventive guardrails block an action, and detective guardrails report when a setting drifts out of line. Account Factory is the provisioning path that creates a new account already enrolled with those rules.

Worked example: a team needs a production account for payments. Step 1, the platform team asks Account Factory for an account named payments-prod placed in the Production OU. Step 2, Control Tower creates the account and applies the baseline logging and guardrails. Step 3, the account's costs roll into the organization's combined bill. Step 4, the account is governed from its first minute, and nobody had to click through the console to make it so.

Common mistake: running ordinary workloads in the management account. Service control policies do not restrict the management account, so anyone with admin rights there sits outside the organization-wide controls, and the billing and identity of the whole organization share one blast radius.

The consequence is that the management account should hold only governance tooling, and every workload should live in a member account under an OU.

questions.prompt: Harbor Co. wants its developers kept out of regions the company has not approved. The platform team follows these steps. Step 1: the team attaches a service control policy that denies actions outside approved regions to the Development OU. Step 2: the policy is inherited by the member accounts ledger-dev, ledger-test and ledger-qa, which all sit in that OU, so developer actions there are blocked. Step 3 is missing. Choose the sentence that correctly completes Step 3, which describes what happens for an admin who acts inside the management account.
choices: The policy does not restrict the management account, so its admins keep the action and workloads should not run there.
It is removed once the accounts join the Development OU.
It is copied into each account, so the management account gets an editable copy.
It also blocks the management account admins, since the policy sits at the top of the OU tree.
questions.why: Service control policies apply to member accounts through the OU tree and do not restrict the management account, so the correct completion states that management account admins are unaffected and that workloads belong in member accounts.

questions.prompt: Which statement about an organizational unit (OU) is accurate?
choices: An OU is a separate AWS account that holds billing for its members.
An OU is a copy of the management account's permissions given to each member.
An OU is a named group of accounts that one rule can cover.
An OU is the place where a new account's logging bucket is created by hand.
questions.why: An OU is a named group you place accounts into so a rule can apply to the whole group at once, which matches the second choice and no other.

questions.prompt: A retailer with 12 member accounts needs a new account for a marketing website. Where should the account be created, and where should the website run?
choices: In a new account signed up for by hand at the sign-up page, then moved into an OU later.
In the management account, since it already pays the combined bill and has the most admin rights.
A new account from Account Factory, placed in the right OU, so rules apply from the start.
In the existing member account marketing-old, to avoid the cost of a new account.
questions.why: Account Factory creates a new account already enrolled with the guardrails and placed in a chosen OU, and workloads belong in member accounts rather than the management account.

questions.prompt: A guardrail reports that an S3 bucket's encryption setting has drifted out of line, but the change has already happened and was not stopped. Which kind of guardrail is this?
choices: A service control policy, since it always reports drift in member accounts.
A landing zone, since it deletes settings that have drifted.
A detective guardrail, since it reports drift rather than blocking the action.
A preventive guardrail, since it blocks the change.
questions.why: Detective guardrails report when a setting drifts out of line, while preventive guardrails block an action before it happens, so a reported after-the-fact drift is detective.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate proposes putting all of our services in one account to keep things simple, and says AWS Organizations and Control Tower are overkill. Explain to them, in your own words, what separate accounts under an organization buy us and what the real tradeoff is.
lessons.modelAnswer: Separate accounts give each environment a hard boundary: a permission mistake or a runaway cost in the sandbox cannot touch production, and each account has its own limits and its own billing line. Organizations lets us create those accounts programmatically and group them into OUs, so one policy can cover all production accounts at once. Control Tower gives a standard baseline with a logging account, an audit account, and guardrails, so every new account starts with the same controls instead of relying on someone remembering to set them up. The tradeoff is more to manage: cross-account access has to be designed, shared services need a home, and each account adds to what we must monitor. For one small product, a single account can be simpler at first, but we pay for that later when we need isolation.
rubricPoints: Separate accounts create hard boundaries for permissions, limits, and billing
Organizations groups accounts into OUs so one policy covers many accounts
Control Tower supplies a standard baseline and guardrails so new accounts start governed
The real tradeoff is added management overhead, such as cross-account access and monitoring

suggested.rationale: The core skill is explaining account structure and its tradeoffs to a teammate, and no listed mission or planned engine covers account governance directly.

lessons.plain: Imagine a company that runs many separate workspaces, called accounts. A central office, the organization, can set house rules that apply to every workspace at once, such as 'nobody may turn off audit logging'. These rules are called service control policies. They never hand anyone new powers. They only mark the outer edge of what is allowed, and inside that edge each person or program still needs its own permission. Role assumption is the second idea: instead of keeping a permanent key for another workspace, a program asks for a temporary badge that lets it act there for a short time. Together these let one team govern many accounts without sharing long-lived secrets.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your company has ten cloud accounts. A central policy says 'no one may disable audit logs', and a developer's own permissions allow them to edit log settings. Can that developer disable audit logs in a member account? Why or why not?
lessons.teach:
AWS Organizations is the service that groups accounts into a tree, with a management account at the top and member accounts below it. Organizational units, or OUs, are folders in that tree. A service control policy, or SCP, is a policy attached to the root, an OU, or a single account. It sets the maximum set of actions that accounts beneath it may perform. An IAM principal is a user or role that makes requests, and an identity policy is a permission document attached to that principal. A role's trust policy names which principals are allowed to assume it. AWS STS, the Security Token Service, issues the temporary credentials that result from assuming a role.

The core rule is that an SCP never grants access. A request in a member account is allowed only if the SCP allows it, the identity policy allows it, and no explicit deny applies anywhere along the way. The management account is not restricted by SCPs.

Worked example: a pipeline role in a tooling account calls AssumeRole on a deploy role in a production account. First, the deploy role's trust policy must name the pipeline role, and the pipeline role's own policy must allow sts:AssumeRole on that deploy role. STS returns temporary credentials. Next, the deploy role tries cloudtrail:StopLogging. An SCP on the production OU explicitly denies that action, so the request fails even though the deploy role's identity policy allows it. Then it tries s3:PutObject. The SCP does not deny it, the identity policy allows it, so it succeeds.

Common mistake: believing that adding an action to an SCP makes it work. The SCP only narrows the allowed set; the identity policy must still grant the action. Another mistake is forgetting that SCPs also limit the root user of member accounts.

In a running system, this shows up as a pipeline that worked yesterday and now fails with AccessDenied after someone attaches a new SCP to an OU. The error rarely names the SCP, so you must check policies at every level of the tree.

questions.prompt: A reporting role in account 4417 calls AssumeRole on a role named analytics-reader in account 902. First, analytics-reader's trust policy names the reporting role, and the reporting role's policy allows sts:AssumeRole on analytics-reader, so STS returns temporary credentials. Next, the role calls s3:GetObject on a bucket in account 902. The SCP on the Analytics OU does not deny it, the identity policy allows it, so the call succeeds. Then the role calls logs:DeleteLogGroup. The SCP on the Analytics OU explicitly denies that action, and analytics-reader's identity policy allows it. The result of this last call is: ___
choices: It fails, because an explicit deny anywhere along the way blocks the request even when the identity policy allows it.
It fails, because the trust policy must be checked again for every API call.
It succeeds, because the identity policy allows the action.
It succeeds, because SCPs only restrict the root user of member accounts.
questions.why: An explicit deny in any SCP on the path blocks the request regardless of what the identity policy grants.

questions.prompt: An SCP attached to the root of the organization denies ec2:RunInstances for every member account. Assuming each principal's identity policy allows the call, which principal can still run the action successfully?
choices: A developer role in member account 5530
The admin role in the management account 1001
A pipeline role in member account 8820
The root user of member account 7712
questions.why: The management account is not restricted by SCPs, so only its own identity policies decide the outcome.

questions.prompt: A team adds s3:DeleteObject to the SCP on their OU so that their pipeline role can delete objects. The pipeline still gets AccessDenied. What is the most likely reason?
choices: The identity policy of the pipeline role also has to grant s3:DeleteObject, because an SCP only narrows the allowed set
The pipeline role must be the management account's root user to delete objects
The SCP must be attached to the account rather than the OU to take effect
SCPs cannot allow any action, so the team must use a permissions boundary instead
questions.why: An SCP never grants access; the identity policy must still allow the action, so adding it to the SCP alone changes nothing.

questions.prompt: A role in account 2290 calls AssumeRole on a deploy role in account 4481 and gets AccessDenied before any temporary credentials are issued. The SCP on account 4481's OU allows all sts actions. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The SCP is blocking the STS call, so the OU must be detached
The deploy role's temporary credentials have expired
STS only issues credentials to users, not to roles
The deploy role's trust policy does not name the calling role, or the calling role's policy does not allow sts:AssumeRole on the deploy role
questions.why: Assuming a role needs both the trust policy on the target role and an allow in the caller's own policy, and the SCP is not the issue here.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a service control policy and a role's identity policy combine to decide whether a deploy job can perform an action in a member account. Name one limit or tradeoff of relying on SCPs for security.
lessons.modelAnswer: An SCP is attached at the organization root, an OU, or an account, and it defines the maximum set of actions that accounts below it can perform. It never grants permission by itself. A deploy job running as an assumed role in a member account can perform an action only if the SCP allows it, the role's identity policy allows it, and no explicit deny applies. The management account is outside SCP control, so it needs careful handling. A tradeoff is that SCPs are blunt: a broad deny can break legitimate workloads in ways that are hard to trace, because the error message does not name the SCP. Also, an SCP cannot stop a user who has permission at the resource level from using it if the SCP allows it, so SCPs must be paired with identity policies and resource controls.
rubricPoints: An SCP sets a maximum boundary and never grants permissions on its own.
An action succeeds only if the SCP, the identity policy, and the absence of explicit denies all agree.
Role assumption requires both a trust policy on the target role and an sts:AssumeRole permission on the caller.
A tradeoff exists, such as broad SCP denies breaking workloads with hard-to-trace AccessDenied errors.

suggested.rationale: The authorization policy evaluator engine would let the learner trace how SCPs, identity policies, and explicit denies combine for a given request, which is the core skill of this objective.

lessons.plain: Governance and security controls at scale are automatic rules that keep many cloud accounts safe and consistent without someone checking each one by hand. Think of a large office building. Some doors lock by themselves, some have cameras that record and alert a guard when something odd happens, and there is a catalogue of approved furniture that anyone can order from. In AWS, separate services play these roles: one builds the governed building, one records how every resource is configured, one detects threats, one gathers alerts in a single place, one helps investigate what happened, and one publishes a catalogue of approved templates. Knowing which tool does which job is the core skill for this topic.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team runs 40 AWS accounts. At 2 a.m., someone makes a storage bucket publicly readable in one of them. Without any tooling, how would the team find out? What would you want automation to do about it: stop it, report it, or both, and why?
lessons.teach:
Start with the definitions. A guardrail is a rule applied across many accounts. A preventive guardrail blocks an action before it happens; in AWS this is usually a service control policy (SCP), an organization-wide permission ceiling. A detective guardrail notices a non-compliant state after it exists. AWS Control Tower builds a governed multi-account setup, called a landing zone, and installs a standard set of guardrails. AWS Config records how resources are configured over time and evaluates them against rules, so you can see what changed and whether it complies. AWS Security Hub gathers findings from many sources, including Config and GuardDuty, and checks them against security standards. Amazon GuardDuty analyses logs such as account activity and network traffic to flag threats; it detects but does not fix. Amazon Detective helps you investigate a finding by linking related activity, such as which role made a change and from where. AWS Service Catalog lets a central team publish approved templates in portfolios that other accounts can launch, with constraints on what each user may choose.

Why it works: prevention and detection are layered. An SCP stops someone from disabling logging. If a bucket still becomes public, a Config rule flags it, Security Hub shows the finding beside others, and Detective traces the actor.

Worked example. At 2 a.m. a role sets a bucket to public. Step 1: AWS Config records the configuration change. Step 2: a Config rule marks the bucket non-compliant. Step 3: Security Hub creates a finding. Step 4: an engineer opens Detective to see the role, its session and the source address. Step 5: the team removes the public setting, and an SCP prevents that action in the account going forward.

Common mistake: assuming GuardDuty or Security Hub will repair a problem. They report; remediation is a separate action you must design, such as an automated response.

Consequence: until remediation runs, the bucket stays exposed, and every hour of exposure is a window for data access. Detection shortens that window but never closes it on its own.

questions.prompt: A new example in a sandbox account: a contractor's role opens a security group to the whole internet on port 3389, which is the remote desktop port. Step 1: AWS Config records the security group change. Step 2: a Config rule marks the group non-compliant. Step 3 is missing: the non-compliant result is passed into Security Hub, where it appears as a finding beside findings from other sources. Step 4: an engineer opens Detective to see the contractor's role and the source address of the session. Step 5: the team tightens the group and adds a preventive control. Which action belongs in the missing step 3?
choices: GuardDuty deletes the offending inbound rule automatically.
An SCP is applied retroactively to undo the rule change.
Detective blocks the contractor's role from making further calls.
Security Hub records the Config non-compliance as a finding, next to findings from other sources.
questions.why: Security Hub gathers findings from sources such as Config, so the non-compliant Config result becomes a Security Hub finding; the other options describe repair or blocking, which the named services do not do in that position.

questions.prompt: Which kind of guardrail stops an action before it happens?
choices: A portfolio in Service Catalog
A detective guardrail
A preventive guardrail
A landing zone
questions.why: A preventive guardrail blocks an action before it takes effect, while a detective guardrail only notices a non-compliant state after it exists.

questions.prompt: A central team wants to stop any member account in its organisation from turning off audit logging, even for administrators there. Which control fits best?
choices: A service control policy that denies the logging-disable action
A Security Hub finding that flags logging as disabled
An AWS Config rule that reports when logging is off
A Detective investigation opened after logging is disabled
questions.why: A service control policy is an organisation-wide permission ceiling that can deny the action before it happens, whereas the other options only detect or investigate after the fact.

questions.prompt: A team sees a GuardDuty finding that an access key is making unusual API calls. Their manager assumes GuardDuty will revoke the key by itself. What is the correct understanding?
choices: Security Hub revokes the key as part of its standard checks
GuardDuty only detects the threat; a separate, designed remediation must act on the key
Detective revokes the key after it finishes tracing the activity
GuardDuty revokes the key once the finding reaches high severity
questions.why: GuardDuty analyses logs to flag threats but does not fix them, so someone or some automated response must be designed to take action on the key.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who is new to AWS how preventive and detective controls differ, name the AWS services you would use for each, and describe one limit of relying on detection alone.
lessons.modelAnswer: A preventive control stops a bad action before it happens. In AWS, an organization-wide service control policy can deny actions such as turning off audit logging in any account, and Control Tower can install those guardrails for you. A detective control notices a bad state after it exists. AWS Config rules check resource settings against what is allowed, Security Hub collects those findings with others and scores them against standards, GuardDuty flags suspicious activity in logs, and Detective helps trace how it happened. The main limit of detection alone is timing: the bad state exists from the moment it is created until someone or something responds, so a public bucket can be read during that gap. Detection also does not repair anything by itself, so the team needs a designed response, or it will just have an accurate list of problems. That is why strong setups use preventive controls for the worst outcomes and detective controls for everything else.
rubricPoints: Defines preventive controls as blocking actions before they happen, with an example such as an SCP
Defines detective controls as finding non-compliant state after the fact, with an example such as a Config rule
Names the right service for each role: Control Tower, Config, Security Hub, GuardDuty, Detective
States that detection does not fix problems and leaves a window of exposure

suggested.rationale: Telling which governance service does which job is best learned by reasoning through an exam-style incident scenario, and no listed mission or planned engine covers this content directly.

lessons.plain: Imagine a fleet of rental cars that someone must keep inventoried, serviced, and fixed after safety recalls, without walking the lot each morning. Here the cars are servers and databases in the cloud. Some services keep a live list of the machines and the software on them. Others record how each resource's settings change over time and whether they match the rules you chose. Others apply the desired settings and install updates on a schedule. This objective is about combining these so a fleet is described, configured, and patched by software, not by someone logging in to each machine one at a time.
lessons.guessPrompt: You run forty servers. Last week one of them had a security update installed by hand and the others did not. How would you find out, today, which servers are missing it, without logging in to each one?
lessons.teach: Inventory is a machine-readable record of what a server has: its operating system, installed software and versions, and whether its management agent is reporting. Configuration management means stating the settings you want, called a desired state, and having software apply them. Patch management means choosing which updates must be installed and when. Drift is the gap between the desired state and what is actually running. Two AWS services split this work. AWS Systems Manager runs a small agent on each managed machine and does the acting: it collects inventory, scans for missing patches against a patch baseline (a set of rules saying which update classes and severities count as required), installs them during a maintenance window (a scheduled time slot), and re-applies a stored desired state on a schedule through an association in State Manager. AWS Config records how resources are configured over time and checks them against rules, labelling each as compliant or noncompliant. Config judges and remembers; Systems Manager changes things. Worked example: a baseline requires critical security updates within seven days. A nightly scan finds that host B is missing one. A Config rule sees the host as noncompliant. The Monday maintenance window installs the update, the next scan confirms it, and the Config status returns to compliant. Common mistake: treating a scan as a fix. A scan only reports. Without an install operation, the host stays exposed while the dashboard looks busy. Consequence: a machine without the agent, or without the instance permissions the agent needs, is invisible to both services, so it appears as neither patched nor failing. Automation is only as complete as the list of machines it can reach.

questions.prompt: Ridgeline Clinic runs 12 Windows servers. Its patch baseline (the rule set saying which updates are required) counts security updates rated Important as required. A scan on Tuesday finds that server WS-07 is missing one such update, and AWS Config, which checks resources against rules, marks WS-07 noncompliant. Step 1: the scan records the missing update. Step 2: [missing step]. Step 3: the next scan confirms the update is present, and Config returns WS-07 to compliant. Which choice correctly fills step 2?
choices: An administrator edits the baseline so that Important updates are no longer required.
Systems Manager runs the scan a second time, because two scans are needed before anything can install.
Systems Manager installs the update during a maintenance window, because a scan only reports and does not change the server.
AWS Config installs the update during its next rule evaluation, because it enforces the rules it checks.
questions.why: Scanning only reports gaps, and Systems Manager is the service that acts, so it must run an install operation during a scheduled window before the next scan can confirm the fix.

questions.prompt: Which service records how resources are configured over time and labels each one as compliant or noncompliant against its rules?
choices: AWS Config
The Systems Manager agent on each machine
AWS Systems Manager Patch Manager
Systems Manager State Manager
questions.why: AWS Config keeps the configuration history and judges each resource against rules, while the other choices either act on machines or store desired settings.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm has a server whose management agent has stopped reporting, and its instance permissions no longer let the agent communicate. What does a team see for that server in Systems Manager and AWS Config?
choices: It appears as patched, because no scan has found a gap on it.
Config marks it noncompliant, because missing patches are always reported as failures.
Systems Manager patches it in the next window through a fallback channel.
It appears in neither the patched nor the failing views, because neither service can reach it.
questions.why: Without the agent and its permissions, the machine is invisible to both services, so it shows as neither patched nor failing, which is why reach matters for automation.

questions.prompt: A company wants a stored setting, such as a required configuration on 30 Linux hosts, re-applied automatically every six hours so that drift does not persist. Which Systems Manager feature does this?
choices: A patch baseline, since it stores the values that the setting should have.
A maintenance window, which applies settings only once each time the window opens.
An AWS Config rule, which changes the setting itself whenever drift is found.
A State Manager association, which re-applies the stored desired state on a schedule.
questions.why: A State Manager association holds the desired state and re-applies it on a schedule, whereas Config only reports drift and a patch baseline defines which updates are required.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would use Systems Manager and AWS Config together to find which servers are missing a required patch and to stop their settings drifting. Name one limit or tradeoff of relying on this setup.
lessons.modelAnswer: Systems Manager is the part that acts. Its agent on each server reports inventory and scans it against a patch baseline that defines which updates are required and how fast. Missing patches are installed in a maintenance window, and a State Manager association re-applies the settings we want on a schedule. AWS Config is the part that judges and keeps history. It records each resource's configuration and checks it against rules, so we can see which servers are noncompliant and when they drifted. The main limit is coverage. A server without a working agent or the right instance permissions is invisible to both, so the dashboard can look green while that machine is unpatched. We have to reconcile the managed-instance list against the real fleet, not trust the compliance summary alone.
rubricPoints: Systems Manager collects inventory, scans against a patch baseline, and installs patches or applies desired state
AWS Config records configuration history and evaluates resources against rules as compliant or noncompliant
A scan or a Config finding only reports; an operation is needed to change the machine
Machines without the agent or permissions are invisible to both services, so coverage must be checked separately

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine practises this service-level configuration, so reading the product behaviour and tracing the example is the best fit.

lessons.plain: Some automations are too big for one small piece of code. Picture a checklist for a new hire: request an account, wait for it to be ready, apply the standard settings, and if a step fails, undo the earlier ones. In AWS, a Lambda function is a small piece of code that runs when something triggers it, so you do not manage a server for it. The AWS SDKs are language libraries that let that code call AWS services directly. AWS Step Functions is a conductor that runs several steps in order, remembers where it is, waits, retries, and branches. This objective is about building multi-step automations that keep working when individual steps fail.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose a function creates a customer record, then charges a card, and it times out after the charge succeeds but before it reports back. The platform then retries the whole function. What could go wrong, and what would have to be true to stop the second run from doing the damage again?
lessons.teach:
A Lambda function is a piece of code that AWS runs when a trigger fires, such as a schedule or an incoming event, and you pay only for the time it runs. It has a fixed time limit, and it keeps no memory between runs unless you store state somewhere else. The AWS SDK is a language library that lets that code call AWS services, for example to request a resource or read a table. A Step Functions state machine is a workflow definition: a set of named steps, called states, with rules for what runs next. A task state calls a function or service, a wait state pauses, a choice state branches on data, and a parallel state runs branches at the same time. Step Functions records each step's output, so the workflow carries its state forward and can retry a failed task with set backoff, or route the error to a catch path.

Why this works: one long function hits its time limit and loses its place. Splitting the work into states keeps each piece short, and the workflow can pause for hours without a server sitting idle.

Worked example: onboarding a new account. State 1 is a task that calls an SDK function to request account creation and returns a request identifier. State 2 waits 60 seconds. State 3 is a task that checks the request status. A choice state sends control back to the wait while the status is pending, and forward once it reads ready. State 4 runs two baseline setups in parallel. If State 4 raises an error, a catch sends control to a cleanup state that closes the request, and the execution is marked failed for a person to review.

Common mistake: retrying a task that is not idempotent, meaning repeating it changes the outcome, such as sending a charge twice. A retry is safe only when the step can check whether its work already happened, for example by sending a stable request key with every attempt.

Consequence: a running onboarding that retries a non-idempotent step can create two accounts for the same request, and the next team has to untangle them by hand.

questions.prompt: A mail-order pharmacy runs a Step Functions workflow that generates prescription label PDFs. State 1 is a task that calls the SDK to start a PDF render job and returns a job identifier. State 2 is a wait of 45 seconds. State 3 is a task that checks the job status. A choice state loops back to the wait while the status is 'rendering' and moves forward once it reads 'done'. The team has configured State 1 to retry up to three times with a 2-second backoff, and every attempt sends the prescription batch number as a stable request key, so a retried start finds the job it already created instead of making a second one. Missing step: if State 3 still fails after its own retries are used up, the workflow must ___ .
choices: restart State 1 without the batch key so that a fresh job is guaranteed
route the error to a catch path that runs a cleanup state, then marks the execution failed so a person can review it
keep returning to the wait state until the render job finally reports done
mark the execution as succeeded so that the batch is skipped and nobody is paged
questions.why: A catch path is the route the workflow takes when a task fails after its retries, and here it hands control to a cleanup state and leaves the execution marked failed for human review, which is the behaviour the situation needs.

questions.prompt: In a Step Functions state machine, which kind of state is designed to pause the workflow for a set period before the next step runs?
choices: A parallel state, because it runs branches at the same time
A wait state, because it holds the workflow for a set time
A task state, because it calls a function or service
A choice state, because it branches on data
questions.why: A wait state is the state type that pauses the workflow, while a choice state branches, a parallel state runs branches together, and a task state performs work.

questions.prompt: A Lambda function that prints shipping labels calls a carrier API through the SDK and is wrapped in a Step Functions retry with three attempts. The carrier sometimes times out after it has already created the label, so a retry creates a second label for the same parcel. Which change fixes the failure without removing the retry?
choices: Lower the retry count to one so that a second attempt never happens
Increase the Lambda time limit so the first call never times out
Replace the retry with a catch that moves straight to a failed state
Send a stable request key taken from the parcel identifier with every attempt, so a repeated call can recognise work already done
questions.why: Because the step is not idempotent, a retry is only safe when each attempt carries a stable key the service can use to detect that the work already happened, which is the fix described for repeated charges and duplicate accounts.

questions.prompt: A team runs a data import in one Lambda function. The vendor takes about six hours to confirm each batch, and the team is considering a loop inside the function that sleeps until the confirmation arrives. Which approach does the teaching text support?
choices: Raise the Lambda memory setting so the function can stay alive for six hours
Split the work into states in a Step Functions workflow with a wait state, because one long function hits its time limit and loses its place
Keep the sleep loop, because a Lambda function keeps its memory between runs and can resume
Store nothing and rely on the function's trigger to fire again each time the vendor replies
questions.why: The text says a Lambda function has a fixed time limit and keeps no memory between runs, so a long sleep inside it fails, while a workflow with a wait state can pause for hours without a server sitting idle.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate when you would automate a multi-step account onboarding with a single Lambda function and when you would use a Step Functions workflow instead, and name one limit or tradeoff of the workflow approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would use a single function when the job is short, has one step, and finishes well inside the time limit, such as tagging one resource. Once the job has several steps, waits on something outside our control like an account becoming ready, or needs different retry rules for different steps, I would put it in a Step Functions workflow. Each step becomes its own short function or service call, and the service stores the state between them. The main tradeoff is extra moving parts: the workflow definition is another thing to version and test, and each state transition adds cost and some latency. A workflow is also only as safe as its steps. Any step that retries must still be idempotent, or a retry duplicates work. So I would keep steps small, attach a stable request key to each external call, and set explicit timeouts and catch paths.
rubricPoints: Defines a single Lambda function as suited to short, one-step work within its time limit
Explains that a Step Functions workflow keeps state between steps and handles waits, retries and branches
Names a tradeoff such as extra definition to maintain or per-transition cost and latency
Notes that retried steps must be idempotent, for example through a stable request key

suggested.rationale: A workflow state machine engine would let the learner trace states, retries and catch paths directly, which is the core skill of this objective.

lessons.plain: Configuration management means keeping the settings and installed software on your servers matching a written description of how they should be. Imagine a checklist posted on the wall that a robot checks every hour and fixes any box someone has changed. You describe the desired state once, and an automated service keeps reality close to it, instead of relying on a person remembering to log in and repair things. AWS offers several services for this. This lesson covers one older managed option, OpsWorks, and the Systems Manager feature called State Manager.
lessons.guessPrompt: A server was set up correctly last month, then someone changed a setting by hand and never reverted it. What would you want an automated system to do about it, and how often would it check?
lessons.teach:
Desired state is the configuration you want a machine to have, written down in a form software can check. Drift is what happens when reality moves away from that description, usually because someone edited a file or stopped a service by hand. Configuration management is the practice of detecting and correcting drift automatically.

Two AWS services are central to this objective. AWS OpsWorks was a managed service for running Chef or Puppet, tools that express desired state as code (recipes or manifests) and apply it to servers grouped into stacks. AWS has been retiring OpsWorks, so check its current status in AWS's own documentation before relying on it for new work. AWS Systems Manager is a broader operations service, and State Manager is its feature for associations. An association pairs a document (a stored definition of steps or desired settings), a set of targets (instances selected by tag or ID), and a schedule. On each run, State Manager applies the document to each target and records whether that target is compliant.

Why it works: the document is written to be idempotent, meaning that running it on a machine already in the right state changes nothing. That makes repeated runs safe, so drift is corrected at the next scheduled run rather than whenever someone happens to notice.

Worked example. An association installs a monitoring agent and ensures its service is running. It targets all instances tagged env=prod and runs every 30 minutes. Step 1: at 10:00 the run finds the agent present and running, so the instance is compliant. Step 2: at 10:12 an engineer stops the agent while debugging. Step 3: at 10:30 the association runs, finds the service stopped, starts it, and reports compliant again. The change was reverted within one interval.

Common mistake: assuming an association is a one-time install. It repeats indefinitely, so a manual change that should persist will be undone. The correct fix is to change the desired state in the document, not on the machine.

Consequence: in a running fleet, hand edits are silently reverted at the next run. That can surprise people who fixed something live, and it can cause an incident if the document itself is wrong, because the wrong state is pushed everywhere on schedule.

questions.prompt: A payments team uses a State Manager association that targets all instances tagged team=payments and runs every 15 minutes, at :00, :15, :30 and :45 past the hour. Its document sets log rotation to daily. Step 1: at 09:05 a new payments instance launches, and no run has happened on it yet. Step 2: at 09:15 the association runs, applies the daily setting, and the instance reports compliant. Step 3: at 09:20 an engineer changes that instance's log rotation to weekly by hand. Step 4 is missing. Which outcome is correct at the next run, 09:30?
choices: It reports the instance noncompliant and waits for an engineer to approve the change before doing anything.
It runs the document once more and then removes the association from the instance.
It leaves the weekly setting in place, because the instance was already reported compliant at 09:15.
It finds the weekly setting differs from the document, resets it to daily, and reports compliant.
questions.why: Each scheduled run compares the machine with the document and reapplies the desired state, so the hand edit is reverted at 09:30 and the instance reports compliant again.

questions.prompt: In AWS Systems Manager State Manager, what is an association?
choices: A record of which software packages an operator installed on each server by hand.
A tag placed on instances so that people can group them in reports.
A one-time command sent to a single instance to run immediately.
A pairing of a document, a set of targets, and a schedule that repeats on each run.
questions.why: An association combines the stored document, the chosen targets and a schedule, and it keeps applying the document on each scheduled run.

questions.prompt: A State Manager document is supposed to ensure a config file contains the line retention=30. Instead of checking whether the line exists, it appends the line on every run. After four scheduled runs with no manual changes, what is the most likely state of the file?
choices: The association stops after the first change, so the file has only the original line.
The file is restored from backup on each run, so it contains no copies of the line.
The file contains one copy of the line, because State Manager removes duplicate lines automatically.
The file contains four copies of the line, because the document is not idempotent.
questions.why: A step that always adds content without checking first is not idempotent, so repeated runs keep changing a machine that is already correct.

questions.prompt: An engineer fixes a library version directly on one production server, and the next scheduled association run puts the old version back. Which change makes the new version persist across the fleet?
choices: Add that one server to an exclusion list so the association skips it.
Stop the association for a week so the server keeps the engineer's fix.
Remove the env=prod tag from the server so it is no longer targeted.
Update the desired version in the document so the next run applies it to every target.
questions.why: The desired state lives in the document, so a lasting change must be made there, since a hand edit on the machine is reverted at the next run.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how State Manager keeps a fleet in its desired state, and name one limit or risk of relying on it.
lessons.modelAnswer: State Manager is a scheduled desired-state enforcer. You create an association that ties a document, which describes the settings or software we want, to a group of instances picked by tag. On each run it checks each target, applies the document, and reports compliance per instance, so anything that drifted gets corrected. The useful property is that the document is idempotent, so repeated runs are safe. The limit is that it only corrects what the document describes. If a setting is not in the document, drift there goes unnoticed. A bad document is also pushed to every target on schedule. It depends on the agent being installed and the instance being reachable; an offline instance shows as noncompliant rather than fixed. So I would keep the document in version control, test it on a small tagged group first, and check compliance reports after each change.
rubricPoints: Desired state is a written description that the system checks and corrects on a schedule.
State Manager pairs a document, targets and a schedule through an association.
Documents must be idempotent so repeated runs are safe.
Limit: only settings in the document are enforced, so unlisted drift goes unnoticed.
Risk: a faulty document is applied to every target on schedule, so test on a small group first.

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through an exam-style situation about drift, schedules and compliance adds the most here, and no listed mission or planned engine covers this objective directly.

lessons.plain: Software compliance means every server in a fleet has the approved updates and settings it is supposed to have, and you can prove it. AWS Systems Manager is a service that lets you manage many machines from one place, without logging into each one. Managed nodes are the machines it can manage. For compliance, you define what correct looks like, such as which security patches must be installed or which software must be present. Systems Manager then checks each machine against that definition, reports the ones that have drifted, and can apply the fix on a schedule. The core habit is to write the standard down, measure against it continuously, and fix the gaps by machine rather than by hand.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose 200 servers should all have the same security patch installed, and a check finds that 12 of them are missing it. What would you want a tool to do, and what would you need to tell it first?
lessons.teach:
A managed node is any machine, virtual or on-premises, that runs the Systems Manager agent (a small program that reports back to the service) and has permission to talk to Systems Manager. Compliance here means a machine matches a written standard. A patch baseline is a set of rules that says which patches are approved for installation and how urgent they are. A State Manager association is a stored instruction that says which task should run on which machines, on what schedule, and what state they should end up in. Compliance status is the result each machine gets for a scan or association: compliant or non-compliant.

Why it works: there are two separate jobs. A scan asks each node what it currently has and compares that with the standard. Scanning only reads, so it is safe to repeat often. An install or apply step changes the machine, and it usually runs inside a maintenance window, a planned time slot. Separating checking from changing lets you see drift before you decide how to fix it.

Worked example: a baseline approves a critical security patch with a seven-day deadline. Step 1, a scan runs nightly across 200 nodes. Step 2, 188 report the patch present, so they are compliant. Step 3, 12 report it missing, so they are non-compliant. Step 4, an install task runs in the Sunday window against those 12. Step 5, the next scan shows all 200 compliant.

Common mistake: treating the scan as the fix. A non-compliant report changes nothing by itself; without an install task or association, the gap stays open.

Consequence: a missing patch on a serving node can remain unseen for weeks if nobody reads the report, and an install run during business hours can cause the restart outage it was meant to prevent. Compliance is only as good as the schedule and the attention behind it.

questions.prompt: A regional clinic network runs 64 managed nodes. Its patch baseline approves a high-severity browser update with a 14-day deadline. Step 1: a scan runs at 02:00 across all 64 nodes. Step 2: 51 nodes report the update present and are compliant, while 13 report it missing and are non-compliant. Step 3 is left blank for you to fill in. Step 4: the next scan shows all 64 nodes compliant. Which action belongs in Step 3?
choices: Run the same scan again straight away to confirm the 13 gaps
Run an install task on the 13 nodes inside a maintenance window
Change the baseline so the browser update is no longer approved
Mark the 13 nodes compliant in the report so the dashboard looks clean
questions.why: Only an install step changes the machines; a scan just reads and reports, so the 13 gaps close only when an install runs in a planned window.

questions.prompt: Which description best fits a State Manager association?
choices: A stored instruction naming a task, its machines, and its timing
A small agent program installed on each machine
A list of approved patches ranked by urgency
A written record of each machine's compliant or non-compliant result
questions.why: A State Manager association is a stored instruction that says which task runs on which machines, on what schedule, and what state they should end up in.

questions.prompt: A team scans 35 nodes on Tuesday morning and 9 report non-compliant against their baseline. Which statement is accurate?
choices: The baseline has been removed from those nine machines
The 9 machines lack an approved patch; no install has run yet
The scan patched those nine machines during its run
The other 26 machines will become non-compliant by Friday
questions.why: A scan only compares what each node has against the standard, so the 9 non-compliant nodes are missing an approved patch and remain unchanged until an install step runs.

questions.prompt: An engineer reads a nightly report showing 6 non-compliant nodes and concludes the patches will be installed automatically because the scan runs every night. What is the flaw?
choices: Nightly scans cannot report non-compliance, so the report must be wrong
The engineer should wait for the baseline deadline before reading the report
The agent installs patches only when a node reboots during business hours
A scan only reads; with no install task, the gap stays open
questions.why: Scanning only reads the machine's state, so the gap is closed only by a separate install step such as a task or association, which the engineer has not confirmed exists.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how Systems Manager keeps a fleet patched and in line with its settings, and name one limit or tradeoff of relying on it.
lessons.modelAnswer: I'd describe it as a loop. We write down the standard: a patch baseline says which patches are approved and how urgent they are, and State Manager associations say which tasks should run on which machines. The service then scans each managed node and marks it compliant or non-compliant against that standard. Scanning is read-only, so we can run it often. Fixing is a separate, deliberate step: an install task runs inside a maintenance window, so restarts happen when we expect them. The limit is that a node only shows up if it is a managed node with a working agent and permission to talk to the service. A machine that is offline or unregistered simply doesn't appear in the report, so it can look compliant by absence. Watching for nodes that stop reporting is part of the job.
rubricPoints: Defines the standard via a patch baseline or association, then compares machines against it
Separates the read-only scan from the change step run in a maintenance window
Notes that a non-compliant result alone does not fix anything
Names a limit such as unmanaged or silent nodes appearing compliant by absence

suggested.rationale: This objective is mostly service facts and console behaviour (baselines, associations, compliance reports), which the read modality covers better than any current mission or planned engine.

lessons.plain: A multi-AZ or multi-Region design means keeping copies of your system in more than one physical location, so that when one location fails, the rest keeps serving users. Think of a shop with branches in several neighborhoods: if one branch floods, customers still get served elsewhere, but only if each branch has enough staff to absorb the extra customers. The idea covers both the servers that run your code and the storage that holds your data. The hard part is not placing copies in two places; it is making sure the surviving copies have enough capacity and can take over quickly, and proving that by testing.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your web app runs on 4 servers split evenly across two data centers, and at peak it needs 3 servers' worth of capacity. If one data center goes offline, will users notice? Why or why not?
lessons.teach:
An Availability Zone (AZ) is one or more separate data centers inside a Region, which is a geographic area such as a country or metro area. Each AZ has its own power and networking, so a failure in one is usually contained. Multi-AZ means running copies of your workload in at least two AZs. Multi-Region means doing the same across two Regions, which protects against losing an entire area but adds distance, latency, and the cost of copying data across it. At the compute layer, you spread instances or containers across AZs, use an auto scaling group to keep a desired count in each, and use a load balancer that sends traffic only to healthy targets. At the data layer, a managed database can keep a synchronous standby in another AZ that takes over during failure, while cross-Region copies are usually asynchronous, so the newest writes can be lost in a regional failover.

Worked example: peak traffic needs 3 instances of capacity. Option A runs 2 instances in each of 2 AZs, for a total of 4. Step 1: count the capacity per AZ, which is 2 each. Step 2: remove one AZ, leaving 2 instances. Step 3: compare 2 with the peak of 3. The result is a shortfall, so users see errors until replacements launch. Option B runs 3 instances per AZ, for 6 total. Losing one AZ leaves 3, which meets peak.

Common mistake: treating a standby or a second AZ as proof of resilience without testing it. The consequence in a running system is that the first real outage exposes missing capacity, health checks that never removed a dead target, or a standby that was never promoted. Failover has to be rehearsed on purpose, and the surviving capacity has to be sized for peak, not for average load.

questions.prompt: A team runs a stateless order API. Each of two Availability Zones (AZs, which are separate data centers inside one Region) runs 5 instances, so 10 in total. Peak traffic needs 6 instances. Complete the capacity check. Step 1: each AZ supplies 5 instances. Step 2: [missing]. Step 3: compare the surviving count with the peak of 6. Which step 2 completes the check?
choices: Add both AZ counts together to get 10 and compare that with 6
Double the peak to 12 so there is headroom for a second failure
Remove one AZ from the count, leaving 5 instances that still serve traffic
Confirm the load balancer health checks pass in both AZs before counting
questions.why: Losing one AZ removes its 5 instances, so the 5 surviving instances are the figure to compare with peak demand.

questions.prompt: Which description best matches a multi-Region deployment, as the term is used for resilience?
choices: Keeping a synchronous standby database in a second Region so that no writes are ever lost
Running the same workload in two Regions, which protects against losing a whole geographic area at the cost of added latency and cross-Region data copying
Using one large instance in a single AZ with automatic restarts for recovery
Running the same workload in two AZs of one Region, which protects against a single data center failure
questions.why: A multi-Region deployment copies the workload across two geographic Regions, trading latency and copy cost for protection against losing an entire area.

questions.prompt: A payments service uses a managed database with a synchronous standby in a second AZ of its primary Region, and an asynchronous copy in a second Region. The whole primary Region becomes unavailable and the team fails over to the Region-level copy. Which data is at risk of being missing?
choices: Nothing, because the standby in the second AZ received every write synchronously
The newest writes that had not yet reached the cross-Region copy when the Region failed
Every write made during the most recent AZ failover, because the standby took over at that time
Only records older than the last nightly backup
questions.why: Cross-Region copies are asynchronous, so writes committed in the primary but not yet copied can be lost, while the same-Region standby is also unavailable during a Region-wide failure.

questions.prompt: A team says its service is resilient because it runs 6 instances, 3 in each of 2 AZs. Peak traffic needs 5 instances. The team assumes a single AZ outage is fine because the total is above peak. What is the most accurate assessment?
choices: Inadequate, because one AZ outage leaves 3 instances, below the peak of 5, so users will see errors until replacements launch
Adequate, because the load balancer will spread the traffic across the one AZ that remains without any further action
Inadequate, because two AZs are never enough and a second Region is required for any capacity
Adequate, because 6 is greater than 5 so the total capacity covers peak
questions.why: Capacity that survives an AZ loss must be sized for peak on its own, and here 3 surviving instances fall short of 5 regardless of how many instances existed in total.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between being spread across two Availability Zones and being able to survive losing one of them. Name one limit or tradeoff of a multi-Region design compared with multi-AZ.
lessons.modelAnswer: Being spread across two AZs means copies of the app and its data exist in two separate data center groups, so one site failing does not take everything down. Surviving the loss is different: the remaining copies must have enough capacity for real peak load and must be detected as healthy by the load balancer. For example, two AZs with two instances each is not enough if peak needs three, because losing one AZ leaves a shortfall. A tradeoff of multi-Region is that data copied across Regions is usually asynchronous, so the newest writes may be lost during a regional failover, and the extra distance adds latency and cost. Multi-AZ is usually the default for availability; multi-Region is a deliberate choice when the business accepts those costs to survive an entire area failing.
rubricPoints: Distinguishes spreading copies across AZs from having enough surviving capacity to absorb a loss
Explains that surviving capacity must be sized for peak load, not average load
Names a tradeoff of multi-Region such as asynchronous replication, latency, or cost
Notes that failover must be tested rather than assumed

suggested.rationale: A planned disaster-recovery planner would have the learner place compute and data copies across AZs or Regions and check whether surviving capacity meets a stated peak and recovery target.

lessons.plain: Every system carries a promise about how much it should be up and how fast it must recover when something breaks. Before you design anything, you have to turn a sentence like the dispatch board must never go dark into numbers an engineer can build against: how much downtime is allowed in a month, how much recent data we can afford to lose, and how long we can take to get back running. Those numbers, not gut feeling, decide whether one data centre zone is enough or whether you need a second region far away. Think of a restaurant asking how long a customer can wait and how many orders can be lost in a fire, then choosing its kitchen setup to match.
lessons.guessPrompt: A manager says the vehicle dispatch board must be available 99.9 percent of the time and must never lose more than five minutes of updates. Before reading on, what would you ask the manager first, and why would the answer change your design?
lessons.teach: Start with the business words. A service level agreement, or SLA, is a promise made to a customer, often with a penalty if it is broken. A service level objective, or SLO, is the internal target an engineering team sets to keep that promise. A service level indicator, or SLI, is the measurement you use to check it, such as the share of requests that succeeded. Two recovery terms matter most. The recovery time objective, or RTO, is the longest acceptable time to restore service after a failure. The recovery point objective, or RPO, is the longest acceptable window of data loss, measured as time since the last safe copy. Why does this translation work? Because an availability percentage becomes a fixed budget of downtime, and an RPO tells you how often data must be copied. A failed availability zone, which is an isolated data centre inside one region, is a fault you can absorb with a second zone. A whole region going dark is rarer but costs far more to survive, so it should only be bought when the numbers demand it. Worked example: the business wants 99.95 percent monthly availability on a 30-day month. That month has 43,200 minutes, and 0.05 percent of that is 21.6 minutes of allowed downtime. A zone failover that takes 30 minutes spends the budget and breaks the promise, so the design needs faster failover. Common mistake: treating a vendor's published availability as your system's availability. If your service depends on two components that are each 99.9 percent available and both must work, the chain is closer to 99.8 percent. Consequence in a running system: an RPO of five minutes cannot be met by a nightly backup, and a backup that has never been restored has an unknown RTO. The requirement, not the architecture, sets the target, and every target must be tested.

questions.prompt: A ticketing service promises 99.9 percent availability in a 31-day month. Step 1: 31 days is 44,640 minutes. Step 2: 0.1 percent of 44,640 is 44.64 minutes of allowed downtime. Step 3: one zone failover is measured at 25 minutes, so a single failover fits inside the budget. Step 4 is missing: the team wants to know whether a month with two such failovers still keeps the promise. Which completion gives the correct step 4?
choices: Compare 25 minutes against 44,640 minutes, which passes easily, so two failovers are fine.
Ignore failover time, since only the number of zones matters for availability.
Divide 44.64 by 2 and conclude each failover must take under 44.64 minutes, so both pass.
Add the two failovers to get 50 minutes and compare with 44.64; 50 is larger, so the promise breaks.
questions.why: Downtime from both failovers adds together to 50 minutes, which exceeds the 44.64-minute monthly budget, so the promise is broken.

questions.prompt: A payments API promises 99.99 percent availability in a 30-day month. How many minutes of downtime does that allow?
choices: 0.432 minutes
21.6 minutes
4.32 minutes
43.2 minutes
questions.why: A 30-day month has 43,200 minutes, and 0.01 percent of that is 4.32 minutes.

questions.prompt: A customer request needs three components to all work at once: a load balancer at 99.95 percent availability, an application server at 99.9 percent, and a database at 99.9 percent. Which is the best estimate of the combined availability of the chain?
choices: About 99.95 percent
About 99.9 percent
About 99.99 percent
About 99.75 percent
questions.why: When every component in a chain must work, their unavailabilities add up roughly (0.05 + 0.1 + 0.1 = 0.25 percent), giving about 99.75 percent, which is lower than any single component.

questions.prompt: A logging platform must recover data with an RPO of 15 minutes. Its only protection is a full copy taken once every 24 hours. Which conclusion is correct?
choices: It passes, because restore time is what gets measured against the RPO.
It fails: the worst-case data loss is close to 24 hours, so copies must be taken at least every 15 minutes or replicated continuously.
It passes if the daily copy is compressed, because compression shortens the loss window.
It fails only if the restore itself takes longer than 15 minutes.
questions.why: The RPO measures the time since the last safe copy, so a daily copy can leave up to about 24 hours of data unprotected, far beyond 15 minutes.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would turn a business statement like 99.95 percent availability and five minutes of acceptable data loss into technical resiliency needs. Name one limit or tradeoff of the approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would first separate the promise from the measurement. A 99.95 percent monthly target leaves about 21.6 minutes of downtime in a 30-day month, so that is the budget the whole design has to fit inside. Then I would map it to RTO and RPO. Five minutes of acceptable data loss means replication must be continuous, not a nightly backup. The downtime budget decides whether a second availability zone with automatic failover is enough. The main tradeoff is cost and complexity: a second region might meet a stricter target, but it adds money and operational work, and I would only recommend it if the business accepts that cost. I would also flag that the number is only as good as the test that proves it.
rubricPoints: Converts an availability percentage into a concrete downtime budget for a stated period
Distinguishes RTO (time to recover) from RPO (data loss window) and maps each to a design choice
Notes that a component chain lowers the combined availability below each part
Names a tradeoff such as cost or complexity of multi-region versus multi-zone, and states that targets must be tested

suggested.rationale: The core skill is reasoning from business wording to numbers and explaining the tradeoff back, which no listed mission or planned engine directly drills.

lessons.plain: A stateful service is anything that remembers things, such as a database, a cache, or a file store. If it fails, its memory is lost unless a copy exists somewhere else. Replication means keeping one or more copies of that memory in other places and updating them continuously. Failover means that when the main copy becomes unavailable, traffic is switched to a copy so the system keeps working. The engineering questions are how fresh the copy must be and how quickly the switch must happen. Those two answers decide which replication and failover method you choose, and each choice costs money, write speed, or both.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your team runs a database with one copy in the same data centre area. Someone says we are resilient because a copy exists. What single question would you ask before agreeing?
lessons.teach:
Definitions. A stateful service keeps data that must survive restarts, such as a relational database, a key-value store, or a message log. A Region is a geographic area with several Availability Zones (AZs), which are separate data centres with independent power and networking. Replication copies every change from a primary copy to one or more replicas. Synchronous replication waits until the replica confirms a write before the primary reports success, so no acknowledged write is lost, but each write is slower. Asynchronous replication reports success immediately and ships the change in the background, so writes are fast but a replica can trail behind by some delay, called replication lag. Failover means promoting a replica to become the new primary and pointing clients at it. Recovery point objective (RPO) is how much recent data you can afford to lose, measured as time. Recovery time objective (RTO) is how long the service may be unavailable.
