DNS sends the Seoul user to Frankfurt at once, because distance matters more than health checks.
The reservation is copied back from Frankfurt to Tokyo before any failover, so Tokyo ends up holding the newest data.
questions.why: Step 4 is a read in the secondary Region, and because the reservation is still in transit, that read can return a value several seconds out of date.

questions.prompt: A team says it runs its workload in two Regions for resilience. Which statement best describes what a second Region adds that a second Availability Zone inside the same Region does not?
choices: It makes every write faster because writes are split across Availability Zones.
It stores a copy in the same building so that it can be restored quickly.
It gives a separate failure boundary at Region level, so a whole-Region outage does not stop the workload.
It removes the need for health checks, since traffic always goes to the nearest location.
questions.why: A Region is the largest failure boundary a team can add, so a second Region protects against an outage that takes down a whole Region, which a second Availability Zone in the same Region does not.

questions.prompt: A team copies its order database to a second Region but never tests restoring or serving from that copy. The copy depends on an encryption key that exists only in the primary Region. The primary Region then degrades. What is the most likely result?
choices: The second Region is a working backup, and the only risk is a few minutes of extra latency.
Replication lag disappears, so no data is missing from the copy.
The copy may be unusable when it is needed, because it depends on a resource that fails along with the primary Region.
The copy fails over automatically, because replicas always recover without outside help.
questions.why: A copy that has never been tested, or that relies on something existing only in the failed Region, may not work during an actual failover, which is the common mistake the teaching text warns about.

questions.prompt: A secondary Region runs about 12 seconds behind its primary because of replication lag. The primary Region fails suddenly and traffic moves to the secondary. Which recovery point should the team promise?
choices: Zero data loss, because the health check confirmed that every write reached the secondary.
About 12 hours, because failover always requires rebuilding the database from a backup.
Only writes from the last second, because replication is instant after the first copy.
Roughly the last 12 seconds of writes may be lost, so the promised recovery point should be about 12 seconds.
questions.why: The recovery point must match how far behind the replica runs, so writes not yet replicated during those roughly 12 seconds are at risk of being lost in a sudden failover.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why running a workload in two Regions does not by itself make it resilient, and name one trade-off of keeping data replicated between those Regions.
lessons.modelAnswer: Two Regions only help if traffic can actually move to the surviving one and the data is there when it does. If the second Region has never been tested, or depends on something that exists only in the first, it fails at the moment it is needed. Data is the main issue. Writes are copied between Regions with a delay, so the replica can lag behind the primary. The trade-off is that the stronger you make consistency across Regions, the slower each write becomes for users far from the primary; the looser you make it, the more recent writes can be lost during a failover. So before we promise a recovery point, we have to measure the replication lag and test that the failover really works.
rubricPoints: A second Region protects against a whole-Region failure, but only if traffic can be shifted and the copy is tested.
Stateless compute is easy to replicate; stateful data needs an explicit replication method.
Replication lag means a replica can return slightly old data and failover can lose recent writes.
Stronger cross-Region consistency adds write latency, so the trade-off must be chosen per data type.

suggested.rationale: A disaster-recovery planner would let the learner model failover paths and recovery points across Regions, which this objective needs practice with.

lessons.plain: Disaster recovery (DR) is the plan for getting a system working again after a serious failure, such as a whole site going offline or a bad change destroying data. Two numbers shape the plan. The recovery time objective (RTO) is how long the business can accept the service being down. The recovery point objective (RPO) is how much recent data, measured in time, the business can accept losing. DR strategies such as pilot light and warm standby describe how much of a copy of the system already runs in a second location before anything goes wrong. The more you keep running ahead of time, the faster you recover, but the more you pay while things are calm.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company copies its order database to a second city every hour. The first city fails at 10:50 and the last copy was made at 10:00. How much recent order data could be lost, and what would decide how quickly the service comes back?
lessons.teach:
Recovery time objective (RTO) is the longest a service may stay down after a disaster before the outage becomes unacceptable to the business. Recovery point objective (RPO) is the longest span of recent data the business can afford to lose, counted back from the moment of failure. Both are business targets, and the engineering job is to choose a strategy that meets them. A pilot light keeps only the minimum running in the recovery Region (a separate geographic area with its own data centres): the core database is replicated continuously, while the application servers are defined but switched off. A warm standby keeps a scaled-down but fully working copy of the whole stack running, ready to take traffic once it is scaled up. Why it works: the data replication sets the RPO, because anything not yet copied is lost. Server readiness and the switch of traffic (for example, moving the DNS record, which is the naming entry that points a web address at servers) set the RTO, because they take time after the failure is declared.

Worked example. Target: RPO 5 minutes, RTO 60 minutes. Pilot light design: the database replicates continuously, so the last copied write is about 2 minutes before the failure, which meets the RPO. Then the team starts and configures servers (about 35 minutes), runs health checks (about 10 minutes), and moves DNS to the recovery Region (about 10 minutes). Total is about 55 minutes, which meets the RTO with little margin. A warm standby starts from a running stack, so it might finish in about 15 minutes, but it costs more to keep that capacity running.

Common mistake: sizing the RTO from the database alone and forgetting that starting servers, deploying the latest release, and waiting for DNS changes to take effect all take time. Another mistake is assuming the standby works because it was built once and never tested.

Consequence: if a replication job silently stopped three days ago, the real RPO is three days, and you only learn this during the outage. Scheduled failover tests are how you find this out first.

RTO and RPO are the two numbers every DR design must be checked against.

questions.prompt: A dental practice runs its booking system on a pilot light design in a recovery Region. Its targets are RPO 10 minutes and RTO 30 minutes. Replication copies the database every 4 minutes, so the worst-case data loss is about 4 minutes, which meets the RPO. Starting and configuring the servers takes 12 minutes, and health checks take 5 minutes. The one step still unknown is the DNS switch to the recovery Region, whose duration has not been measured. The team wants the largest DNS switch time that still meets the 30-minute RTO. What is that largest value?
choices: 8 minutes
13 minutes
18 minutes
30 minutes
questions.why: The RTO covers every step after the failure is declared, so the DNS time is the RTO minus server start (12) and health checks (5), which is 13 minutes.

questions.prompt: A payroll company says its recovery point objective is 15 minutes. Which description matches that target?
choices: The number of servers kept running in the recovery Region at all times
The longest span of recent data the company can afford to lose, counted back from the failure
The time it takes to switch DNS to the recovery site after a failure is declared
The longest time the service may be offline after a disaster before the business is harmed
questions.why: RPO is a business limit on how much recent data may be lost, measured back from the moment of failure, and not a measure of downtime or capacity.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm must be back within 15 minutes of a disaster. Its pilot light design keeps the database replicating continuously, but the switched-off servers take 20 minutes to start and configure after the failure is declared. What is the most accurate conclusion?
choices: The design misses the target because server start-up sets the recovery time, not the database
The design meets the target if the database replication interval is shortened
The design meets the target because the database replicates continuously
The design meets the target because DNS changes are usually instant
questions.why: Continuous replication sets the RPO, while server readiness and traffic switching set the RTO, so a 20-minute start-up alone breaks a 15-minute RTO regardless of replication speed.

questions.prompt: A team's replication setting reads continuous, but the replication job silently stopped four days ago and nobody noticed. If a disaster happens today, what is the real data-loss exposure?
choices: Zero, because the setting still reads continuous
About four days of data, the time since the last successfully copied write
Only the time needed to start the servers, which is the RTO
Only the 15 minutes since the last health check
questions.why: Data loss is counted from the last write that actually reached the recovery site, so a silently stopped job means the real RPO is the four days since then.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a pilot light differs from a warm standby, and how each one is judged against RTO and RPO. Name one limit or tradeoff of each.
lessons.modelAnswer: A pilot light keeps only the data layer running in the recovery Region. The database is replicated continuously, so RPO is driven by how far behind that replication is. The servers exist as definitions but are switched off, so after a disaster we must start them, deploy the current release, check health, and move traffic. That makes RTO longer, and the time is hard to predict unless we have rehearsed it. A warm standby runs a scaled-down copy of the full stack, so the servers are already up. Scaling up and moving traffic is faster, which gives a shorter RTO, and RPO is still set by replication. The tradeoff is cost: the standby capacity is paid for every hour even when nothing fails. A pilot light is cheaper but slower. Either one is only as good as its last failover test.
rubricPoints: RTO is the maximum acceptable downtime and RPO is the maximum acceptable data loss, both set by the business.
A pilot light keeps only the data layer replicated with compute switched off, so recovery means starting servers.
A warm standby keeps a scaled-down full stack running, so recovery is faster but costs more while idle.
Both strategies must be checked by testing failover, since untested recovery paths often fail or run slower than planned.

suggested.rationale: The planned disaster-recovery planner would let the learner set RTO and RPO targets and check which strategy meets them, which is the core skill here.

lessons.plain: Testing failover means deliberately breaking part of a system that is supposed to survive failures, then checking that it recovers on its own and measuring how long that takes. Many teams build a backup copy in another data center or another geographic region and assume it will take over. Until you trigger a failure on purpose and watch, you do not know whether traffic actually moves, how long users were affected, or whether recent data was lost. It is like a fire drill: the exits exist on paper, but only the drill shows whether people can use them under pressure.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose your web app already has a standby copy running in a second data center. What two numbers would tell you the standby really works, and what could still go wrong even though the standby exists?
lessons.teach:
A failover is the switch from a failed component to a healthy standby. An Availability Zone (AZ) is an isolated data center inside one Region, a geographic area of the cloud provider. Multi-AZ designs spread copies of a workload across AZs so that one facility failing does not stop the service. Multi-Region designs repeat that idea across separate Regions. Two targets judge any drill: the recovery time objective (RTO), the longest outage the business accepts, and the recovery point objective (RPO), the most recent data you can afford to lose. Replica lag, how far a standby database trails the primary, is a common measure of RPO.

Why testing matters: a standby is only proven when traffic actually moves to it. Failover is a chain. Health checks must notice the failure, the load balancer or DNS must stop sending traffic to the dead target, a standby database must be promoted, and the application must reconnect. Each link adds delay. DNS time-to-live (TTL), the period resolvers cache an answer, can keep users pointed at the failed Region long after you changed the record.

Worked example: a load balancer spreads traffic over instances in two AZs. In a planned drill at 10:00:00 you stop the instances in AZ-a. Health checks run every 30 seconds and need two failures, so the balancer stops sending traffic to them around 10:01:00. Measured traffic recovery is about 60 seconds. Replica lag was 2 seconds just before the drill, so the database RPO is about 2 seconds of writes. Compare 60 seconds with the RTO and 2 seconds with the RPO. If either target is missed, that is a finding to fix, not a pass.

Common mistake: treating a configured standby as a tested one, or running one drill and never repeating it. Configuration drifts; a standby that worked last year may lack a new secret or permission.

Consequence: in a real outage, the team finds the standby missing a setting, DNS caches still holding the old answer, and downtime far past the RTO. A failover test is a measured experiment with an expected result, a stop condition, and a rollback plan.

questions.prompt: A ticketing service runs behind a load balancer spread across AZ-b and AZ-c, where AZ is an Availability Zone, an isolated data center inside one Region. The team runs a drill: at 09:15:00 they stop every instance in AZ-b. Health checks run every 10 seconds and need three consecutive failures, so the balancer stops sending traffic to the dead instances by about 09:15:30. Measured traffic recovery is 44 seconds after the stop, so traffic is back at 09:15:44. Replica lag, how far the standby database trails the primary, was 6 seconds just before the drill. The targets are an RTO of 60 seconds and an RPO of 10 seconds. The one step not yet written is the final check of the drill against those two targets. Which completion of the drill is correct?
choices: Only the RTO matters for a drill, because the RPO describes the longest outage the business accepts, so the 6-second lag can be ignored.
Both targets are met: 44 seconds is under the 60-second RTO, and 6 seconds of possible lost writes is under the 10-second RPO, so the drill passes.
The RTO is missed because the 44-second recovery is longer than the 30-second detection window, so the whole drill must be rerun before any result is recorded.
The balancer stopped sending traffic at 09:15:30, which is before the RTO, so the recovery target is met and the RPO question does not apply.
questions.why: The RTO is compared with the measured 44 seconds of recovery and the RPO is compared with the 6 seconds of replica lag, and both fall within their targets, so the drill passes.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm's order-intake service must be back within 4 minutes of an outage. In resiliency terms, what does this 4-minute figure define?
choices: The most recent data the firm can afford to lose, measured as writes not yet copied to the standby.
The average response time of the service under normal daily load.
The longest outage the business accepts before the service must be running again, which is the recovery time objective.
How often the health checks are scheduled to run against each instance.
questions.why: The recovery time objective is the longest outage the business will accept, so a 4-minute figure sets that limit; the other options describe RPO, latency, or health check scheduling.

questions.prompt: A bank fails over to a second Region and the switch is finished at 12:00. At 12:40, some customers still reach the failed Region even though the DNS record was changed at 12:00. Which factor best explains this?
choices: The standby database was promoted before the application reconnected, which caused the traffic to be sent to the old Region.
The load balancer health check interval was set too short, so it reacted before the failure was real.
Resolvers may still hold the old DNS answer in cache for the record's time-to-live period, so users keep reaching the failed Region.
Replica lag was above zero when the switch happened, so the standby held stale data and rejected the requests.
questions.why: DNS time-to-live is the period resolvers cache an answer, so an old answer can keep users pointed at the failed Region after the record has been changed.

questions.prompt: A team's failover drill passed last year with a recovery time well inside its target. This year the same drill fails at the standby step, and nothing in the drill procedure has changed. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: Configuration drifts over time, so a secret or permission added since the last drill may be missing from the standby even though the drill steps are unchanged.
A drill that passed once proves the recovery time holds for every later change, so the failure must come from the test tool.
Replica lag is always zero, so the failure must have come from DNS rather than from the standby.
The drill was run too often, which wore out the standby and made it slower to accept traffic.
questions.why: A passing drill proves the standby worked at that time only, and configuration changes made since can break it without any change to the drill itself.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says our multi-Region database failover is fine because a replica already exists in another Region. In your own words, explain how you would test that failover, what you would measure, and one limit or tradeoff of running the test.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would not accept the replica as proof. I would write down the expected result first: the RTO and RPO the business needs. Then I would run a planned drill in a quiet window, with a rollback plan and a stop condition, such as error rates above an agreed level. During the drill I would timestamp each step: the failure, the moment health checks marked the primary unhealthy, the promotion of the replica, the DNS change, and the first successful writes from the application. I would also check replica lag just before the failure to estimate how much data would be lost. The main limit is that a real Region-level test can cause real user impact and cost, so we would often test with a partial failure first, then repeat the full test on a schedule so the result stays current.
rubricPoints: States that a standby counts only after a test shows traffic and writes actually moving to it.
Measures recovery time against the RTO and data loss against the RPO, using replica lag as a proxy.
Traces the failover chain: detection, traffic redirection, promotion, and application reconnection.
Names a real limit or tradeoff of testing in production, such as user impact or cost, and how to reduce it.

suggested.rationale: A planned disaster-recovery engine would let the learner set RTO and RPO targets and rehearse timed failover drills against them, which this objective needs.

lessons.plain: Cross-Region backup and recovery means keeping copies of your data and service settings in a second, geographically separate area of the cloud, so that if the main area suffers a large outage you can rebuild elsewhere. Think of keeping a spare set of house keys at a relative's home across town rather than only in your coat pocket. The real skill is deciding how often copies are made, how old the newest usable copy may be, and how quickly the service must return. Several cloud services help: one schedules and copies backups, one stores files and can replicate them to another region, and one runs the restore steps in a fixed order so recovery is repeatable.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your main region suffers a day-long outage. Your only backups are stored in that same region, taken every night. What is the risk, and what single change would reduce it?
lessons.teach:
Cross-Region backup and recovery means keeping copies of your backups in a different geographic region from the one that runs your service, so a regional failure does not destroy every copy. A region is a separate geographic area of the cloud made of several availability zones, which are isolated data centres. Two numbers guide the design. The recovery point objective (RPO) is the most data, measured in time, you can afford to lose. The recovery time objective (RTO) is how long the service may stay down before it is back. AWS Backup is a managed service that schedules backups, stores them in vaults, and can copy recovery points to a vault in another region. Amazon S3 is object storage; cross-region replication copies new objects to a bucket in another region and requires versioning on both buckets. AWS Systems Manager Automation runs ordered runbook steps, so restore actions are repeatable rather than typed by hand under pressure.

Worked example: the RPO is 4 hours. A backup plan runs every 4 hours and copies each recovery point to a second region. At 14:00 the primary region fails. The newest copy in the second region was made at 12:00, so at most 2 hours of data is lost, within the 4-hour RPO. A runbook restores from that copy in 90 minutes, within a 2-hour RTO.

Common mistake: assuming copies exist because the backup job reported success in the primary region. Copies only exist in the second region if the copy rule is configured and the target vault is reachable, and a restore must be tested to prove it works.

Consequence: if every copy lives in the failed region, recovery is impossible no matter how frequent the backups were. The copy in another region is what makes the RPO and RTO promises real.

questions.prompt: A media company keeps its photo archive in region A. AWS Backup takes a recovery point every 6 hours and copies each one to a vault in region B. Its recovery point objective (RPO, the most data it can afford to lose, measured in time) is 6 hours, and its recovery time objective (RTO, how long the service may stay down) is 3 hours. At 22:30, region A fails. Step 1: the newest copy in region B was made at 18:00. Step 2: the data at risk is 4.5 hours, which is within the 6-hour RPO. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: a Systems Manager Automation runbook restores from that copy in 100 minutes, which is within the 3-hour RTO. Which step fills the gap at Step 3?
choices: Count the recovery points still stored in region A to confirm the scheduled backups ran.
Compare the RTO against how long region A took to recover in its last maintenance window.
Shorten the backup schedule to every hour so that the RPO is met for future failures.
Confirm that the copy rule to region B exists and that a test restore from the region B copy has succeeded.
questions.why: A copy only protects you if it exists in the second region and a restore from it has been proven to work, so checking the copy rule and running a test restore fills the gap.

questions.prompt: A payments team says its RPO is 2 hours. Which statement describes what that means?
choices: Each restore job is allowed to take up to 2 hours to finish.
The service must be running again within 2 hours of a failure.
The team may lose at most about 2 hours of the most recent data when recovering.
Backups are kept for 2 hours before they are deleted.
questions.why: RPO is the maximum amount of recent data, measured in time, that can be lost, while the statement about getting service back describes RTO instead.

questions.prompt: A freight firm has an RTO of 24 hours and copies its nightly recovery points to a second region. Its primary region fails at 09:00 and the team restores from the copy in 5 hours. Which conclusion is correct?
choices: The RPO has been breached because the restore took more than 4 hours.
The RTO is breached because backups only run once a day.
The RTO is met because service returned in 5 hours, well inside the 24-hour limit.
The RPO is irrelevant because the RTO was met, so no data loss is possible.
questions.why: The 5-hour restore is well within the 24-hour RTO, so the RTO is met; the other choices confuse RPO with restore duration or assume a relationship the teaching text does not describe.

questions.prompt: A retail company's AWS Backup plan reports every nightly job as successful in its primary region. No copy rule to a second region was ever configured. The primary region then becomes unavailable for a long period. What is the most accurate outcome?
choices: The restore works in about the same time as usual because the job reported success.
The team can restore quickly from the primary region's vault after a short wait.
No recovery point exists outside the failed region, so the data cannot be recovered from backups however often they were taken.
The backups are recovered automatically from the primary region once it comes back.
questions.why: Successful backup jobs in the primary region do not create copies elsewhere, so without a copy rule, a regional failure can destroy every recovery point.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why a backup stored in the same region is not enough for disaster recovery, and name one limit or tradeoff of copying backups to another region.
lessons.modelAnswer: A backup in the same region protects against losing a single resource, such as a deleted table, but not against losing the whole region, because the copy fails with the original. To survive a regional outage, we copy recovery points to a vault or bucket in a second region. The tradeoff is cost and time: cross-region copies add storage charges, data transfer charges, and a delay, so the newest copy in the second region is always somewhat behind the primary. That delay sets the real RPO, so we must check it against the business's allowed data loss. We also have to test restores in the second region, because a copy that was never restored may still be unusable.
rubricPoints: A same-region backup shares the failure of its source, so a regional outage can destroy both.
A cross-region copy must exist and be reachable, and it should be checked, not assumed.
The copy schedule and copy delay determine the achievable RPO.
Restores should be tested and automated to meet the RTO.

suggested.rationale: Setting RPO and RTO targets and checking copy schedules against them is a planning exercise the planned disaster-recovery planner engine would drive, and no listed mission covers it yet.

lessons.plain: A load balancer is a traffic director that sits in front of several copies of the same service and hands each incoming request to one of them. If one copy breaks, the director should stop sending it work so users keep getting answers from the healthy copies. The skill here is teaching the director how to tell a broken copy from a working one, and how quickly to react. Think of a shop with several cashiers and a supervisor who waves customers away from any cashier who has stopped responding.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose a load balancer has three identical servers behind it and one of them crashes at 2 a.m. Without anyone touching the balancer, what should happen to requests that arrive in the next minute, and how would the balancer know the server is gone?
lessons.teach: A backend is the server or group of servers that actually does the work behind a load balancer. Each server registered with the balancer is called a target. A group of targets that the balancer treats as one pool is called a target group. To decide whether a target is alive, the balancer runs a health check: it sends a small test request on a fixed schedule and judges the reply. Four settings control this. The interval is the time between checks. The timeout is how long to wait for a reply. The unhealthy threshold is how many failed checks in a row mark a target as broken. The healthy threshold is how many passing checks in a row bring a broken target back into service. Once a target is marked unhealthy, the balancer stops sending it new requests, and the remaining targets absorb the load. Worked example: the interval is 10 seconds and the unhealthy threshold is 2. A server dies just after a passing check at time 0. The check at 10 seconds fails, the check at 20 seconds fails, and the server is marked unhealthy at about 20 seconds. Requests sent in those 20 seconds may still reach the dead server and fail, so recovery is never instant. A common mistake is a health check that only confirms the web process answers while ignoring the application and its database, so traffic keeps flowing to servers that cannot do real work. The opposite mistake is a check that depends on a shared database; a brief database blip then marks every target unhealthy at once. Some balancers, when every target looks unhealthy, fall back to sending traffic to all of them, so you must confirm what yours does. Recovery speed is a direct product of these four numbers, and they should be chosen on purpose, not left at defaults.

questions.prompt: A payments API team runs health checks every 30 seconds with a healthy threshold of 3. They repair a broken target just after a failing check at time 100 seconds. Step 1: the check at 130 seconds passes. Step 2: the check at 160 seconds passes. Step 3: the target is returned to service when the next check, at 190 seconds, passes. Why 190 seconds?
choices: Because 190 seconds is the third consecutive pass, which meets the healthy threshold of 3
Because 130 seconds is the first pass and the target counts as recovered after one good reply
Because 220 seconds is one full interval after the third pass, and the balancer waits that extra interval before trusting it
Because 160 seconds is when the second pass happens, and two passes are enough once a target has been broken
questions.why: The healthy threshold counts consecutive passing checks, so the third pass in a row at 190 seconds is the moment the target returns to service.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what does the unhealthy threshold control in a load balancer's health check?
choices: How many failed checks in a row it takes to mark a target as unhealthy
How many passing checks in a row a broken target needs before it is returned to service, which is a separate setting from the one asked about here
The time between one health check and the next one
How long the balancer waits for a reply before it gives up on a single check
questions.why: The unhealthy threshold is the count of consecutive failed checks that marks a target broken; the other options describe the interval, the timeout, or the healthy threshold.

questions.prompt: A web application's health check only requests a small static page from each web server. The order database behind the servers goes down, and the static page still loads. What happens to customer orders?
choices: Nothing changes, since the static page still answers and the check passes
The balancer removes each web server from the pool on the first failed customer request
The balancer keeps sending orders to targets that cannot finish them, because the check never tests the database
The balancer marks every target unhealthy at once, because the database is shared
questions.why: A check that only confirms the web process answers cannot detect a failed database, so unhealthy-in-practice servers stay in the pool and keep receiving work.

questions.prompt: A matchmaking service's health check runs every 20 seconds with an unhealthy threshold of 2. A target crashes just after a passing check at time 0. Roughly when does the balancer stop sending it new requests?
choices: About 40 seconds after the failure, when the second consecutive check at 40 seconds fails
About 60 seconds after the failure, because the timeout adds to the wait for each check
About 20 seconds after the failure, when the first check fails
Immediately at 0 seconds, because the last check passed
questions.why: With a 20-second interval and a threshold of 2, the checks at 20 and 40 seconds both fail, so the target is marked unhealthy at about 40 seconds, and requests may still reach it until then.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says our load balancer handles backend failure, so we do not need to worry about it. Explain to them in your own words how recovery actually works, and name one limit or tradeoff of the setting you would tune first.
lessons.modelAnswer: The balancer does not know a server is dead by magic. It sends a health check on a schedule, and after a set number of consecutive failures it marks that target unhealthy and stops routing to it. Until that happens, some requests still reach the broken server and fail, so there is a detection window. Recovery is therefore a function of the check interval, the timeout, and the unhealthy threshold. The setting I would tune first is the unhealthy threshold. A low value removes servers quickly but can eject healthy servers after one slow reply or a brief network hiccup, which shrinks capacity for no reason. A high value avoids that noise but lengthens the window in which users see errors. I would also check what the health-check path actually tests. A path that only returns a static page proves little, while a path that depends on a shared database can take every target out at once when that database blips. The balancer handles failure only as well as its health check describes it.
rubricPoints: Health checks on an interval decide which targets receive traffic, and failed checks mark a target unhealthy.
There is a detection window during which some requests still reach a failed target.
The unhealthy and healthy thresholds trade speed of recovery against false alarms.
The health-check path must test something meaningful without depending on a shared resource that can fail for everyone at once.

suggested.rationale: An exam-style scenario asking which health-check settings meet a stated recovery time best adds more than any listed mission, since none of them drills load balancer health checks directly.

lessons.plain: CloudWatch is the AWS service that stores numbers measured over time, such as how busy a server is or how many errors a load balancer returned. Each stream of numbers is called a metric. To keep thousands of streams organized, each metric sits inside a namespace, which is a container name that groups related metrics, often by the service that produced them. Dimensions are labels attached to a metric, such as the ID of one specific server, so you can tell two servers' readings apart. Resolution is how often the numbers are recorded. Knowing these four pieces tells you exactly which numbers you are looking at before you decide what to watch.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose you run ten web servers and want to see the CPU use of just one of them. What information would you need to give a monitoring system so it returns that one server's numbers and not all ten mixed together?
lessons.teach: A CloudWatch metric is a time-ordered series of data points for one measurement. Each data point has a timestamp and a value. Three parts identify a metric: the namespace, the metric name, and the set of dimensions. A namespace is a container name, such as one used for a particular AWS service or for your own application, so names from different sources do not collide. The metric name says what is measured, such as CPUUtilization. A dimension is a name and value pair that narrows the series to one resource, such as an instance ID with a specific value. Two series with the same namespace and name but different dimensions are separate metrics. Resolution is the interval at which data points are stored. Standard resolution stores one data point per minute. High-resolution metrics, which you publish yourself, can be stored every second. When you read a metric, you choose a period, the window over which points are combined, and a statistic such as Average, Sum, or Maximum. A period shorter than the stored resolution gives you nothing finer than the data you actually have. Worked example: a load balancer's 5xx error count is stored under a namespace for that service, a metric name for 5xx errors, and a dimension naming one load balancer. Each minute the service records a count. You ask for Sum over a five-minute period. CloudWatch adds the five one-minute counts and returns one value. Common mistake: querying with the namespace and name but leaving out the dimension, or using the wrong dimension value, so you see no data or a blend of several resources. Another is putting a unique value such as a user ID into a dimension, which creates a new metric for every value and multiplies cost. Consequence: an alarm pointed at a dimension set that never receives data sits in an insufficient-data state and stays quiet while the real resource fails. A metric is found by its namespace, name, and dimensions together, and its resolution sets the finest detail you can ever see.

questions.prompt: A batch team publishes a custom metric in the namespace Billing/Reconciler, with the metric name RowsRejected and the dimension Stage set to prod. They publish one count per minute. They want the total number of rejected rows across a 15-minute window. Step 1: they confirm the namespace, name, and dimension match the published series exactly. Step 2: they set the period to 900 seconds so CloudWatch combines fifteen one-minute points into one window. Step 3 is missing: which statistic should they choose so the fifteen counts are added together to give the total?
choices: Minimum
Average
Maximum
Sum
questions.why: The counts are per-minute totals that must be added across the window, and Sum is the statistic that adds the points together, while Average, Maximum, and Minimum return a mean, peak, or lowest single value instead.

questions.prompt: Two series share the namespace Checkout/Gateway and the metric name RetryCount. One series has the dimension Region set to us-east-1 and the other has Region set to eu-west-1. Are these one metric or two?
choices: One metric, because the namespace and metric name match
One metric whose dimension values are merged automatically
Two metrics, but only if their namespaces also differ
Two separate metrics, because their dimension values differ
questions.why: A metric is identified by namespace, name, and dimensions together, so differing dimension values make two separate series even when the namespace and name are the same.

questions.prompt: A team adds a dimension called RequestId to a custom metric so they can find slow requests later. Each request gets a new, unique value for RequestId. Which outcome is the most direct result of this change?
choices: The stored resolution of the metric becomes one second
Alarms on the metric stop evaluating and must be recreated
Every new request value creates a separate metric, which raises cost
The existing data points are rewritten to the new dimension
questions.why: Each unique dimension value defines a new series, so a per-request value multiplies the number of metrics and the cost, and the other options describe effects that dimensions do not have.

questions.prompt: A custom metric is published at standard resolution, so one data point is stored per minute. An engineer requests the metric with a 10-second period, expecting finer detail. What will the engineer actually see?
choices: An error response, because the period and the resolution must be identical
Ten-second data points, because the requested period determines the stored resolution
Only the one-minute data points that were stored, since a period shorter than the stored resolution gives nothing finer
One data point per hour, because CloudWatch rounds up short periods
questions.why: Resolution is the interval at which points are stored, so a shorter period cannot reveal detail that was never stored, and the engineer sees only the one-minute data.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how CloudWatch tells two servers' CPU metrics apart, and name one limit or tradeoff of using high-resolution metrics.
lessons.modelAnswer: Both servers publish CPUUtilization under the same namespace and metric name, so the namespace and name alone are not enough. The difference is the dimension, which holds a value such as each server's instance ID. CloudWatch treats each distinct combination of namespace, name, and dimension values as its own series, so reading with the right dimension returns one server's data. The tradeoff with high-resolution metrics is that the finer interval gives more detail but produces more data points, which costs more to store and read, and alarms on very short periods can be noisier. Standard one-minute resolution is often enough unless you need to catch spikes that last only seconds.
rubricPoints: Namespace and metric name alone do not identify one resource's series.
Dimensions are name and value pairs that separate series for each resource.
Each unique combination of namespace, name, and dimensions is its own metric.
High resolution gives finer detail but adds cost and possible alarm noise.

suggested.rationale: Choosing the right namespace, dimensions, and period is the core skill when building a metric alarm, which this planned engine would practise.

lessons.plain: Logs are the running notes a system writes about what it did: requests, errors, logins, and changes. Storing them securely means deciding who can read them, who can delete or change them, how they are scrambled so a stolen copy is useless, and how long they are kept. A log can contain customer details, internal addresses, or evidence of an attack, so it is sensitive data in its own right. Treat the log store like a locked filing cabinet, not like a notice board in the lobby.
lessons.guessPrompt: A developer wants to read last week's application logs to fix a bug, and a security colleague says those logs should not be readable by everyone in the company. Why might the colleague be right, even though the logs really do help debugging?
lessons.teach:
A log group is a named container that holds related log messages, such as all output from one service. A log stream is one sequence of messages inside that group, usually from one process or machine. Retention is the number of days a log group keeps its messages before they are deleted automatically. Encryption at rest means the stored data is scrambled on disk, so it is only readable by something holding the right key. A customer-managed key is an encryption key you create and control in AWS Key Management Service (KMS), a service that stores keys and performs encryption for other services. Least privilege means giving each person or machine only the permissions the job needs.

Worked example. A payment service accidentally logs a card token. First, the log group is encrypted with a customer-managed KMS key, so copies on disk are unreadable without permission to use that key. Second, read access goes only to an on-call role, not to every developer. Third, retention is set to 30 days, so the bad line is deleted on schedule. Fourth, the code is fixed so the token is never written, and old lines are left to expire. Each step narrows who can see the data and how long it exists.

Common mistake: assuming that because logs are in a managed cloud service they are private by default. Granting broad read or delete rights 'so people can debug' is the usual error, and keeping logs forever 'just in case' multiplies the exposure.

In a running system, an over-permissioned role lets anyone with access pull customer data out of the logs. If the KMS key is disabled or deleted, the encrypted logs become unreadable, which can destroy the audit trail you need during an incident.

questions.prompt: A bike-share company stores ride logs in a log group. The logs sometimes contain rider email addresses. The platform team applies three controls in order. Step 1: they encrypt the log group with a customer-managed KMS key, so stored copies cannot be read without permission to use that key. Step 2: [missing step]. Step 3: they set retention to 14 days, so any sensitive line is deleted automatically after two weeks. Which missing step best completes the plan?
choices: Keep retention at never-expire so the audit trail is always available.
Grant read access to every engineer so debugging is faster.
Restrict read access to the named support role only, not to all developers.
Delete the KMS key so the stored logs no longer contain readable data.
questions.why: Step 2 should narrow who can read the data, and restricting reads to the named support role does that, while the other choices either widen access, keep data forever, or make the encrypted logs permanently unreadable.

questions.prompt: In a log group, what is a log stream?
choices: The number of days the group keeps its messages before deleting them.
The full set of related messages from one service, held together under one name.
The customer-managed key that scrambles the stored messages on disk.
One sequence of messages inside the group, usually from one process or machine.
questions.why: The teaching text defines a log stream as one sequence of messages inside a group, usually from one process or machine, which is the first choice.

questions.prompt: A team sets retention to 365 days on a log group that receives debug output containing session tokens, saying they might need the history later. Which statement best describes the main risk?
choices: Retention automatically rotates the encryption key once a year, which exposes the tokens.
Long retention makes the logs unreadable to the on-call role after the first month.
Keeping sensitive messages longer multiplies how long they can be exposed.
Long retention only affects storage cost and does not change who can see the data.
questions.why: Retention controls how long messages exist, so keeping a sensitive token for a year extends the period during which it can be read, which the teaching text names as the multiplying effect of keeping logs forever.

questions.prompt: A monitoring dashboard only needs to display error counts from one log group. Which access setup best applies least privilege?
choices: A role allowed to read and delete every log group in the account.
A role allowed to read every log group in the account, but not delete them.
A role allowed only to read the one log group the dashboard needs.
A single admin role shared by the whole engineering team.
questions.why: Least privilege means giving only the permissions the job needs, and reading just the one required log group matches the dashboard's task, while the other choices grant more access than it requires.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would store application logs securely, and name one limit or tradeoff of the approach you choose.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would put each service's logs in its own log group, encrypt that group with a customer-managed KMS key, and give read access only to the roles that need it, such as on-call engineers and the security team. Delete rights would go to a much smaller set of roles, and any change to retention or key policy would be audited. I would set retention to match what the business and compliance need, not forever. The main tradeoff is operational: restricted access slows down debugging, because a developer who needs logs during an incident has to request a role or go through an on-call process. Keeping the key under our control also means we are responsible for its policy. If someone disables or deletes that key, the logs become unreadable, so key deletion needs a waiting period and approval. Shorter retention reduces risk but can remove evidence we later need for a security investigation.
rubricPoints: Logs are sensitive data and need explicit access rules, not open read access
Encryption at rest with a key the team controls, and the risk if that key is disabled or deleted
Retention should match business and compliance need, so data expires on purpose
A real tradeoff: tighter access and shorter retention slow debugging or remove investigation evidence

suggested.rationale: No listed mission walks through choosing who can read, encrypt, and expire logs, so a situation to reason through adds the most here.

lessons.plain: Encryption means scrambling data so only someone holding the right key can read it. Logs and metrics are records of what your systems did, and they often contain account numbers, IP addresses, or request details, so they need protection in two places: while they sit in storage (at rest) and while they travel across a network (in transit). This objective is about choosing how those two protections are set up for monitoring data, and about using AWS Key Management Service (KMS), a managed service that creates and guards the keys. Think of it like a locked filing cabinet, a sealed courier envelope, and a key that only certain staff are allowed to use.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company's log storage is already encrypted by the cloud provider, so why would its security team still want its own key for the log group that holds customer IDs? Make a guess before reading on.
lessons.teach: Encryption at rest means data is stored in scrambled form, so it is unreadable without a key. Encryption in transit means data is scrambled while moving between systems, usually using TLS, the protocol behind HTTPS. Monitoring services encrypt stored data by default and receive calls over HTTPS. The stronger option for logs is a customer managed key: a symmetric key you create in AWS Key Management Service (KMS), which holds keys and performs encryption and decryption without showing you the raw key material. You associate that key with a log group. The key's policy must allow the CloudWatch Logs service to use it, or ingestion fails. The protection works through envelope encryption. For each batch, the service asks KMS for a fresh data key, uses that data key to encrypt the log events, and stores an encrypted copy of the data key beside them. To read the events later, the service sends the encrypted copy back to KMS, which returns the usable key only to a caller allowed to use your KMS key. Worked example: log group ops-api is associated with key K. A batch of events arrives. The service requests a data key from KMS, receives a plaintext copy and an encrypted copy, encrypts the batch with the plaintext copy, discards the plaintext copy, and stores the ciphertext with the encrypted copy. Common mistake: assuming the association protects old data. It applies to events ingested afterward; earlier events keep the encryption they were written with. Consequence in a running system: if key K is disabled or scheduled for deletion, ingestion into ops-api fails and stored events cannot be read until the key is restored, so a key change can cause a monitoring outage. Metrics are encrypted by the service at rest, and calls to them travel over HTTPS, so the choices you make mainly concern log groups and other stores that receive monitoring data.

questions.prompt: Riverside Clinic keeps its patient portal audit events in a log group called portal-audit, which is associated with a customer managed key called rc-audit-key. An analyst asks to read Monday's audit events. Trace what happens. Step 1: the service looks up the stored encrypted copy of the data key for Monday's batch. Step 2: the service sends that encrypted copy to KMS. Step 3: KMS checks that the caller is allowed to use rc-audit-key. Step 4: [missing step]. Step 5: the service uses the usable data key to decrypt Monday's events and returns them to the analyst.
choices: KMS returns the usable data key to the permitted caller, which uses it to decrypt the batch
The service writes the encrypted copy of the data key into a new log group so it can be read later
KMS deletes the encrypted copy of the data key, which lets the service read the events in plaintext
KMS sends the usable data key directly to the analyst's browser, and the service is not involved
questions.why: Envelope encryption means KMS only hands back the usable data key to a permitted caller, and that key is then used to decrypt the stored events.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what does envelope encryption mean for a log group that uses a customer managed key?
choices: Each log event is encrypted directly by KMS one at a time, and the data key is never created
Each batch gets its own fresh data key, which encrypts the events and is itself stored in encrypted form beside them
The log group stores a single master key in plaintext next to the events so reads are faster
The events are sent to a separate envelope service that holds them until the key is rotated
questions.why: Envelope encryption uses a fresh data key per batch to encrypt the events, and the data key is stored only in encrypted form next to them.

questions.prompt: A payments team wants to switch the CPU and latency metrics for its checkout service to a customer managed key in KMS, expecting that to be the only way to protect them at rest. Which statement is accurate?
choices: Metrics must be encrypted with a key the team creates, or they are stored in plaintext
Metrics cannot be encrypted at rest at all, so the team must move the data to a log group instead
Metrics are encrypted only in transit, so switching keys would change nothing about their storage
Metrics are already encrypted at rest by the monitoring service, and the customer managed key choice mainly concerns log groups and other stores that receive monitoring data
questions.why: The teaching text says metrics are encrypted by the service at rest and calls travel over HTTPS, so customer key choices mainly apply to log groups and similar stores.

questions.prompt: On February 3, the Northwind platform team associates a customer managed key with its edge-proxy log group. Events ingested on January 10 were written before the association. What happens to them?
choices: They become unreadable until the team deletes the old key and creates a new one
They are copied into a new log group that uses the new key by default
They are re-encrypted with the new key automatically as soon as the association is saved
They keep the encryption they were written with, and only events ingested after February 3 use the new key
questions.why: The association applies only to events ingested afterward, so January 10 events keep their original encryption.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what encryption at rest and encryption in transit each protect for logs and metrics, what AWS KMS does in a customer managed key setup, and one limit or risk of using your own key.
lessons.modelAnswer: Encryption at rest protects stored logs, so someone who gets the disk or storage files still cannot read them. Encryption in transit protects data moving between the sender, the monitoring service, and any destination, usually through TLS, so someone watching the network sees only scrambled bytes. KMS is the managed service that holds the key. With a customer managed key, the log service uses envelope encryption: it gets a data key from KMS, encrypts the log batch, and stores the encrypted data key alongside it. The tradeoff is operational. If the key is disabled, its policy blocks the logging service, or it is scheduled for deletion, new events fail to ingest and old events become unreadable. So we treat the key like production infrastructure, with careful key policies, rotation, and alarms on access errors.
rubricPoints: Distinguishes encryption at rest from encryption in transit, with an example of each for logs or metrics
Explains that KMS holds and controls the key, and that envelope encryption uses a data key wrapped by the KMS key
Notes that a key association applies to newly ingested data, not to events already stored
Names a real risk: disabling or deleting the key or a wrong key policy breaks ingestion and reads

suggested.rationale: The planned envelope encryption lab lets the learner wrap and unwrap data keys hands-on, which is the core mechanism this objective depends on.

lessons.plain: A log collector is a small helper program that reads your application's log lines and sends them to a central service where you can search them later. Before it can send anything, it has to prove who it is to that service. An IAM role is a named set of permissions that a machine, not a person, can temporarily take on. This objective is about giving the collector just enough permission to create its log groups and streams and write events into them, and nothing more. If the permissions are wrong, logs quietly stop arriving, which is one of the most common ways a monitoring setup fails without anyone noticing.
lessons.guessPrompt: A small agent running on a server needs to write log lines to a central logging service. Should you give it your own administrator login, a password stored in a file on the server, or a role with only the log-writing permissions? Which would you pick, and why?
lessons.teach:
An IAM role is an identity in AWS Identity and Access Management that has no fixed password or long-lived key. Instead, something trusted can assume it and receive short-lived credentials. A permission is a statement in a policy that allows or denies an action, such as writing log events, on a resource, such as one log group. A trust policy is the part of a role that names who may assume it, for example the EC2 service acting on a server. An instance profile is the container that attaches a role to an EC2 server. An Amazon Resource Name (ARN) is the unique address of a resource, which lets a policy point at exactly one log group.

Why it works: the collector never stores a secret. When it starts on a server with a role attached, it requests temporary credentials, which expire and rotate on their own. It then calls the logging service, and the service checks the request against the role's permissions. Anything not explicitly allowed is denied.

A collector usually needs a small set of actions: create a log group, create a log stream, describe existing streams so it knows where it left off, and put log events. Create actions can be dropped if someone creates the group ahead of time, which is safer.

Worked example: an application on an EC2 server writes to a log group named orders-api. Step 1: the role's trust policy lets EC2 assume it. Step 2: the instance profile attaches the role to the server. Step 3: the collector obtains temporary credentials and calls PutLogEvents on orders-api. Step 4: the policy allows that action on that group's ARN, so the request succeeds. If the policy named a different group, the call is denied, and the central group stays empty.

Common mistake: attaching an administrator or wildcard policy so everything works. This hides the scoping problem and widens the damage if the server is compromised.

Consequence: a denied collector does not crash the application, so nothing looks broken. Dashboards and alarms built on those logs go silent, and the first sign of an outage may be a customer report.

questions.prompt: A payments team runs a reconciliation worker on an EC2 server, which is a virtual machine in AWS. They want its output in a log group called ledger-recon-prod, where a log group is the container that holds related log streams. They create a role named recon-worker-role with a trust policy that lets the EC2 service assume it. They attach the role to the server through an instance profile, the container that connects a role to a server. The collector then obtains temporary credentials and calls PutLogEvents, the action that writes log entries. Step 4 is missing: what the role's permission must contain for that call to succeed. Which completion fills the gap correctly?
choices: The permission allows PutLogEvents on the ARN of ledger-recon-prod, the unique address of that one group
The role is given AdministratorAccess so that no log action can be denied, which keeps the collector working even if group names change
The trust policy lists the ARN of ledger-recon-prod as the principal, so the log group itself can assume the role and make the call
The access key ID and secret for the role are copied into a configuration file on the server so the collector can sign its requests
questions.why: A permission statement must allow the action on the specific resource address (ARN) of the group, and the service then checks the request against it; the other options either confuse trust with permission or store a secret the design avoids.

questions.prompt: In an IAM role, what is the trust policy for?
choices: It names which identity, such as the EC2 service, is allowed to assume the role
It lists the log actions the role's holder may perform on each log group
It attaches the role to one specific server through a container called an instance profile
It stores the long-lived password the server uses to sign in to the logging service
questions.why: The trust policy answers who may assume the role; what the role may do is governed by its permissions, and the instance profile is only the attachment mechanism.

questions.prompt: A collector on an EC2 server has been delivering to the log group checkout-logs. Last week the team renamed the group to checkout-events, but the role's permission still names the old group's ARN. What is the most likely result?
choices: The application crashes on startup because its log group no longer exists
The collector follows the rename automatically and writes to checkout-events
The log calls are denied, the application keeps running, and the central group stays empty
The temporary credentials expire immediately and the server shuts itself down
questions.why: The permission matches only the old ARN, so requests to the renamed group are denied without crashing the application, which is why the silence can go unnoticed.

questions.prompt: A team has already created a log group named billing-prod ahead of time. Its collector only needs to make the calls that write entries and track where it left off. Which permission set is the smallest that still lets it work?
choices: logs:* on every resource, so future log groups are covered without edits
logs:PutLogEvents alone on the account root, since nothing else is ever needed
logs:CreateLogStream, logs:DescribeLogStreams and logs:PutLogEvents, scoped to the ARN of billing-prod
logs:CreateLogGroup, logs:CreateLogStream, logs:DescribeLogStreams and logs:PutLogEvents on every resource in the account
questions.why: The group already exists so its creation action can be dropped, and the remaining actions are scoped to that one group's ARN, which is the smallest set the collector needs.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why a log collector on an EC2 server should use an IAM role rather than an access key stored in a config file, and name one limit or tradeoff of scoping its permissions tightly.
lessons.modelAnswer: A role gives the server temporary credentials that the platform rotates and expires, so there is no long-lived key sitting in a config file where it can leak into a repository or an image. The permissions attached to the role decide what the collector can do, so I would keep them to describing streams and putting log events, scoped to the ARN of this service's log group. The tradeoff is that tight scoping means every new log group or new encryption key needs a permission update, or the collector is silently denied. If the agent also creates groups, it needs create permissions, which widens the role a little. So I would pre-create the groups with retention set, and keep create permissions off unless they are needed. After any change, I would confirm that events are still arriving, because a denial does not crash anything.
rubricPoints: Explains that a role provides temporary, rotated credentials instead of a stored long-lived secret
Describes the minimum actions needed, such as creating streams and putting log events
Explains scoping permissions to specific log group ARNs rather than wildcards
Names a tradeoff, such as new groups or keys needing permission updates or silent denials
Notes that denied log writes do not crash the application, so verification is needed

suggested.rationale: Deciding whether a collector's request is allowed means working out which policy statements match, which the planned authorization policy evaluator would practise directly.

lessons.plain: Your application writes log lines, a running diary of what it does. A metric filter is a rule that reads that diary as each line arrives and counts the lines that match a pattern, such as every error. Each match becomes a number stored over time, so you can graph it or set an alarm on it. You do not have to change the application to get the count. The rule only looks at new lines from the moment it is created, and it has no memory of earlier ones.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your web app writes one log line for every failed login, but it has no metrics code at all. You want a graph of failed logins per minute and an alarm when they spike. Without changing the app, what would you attach to the logs, and what would it need to look for?
lessons.teach: A log group is a named collection of log streams, which are the stored lines a service writes. A metric filter is a rule attached to one log group. It has a filter pattern, a text expression that decides whether a given log event matches, and a metric transformation, which says what number to publish when it matches. A metric is a named time series of values inside a namespace, which is a container that groups related metrics. Publishing a metric means sending a data point with a timestamp and a value into that series. Why it works: the rule runs as events arrive, so the application needs no change. Each matching event produces a data point. The usual value is 1, so summing the points over a minute counts the matches. The value can also be taken from a field inside the log line, such as a response time, which lets you track averages. Worked example: a log group receives the line 'ERROR payment timeout 2300ms'. A pattern that matches lines containing ERROR matches it. The transformation publishes the value 1 to a metric named PaymentErrors in a namespace called Shop. Two more matching lines arrive within the same minute. Summed over that minute, PaymentErrors equals 3. An alarm can now fire when that sum is above 10 for five minutes. Common mistake: expecting a filter to count history. It only applies to events ingested after it exists, so a brand-new filter shows no past errors. A second mistake is a pattern that is too broad, which inflates the count and produces false alarms. Consequence in a running system: if a developer changes the wording of the error message, a pattern tied to the old wording stops matching. The metric then drops to zero or stops publishing, and an alarm built on it looks healthy while failures continue. Treat missing data as a warning sign, not as proof that all is well.

questions.prompt: Lumen Bikes runs a ride-matching service that writes lines to a log group. A metric filter with the pattern WARN and a transformation that publishes the value 1 to the metric SlowedRequests in the namespace Rides is created at 09:00. Step 1: at 08:58, a line 'WARN rate_limited driver=88' is written to the log group. Step 2: at 09:02, two more WARN lines arrive, both within the 09:02 minute. Step 3 is missing. Step 4: summed over the 09:02 minute, SlowedRequests equals 2. What is the missing Step 3?
choices: The filter must be restarted at 09:02 before any line can match.
The 08:58 line is counted retroactively, so the 09:00 minute total includes it.
The filter publishes the value from the driver field, so the 09:02 sum is 88 plus 88.
The 08:58 line is not counted, because the filter only applies to events ingested after it was created at 09:00.
questions.why: A metric filter only applies to events ingested after it exists, so the 08:58 line written before the 09:00 creation is not counted, which is consistent with the stated sum of 2.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what is a metric filter?
choices: A dashboard widget that graphs log lines over time without storing any data points.
A scheduled job that copies log lines from one log group into another.
A permission policy that controls which engineers may read a log group.
A rule attached to one log group that has a filter pattern deciding which events match and a transformation deciding what number to publish.
questions.why: The teaching text defines a metric filter as a rule on one log group made of a filter pattern (which events match) and a metric transformation (what number to publish).

questions.prompt: A checkout service writes lines like 'INFO checkout ok latency=412' to a log group. The team wants to track average checkout latency, not a count of checkouts. Which approach fits?
choices: Create an alarm that fires whenever the word INFO appears more than 50 times in five minutes.
Enable encryption on the log group so the latency values are stored more securely.
Set the transformation to take its value from the latency field in the line, so each matching event publishes its response time.
Use a pattern that matches the word checkout and publish the value 1 for each match, then average the counts.
questions.why: The teaching text says the published value can be read from a field inside the log line, such as a response time, which lets you track averages instead of counting matches.

questions.prompt: An authentication service's filter matches the wording 'login rejected'. A developer later changes the message to 'sign-in refused'. Afterward, the filter's metric drops to zero and an alarm on it stays green while users report failures. What is the right reaction?
choices: Delete the alarm, because a metric that reads zero cannot be trusted at all.
Conclude the service is healthy, since an alarm that stays green means nothing is wrong.
Treat the zero or missing data as a warning sign, then check whether the filter pattern still matches the current wording of the log lines.
Backdate the filter so it counts the failures that happened before the wording change.
questions.why: The teaching text warns that a pattern tied to old wording stops matching, so the metric falls to zero or stops publishing while failures continue, and missing data should be treated as a warning rather than proof of health.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a metric filter turns log lines into a metric that an alarm can watch, and name one limit or tradeoff you would warn them about before they rely on it.
lessons.modelAnswer: A metric filter sits on a log group and checks each new log line against a pattern. When a line matches, it publishes a data point into a named metric, usually with the value 1, so summing those points over time gives a count of matching events. That metric can then be graphed or alarmed on like any other metric. The main limit is that it applies only going forward. It does not create metrics from log lines written before the filter existed, so you cannot use it to explain an incident that happened last week. The other tradeoff is pattern precision. A loose pattern overcounts and fires false alarms. A pattern tied to exact wording silently stops matching when developers change the message, so the alarm goes quiet while the failure continues. I would tell the teammate to test the pattern against real sample lines first, and to set the alarm to treat missing data as a warning too.
rubricPoints: A metric filter attaches to a log group and matches new log events against a pattern.
Each match publishes a data point to a named metric, so the count can be graphed and alarmed on.
It only applies to events ingested after the filter is created, not to past logs.
A pattern that is too broad overcounts, and one tied to exact wording can silently stop matching.

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through a situation where a log pattern drives an alarm adds the most here, and no listed mission teaches log-to-metric conversion directly.

lessons.plain: CloudWatch already keeps measurements about your systems, such as how busy a server is or how many errors a web app returned. Normally a tool has to ask for those numbers again and again. A metric stream flips that: CloudWatch pushes a copy of the numbers out as they arrive, to a destination you choose. The usual destinations are a storage bucket, where you keep a long history cheaply, or a delivery service that batches the data and forwards it onward. Think of it as a tap on a water pipe that fills a barrel, instead of walking to the reservoir with a cup every minute.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you wanted every CPU reading from a fleet of 200 servers kept for a year for later analysis, would you rather have a tool ask CloudWatch for those numbers every minute, or have CloudWatch send them to you as they arrive? Which one do you expect to scale better, and why?
lessons.teach:
A metric stream is a CloudWatch feature that continuously sends metric data points to a destination as they are published, instead of waiting for something to request them. The stream has three parts. The source is the set of metrics it includes, which you can narrow by namespace (a namespace is a group name for metrics, such as the group for one service) using include or exclude filters. The destination is where the data lands. For Amazon S3, the stream goes through Amazon Data Firehose, a delivery service that collects records, buffers them for a short time or until a size limit is reached, and writes them as batched files to a bucket. The third part is an IAM role, a set of permissions that lets CloudWatch write into the Firehose delivery stream.

Why it works: the data is pushed, so you do not pay for repeated polling, and batching keeps storage writes efficient.

Worked example: you create a stream that includes only the namespace for your load balancer. Step 1, the load balancer produces a 5xx error count and CloudWatch publishes that metric. Step 2, the stream matches the namespace and forwards the data point. Step 3, Firehose holds it in its buffer. Step 4, when the buffer fills or its time window ends, Firehose writes one file containing many points into your bucket. Step 5, a later analysis job reads those files.

Common mistake: assuming the stream is a dashboard or an alarm source. It only moves data. Alarms still run inside CloudWatch, and the copy in S3 arrives with a delay measured in minutes, so it cannot replace a live alarm.

Consequence: if the IAM role lacks permission to write to the delivery stream, gaps appear in the bucket while the rest of your system looks healthy, which is why you verify that files are arriving after you create a stream.

questions.prompt: A food delivery company wants its checkout service metrics kept in long-term storage for later review. An engineer sets up a CloudWatch metric stream that includes only the namespace Orders/Checkout, with Amazon Data Firehose as the destination and an S3 bucket behind it. Step 1: the checkout service publishes a p99 latency metric to CloudWatch. Step 2: the stream includes that namespace and picks up the data point as it is published. Step 3: [missing step]. Step 4: Firehose holds the point in its buffer until the buffer fills or its time window ends. Step 5: Firehose writes one batched file containing many points to the S3 bucket. Which statement correctly fills the missing Step 3?
choices: The stream sends the data point to the Firehose delivery stream, using the IAM role's permission to write into it.
The S3 bucket polls CloudWatch every hour and copies any new metric values it finds.
CloudWatch compares the latency value with an alarm threshold and pages the on-call engineer if it is exceeded.
The engineer exports the metric from the CloudWatch dashboard by hand so Firehose can receive it.
questions.why: The stream pushes each matched data point to the Firehose delivery stream, and the IAM role is what grants CloudWatch the permission to do that write.

questions.prompt: Which description best defines a CloudWatch metric stream?
choices: A feature that continuously sends metric data points to a destination as they are published, rather than waiting to be asked for them.
A dashboard widget that graphs metrics from several namespaces on a single screen.
A rule that changes the threshold of an alarm when a metric crosses a certain level.
A scheduled job that polls CloudWatch for metric values once a day and saves a report.
questions.why: A metric stream pushes each data point to its destination as it is published, which is different from polling, dashboards, or alarm rules.

questions.prompt: A data team's metric stream to S3 through Firehose has been running for a week, but the bucket is missing files for one namespace. The other namespaces arrive normally. The team checks and finds the IAM role was never given permission to write into the Firehose delivery stream. What is the most accurate account of what has happened?
choices: The metric stream has stopped publishing metrics to CloudWatch, so the alarms for that namespace are also silent.
The namespace is excluded automatically by the stream, so no data was ever meant to reach the bucket.
Firehose has deleted the earlier files for that namespace to free space, which is why the bucket looks incomplete.
CloudWatch alarms still evaluate normally inside CloudWatch, but the S3 copy of that namespace has gaps because the role could not write.
questions.why: The missing IAM permission only blocks the write into Firehose and the S3 bucket, while the source metrics and their CloudWatch alarms keep working.

questions.prompt: An on-call team wants to be paged within about one minute when a payment API error metric spikes. Someone proposes using the metric stream's files in S3 as the trigger, since the data is already being stored there. What is the best response?
choices: Remove the IAM role so the stream sends data directly to the alarm.
Use the S3 files, because the copy in the bucket is always current and arrives in seconds.
Keep the alarm inside CloudWatch, because the S3 copy arrives with a delay of minutes and the stream only moves data.
Use the S3 files, but only if the bucket is in the same region as the payment API.
questions.why: Alarms run inside CloudWatch, and the stream's S3 copy is delayed by minutes, so it cannot serve as a live alarm source.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what a CloudWatch metric stream to S3 or Data Firehose does, and name one limit or tradeoff they should weigh before choosing it over polling the metrics.
