lessons.modelAnswer: A metric stream pushes CloudWatch metric points out to a destination as they are published, so the data does not have to be requested again and again. It is set up with a set of included namespaces and an IAM role that lets CloudWatch write into an Amazon Data Firehose delivery stream. Firehose buffers the points and writes batched files to S3, which suits long retention and later analysis. The main tradeoff is that the copy is delayed by the buffer and is not a live alarm source; alarms still run inside CloudWatch. Each stream also costs money per metric update it carries, so including a broad namespace can be expensive. A missing role permission means files stop appearing without an obvious error in your application. Filtering to the namespaces you actually need keeps both cost and noise down.
rubricPoints: A metric stream pushes metric data continuously to a destination instead of being polled.
Data going to S3 passes through Firehose, which buffers and writes batches.
An IAM role must allow CloudWatch to write into the delivery stream.
The stream copy is delayed and does not replace live alarms, and cost grows with the metrics included.

suggested.rationale: This objective is mostly setup facts and product wiring that a short reading with clear definitions covers best, and no listed mission or planned engine targets it directly.

lessons.plain: Normally a cloud server reports only basic health numbers, such as how busy its processor is. Many real problems, like a disk nearly full or memory running low, stay invisible to those basics. A small helper program called the CloudWatch agent runs on the server, reads extra measurements you choose, and sends them to a monitoring service as custom metrics. It works like a field inspector who checks the gauges the standard dashboard leaves out and reports them to a control room on a schedule. Once the numbers arrive, you can graph them and set alarms on them, just as you would with built-in numbers.
lessons.guessPrompt: A server's CPU graph looks calm, yet users report that the application stopped saving files. Why might the cloud provider's default graphs miss the cause, and what kind of measurement would reveal it?
lessons.teach:
A metric is a named number recorded over time, such as the percentage of disk space in use. A namespace is a container that groups related metrics so their names do not collide with others. A dimension is a name and value pair, such as InstanceId equals a particular server ID, that splits one metric into a separate series for each server. A custom metric is one you publish yourself, as opposed to the metrics the cloud provider publishes automatically. The CloudWatch agent is software installed on the server that gathers chosen measurements and publishes them. Its behaviour is set by a configuration file, written in JSON, that lists which measurements to collect, how often, which namespace to use, and which dimensions to attach.

Why it works: the provider sees the virtual machine from outside, so it knows CPU and network traffic but not what happens inside the operating system. Memory use and the fullness of each disk partition exist only inside the guest, so only a program running on the machine can read them. The agent is that program. It samples the operating system counters on a fixed interval and sends the values using the permissions attached to the server.

Worked example: you want an alarm when the root disk passes 85 percent used. Step 1: in the configuration, add a disk measurement for the used-percent value with a 60-second collection interval. Step 2: set a namespace such as ExampleApp/Host so it stays separate from built-in metrics. Step 3: attach the InstanceId dimension so each server gets its own series. Step 4: the agent samples the disk and publishes a value each minute under that namespace and dimension. Step 5: an alarm watches that exact namespace, metric name and dimension, and fires when the value stays above 85 for the chosen number of periods.

Common mistake: writing the alarm against the default namespace, or using a dimension value that does not match what the agent publishes. The alarm then never receives data and sits in an insufficient-data state. Nothing errors loudly.

Consequence: in a running system this silence is dangerous, because nobody learns the disk is full until writes start failing. A custom metric is only as useful as the exact name, namespace and dimensions that the alarm is written to match.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm called Ridgeway Freight runs 12 order-API servers in an auto scaling group named api-prod. The team wants an alarm when memory use stays above 80 percent. Step 1: in the agent configuration, add a memory measurement for the used-percent value with a 30-second collection interval. Step 2: set the namespace to RidgewayApi/Memory so it is separate from built-in metrics. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: the agent samples memory every 30 seconds and publishes each value under that namespace, metric name and dimension. Step 5: an alarm watches that exact namespace, metric name and dimension and fires when the value stays above 80 for three consecutive periods. Which completes step 3?
choices: Attach an AutoScalingGroupName dimension with the value api-prod to the measurement, so each server's series is split by group, and write the alarm against the same namespace, metric name and dimension.
Create the alarm with no dimension, because alarms match on the namespace and metric name alone and ignore dimensions.
Raise the collection interval to 300 seconds so the alarm has fewer data points to evaluate.
Point the alarm at the default AWS/EC2 namespace so it inherits the memory series automatically.
questions.why: The alarm only receives data when its namespace, metric name and dimension match exactly what the agent publishes, so the dimension must be attached in the configuration and then matched in the alarm.

questions.prompt: In CloudWatch, what is a dimension?
choices: A name and value pair attached to a metric that splits it into a separate series for each matching resource.
A JSON file on the server that lists which measurements the agent should collect.
The fixed time gap between two samples taken by the agent.
A container that stops metric names from colliding with other metric names.
questions.why: A dimension is a name and value pair, such as a server ID, that divides one metric into separate series, one per resource.

questions.prompt: A team at Harbor Yard Cargo sets the agent namespace to HarborYard/Gate and the metric name to queue_depth. Their alarm watches the namespace HarborYard/gate with the same metric name. What is the most likely result?
choices: The alarm fires immediately because it treats both spellings as the same series.
The alarm never receives data, so it sits in an insufficient-data state without any loud error.
The agent refuses to start because the namespaces differ in case.
The alarm reads the wrong data but CloudWatch flags a configuration error in the console.
questions.why: Namespaces must match exactly, so the alarm watches an empty series and silently stays in insufficient data.

questions.prompt: Why does a team need the CloudWatch agent to collect swap usage on a virtual machine, instead of relying on the cloud provider's default metrics?
choices: Swap usage is only exposed by the provider after the agent is installed, so the agent is the only way to see it at all.
Default provider metrics do not support any value that is a percentage.
Swap usage is billed separately, so the provider hides it from default metrics.
Swap usage is held in the virtual machine's operating system, which the provider cannot see from outside, so only a program running on the machine can read and publish it.
questions.why: Values inside the guest operating system, such as swap and disk partition fullness, are invisible from outside the virtual machine, so software on the machine must read and publish them.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why a server needs the CloudWatch agent to report disk usage, and name one limit or cost of publishing custom metrics.
lessons.modelAnswer: The cloud platform sees a server from outside, so it reports things like CPU and network traffic automatically but cannot see inside the operating system. Disk fullness and memory use are only visible from within, so the CloudWatch agent runs on the server, reads those counters on a set interval, and publishes them as custom metrics under a namespace and dimensions we choose. The limit is that these metrics are only as good as the configuration. If the agent is not installed, its permissions are missing, or the alarm names a different namespace or dimension, the alarm gets no data and stays in insufficient-data without warning. Custom metrics also cost money per metric, so we collect only what an alarm or dashboard actually needs, and we confirm the agent is publishing with a test read after every rollout.
rubricPoints: The cloud provider sees only what is outside the virtual machine, so in-guest values like disk and memory need an agent.
The agent reads chosen counters on an interval and publishes them as custom metrics under a namespace and dimensions.
The alarm must match the exact namespace, metric name and dimensions, or it receives no data.
Custom metrics have a cost, so collect only what alarms and dashboards need.

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through an exam-style scenario where an alarm stays silent because the agent's namespace or dimensions do not match adds the most here.

lessons.plain: Logs are the diary a system writes about itself, and they pile up fast. Storage lifecycle management is the set of rules that decides how long each kind of log is kept, when it moves to cheaper storage, and when it is deleted. Without rules, you pay for old logs nobody reads. With rules set too aggressively, you delete the evidence you need during the next outage or audit. On AWS this happens in two main places: files in object storage (S3) and log groups in the monitoring service (CloudWatch Logs). Each has its own settings, and the skill is choosing the right value for each based on how long the logs stay useful and what rules you must follow.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your application writes a log line for every request, and the team keeps all of them forever. Over a year, name one thing that goes wrong for cost and one thing that goes wrong for risk, and say which you would fix first.
lessons.teach:
A log lifecycle is the timeline a log follows from creation to deletion. Two AWS features control parts of that timeline, and you need to know which setting belongs to which store.

In CloudWatch Logs, logs are grouped into log groups. Each log group holds log streams, one per source such as an instance or a container. Every log group has a retention setting, the number of days after which its log events are deleted automatically. The default is to never expire. Shortening retention also removes older events that already exist, so a change applies to past data as well as future data.

In Amazon S3, an object store, a lifecycle policy is a set of rules attached to a bucket. A rule can apply to a prefix (a name shared by a group of objects, often shaped like a folder path) or to tags. Its actions include transition, which moves objects to a cheaper, slower storage class after a set number of days, and expiration, which deletes them. In a versioned bucket, a rule can also expire noncurrent versions, the older copies kept when an object is overwritten. Some cheaper storage classes charge a minimum storage duration, so deleting or moving an object too early costs more than leaving it alone.

Worked example: a bucket holds logs under the prefix app/. The rule says: after 30 days, transition to an infrequent-access class; after 90 days, transition to an archive class; after 365 days, expire. Step by step, an object written on day 0 sits in the standard class, moves on day 30, moves again on day 90, and is deleted on day 365. Lifecycle actions run asynchronously, so the deletion may happen a day or two after the target day rather than at that exact moment.

Common mistake: assuming that exporting logs from CloudWatch to S3 moves them. An export creates a copy. The original in CloudWatch still follows its own retention, and the S3 copy follows its own rules.

Consequence: if a log group keeps events for 3 days but a security review needs 90 days of history, the evidence is gone before anyone asks for it. Set retention for each store from the questions those logs must answer, not from the default.

questions.prompt: The payments team has a CloudWatch log group named /ledger/api with no retention setting, so its events are kept indefinitely. On day 100 they set retention to 21 days. Step 1: the cutoff is 21 days before the change, which is day 79. Step 2: events written before the cutoff become eligible for deletion. Step 3: an event written on day 85 is inside the window, so it is kept. Step 4 is missing. Which statement completes the trace for an event written on day 40?
choices: It is deleted at the exact moment the setting changes on day 100.
It is copied to an S3 bucket automatically and then deleted from CloudWatch.
It is kept, because a retention change only applies to events written after the change.
It is eligible for deletion and is removed within a day or two after day 100, because deletion runs asynchronously.
questions.why: The event is older than the cutoff, so it is eligible, and the removal happens asynchronously, so it may complete a day or two later rather than instantly.

questions.prompt: Which setting in CloudWatch Logs decides how long log events are kept before they are deleted automatically?
choices: The tags attached to the individual log events
The log stream name for each container or instance
The number of days set as the log group's retention
The storage class chosen for the S3 bucket that receives exports
questions.why: Retention is a per-log-group setting measured in days, and the log stream name, S3 storage class, and tags do not control CloudWatch deletion.

questions.prompt: A team versions an S3 bucket and writes a lifecycle rule that expires current versions after 60 days. After a year they find many older overwritten copies still stored and costing money. What is the most likely reason?
choices: The rule only covers current versions, so noncurrent versions need their own expiration action.
The rule was applied to a tag instead of a prefix, so it matched nothing.
Lifecycle rules never delete anything in a versioned bucket.
The deletion ran too early and the copies were restored from archive.
questions.why: A rule that expires current versions does not touch the older noncurrent copies, which need an explicit expiration action in the rule.

questions.prompt: An object in an S3 bucket is moved to an archive class and then deleted after only 20 days, although the archive class charges for a minimum storage duration longer than that. What should the team expect on the bill?
choices: A charge for the minimum storage duration, because early deletion does not remove that obligation.
A refund of the transition fee when the object is deleted early.
A charge only for the days beyond the 20-day mark.
No charge, because deleting an object always cancels its storage cost.
questions.why: Some cheaper storage classes bill for a minimum storage duration, so deleting early still incurs the cost of the full minimum period.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would set retention for a service's application logs and for its audit logs, and name one limit or tradeoff of the choice you make.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would separate the two by purpose. Application logs are mostly for debugging recent incidents, so I would keep them in the CloudWatch log group for a short period, maybe two to four weeks, which keeps searching cheap and fast. If the team wants longer history, I would export them to S3 and apply a lifecycle policy there that moves older objects to cheaper storage classes and expires them later. Audit logs are different because a review may ask for months of history, so I would set a longer retention on their log group and keep an archived copy in S3 under a separate prefix with its own rules. The main tradeoff is cost against access speed: the cheaper archive classes are slower to read and may charge a minimum storage duration, so a log retrieved in a hurry costs more than expected. I would also note that the exported copy is not the same object as the CloudWatch one, so both need their own retention settings.
rubricPoints: Retention is set per log group in CloudWatch Logs and applies to events, with the default never expiring
S3 lifecycle rules use prefixes or tags to pick objects, then transition to cheaper classes or expire them
Exporting logs creates a copy, and each copy follows its own retention or lifecycle rules
Retention should match the questions the logs must answer, such as incident debugging or audit history
Cheaper archive classes trade access speed and minimum storage duration for lower cost

suggested.rationale: Choosing retention for different log types under cost and evidence constraints is best practised by reasoning through exam-style scenarios, which no existing mission covers directly.

lessons.plain: CloudWatch Logs is where your applications send their log lines, grouped into named buckets called log groups. A subscription filter is a rule attached to one log group that says: copy the lines that match this pattern, and send the copies to a second place as they arrive. That second place can be a stream that other programs read, a function that runs your own code on each batch, or a delivery pipe that loads the lines into a search service. Think of a mail sorter that photocopies every letter with a certain stamp and forwards the copies while the originals stay where they are.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you want every error line from an API's logs to be searchable in a dashboard tool within seconds of being written, what would you connect to the log group, and what happens to lines written before you set that connection up?
lessons.teach:
A log group is a named collection of log events in CloudWatch Logs, and a log stream is one sequence of events inside it, usually from one source such as a single server or container. A subscription filter attaches to a log group and holds two things: a filter pattern, which decides which events qualify, and a destination, which receives the qualifying events. Supported destinations are an Amazon Kinesis Data Stream, an Amazon Data Firehose delivery stream, or an AWS Lambda function. Amazon OpenSearch Service is not a direct destination; you reach it by sending events through Firehose, which buffers them and writes them into an OpenSearch index. CloudWatch Logs also needs permission to write into the destination, granted through an IAM role the subscription uses; that role is covered elsewhere in this unit.

Why it works: forwarding happens as events arrive, so nothing has to poll the logs. Events are sent in batches, compressed and encoded, which is efficient but means the receiver must unpack them before reading.

Worked example: a log group called shop-api receives the line 'ERROR payment timeout order=8812'. The filter pattern ERROR matches it, so CloudWatch Logs packages it with the group name, stream name and timestamp into a batch. The batch is compressed and delivered to a Firehose stream, which buffers it briefly and then writes it into an OpenSearch index. A line containing only INFO does not match, so it never leaves CloudWatch Logs.

Common mistake: expecting a subscription to forward history. It only sees events written after the filter exists, so earlier error lines stay only in the log group.

Consequence: delivery can fall behind when the destination throttles or fails, so you must watch the destination's own metrics and errors rather than assuming every line arrived.

questions.prompt: A logistics team has a log group called parcel-tracker and wants lines containing TIMEOUT searchable in an OpenSearch index. Their path has five steps. (1) A subscription filter with the pattern TIMEOUT is attached to parcel-tracker. (2) A matching event is packaged into a batch with its group name, stream name and timestamp. (3) The batch is compressed and sent to the subscription's destination. (4) The blank step, which is the only missing step. (5) The event becomes searchable in the OpenSearch index. Which choice belongs in step 4?
choices: The batch is copied into an S3 bucket, and OpenSearch reads that bucket on a schedule.
The batch goes straight from CloudWatch Logs into the OpenSearch domain, with no intermediate service.
The batch is handed to an Amazon Kinesis Data Stream, which writes it into the OpenSearch index.
The batch goes to a Firehose delivery stream, which buffers it briefly and writes it into the OpenSearch index.
questions.why: OpenSearch Service is not a direct subscription destination, so events must pass through Firehose, which buffers them and writes them into the index.

questions.prompt: A team created a subscription filter on the group billing-worker today and now expects last week's error lines to appear in their Kinesis stream. Which statement explains why they will not?
choices: Subscriptions replay the whole log group history once when the filter is first created, but only for Lambda destinations.
The filter pattern must be rewritten with a timestamp before it can match events from earlier dates.
Kinesis streams reject any event older than seven days, so older lines are dropped before delivery.
Subscriptions only see events written after the filter exists, so earlier lines remain only in the log group.
questions.why: A subscription filter only forwards events that arrive after it is in place, so older events stay in the log group and are never sent to the destination.

questions.prompt: A log group named warehouse-scanner receives these three lines in order: 'ERROR scan=77 jam at dock 4', 'INFO scan=78 ok', 'ERROR scan=79 label unreadable'. A subscription filter with the pattern ERROR is attached and was created before any of these lines were written. How many events does the filter forward to its destination?
choices: Two, the two lines that contain the pattern ERROR.
Three, because every line in one batch is forwarded once the filter matches any line.
Zero, because the filter must match the full line exactly and none of these lines do.
One, because a batch only ever contains the most recent matching event.
questions.why: The filter forwards each event whose content matches the pattern, and the two ERROR lines match while the INFO line does not.

questions.prompt: A team's subscription sends events from a log group to an Amazon Kinesis Data Stream. The log group shows events being written normally, but the team notices the downstream reader is missing recent entries. What is the most useful first step?
choices: Delete the subscription filter and create it again so the backlog is resent from the log group.
Increase the filter pattern's length so more events qualify and are pushed through.
Assume the events were delivered, since CloudWatch Logs shows that they were written.
Check the destination's own metrics and errors, because forwarding can fall behind when the destination throttles or fails.
questions.why: Events written to the log group do not prove delivery, so the destination's own metrics and error records are the place to see whether it is throttling or failing.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has only read log files on a server how a CloudWatch Logs subscription sends log events to Kinesis, Lambda or OpenSearch, and name one limit or tradeoff they must plan for.
lessons.modelAnswer: A subscription filter sits on one log group and copies events that match its pattern to one destination as they arrive, so we are not reading logs on a schedule. The events can go to a Kinesis stream for other consumers, to a Lambda function that runs our code per batch, or through a Firehose delivery stream into OpenSearch for searching. The limit I would flag is that it only forwards events written after the filter exists, so backfilling old lines needs a separate export. The other tradeoff is that the filter pattern controls volume and cost: a broad pattern floods the downstream system, and a Lambda receiver has to decode the batched, compressed payload before it reads anything. We should also watch the destination's own metrics, because the pipeline can fall behind even when the source looks healthy.
rubricPoints: A subscription filter sits on a log group, matches a pattern, and forwards matching events to one destination as they arrive.
Destinations are Kinesis Data Streams, Firehose (which can feed OpenSearch), or Lambda; OpenSearch is reached through Firehose.
Names a limit: only events written after the filter exists are forwarded, not history.
Notes that the receiver must handle batched, compressed payloads, or that the filter pattern drives volume and cost.

suggested.rationale: Choosing between Kinesis, Firehose-to-OpenSearch and Lambda for a given log flow is best practised as an exam-style scenario, and no listed mission covers it directly.

lessons.plain: When a system writes thousands of log lines, finding the few that matter by hand is slow. CloudWatch Logs, the AWS log storage service, supports two search tools. A filter pattern is a small rule that keeps only the lines matching a condition. Logs Insights is an interactive query tool that can search, count, group and chart what it finds over a chosen time window. Think of a filter as a targeted search box and an Insights query as a spreadsheet-style question you ask about many lines at once. You use filters for quick checks and queries when you need to answer a question about patterns over time.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose a web server writes one line per request, and you want only the requests that returned a server error. Before reading further, how would you describe the search rule you would give a log tool, and what could go wrong if the rule only looked for the digits 500 anywhere in the line?
lessons.teach:
A log event is one record written to a log group, which is a named collection of log streams. A filter pattern is a rule CloudWatch Logs applies to each incoming event, keeping only those that match. There are three styles to recognise. Plain terms match text anywhere in the event: a bare word is a case-sensitive substring test, a quoted phrase must appear exactly, and terms separated by spaces must all be present. A question mark before a term gives OR, and a minus sign excludes a term. JSON patterns begin with a brace and refer to fields with a dollar-sign path, so the rule compares a real field with a number instead of searching text. Space-delimited patterns put names in square brackets for each position in a fixed-format line, such as an access log.

Logs Insights is a query language. You pick log groups and a time range, then chain commands with pipes. Filter keeps matching rows, parse pulls values out of free text into named fields, stats aggregates with count, sum or average, and bin groups results into time buckets.

Worked example: each JSON log event has a status field and a latency field. A filter pattern for slow server errors reads a brace, then a dollar-sign path to status greater than or equal to 500, then a condition on latency. Step one: the service reads each event's status. Step two: it reads the latency. Step three: only events passing both conditions are kept. An Insights version would filter messages containing the word timeout, then run stats count grouped by five-minute bins to show the trend.

Common mistake: writing a plain-text filter that matches a word in any field, so a user named error triggers an error count. Consequence: a metric filter built on a loose pattern can raise false alarms, while an overly strict one silently counts nothing, leaving the alarm green during a real outage. Pattern accuracy is therefore a reliability concern, not just a tidiness one.

questions.prompt: A checkout service writes JSON events with a level field, but the retry count appears only inside the message text as retry=N. A learner builds this Logs Insights query to find the average retry count for ERROR events in 15-minute buckets: filter level = 'ERROR' | ??? | stats avg(retries) by bin(15m). Which command must fill the blank so that retries exists before stats runs?
choices: stats count() by retries
parse @message 'retry=*' as retries
bin(15m) as retries
sort retries desc
questions.why: The parse command pulls the number out of the free-text message into a named field called retries, which the stats command can then average.

questions.prompt: A team uses the filter pattern 'payment failed' -test on their application log group. Which events does this pattern keep?
choices: Events where the phrase appears in any letter case
Events containing the word test that also include the phrase
Events containing payment or failed, excluding any event with the word test
Exact phrase 'payment failed' and no term test
questions.why: A quoted phrase must appear exactly, and a minus sign excludes a term, so only events with that exact phrase and without test are kept.

questions.prompt: A team counts access denials with the plain-text filter pattern Denied. Their log lines write the word in lowercase as denied. What happens to the count?
choices: Matches lowercase too, because the pattern is a substring test on the whole event
Matches every line that contains any word, so the count is inflated
Matches only when the word is wrapped in quotes inside the event
Matches nothing, since plain terms are case-sensitive
questions.why: A bare word is a case-sensitive substring test, so Denied does not match denied, and the count stays at zero even during a real problem.

questions.prompt: A Logs Insights query must show the number of 404 responses in each ten-minute window. Which command produces both the count and the time buckets?
choices: sort @timestamp by 10m
parse 404 as window
filter bin(10m) = 404
stats count() by bin(10m)
questions.why: The stats command aggregates with count, and grouping by bin(10m) places those counts into ten-minute time buckets, whereas filter, sort and parse do not aggregate or bucket.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between a log filter pattern and a Logs Insights query, and name one limit or tradeoff of using each to investigate an incident.
lessons.modelAnswer: A filter pattern is a rule applied to each log event as a yes or no test. It keeps matching lines, and it is fast for a targeted check, but it can only express conditions on text or on named fields, so it cannot count or group results. A Logs Insights query is an ad hoc pipeline over a chosen time range. It can filter, extract fields, aggregate and bucket by time, which makes it good for answering how often something happened and when. The tradeoff with Insights is cost and scale: it scans the data in the selected groups and time window, so a wide range over large groups is slow and billed by data scanned. The tradeoff with filters is precision: a loose plain-text pattern can match the wrong field and produce false results, so the pattern needs checking against real sample events before anyone trusts it.
rubricPoints: A filter pattern keeps or drops individual events using text, phrase, JSON field or positional rules.
Logs Insights is a piped query over selected log groups and a time range, able to aggregate and bin by time.
Insights costs grow with the data scanned, so a narrow time range and log group selection matter.
A loose filter pattern can match the wrong field and create false results, so test patterns against real events.

suggested.rationale: That mission has the learner hunt for the cause of an API failure in logs, which practises the search-and-narrow skill this objective needs.

lessons.plain: An anomaly detection alarm watches a number, such as how many requests a service handles each minute, and learns what normal looks like for that number, including daily and weekly rises and falls. Instead of you picking one fixed line such as 'alert above 500', the alarm draws a band of expected values around the learned pattern and raises a flag when the number leaves that band. It is useful when normal levels change by hour or by day, because a fixed line would either fire every busy morning or miss real trouble at quiet times.
lessons.guessPrompt: A service handles about 300 requests a minute at 9 am on weekdays and about 20 a minute at 3 am. Why would one fixed alarm line be a poor choice for this service, and what would you want an alarm to compare against instead?
lessons.teach:
A metric is a numeric measurement recorded over time, such as requests per minute. A threshold alarm compares each data point with one fixed number you choose. An anomaly detection alarm instead uses a model that learns the metric's expected pattern from its history, including repeating daily and weekly cycles and slow trends. The model produces an expected band with an upper and a lower boundary around the predicted value. Band width is expressed in standard deviations, a measure of how spread out typical values are, so a wider band fires less often than a narrower one.

Why it works: a fixed line assumes normal never moves. The learned band moves with the cycle, so 9 am traffic is compared with what 9 am usually looks like, not with 3 am. You choose the alarm condition: fire above the upper boundary, below the lower boundary, or outside either. You also set how many consecutive data points must breach before the alarm changes state, which filters out single blips.

Worked example. The metric is requests per minute and the learned band at 9 am on weekdays is roughly 280 to 320. Step 1: at 9:05 the value is 310, inside the band, so the alarm stays OK. Step 2: at 9:10 the value drops to 90, below the lower boundary. The condition is 'less than lower boundary' with 3 of 3 datapoints required, so the first breach only starts the count. Step 3: if the next two also breach, the alarm enters ALARM and notifies the on-call topic. A single dip would page nobody.

Common mistake: treating the model as a replacement for history. A new metric has little data, so its band is wide and unreliable and the alarm can stay quiet when it should not. Another mistake is alarming in both directions when only a drop matters, which doubles the noise.

Consequence: a slow loss of capacity can be absorbed into the learned baseline over weeks, so the band moves with the problem and the alarm stays silent. Pair anomaly alarms with a fixed limit for any ceiling you can never accept.

questions.prompt: A food-delivery app tracks orders per minute on Sunday evenings. Its learned band at 8:00 pm is about 140 to 175 orders per minute. The alarm fires when the value goes below the lower boundary, and it requires 2 of 2 datapoints to breach. Step 1: at 8:00 pm the value is 160, inside the band, so the alarm stays OK. Step 2: at 8:05 pm the value falls to 95, below the lower boundary. This is the first breach, so the count starts but the alarm does not change state. Step 3 (missing): at 8:10 pm the value is 98, still below the lower boundary. The alarm is now in which state?
choices: Still OK, because the alarm waits for a full hour of breaches
INSUFFICIENT_DATA, because the band was learned only from weekday data
ALARM, because the second consecutive breach meets the 2 of 2 requirement
ALARM, but only if the upper boundary is also breached
questions.why: The alarm needs two consecutive breaches, and the 8:05 and 8:10 points are both below the lower boundary, so the alarm changes to ALARM.

questions.prompt: A team runs a message queue for a ticketing site. Which statement best describes the difference between a fixed threshold alarm and an anomaly detection alarm?
choices: Both alarms compare against one number, but the anomaly alarm uses a larger number
A fixed threshold compares each point with one chosen number, while an anomaly alarm compares it with a band learned from history that moves with cycles
An anomaly alarm only works for metrics that never change, so it ignores daily cycles
A fixed threshold alarm learns the expected pattern, while an anomaly alarm uses one number chosen by hand
questions.why: A threshold alarm uses one fixed number, whereas an anomaly alarm uses a learned band that shifts with repeating daily and weekly patterns and slow trends.

questions.prompt: A new internal payment API has been live for three days, and its anomaly alarm shows a very wide band. A colleague says the alarm is reliable because it uses a learned model. What is the best response?
choices: The colleague is right, since the model is reliable from the first hour of data
Set the datapoint count to 1 so the wide band fires more often
Delete the metric, because wide bands always mean the data is corrupt
Keep it, but expect quiet misses; add a fixed limit for any ceiling you can never accept
questions.why: A new metric has little history, so its band is wide and unreliable and can miss real problems, so a fixed limit should cover any ceiling that must never be exceeded.

questions.prompt: An storage team's anomaly alarm on write latency has stayed silent for six weeks while latency has climbed steadily. Which is the most likely cause?
choices: The datapoint count was set to 1, so single blips paged the on-call team each time
The alarm was set to fire in both directions, which hides drops in latency
The learned band drifted upward with the slow trend, so the rise looked normal
Anomaly alarms cannot monitor latency metrics at all because latency is not a count
questions.why: A slow loss of performance can be absorbed into the learned baseline over weeks, so the band moves with the problem and the alarm stays silent.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate wants to replace our fixed 500-requests-per-minute alarm with an anomaly detection alarm on the same metric. Explain to them what the new alarm does differently, and name one limit or tradeoff they should weigh before switching.
lessons.modelAnswer: The fixed alarm fires whenever the requests-per-minute count goes above 500, regardless of the time of day. An anomaly detection alarm instead learns the metric's normal pattern from its history, including daily and weekly cycles, and builds an expected band. It fires when the value leaves that band, so a busy 9 am is judged against typical 9 am traffic rather than one number. The tradeoffs are that the model needs enough history to be reliable, so a new or irregular metric gets a wide, weak band; the band width and the number of datapoints required to alarm control how often it fires and must be tuned; and because the baseline adapts, a slow decline can be learned as normal. For a hard ceiling we can never accept, I would keep a fixed threshold alarm alongside it.
rubricPoints: Explains that the anomaly alarm compares values to a learned expected band rather than a fixed number.
Notes that the band follows daily and weekly patterns, so time-of-day normal is handled.
Names a real limit such as needing enough history or a wide band on new metrics.
Mentions that slow drift can be absorbed into the baseline, so a fixed limit may still be needed.

suggested.rationale: Choosing band width, condition direction and datapoint counts is best practised by building alarms against a metric, which the planned metric alarm builder would let you do.

lessons.plain: When a computer system is in trouble, it usually leaves signs before users complain. This objective is about knowing which signs matter most. Three common ones are how hard a virtual server's processor is working, how many disk requests are piling up waiting for a database's storage, and how often a load balancer hands out server-error responses. Each is a number collected over time, and an alarm watches it and reacts when it crosses a line you chose. The skill is picking the right signal for the symptom, not collecting everything.
lessons.guessPrompt: A web application's servers show 95% CPU for ten minutes, but users say pages still load normally. Would you wake someone up immediately, and what other number would you check before deciding?
lessons.teach:
A metric is a number recorded at regular intervals, such as a server's CPU percentage each minute. A threshold is the line a metric is compared against. An alarm is a rule that watches one metric and changes state when the value stays past its threshold for a set number of consecutive periods. A period is one fixed interval of time, such as one minute. Three signals are central here.

EC2 CPU utilization, where EC2 is Amazon's virtual server service, is the share of a server's processor in use. It shows whether compute is the bottleneck. A high number alone is not proof of a fault, because a server doing planned batch work at full speed is healthy. Read it together with latency or queueing.

RDS queue length, where RDS is the managed relational database service, is usually measured as disk queue depth: the count of storage requests waiting to be served. A growing queue means storage is slower than demand, which delays every query behind it.

Application Load Balancer 5xx errors count server-error responses. A 5xx code means the server side failed. The count can come from the load balancer itself, for example when no healthy target exists, or from a target, meaning the application behind the balancer. Separating the two tells you whether to look at the balancer's health checks or at application code.

Worked example: a target 5xx alarm has a threshold of 10 per minute and needs three consecutive periods. Counts of 40, 3, then 40 reset the streak, so nothing fires. Counts of 40, 40, 40 move the alarm to ALARM on the third period, so one blip does not page anyone.

Common mistake: alarming on CPU alone with a threshold picked by guesswork, so the alarm fires during normal peaks and people learn to ignore it.

Consequence: when the database disk queue climbs during a traffic surge, query latency rises for every service that depends on it, and the first visible symptom is often a rise in load balancer 5xx errors.

questions.prompt: A checkout API sits behind an Application Load Balancer. Its target 5xx alarm has a threshold of 25 per minute and needs 4 consecutive periods. Period 1 counts 30 (above threshold, streak 1). Period 2 counts 30 (streak 2). Period 3 counts 30 (streak 3). Period 4 counts 12, which is below the threshold, so the streak resets to 0. Periods 5, 6, 7 and 8 each count 30. In which period does the alarm move to ALARM?
choices: Period 9, because the alarm waits one extra period after a reset
Period 5, because the streak restarts from the first high count after the reset
Period 7, because only three high periods follow the reset
Period 8, because the fourth consecutive high period after the reset is period 8
questions.why: After the reset at period 4, the streak counts 1 at period 5, 2 at period 6, 3 at period 7 and 4 at period 8, so the alarm enters ALARM at period 8.

questions.prompt: A reporting database on a managed relational service shows low CPU but its disk queue depth climbs steadily through the afternoon. What does the growing queue most directly indicate?
choices: The database has too many idle connections and needs a larger instance class
The processor is the bottleneck and queries are being scheduled unevenly
The load balancer is returning more server errors because of the database
Storage requests are arriving faster than the disk can serve them, so queries wait behind the backlog
questions.why: Disk queue depth counts storage requests waiting to be served, so a steadily growing queue means storage is slower than demand, which delays every query behind it.

questions.prompt: A video encoding fleet runs at 96% CPU for two hours each night while job completion times and queue wait times stay flat and within target. An engineer proposes an alarm that pages on-call whenever CPU exceeds 90%. What is the main flaw?
choices: The alarm will page for planned full-speed work that is healthy, so people will learn to ignore it
Alarms can only be attached to load balancer metrics, not instance metrics
Ninety percent is always too low a threshold for any server
CPU percentage cannot be collected by monitoring at all on batch servers
questions.why: High CPU during planned batch work is healthy, and CPU alone does not show a fault, so a CPU-only alarm fires during normal operation and trains people to ignore it.

questions.prompt: An Application Load Balancer starts returning 503 responses for a new service. Its target group shows zero healthy targets, and the application logs show no requests reaching the code. Where should the investigation start?
choices: In the database, looking for slow queries that caused the targets to time out
At the load balancer side, checking target registration and health check configuration
In the application code, looking for an unhandled exception in the request handler
By increasing the alarm period so the 503s are averaged out
questions.why: A 5xx produced with no healthy target originates from the load balancer itself, so the health checks and target registration are where to look rather than application code.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why a team should not alarm on CPU alone. Name one limit of each of the three signals that you would still have to check before acting on an alarm.
lessons.modelAnswer: CPU alone tells you a processor is busy, not that users are suffering. A server can run at high CPU during planned, healthy work, so an alarm on that number alone fires on normal peaks and gets ignored. A better alarm pairs CPU with a user-facing symptom, such as latency or error rate, and uses a threshold tied to real capacity, held for several periods. Each signal has limits. High CPU can hide a waiting-on-I/O problem, so check it alongside other measures. A growing RDS disk queue depends on the storage type and workload, so compare it to a baseline. Load balancer 5xx errors need the split between balancer-generated and target-generated counts, because the fix differs. A single number never settles the diagnosis.
rubricPoints: Explains that CPU alone does not show user impact and can fire during healthy peak work
Notes that alarms should combine a signal with a user-facing symptom and sustained periods
Names a limit of CPU utilization, such as hiding I/O waits
Explains that RDS disk queue depth must be read against a baseline and workload
Distinguishes load-balancer-generated from target-generated 5xx errors and why the split matters

suggested.rationale: Choosing which signal and threshold should page someone is best practised by building alarm rules against changing metric values.

lessons.plain: Some monitoring does not watch how fast things run. It watches whether things are safe and set up correctly. Amazon Inspector looks for known software weaknesses on servers and container images and reports each one as a finding. AWS Config keeps a record of how each resource is configured over time and checks those settings against rules you choose, such as 'storage must not be public.' Both produce signals you can route to alarms or automatic fixes, so a problem gets noticed without a person having to go looking for it.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a server is running software with a known security flaw, or a storage bucket was made public last Tuesday, how would you find out without someone checking by hand? What would need to run in the background to notice it?
lessons.teach: A finding is a single problem report, such as a software weakness on one server. A resource is any cloud object you manage, such as a server, a bucket, or a database. Amazon Inspector is a vulnerability scanner: it checks servers, container images, and some functions against lists of known weaknesses and creates a finding for each match. Older Inspector setups used assessment templates, which are saved scan definitions that say what to assess, which rule sets to use, and how long to run. The current service scans continuously, so you should know the concept of a saved scan definition for exam questions, but do not assume every account still uses templates. AWS Config records a configuration item, which is a snapshot of one resource's settings each time they change. A Config rule is a check that compares those settings with a desired state. A managed rule is prebuilt by AWS; a custom rule is one you write. Each resource gets a compliance status, compliant or non-compliant. Rules evaluate on configuration change, on a schedule, or both. A remediation action can run an automation document to correct the setting. Worked example: a rule requires buckets to block public access. At 10:02 someone changes bucket B. Config records the change, the rule evaluates, and B becomes non-compliant. The attached remediation re-enables the block, and B returns to compliant, while the history still shows the change. Common mistake: treating a compliance status or a finding as the fix itself. Neither changes anything unless an action is wired to it. If findings only sit on a dashboard, nobody is woken, so route them to an alarm or an event rule.

questions.prompt: A platform team uses a Config rule that requires every load balancer to carry an owner tag. Here is how one change plays out in a different account. At 09:15 an engineer creates load balancer LB-4 with no owner tag. Config records a configuration item for LB-4 showing the new settings. The tag rule evaluates that item and marks LB-4 non-compliant. Step four is missing. Which step completes the chain so that LB-4 actually gets its owner tag?
choices: The compliance dashboard refreshes and shows LB-4 in red, which adds the tag automatically.
The configuration item for LB-4 is overwritten so the history of the missing tag disappears.
Config deletes LB-4 because it breaks the rule, and the engineer must recreate it with the tag.
A remediation action runs an automation document that adds the owner tag, and the rule then evaluates LB-4 again as compliant.
questions.why: A compliance status changes nothing by itself, so the tag is only added when a remediation action is attached to the rule and runs an automation document that corrects the setting.

questions.prompt: In AWS Config, what does a configuration item represent?
choices: A snapshot of one resource's settings, recorded each time those settings change.
A running alarm that fires when a resource drifts from its desired state.
A prebuilt check that AWS maintains for common security settings.
A saved scan definition that says which rule sets to use and how long to run.
questions.why: The teaching text defines a configuration item as a snapshot of one resource's settings each time they change, which is different from alarms, managed rules, and saved scan definitions.

questions.prompt: A security scanner has produced a critical finding on a fleet of web servers, and the finding is visible on the console dashboard. Nobody on call has been contacted. What is the most accurate explanation?
choices: Findings always page the on-call engineer automatically, so the scanner must have failed to send it.
The scanner has already fixed the weakness, and the dashboard is just a record of past repairs.
The finding is only on a dashboard, so nothing wakes anyone; it needs to be routed to an alarm or an event rule.
The finding is stored as a configuration item, which only sends alerts when the resource is deleted.
questions.why: The teaching text says findings sitting on a dashboard do not wake anyone, and they must be connected to an alarm or event rule so that someone is notified.

questions.prompt: A team has a Config rule that checks whether a database has automated backups turned on. The team wants the rule to be checked only once a day at midnight, and not every time a setting changes. Which evaluation setting matches this requirement, and what kind of rule is it if the team wrote the logic themselves?
choices: Evaluate on a schedule only, which makes it a custom rule when the team writes the logic.
Evaluate on configuration change and on a schedule, which makes it a managed rule.
Evaluate on a schedule only, which makes it a managed rule because AWS prebuilt it.
Evaluate on configuration change only, which makes it a managed rule by default.
questions.why: Rules can evaluate on a schedule, on configuration change, or both, and a rule is custom when you write it yourself rather than using one prebuilt by AWS.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what Amazon Inspector and AWS Config each contribute as monitoring inputs, and name one limit or tradeoff of relying on them for detection.
lessons.modelAnswer: Amazon Inspector scans workloads such as servers and container images for known vulnerabilities and produces findings, so it tells you what is weak in the software. AWS Config records how each resource is configured and evaluates rules against those settings, so it tells you when something drifted from the required state and keeps the history of the change. Both are inputs, not responses: a finding or a non-compliant status does nothing by itself until an alarm, event rule, or remediation action picks it up. One limit is that Inspector only knows about weaknesses in its catalogue, so an unknown flaw or a misconfigured custom app can pass unnoticed. Config rules are only as good as the rules you chose, and periodic evaluations can leave a gap between the change and the detection.
rubricPoints: Inspector reports vulnerabilities in workloads such as servers and container images as findings.
AWS Config records resource configuration history and evaluates it against rules with a compliance status.
Findings and non-compliant statuses are inputs that need an alarm, event rule, or remediation to act on them.
A stated limit: Inspector only detects known weaknesses, and Config only checks the rules you chose.

suggested.rationale: Deciding which findings and non-compliant states should trigger an alarm or automatic fix is an exam-style scenario that benefits from reasoning through a situation, and no listed mission covers it directly.

lessons.plain: CloudTrail is a record-keeping service for a cloud account. Every time someone or something uses the account to do a task, such as creating a server, changing a permission, or deleting a firewall rule, the service writes a note saying who did it, when, from where, and whether it worked. Each note is one event. Later, these notes let you answer what changed, who changed it, and whether it was allowed. Think of it as the visitor log and security camera for a building.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a colleague says a production firewall rule was deleted last night, what details would you want written down so you could find out who did it, when, and from which machine?
lessons.teach:
CloudTrail is the AWS service that records API activity. An API call is a request sent to a cloud service to do something, whether it comes from the web console, the command line, an SDK, or another AWS service acting for you. Each recorded request becomes a log event, a structured JSON record. The key fields are eventTime (when), eventSource (which service, such as EC2), eventName (the action, such as DeleteSecurityGroup), userIdentity (the caller: a person, a role, or a service), sourceIPAddress (where the call came from), requestParameters (what was asked for), and errorCode (present only when the call failed).

Events come in two broad kinds. Management events record control-plane actions such as creating or changing resources. They are recorded by default. Data events record high-volume actions on the data itself, such as reading an object in S3 or invoking a Lambda function. They are not recorded unless you turn them on, and they cost extra.

Why it works: the service sits in front of the API, so the platform writes down every accepted or rejected request, independent of the application being watched. Event history in the console keeps 90 days of management events. A trail is the configuration that keeps events longer. A trail delivers compressed log files to an S3 bucket, can cover all regions, and can send events to CloudWatch Logs so alarms can match on them.

Worked example: at 02:14 a security group is deleted. Step 1: filter for eventName DeleteSecurityGroup. Step 2: read userIdentity, which shows an assumed role named deploy-bot with session name ci-42. Step 3: check sourceIPAddress and errorCode; the error field is empty, so the call succeeded. Step 4: compare eventTime with the change window. You now know who, what, when, and whether it worked.

Common mistake: assuming that because CloudTrail is switched on, every action is recorded. Event history only covers 90 days of management events, and data events need an explicit trail setting.

Consequence: if no trail exists before an incident, the evidence is gone after 90 days, and an investigation can only describe the damage, not explain how it happened.

questions.prompt: A payments team at a retail company wants to know which roles read objects from its invoice S3 bucket last Friday. Their procedure is: Step 1, open the trail and confirm its settings. Step 2, ____. Step 3, filter the log events for eventName GetObject. Step 4, read userIdentity to identify the calling role. They skipped the missing step, searched the event history, and got no results for last Friday. Which entry correctly fills Step 2?
choices: Confirm that data events for the invoice bucket were turned on in the trail before last Friday, because object reads are only logged that way.
Check that the errorCode field is empty on every GetObject event so only successful reads are listed.
Check that the bucket's management events are kept for at least 90 days in the trail's S3 bucket.
Compare the eventTime of each read with the company's Friday change window before filtering.
questions.why: Object reads are data events, which are only recorded when the trail has them switched on, so without that setting the reads were never written as log events and the search correctly came back empty.

questions.prompt: In a CloudTrail log event, which field tells you the caller, meaning the person, role, or service that made the request?
choices: sourceIPAddress, which shows the network address the request came from
requestParameters, which lists what the request asked for
userIdentity, which identifies the caller as a person, role, or service
eventSource, which names the service the request was sent to
questions.why: The userIdentity field holds the caller's identity, which the teaching text describes as a person, a role, or a service.

questions.prompt: A bank's audit team wants to find every API call that the platform rejected during the last week. Which field should they filter on?
choices: userIdentity, because rejected calls are always tied to a role and the role list shows every failure
errorCode, because it is present only when a call failed, so its presence marks a rejected request
eventSource, because it shows which service each rejected request went to and so separates failures by service
eventName, because each rejected request has its own action name that is different from accepted ones
questions.why: The errorCode field appears only on failed calls, so filtering for events that carry it finds the rejected requests.

questions.prompt: A clinic set up a trail that records only management events and delivers them to an S3 bucket. A year later they assume every read of their patient-record bucket was logged. Which statement is accurate?
choices: Management events are kept in the bucket beyond 90 days, but object reads were not recorded because data events were never turned on.
Nothing from the year was recorded at all, because a trail with only management events records nothing until data events are switched on.
The event history in the console keeps all their S3 reads for a year, since the trail covers the full account.
Data events such as S3 object reads were recorded automatically because S3 is a storage service and always logs reads.
questions.why: Management events are recorded by default and a trail can keep them longer than the 90-day event history, but S3 object reads are data events that need an explicit setting, so they are absent.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says CloudTrail tells us everything that happened on our servers. Explain to them, in your own words, what CloudTrail actually records, and name one limit or tradeoff they should plan for.
lessons.modelAnswer: CloudTrail records API activity in the account: each request to create, change, read, or delete a resource, along with who made it, when, from where, and whether it succeeded. It does not record what happens inside the operating system or the application. It will show that someone changed a security group, but not the commands they typed on a server afterward; for that you need server-side logs. The main tradeoffs: management events are recorded by default, but data events such as S3 object reads are off until enabled and add cost. Event history keeps only 90 days, so we need a trail delivering to a protected S3 bucket if we want longer retention. The log files also contain sensitive request parameters, so they need encryption and restricted access.
rubricPoints: CloudTrail records API calls to the account, including who, when, source, action, and success or failure
It does not capture activity inside the operating system or application itself
Management events are on by default while data events must be enabled and cost extra
Event history covers only 90 days, so a trail delivering to S3 is needed for longer retention

suggested.rationale: This objective is mostly facts about event fields, event types, and trail settings, which are best learned by reading the teaching text and then the product documentation.

lessons.plain: A monitoring dashboard is a single screen that gathers the charts you need to judge whether a system is healthy: request counts, error counts, response times, queue depths. Each chart is a widget that reads a measurement collected over time and draws it for a chosen time window. The skill is choosing the few charts that answer the question someone on shift will ask first, and presenting them so a short spike cannot hide inside an average. Dashboards are for looking; they do not wake anyone up. A related tool, QuickSight, builds richer business-style reports from larger data sets for people who are not on call.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your service handled about 1,000 requests a minute all night. For two minutes, 30 percent of requests failed. You open a chart that shows the average error rate over each 15-minute block. Would you expect that chart to make the two bad minutes obvious, and why or why not?
lessons.teach:
A dashboard, in this context, is a saved page of widgets. Each widget shows one metric (a numeric measurement collected over time, such as an error count) or the result of a log query, drawn across a time range you choose. A period is the length of each bucket into which the service groups raw data points, such as one minute or five minutes. A statistic is the function applied inside each bucket: Sum, Average, Maximum, or a percentile such as p99. A dashboard does not decide whether something is wrong. It lets a person see the shape of the data quickly.

Why it works: a chart is only as honest as its statistic and period. Averages hide spikes, and long periods smooth short bursts into a flat line.

Worked example. Raw data is an error count per minute: 0, 0, 40, 0, 0. The widget uses a five-minute period and the Average statistic. Step one: the five raw points fall into one bucket. Step two: the average is (0+0+40+0+0) divided by 5, which is 8. Step three: the chart shows 8 errors per minute, a modest bump. Step four: switch the statistic to Sum. The bucket now shows 40, a clear event. Same data, different story.

Common mistake: putting Average on a count metric and assuming the chart shows the full picture, or leaving the default period when the incident lasted two minutes.

Consequence: during an incident, the on-call engineer reads a flat-looking chart, concludes the problem is small, and delays escalation while customers keep failing.

QuickSight is a separate reporting service. It reads prepared data sets, lets analysts build visuals and share them with non-engineers, and suits trends over days or weeks rather than live operations. Use dashboards in the first minutes of an incident and reports in the review afterward.

questions.prompt: A payments team plots failed card charges per minute for eight minutes: 1, 0, 0, 0, 9, 0, 0, 1. The widget uses a four-minute period, so the eight raw points form two buckets: minutes 1 to 4 and minutes 5 to 8. A bucket is one group of raw data points that the service combines into a single chart value. Step one: the first bucket holds 1, 0, 0, 0. Step two: with the Average statistic, the first bucket shows (1+0+0+0) divided by 4, which is 0.25. Step three is missing. The team switches the statistic to Sum and reads the second bucket, which holds 9, 0, 0, 1. What does the widget show for the second bucket?
choices: 2.5 failed charges
10 failed charges
9 failed charges
1 failed charge
questions.why: Sum adds every point in the bucket, so 9 + 0 + 0 + 1 gives 10 failed charges, which is the spike the Average statistic had flattened.

questions.prompt: A percentile such as p99 is a statistic. What does the p99 statistic report for a bucket of latency values?
choices: The value below which 99 percent of the values in the bucket fall
The average of the slowest 1 percent of values in the bucket
The lowest latency value in the bucket
The total of all latency values in the bucket
questions.why: A p99 percentile is the value that 99 percent of the bucket's data points fall at or below, so it exposes the slow tail that an average hides.

questions.prompt: A disk-usage metric is recorded every 30 seconds. An engineer wants a dashboard widget to keep a 90-second disk spike clearly visible rather than smoothing it away. Which period should the widget use?
choices: Fifteen-minute period
One-minute period
One-hour period
Five-minute period
questions.why: A period is the bucket length, and the shorter the bucket the less a brief burst is blended into surrounding quiet time, so a one-minute period keeps the spike visible better than the longer options.

questions.prompt: During the first five minutes of a production outage, an on-call engineer needs to see how the error count is changing right now. Which choice fits this need best?
choices: A QuickSight visual built from a prepared data set that is refreshed weekly
A CloudWatch widget using the Average statistic over a one-hour period
A CloudWatch dashboard widget on the error count metric with a one-minute period
A QuickSight monthly trend report shared with the finance team
questions.why: CloudWatch dashboards suit live operations because they show raw metrics over short periods, whereas QuickSight reads prepared data sets and suits trends over days or weeks, and a one-hour average would hide a short burst.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why a CloudWatch dashboard that looks calm can still hide an outage, and name one limit of dashboards compared with alarms.
lessons.modelAnswer: A dashboard only shows what its widgets compute, so the statistic and period decide what you see. If a count metric is drawn as an Average over a five-minute period, a burst of 40 errors in one minute shows up as about 8 per minute, which looks like noise. The outage is in the data but the chart has flattened it. The fix is to pick Sum for counts, use a period short enough to match the incident, and check the raw numbers when something looks off. One limit of dashboards is that they need a person looking at them. Nothing on a dashboard notifies anyone or takes action. That job belongs to alarms, which evaluate a condition continuously and can notify a team automatically. A dashboard is a tool for understanding during an incident; an alarm is what gets someone there.
rubricPoints: A dashboard widget shows a metric or query result using a chosen statistic and period.
Averages and long periods can hide short spikes; the statistic must match the data type.
Dashboards need a person to look at them and do not notify or act on their own; alarms do that.
QuickSight suits business-style reports and trends, not live operational watching.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine practises building dashboards, so reading the console-level concepts and checking the chart statistics is the most direct route.

lessons.plain: An alarm is a watcher that keeps checking one number over time. That number is a metric, a measurement such as how busy a server's processor is or how many requests failed in the last minute. Some metrics come built in from AWS services, such as the CPU reading for a virtual server. Others are custom metrics that your own application or a monitoring agent sends in, such as the number of orders waiting in a queue inside your app. When the number stays past a line you chose for long enough, the alarm changes state and can trigger a response, such as sending a message to a person or starting a scaling action. Picking the right metric, and telling the alarm exactly where to find it, decides whether the alarm ever means anything.
lessons.guessPrompt: A service's error count jumps sharply for one minute and then returns to normal. Should an alarm page someone immediately, and what setting would you change so a single brief spike does not cause a page?
lessons.teach:
An alarm is a rule that watches one metric and changes state when the metric crosses a threshold. It finds its metric using four details. The namespace is the container the metric lives in, such as AWS/EC2 for built-in service metrics or a name you choose for your own. The metric name is the measurement itself, such as CPUUtilization. Dimensions are name-value tags that select one specific series, such as InstanceId equal to one server's ID. The alarm's dimensions must match the dimensions the metric was published with exactly, or the alarm watches an empty series.

Standard metrics are published automatically by AWS services. Custom metrics are published by your own code or by an agent you install, using the same namespace, name and dimension model. A metric is published at standard resolution (one data point per minute) or high resolution (as fast as one second). The alarm sets its own period, the window over which data points are combined with a statistic such as Average, Sum or Maximum. The period must be a multiple of the metric's resolution.

Why it works: each period produces one value. The alarm compares that value with a threshold using an operator such as greater than 80. It enters ALARM only after a set number of consecutive breaching periods, called evaluation periods. This stops one noisy spike from waking someone.

Worked example: an alarm on CPUUtilization for one instance, statistic Average, period 300 seconds, threshold 80, three evaluation periods. Step 1: every five minutes the service averages the instance's readings. Step 2: a window averaging 85 is a breach. Step 3: three breaches in a row set the alarm to ALARM. Step 4: two healthy windows afterwards return it to OK.

Common mistake: a custom metric is published with dimension Host set to web-1, but the alarm asks for Host set to web-01. The alarm reads no data, shows INSUFFICIENT_DATA, and stays silent.

Consequence: in a running system, a silent alarm looks the same as a healthy one until an incident occurs, so dimension matching must be checked when the metric is published.

questions.prompt: A payments team publishes a custom metric named RefundsQueued in the namespace Ledger/Payments, with one dimension Region set to eu-west-2. The metric is published at standard resolution, so one data point arrives per minute. The alarm uses statistic Sum, period 60 seconds, threshold greater than 25, and 2 evaluation periods. Trace it. Step 1: each minute the service adds up the refunds published in that minute. Step 2: minute A sums to 31, which is a breach. Step 3: minute B sums to 12, which is not a breach, so the run of consecutive breaches resets. Step 4: minute C sums to 40 and minute D sums to 27, both breaches. Step 5 is missing: state what the alarm does at the end of minute D.
choices: The alarm shows INSUFFICIENT_DATA, because Sum cannot be used with a Region dimension
The alarm enters ALARM at minute C, because a single breach is enough when the period is 60 seconds
The alarm goes to OK, because a Sum above 25 is only meaningful when averaged over the hour
The alarm enters ALARM, because two consecutive breaching periods meet the evaluation count
questions.why: The alarm needs 2 consecutive breaching periods, and minutes C and D are two breaches in a row, so it enters ALARM at the end of minute D.

questions.prompt: A checkout team publishes a custom metric in the namespace Shop/Checkout with two dimensions: Service set to checkout-api and Stage set to prod. Their alarm is configured with only Service set to checkout-api. What does the alarm see?
choices: The alarm reads the most recent value across all stages
The alarm enters ALARM once the threshold is crossed in either stage
The alarm matches the metric because one matching dimension is enough
The alarm watches an empty series and reads no data, since its dimensions must match the published dimensions exactly
questions.why: An alarm's dimensions must match the published dimensions exactly, so an alarm missing the Stage dimension watches an empty series and reads no data.

questions.prompt: A team publishes a custom metric at standard resolution and wants an alarm period of 90 seconds. Which statement is correct?
choices: Valid, since 90 is a multiple of 30 and the alarm accepts it
Invalid, since custom metrics can only use periods of five minutes or more
Valid, since the alarm can combine data over any window length
Invalid, since the period must be a multiple of 60 for standard resolution
questions.why: Standard resolution produces one data point per minute, so the period must be a multiple of 60 seconds, and 90 is not.

questions.prompt: An alarm uses a 60-second period, a threshold breach rule, and 4 evaluation periods. Breaches occur in minutes 2, 3 and 4. Minute 5 is healthy. Breaches then occur in minutes 6, 7, 8 and 9. At which minute does the alarm first enter ALARM?
choices: Minute 4
Minute 8
Minute 6
Minute 9
questions.why: Minutes 6 through 9 are four consecutive breaches, which meets the evaluation count; the earlier run of three was broken by healthy minute 5 and never reached four.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a CloudWatch alarm decides it is in ALARM state, and name one limit or tradeoff of using a very short period with only one evaluation period.
lessons.modelAnswer: The alarm picks one metric by its namespace, name and dimensions. Each period, the service combines the raw data points in that window using the chosen statistic, such as Average. It compares the result to the threshold. If the number of consecutive breaching periods reaches the evaluation count, the alarm moves to ALARM and runs its actions. Otherwise it stays OK or shows INSUFFICIENT_DATA when no data arrives. The tradeoff with a short period and one evaluation period is speed versus noise. The alarm reacts quickly, but a brief spike, a single unusual sample, or a gap in publishing can trigger it. You can reduce false pages by using more evaluation periods, a longer period, or a statistic that smooths the data, though each of those makes the alarm slower to notice a real problem.
rubricPoints: The alarm is tied to one metric by namespace, metric name and dimensions
The period combines raw data points with a statistic, and each period yields one value compared to the threshold
Evaluation periods require consecutive breaches, which filters out brief spikes
Short periods with few evaluation periods react fast but produce more false alarms

suggested.rationale: A planned metric alarm builder would let the learner set namespace, dimensions, statistic, period and evaluation count and watch the state change, which is the core skill here.

lessons.plain: When one user request passes through several services, such as an API front door, a function, and a container, it can be hard to tell which step was slow or failed. AWS X-Ray is a tracing service that follows a single request across those hops and draws a timeline of where the time went. Setting it up means switching on tracing at each point the request passes through and making sure the trace data is collected and sent on. This objective covers doing that for containers, the API Gateway front door, and Lambda functions.
lessons.guessPrompt: A user says checkout takes 9 seconds. The request goes through an API gateway, then a Lambda function, then a database call. Before any teaching, what single piece of information would you most want to see to find which step caused the delay, and why?
lessons.teach:
A trace is the full record of one request as it moves through your system. Each service that handles the request records a segment, which is its own timed piece of work. Smaller timed operations inside a segment, such as one database call, are subsegments. X-Ray is the AWS service that stores and displays these pieces. The X-Ray daemon is a small background program, listening on a network port (UDP 2000 by default), that receives segment data from your application and forwards it to X-Ray. A sidecar is a helper container that runs beside your main container in the same task. The trace header is a small tag, named X-Amzn-Trace-Id, carried with the request so every service attaches its work to the same trace.

Why it works: each service reads the incoming header and passes it on, so separate timelines join into one picture. Sampling decides how many requests are recorded. By default X-Ray records a small share, not every request, which keeps cost down.

Setup by place. For Lambda, turn on active tracing in the function configuration and give the execution role permission to write trace data. For API Gateway, enable X-Ray tracing on the stage; it starts the first segment and forwards the header to the backend. For containers, run the daemon as a sidecar in the task on ECS, or as one daemon per node on EKS, and give the task or pod role write permissions.

Worked example. A request enters API Gateway, which records segment 1 at 9.1 s total. It forwards the header to the function, which records segment 2 at 8.8 s. Inside the function, a database subsegment takes 8.5 s. The timeline places the delay in the database call, not in the gateway.

Common mistake: enabling tracing on the gateway but not the function, so the trace stops at the first hop. Another is forgetting the container's role permission. Nothing fails visibly; the traces simply never appear.

Consequence: a missing header or a missing daemon produces fragmented traces, so the slow step looks like a gap instead of a named cause.

questions.prompt: A team runs a refund service as an AWS Lambda function behind an Amazon API Gateway stage. They have done two of three setup steps: they turned on tracing on the API Gateway stage, which starts the first segment and forwards the trace header, and they turned on active tracing in the function configuration.
