They have not yet given the function's execution role permission to write trace data. Their dashboard shows the gateway segment but no function segment at all. Which action completes the setup?
choices: Raise the sampling rate so every request is recorded, which forces the function segments to appear
Give the function's execution role permission to write trace data
Create a second API Gateway stage with its own tracing setting and send traffic there
Turn off tracing on the API Gateway stage so the header is sent only once
questions.why: The function's execution role must be allowed to write trace data, because without that permission the function's segments fail to reach X-Ray silently, which is the setup gap the text describes.

questions.prompt: A Lambda function's segment in a trace shows 3.2 seconds in total. Inside it, one call to an external pricing service is recorded as a subsegment lasting 2.9 seconds. What does this trace tell you?
choices: The function is fine and the 2.9 seconds is sampling noise
The trace is incomplete because subsegments cannot be nested inside a function's segment
The gateway in front of the function is responsible for most of the delay
The subsegment for the external call is where most of the time goes, so that is the first place to investigate
questions.why: A subsegment is a smaller timed operation inside a segment, so a 2.9-second subsegment inside a 3.2-second function segment places the delay in that external call.

questions.prompt: A container service on Amazon ECS runs the X-Ray daemon as a sidecar in the same task, but the task role was never given permission to write trace data. The application itself runs without errors and returns normal responses. What do the operators most likely see?
choices: A trace showing the daemon as the slowest segment in every request
Traces that never appear in the X-Ray console, with no visible failure in the application
An error in the application logs saying the daemon refused the connection
Automatic fallback to sending the segments directly over HTTP without any permission check
questions.why: Missing role permissions fail silently, so the application keeps working while the traces simply never show up in X-Ray, as the text warns.

questions.prompt: A team turns on tracing for an API Gateway stage, but the Lambda function behind it still has active tracing turned off. A user request takes about 6 seconds end to end. What will the team most likely see in X-Ray?
choices: A trace that stops at the gateway segment, leaving the function's time as an unexplained gap
No trace at all, because tracing must be enabled on both services to record anything
A trace with the 6 seconds attributed entirely to the function
A complete trace with the function segment added automatically by the gateway
questions.why: The gateway starts the first segment and forwards the header, but without tracing on the function no second segment is recorded, so the trace breaks at the first hop and the function's time looks like a gap.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, how you would turn on X-Ray tracing for a request that goes from API Gateway to Lambda to a container. Name one limit or tradeoff of the setup.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would treat it as three switches plus a collector. Turn on tracing on the API Gateway stage, turn on active tracing on the Lambda function, and run the X-Ray daemon beside the container, with the task or pod role allowed to write trace data. Each service passes the trace header along, so the three pieces join into one trace. The tradeoff is sampling: X-Ray records only a share of requests by default, so a rare slow request may not be captured unless we adjust the sampling rule. A second limit is that a trace shows where time went but not why a step was slow. For that we still need logs or metrics.
rubricPoints: Tracing must be enabled at each hop: the API Gateway stage, Lambda active tracing, and the container.
The trace header links the segments from each service into one trace.
Containers need the X-Ray daemon running and write permissions on the task or pod role.
Sampling means not every request is recorded, so rare slow requests can be missed.

suggested.rationale: The objective is per-service configuration facts that no current or planned hands-on mission directly exercises, so reading the setup for each service fits best.

lessons.plain: Think of a stream of log lines from many servers as a river that never stops. Amazon Kinesis Data Streams is a managed AWS service that catches that river, keeps the water in order for a while, and lets people downstream read it as it flows. Instead of waiting for a file to be written at the end of the day, a team can watch errors appear within seconds. This matters because monitoring that arrives late often arrives after the damage is done. You need to know what a stream is made of, how records get sorted into lanes, what happens when one lane fills up, and how to tell whether the readers are keeping pace.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team wants error counts on a dashboard within seconds of each error, but their logs are only exported to a file once an hour. Why does that delay defeat the goal, and what kind of pipeline would you put in its place?
lessons.teach:
Amazon Kinesis Data Streams is a managed service on AWS that accepts a continuous flow of records, such as log lines, and holds them in a stream so that one or more consumers can read them within moments. A record is one unit of data, usually a small JSON document. The stream is split into shards, where each shard is a fixed slice of capacity: it accepts a set amount of writes per second and serves reads to consumers. Each record carries a partition key, a text value chosen by the producer. The service hashes that key to pick a shard, so records with the same key land on the same shard and keep their order. Records stay in the stream for a retention period, 24 hours by default, so a consumer that falls behind can read older records again rather than losing them. A consumer tracks its position with a sequence number, a per-shard ordering marker it saves after processing each batch.

Worked example: a stream with three shards receives five log lines with partition key checkout, then one line with key search. The checkout key always hashes to the same shard, say shard 2, so its five lines are read in the order they were written. Search may land on shard 0. The consumer on shard 2 reads lines 1 to 5 in order, saves sequence number 5, and resumes from there after a restart.

Common mistake: choosing a partition key with very few distinct values, such as log level. If nearly every record is ERROR or INFO, one shard receives almost all the traffic, writes get throttled, and consumer lag grows, so the dashboard shows minutes-old data while the other shards sit idle. Pick a key with many distinct values, such as a service-and-instance identifier.

Consequence: a stream is only as real-time as its slowest consumer. Lag, the age of the oldest unread record, should be watched and alarmed on, because it is the honest measure of whether the monitoring is still current.

questions.prompt: A payments company runs a Kinesis Data Stream with four shards. Each card-terminal record carries the terminal serial number as its partition key, and there are about 20,000 terminals, so keys are spread widely across shards. Terminal T-5531 sends a batch of three records, sequence numbers 40 to 42, which one consumer reads and processes. The consumer then crashes before saving its position. Its last saved sequence number is 39. When the consumer restarts, it resumes from its saved position. Because that position was never advanced past 39, it reads ___ again.
choices: nothing, because the stream never re-sends processed records
records 40, 41 and 42, which were processed but never saved
all records from the start of the shard, because the position was lost
only record 42, because that was the last one read
questions.why: The consumer only moves its saved position after a batch is saved, so with 39 as the last saved position it resumes at 40 and reprocesses 40 to 42 that it handled before the crash.

questions.prompt: A small logistics firm sets its Kinesis Data Stream retention to the default. A consumer goes offline for 30 hours. When it returns, what can it read?
choices: Every record from the 30 hours, because the stream keeps data until it is read
Nothing from before the outage, because consumers must be online to receive records
Only the records from the last 6 hours, because retention is measured per consumer
Only the records from the most recent 24 hours, because older records have aged out of the default retention period
questions.why: The default retention period is 24 hours, so records older than that are no longer in the stream and cannot be read, even though the consumer was only offline for 30 hours.

questions.prompt: A sensor network has 40,000 temperature sensors sending readings into a Kinesis Data Stream. The team is choosing a partition key. Which choice best spreads the load and keeps each sensor's readings in order?
choices: A constant value such as the word readings for every record
The unit of measure, either Celsius or Fahrenheit
The sensor's own identifier, which has tens of thousands of distinct values
The hour of the day in which each reading was taken
questions.why: A key with many distinct values, like a per-sensor identifier, spreads records across shards, while the same key keeps one sensor's records on the same shard in write order; the unit and hour keys have few values and would crowd traffic onto a few shards.

questions.prompt: A consumer of a Kinesis Data Stream reports that its dashboard is showing data that is about 20 minutes old, yet the producers write without errors and the shards show no throttling. Which measure should the team alarm on to detect this problem directly?
choices: The number of shards in the stream, compared to the expected count
The producer application's CPU usage, which reflects how fast it sends
The count of records written per minute by the producers
The age of the oldest unread record, which is the consumer's lag
questions.why: Lag, the age of the oldest unread record, directly shows how far behind a consumer is, which is the measure that reveals stale monitoring data even when writes look healthy.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what Kinesis Data Streams does with a continuous stream of application log lines, and name one limit or tradeoff the team must plan for when choosing the partition key.
lessons.modelAnswer: Kinesis Data Streams takes log records as they are produced and holds them in a stream split into shards. Each record has a partition key, and the service hashes that key to choose a shard. Records with the same key go to the same shard and are read back in order, which is useful when you need to follow one service's events in sequence. Consumers read each shard and save their position with a sequence number, so they can resume after a failure or replay recent data, within the retention period. The main tradeoff is the partition key. A key with few distinct values, like log level, concentrates traffic on one shard, which gets throttled and makes consumer lag grow. A key with many distinct values spreads load but gives up global ordering across the whole stream. The team has to choose the key with both limits in mind and alarm on lag.
rubricPoints: Describes records flowing into shards and being read by consumers in near real time
Explains that the partition key decides the shard and that same-key records keep their order
Mentions retention so consumers can replay or catch up
States the tradeoff of a low-cardinality key causing hot shards and lag
Notes that ordering holds only within a shard, not across the whole stream

suggested.rationale: A messaging engine would let the learner build a producer and consumers and watch lag and hot shards, which is the hands-on core of streaming logs.

lessons.plain: Logs are the record a system keeps of what it did: each line notes a request, an error, or a login. Once you have millions of lines, reading them by eye is hopeless, so engineers ask questions of them instead. This objective covers two ways to do that. One approach queries logs held inside a managed log service, using a short query language to get quick answers about recent events. The other runs SQL, a standard language for asking questions of tables, over log files stored cheaply as objects in storage, which lets you look across months of history. Both let you count errors, find slow requests, or trace one customer's failures. The real skill is choosing where the logs live and writing a question precise enough to give a useful answer.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your web service writes one log line per request, and you need the count of server errors per hour across the last six months. Would you scroll through the service's live log viewer, or ask a question over stored files, and what would you worry about in each case?
lessons.teach:
A log group is a named collection of log streams in CloudWatch Logs, the managed log service on AWS. CloudWatch Logs Insights is a query tool built into that service; it reads events in one or more log groups over a chosen time range and can parse fields, filter, and aggregate them. Amazon Athena is a serverless SQL query engine that reads data sitting in Amazon S3, object storage. You define a table that points at a set of files and their format, and you pay for the bytes each query scans. Partitioning means organising the files into folders by a key such as date, so a query that filters on that key reads only the folders it needs.

Worked example: to count 500-status responses per hour over the last day in a log group, you first set the time range to one day. Second, you filter events whose status field is 500 or higher. Third, you group the matching events into one-hour buckets and count each bucket. The result is a short table you can read in seconds. The same question over six months of archived files works in Athena only if the files are partitioned by date, so the query skips most of them.

The common mistake is querying without a time filter or partition, which forces the engine to read everything. That is slow and costs money, and during an incident it leaves the responder waiting. Retention also matters: a log group deletes events once their retention period passes, so history you need later must be exported to S3 beforehand.

A broad, unfiltered query over the whole archive is the slowest and most expensive way to answer a question, so narrow the time range and partitions first.

questions.prompt: A payments team keeps two years of card-terminal logs in Amazon S3, organised into folders named by date (for example dt=2024-03-04). An analyst wants the number of 503 responses per day for 4 to 10 March 2024, reading as little data as possible in Amazon Athena. Step one: limit the query to the date folders from dt=2024-03-04 through dt=2024-03-10. Step two: keep only rows where the status field is 503. Step three is missing. Which step completes the count?
choices: Export the logs to S3 before the log group deletes them
Remove the date filter so the engine can see every file before counting
Group the matching rows by day and count each group
Sort the matching rows by status in ascending order
questions.why: After narrowing to the right folders and matching status, grouping by day and counting each group produces the per-day totals asked for, while the other choices either re-widen the scan, handle retention rather than the query, or do not produce a count.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what does partitioning mean for log files stored in Amazon S3?
choices: Giving every file a unique name so that no two files collide
Copying the files into two separate buckets so that a backup always exists
Organising files into folders by a key such as date, so that a query filtering on that key reads only the folders it needs
Compressing each file so that it takes fewer bytes to store
questions.why: The teaching text defines partitioning as organising files into folders by a key so that filtered queries skip the folders they do not need, which is what the correct choice states.

questions.prompt: A security team has 90 days of archived firewall logs in S3 stored as one flat set of files with no date folders. They need the count of denied connections during one hour last Tuesday. Which approach best limits the cost and time of the Athena query?
choices: Query the whole flat archive and then filter the results table by hour
Reorganise the files into date folders, then filter the query on that date so only the needed folders are read
Create a second copy of the archive in a new log group so the query runs in parallel
Set the CloudWatch Logs retention period to 90 days so the query is smaller
questions.why: Without date partitions, Athena must read every file regardless of the hour filter, so reorganising by date and filtering on the date is what lets the engine skip most of the data.

questions.prompt: A web team set a 30-day retention period on a CloudWatch log group. An auditor now asks for all events from the last 12 months, and the audit is next month. What must the team have done to be able to answer that request?
choices: Exported the events to S3 before they passed the 30-day retention period
Widened the Logs Insights time range to 365 days when the query runs
Pointed an Athena table at the log group, since Athena reads it directly
Lengthened the alarm evaluation period so older events stay visible
questions.why: A log group deletes events once their retention period passes, so history needed later must already have been exported to S3 before deletion; widening queries or changing alarms cannot recover deleted events.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate asks why we should not send every log to one place and query everything with Athena. In your own words, explain when each tool fits and name one limit or tradeoff you would weigh before choosing.
lessons.modelAnswer: Logs Insights fits when I need a fast answer about recent events in a log group, because it is built into the log service and needs no setup beyond picking a time range. Athena fits when I need history or cross-service analysis, because it reads files in S3 cheaply and at any age. The main tradeoff with Athena is that the answer depends on how the data is laid out: if I have not partitioned the files by date, a query scans far more data than it needs, costs more, and runs slower. The main tradeoff with Logs Insights is retention: once events age out of the log group they are gone unless I exported them first. So before an incident I would check retention and export paths, and during one I would start with a narrow time range in whichever tool holds the data I need.
rubricPoints: Logs Insights queries recent events inside the log service and suits fast, short-horizon questions.
Athena queries files in S3 with SQL and suits long history and cross-source analysis.
Athena cost and speed depend on data scanned, so time filters and partitions matter.
Log groups delete events after retention expires, so older history must be exported to S3 first.

suggested.rationale: An exam-style scenario asking which tool to use, and why, for a given retention and cost situation adds the most value here, and no listed mission has the learner write these queries.

lessons.plain: Instead of someone or some script constantly checking whether something happened, the system tells you when it happens. A file lands in a storage bucket, a server changes state, or a deployment finishes, and the source sends a short message describing what happened. A router passes that message to whoever needs it. Your job is to know which events exist, where they are sent, and what the receiver does with them, so the response runs on its own without anyone watching a dashboard. Think of a smoke alarm that rings a central panel and also a phone, rather than a guard walking every floor with a clipboard.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team wants to know within seconds whenever a new log file is written to a storage bucket, without a script checking the bucket every minute. Before reading on, what would you expect the notification to contain, and what could go wrong if the receiver is slow or the same message arrives twice?
lessons.teach:
An event is a small record that something happened, such as an object being created in an Amazon S3 bucket. S3 is object storage, where files are kept in named containers called buckets. An event source is the service that emits the event. Routing means sending that record to one or more targets. There are two main routes. First, S3 event notifications: you configure a bucket so that matching object actions send a message directly to Amazon SNS (a topic that fans a message out to subscribers such as email addresses or other endpoints), to Amazon SQS (a queue), or to an AWS Lambda function (code that runs when it is invoked). Second, Amazon EventBridge: an event bus receives events from AWS services and your own applications, and a rule with an event pattern (a JSON filter that selects events by source, type and fields) forwards matching events to targets. S3 can also send its events to EventBridge, which allows more filtering and more targets.

Why it works: the sender publishes and moves on without waiting, so watching costs nothing while nothing happens, and the router does the matching.

Worked example: a bucket holds application log archives. A rule matches object-created events whose key starts with a given folder prefix. Step 1: a server uploads a file under the errors prefix. Step 2: S3 emits an object-created event toward EventBridge. Step 3: the rule's pattern matches the bucket name and prefix, so the event is forwarded. Step 4: the SNS topic target delivers a short message to the on-call email subscription. Step 5: a Lambda function subscribed to the same topic reads the object and counts error lines.

Common mistake: assuming delivery happens exactly once and in order. Notifications can arrive more than once or out of sequence, so handlers must be idempotent, meaning safe to run twice with the same result. Another mistake is a function that writes its output back under the prefix that triggers it, which creates an endless loop of invocations.

In a running system, a loop can multiply cost and flood the alert channel within minutes, and a non-idempotent handler will double-count errors. The event reports that something happened; the rule and target decide whether anyone is woken.

questions.prompt: A retail team has a bucket named scans with a rule that matches object-created events whose key starts with incoming/. Step 1: a scanner uploads batch-88.pdf under incoming/. Step 2: S3 emits an object-created event toward EventBridge. Step 3: the rule's pattern matches the bucket name and prefix and forwards the event to a Lambda target. Step 4 is missing: the Lambda function writes its processed copy to a new key. Step 5: the function finishes, and no further invocation happens. Which key choice completes step 4 so that step 5 holds?
choices: incoming/ prefix so the next run can pick it up
the SNS topic directly, bypassing the rule
processed/ prefix, which the rule does not match, so the write cannot trigger another run
the same key name, which S3 quietly overwrites without any event
questions.why: A key outside the matched prefix produces no new event that the rule would forward, so the function is not invoked again and the loop cannot start.

questions.prompt: In Amazon EventBridge, what does the event pattern on a rule do?
choices: It is a JSON filter that selects events by source, type and fields before forwarding them to targets
It encrypts the event payload so only the named target can read it
It keeps a copy of the event for seven days so it can be replayed later
It sets how many times the target retries a failed delivery
questions.why: The teaching text describes the event pattern as a JSON filter that selects events by source, type and fields, and the rule forwards only the events that match it.

questions.prompt: A billing team's Lambda function is subscribed to an SNS topic and adds one to a monthly counter for each notification it receives. After a retry storm, the counter is far too high. Which property of the handler would have prevented this?
choices: Exactly-once delivery, meaning each notification arrives precisely one time
A longer timeout, so the function never has to be retried
Idempotence, meaning running the handler twice with the same notification leaves the same result
Ordering, meaning notifications are guaranteed to arrive in the sequence they were sent
questions.why: Notifications can arrive more than once, so a handler that is safe to run twice with the same notification gives the same count regardless of duplicates.

questions.prompt: A thumbnail function is triggered by object-created events under the uploads/ prefix. Each time it runs, it writes a thumbnail to uploads/thumbs/. What is the most likely result?
choices: S3 rejects the write because thumbs is a reserved folder name
Each thumbnail write matches the uploads/ prefix and triggers another invocation, creating a loop
Each thumbnail is written once and the function then stops
EventBridge merges the two writes into a single event
questions.why: The teaching text warns that writing output under the prefix that triggers a function creates an endless loop of invocations, and uploads/thumbs/ starts with uploads/.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how an S3 upload can end up as an SNS message or a Lambda run, and name one limit or tradeoff of relying on these asynchronous notifications for an alert.
lessons.modelAnswer: When a file is uploaded to a bucket, S3 emits an object-created event. That event can be sent directly to an SNS topic or a Lambda function configured on the bucket, or sent to EventBridge, where a rule with an event pattern selects it and forwards it to targets such as SNS or Lambda. The sender does not wait for the receiver. The main tradeoff is that delivery is asynchronous and can be delayed, duplicated or out of order. So an alert can arrive late, and a handler may see the same event twice. Handlers have to be idempotent, and anything that must never be missed needs a retry or dead-letter path and a check that the alert path actually works.
rubricPoints: Describes the event source, the event, and the route through a bucket notification or an EventBridge rule to a target
Explains that the sender does not wait, so the flow is asynchronous
Names a limit such as possible duplicate, late or out-of-order delivery
Says the handler must be idempotent or that failed deliveries need a retry or dead-letter path

suggested.rationale: The messaging engine planned for OpsForge would let the learner wire events to targets and observe duplicates and ordering, which is the core skill here.

lessons.plain: Auto scaling means a system adds or removes copies of its own workers based on how busy they are, so nobody has to resize things by hand at 3 a.m. Think of a restaurant that calls in extra waiters when the room fills and sends some home when it empties. Cloud services offer this for virtual servers, databases, containers and Kubernetes clusters, each with its own settings. The shared idea is a rule that watches a measurement, compares it with a target, and changes the count within limits you set. Knowing the rule and its limits is what keeps a system both affordable and able to cope with a surge.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your web servers average 90 percent CPU for ten minutes at peak, then drop to 10 percent overnight. Without anyone touching anything, what should happen to the number of servers, and what would you need to decide before letting that happen automatically?
lessons.teach: Auto scaling is a control loop. A monitor measures something, such as average CPU, a policy compares that measurement with a rule, and a controller changes how many units of capacity exist. A unit can be a virtual server in an EC2 Auto Scaling group, a task in an ECS service that a capacity provider places onto compute, a Kubernetes node added by a cluster autoscaler, extra storage added to an RDS database, or read and write throughput for a DynamoDB table. Adding units is scaling out; removing them is scaling in. Three settings appear almost everywhere. The minimum is a floor that is never crossed, protecting availability. The maximum is a ceiling that caps cost and protects downstream systems. The target is the level a metric should hold. A target tracking policy adjusts capacity in proportion to the gap between the measured value and the target, so you state a goal instead of writing step rules by hand. A cooldown is a quiet period after a change during which the controller waits before acting again. Why it works: the controller always acts on old information. Metrics are averaged over a window, new servers take minutes to boot and pass health checks, and a cooldown stops the loop from reacting twice to one spike. Worked example: an EC2 group has minimum 2, maximum 10, and target 60 percent CPU. Average CPU reaches 90 percent with 4 instances. Required capacity is roughly 4 times 90 divided by 60, which is 6. The controller adds 2, the new instances warm up, the average drops to about 60 percent, and the loop settles. Common mistake: setting the target at 95 percent to save money. There is then no headroom, and new capacity arrives after users have already seen timeouts. Another mistake is leaving the maximum at a default that is too low for the next traffic surge. Consequence: when the maximum is reached and load keeps rising, scaling stops and requests fail. A database whose storage ceiling is set too low will refuse writes even though its storage autoscaling is switched on. Scaling is only as good as its limits and its lag, so set both on purpose.

questions.prompt: A ticket-booking service runs an EC2 Auto Scaling group (a set of virtual servers that the platform adds or removes automatically) with minimum 3, maximum 20, and a target tracking policy (a rule that adjusts capacity in proportion to how far a measured value is from a goal) that holds average CPU at 50 percent. The group has 6 instances and average CPU is 80 percent. Step 1: divide 80 by 50 to get 1.6. Step 2: multiply 1.6 by 6 to get 9.6 instances of required capacity. Step 3 is missing. What must happen to 9.6 before the group can be set to that value?
choices: Round down to 9 and accept the 80 percent reading
Divide 9.6 by 3 because the minimum sets the step size
Leave it at 9.6, since the controller can run fractional instances
Round up to 10, which sits inside the 3 to 20 limits
questions.why: Instances are whole units, so the fractional need must be rounded up to 10 to keep enough capacity, and 10 stays within the minimum of 3 and maximum of 20.

questions.prompt: A payments API runs in an EC2 Auto Scaling group with minimum 4, maximum 12, and a target of 55 percent CPU. Overnight traffic falls and the controller wants to remove instances. Which setting decides the lowest number of instances the controller is allowed to reach?
choices: The minimum, because it is a floor that is never crossed
The target, because it is the level the metric should hold
The cooldown, because it sets how long the controller waits
The maximum, because it caps how many instances can exist
questions.why: The minimum is the floor the controller never goes below, protecting availability, while the cooldown only controls timing and the target only controls the metric goal.

questions.prompt: A logistics team sets the target of its target tracking policy to 90 percent CPU on a fleet serving a latency-sensitive search page, reasoning that this uses the hardware fully. What is the main risk of this choice?
choices: The maximum is ignored, so the group can grow past its ceiling
The cooldown is disabled automatically, so the fleet scales in too often
The fleet has no headroom, and new capacity arrives after users already see slow responses because new instances take minutes to boot
The metric is averaged over a shorter window, so the policy becomes less accurate
questions.why: A high target leaves little spare capacity, and because the controller acts on delayed information while new instances take minutes to become ready, users feel the shortage before extra capacity arrives.

questions.prompt: A relational database has storage autoscaling switched on, but its maximum storage limit is set to 200 GiB and the disk is now full at 200 GiB. What happens to new writes?
choices: Autoscaling adds storage beyond the limit automatically once the switch is on
Writes are refused, because the storage ceiling caps growth even though autoscaling is enabled
The cooldown period is bypassed so growth continues immediately
The database deletes its oldest rows to make room for new writes
questions.why: Autoscaling can only grow storage up to the configured maximum, so once that ceiling is reached new writes fail regardless of the autoscaling switch.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says we should just turn on auto scaling for the whole stack and forget it. In your own words, explain what auto scaling does across our EC2 group, our database storage and our container cluster, and name one limit or tradeoff they must plan for.
lessons.modelAnswer: Auto scaling watches a measurement and changes the number of units to keep it near a target, within a minimum and a maximum. For our EC2 group, the target might be 60 percent average CPU, so the group adds instances at peak and removes them overnight, but only between the floor and the ceiling. For RDS storage, the database grows its disk when free space runs low, up to a cap we set. For the container cluster, capacity providers or node autoscalers add compute when tasks cannot be placed. The tradeoff is lag: new capacity takes minutes to become healthy, so a sudden spike can still cause errors, and a scale-in that is too eager can remove capacity right before the next peak. So we must choose sensible limits, cooldowns and alarms, and test them under load rather than trusting the defaults.
rubricPoints: Auto scaling adjusts capacity based on a metric compared with a target, within a minimum and a maximum.
It applies to EC2 groups, RDS storage, DynamoDB throughput, ECS capacity providers and EKS node or pod scaling, each with its own unit.
New capacity takes time to arrive, so sudden spikes can still cause failures.
A real limit or tradeoff is named, such as a ceiling that stops scaling, cost, or scale-in removing capacity too early.

suggested.rationale: The planned autoscale engine would let the learner set targets, minimums, maximums and cooldowns and watch the resulting capacity change, which is the hands-on way to see the control loop work.

lessons.plain: When a computer system runs, it keeps measuring itself, such as how busy its processor is. An alarm is a rule that watches one of those measurements and changes state when the number crosses a line you chose. Beyond showing a changed state, an alarm can do two things. It can send a message to a broadcast channel that reaches people or other software, or it can start a small program that tries a fix. For virtual servers in the cloud there is also a special action that moves a failing machine onto healthy physical hardware without you rebuilding it. This lesson is about choosing those reactions so known problems get handled quickly and people are woken only when a human is truly needed.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose a server's processor stays above 90 percent for a long time, and you want someone told and something tried automatically. Which two different kinds of reaction would you want, and why might one reaction not be enough on its own?
lessons.teach:
A CloudWatch alarm watches one metric, which is a number recorded over time such as CPU percentage, and compares it with a threshold. You choose how long the breach must last, using a period (the length of each measurement window) and a count of consecutive periods that must breach. An alarm has three states: OK, ALARM, and INSUFFICIENT_DATA, which means there is not enough recent data to judge. An alarm action is something the alarm does when its state changes. Two common kinds are publishing to an SNS topic, which is a managed publish-subscribe channel that copies one message to every subscriber such as an email address, a chat hook, or a queue, and invoking a Lambda function, which runs a short piece of code on demand without servers you manage. Notifying a topic lets people or other systems react. Invoking a function lets the system attempt a fix itself. EC2 automatic recovery is a separate alarm action that watches the system status check, which reports problems in the physical host under the virtual machine. When it fires, the platform moves the instance to healthy hardware and starts it again, keeping the same instance ID, private IP address, and attached EBS volumes. Data in instance store is lost, and only some instance types qualify.

Worked example. The alarm threshold is 80 percent, with a 5-minute period and 3 of 3 periods required. Step 1: the 5-minute CPU averages are 85, 88, and 90. Step 2: after the third breach the state moves from OK to ALARM. Step 3: the alarm publishes to the topic ops-alerts. Step 4: the topic delivers the message to the on-call email and to a Lambda subscriber that opens a ticket. Step 5: CPU falls to 40 percent, the state returns to OK, and a recovery message can be sent if you configured one.

Common mistake: treating the alarm as the fix. An alarm only announces a condition or starts a program. A Lambda that restarts a service with no limits can loop forever, and automatic recovery does nothing for a crashed application because the underlying hardware is healthy.

Consequence: when a metric is sparse, the missing-data setting decides whether the alarm flips to ALARM, stays OK, or goes to INSUFFICIENT_DATA, so choose that setting deliberately.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm runs a reporting server on EC2 with an alarm that watches the system status check. The alarm uses a 1-minute period and needs 2 of 2 periods to breach. Steps 1 to 4 are done. Step 1: the system status check fails in minute 10 and minute 11. Step 2: the alarm state moves from OK to ALARM. Step 3: the alarm's EC2 automatic recovery action starts. Step 4: the platform moves the instance to healthy hardware and starts it again, keeping the same instance ID and private IP. Missing step 5: state what happens to the data held in the instance's local instance store during this recovery.
choices: The data is copied to the new hardware and is fully preserved.
The data is lost, while the attached EBS volumes stay intact.
The data is moved to an SNS topic so that the on-call team can restore it.
The data is kept only if the instance was stopped before the failure.
questions.why: Instance store is physical storage tied to the original host, so recovery onto new hardware loses it, while attached EBS volumes persist.

questions.prompt: Which description best matches an SNS topic as used in alarm actions?
choices: A status check that reports failures in the physical host beneath a virtual machine.
A managed publish-subscribe channel that copies one message to every subscriber, such as an email address or a queue.
A short piece of code that runs on demand and attempts a repair on the machine that raised the alarm.
A measurement window that sets how long each metric sample covers before the alarm compares it to a threshold.
questions.why: An SNS topic fans one published message out to all of its subscribers, which is what the alarm relies on to notify people or systems.

questions.prompt: A team configures an alarm to invoke a Lambda function that restarts a web service whenever it fails. The web service keeps crashing because of a bug in its code, and the function has no limit on retries. What is the most likely outcome?
choices: The alarm stops firing permanently after the first restart succeeds.
The alarm state becomes INSUFFICIENT_DATA until a human resets the bug.
EC2 automatic recovery moves the instance to new hardware and fixes the bug.
The function can keep restarting the service in a loop, because an alarm action does not stop itself and the function does not cap its attempts.
questions.why: An alarm action only starts a program, and without limits a restart function can repeat indefinitely, which is why the teaching text warns against treating an alarm as the fix.

questions.prompt: An operations group wants a breach of its database host's CPU threshold to both try an automatic repair and tell the on-call engineers. Which setup fits this goal?
choices: Use only an SNS topic subscription, because a topic restarts failed software on its own.
Set the missing-data option to ALARM so that the engineers are paged without any repair step.
Attach a Lambda function that performs the repair and also publish the same alarm to an SNS topic that the engineers subscribe to.
Use only EC2 automatic recovery, because it notifies people and repairs application faults.
questions.why: An alarm can have more than one action, so a Lambda action can attempt the fix while an SNS publish informs the people who need to know.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between an alarm that publishes to an SNS topic and an alarm that invokes a Lambda function, and name one limit of EC2 automatic recovery.
lessons.modelAnswer: An alarm that publishes to an SNS topic tells people or other systems that something changed, and the topic fans the message out to every subscriber, such as email or a ticket hook. An alarm that invokes a Lambda function runs code straight away, so the system can try a fix on its own. The choice depends on whether a human must judge the situation or the response is safe to automate. A limit of EC2 automatic recovery is that it only handles failures in the underlying physical host, detected by the system status check. If the operating system hangs or the application crashes while the hardware is healthy, recovery never fires. Also, instance store data is lost when the instance moves to new hardware, so it should not hold anything you cannot rebuild. Both reactions need guardrails, such as limits on retries and a clear owner.
rubricPoints: SNS publish notifies humans or systems and fans out to subscribers, leaving the response to people
Lambda invocation lets code react automatically, suited to safe and bounded fixes
EC2 automatic recovery responds only to host-level system status failures
Instance store data is lost on recovery, and the action only works for certain instance types

suggested.rationale: Choosing thresholds, periods, missing-data treatment and alarm actions is best practised by building alarms and seeing their state changes.

lessons.plain: When something happens in a computer system, such as a server stopping or a file being uploaded, the system can announce it as a small message called an event. Event routing services collect these announcements and pass them along. Configuring one to notify you on a particular event pattern means writing a filter that says which announcements matter, such as only a server stopping while ignoring everything else, and attaching that filter to an action like sending an email or posting to a team channel. The filter is the important part: it decides what gets through, so a good one catches the real trouble and stays quiet about the rest. This lesson covers how that filter is written and how it behaves.
lessons.guessPrompt: Imagine every server in your fleet sends a message whenever its power state changes, including starts, stops and restarts. How would you describe to a router that you want an email only when a server stops, and nothing else?
lessons.teach:
An event is a record that something changed, produced by a service and sent to an event bus, which is a shared channel that receives events. A rule is configuration attached to a bus. It holds an event pattern, a JSON-style template describing which events to match, and one or more targets, the places matching events are delivered, such as a notification topic or a function. An event pattern matches by comparing fields. Every field you list must be present in the event and equal one of the values you list in an array; any value in the array counts as a match. Fields you leave out are ignored, so a pattern is a loose filter, not a full copy of an event. Nested fields, such as the state inside the detail section, are written as nested objects inside the pattern.

Why it works: the router checks each incoming event against every rule independently, so producers never need to know who is listening. Adding a listener means adding a rule, not changing the producer.

Worked example. The pattern is {'source': ['aws.ec2'], 'detail-type': ['EC2 Instance State-change Notification'], 'detail': {'state': ['stopped']}}. Event A arrives with source aws.ec2, the right detail-type, and detail state running. The source and detail-type checks pass, but running is not in the list ['stopped'], so the rule does not fire. Event B arrives with detail state stopped. All three checks pass, so the rule delivers it to the notification topic.

Common mistake: misspelling a field name or value, or getting the letter case wrong. The pattern then never matches, nothing reports an error, and the rule shows zero invocations. The team assumes the system is quiet when it is actually unwatched.

Consequence: a missing or overly broad pattern either leaves a real failure silent or floods the team with noise. Test a pattern against a sample event before relying on it, because a rule verified against a real event is the only kind you can trust during an incident.

questions.prompt: A team wants to be told when a nightly backup job fails in the production vault. They write a rule on the event bus with the pattern: source must be com.acme.backup, detail-type must be Backup Job Failed, and detail vault must be nightly-prod. Event A has vault nightly-staging, so the vault check fails and the rule stays silent. Event B has detail-type Backup Job Completed, so the detail-type check fails and the rule stays silent. Event C has source com.acme.backup, detail-type Backup Job Failed, and vault Nightly-Prod. The source check passes and the detail-type check passes. Step 3 is the vault check, and the rule's result depends on it. What happens?
choices: The vault check fails because Nightly-Prod is not an exact match for nightly-prod, so the rule does not fire and nothing reports an error.
The detail check passes because matching ignores letter case, so the rule delivers Event C to the notification topic.
Matching stops after the detail-type check and the rule writes an error to the logs instead of testing the vault field.
The rule fires, but the notification is held back until the next scheduled backup run.
questions.why: Event patterns compare values exactly, including letter case, so Nightly-Prod is not in the list [nightly-prod] and the rule does not deliver the event.

questions.prompt: A rule on an order-processing event bus uses this pattern: source must be com.shop.orders, and detail region must be one of eu-west-1 or eu-central-1. The pattern has no detail-type field. An incoming event has source com.shop.orders, detail-type Order Placed, and detail region eu-west-1. Does the rule fire?
choices: Yes, because the detail-type field is left out of the pattern, so it is ignored, and the other two checks pass.
Yes, but only if the detail-type is also written into the pattern as Order Placed.
No, because the event has a detail-type and the pattern does not list one to compare against.
No, because eu-west-1 is only one of two allowed values and the event must match both.
questions.why: Fields left out of a pattern are ignored, and any single value in an array counts as a match, so the source and region checks both pass and the rule fires.

questions.prompt: A team's rule watches a continuous-integration event bus. Its pattern lists detail-type as Build Timed Out, but the producing tool actually sends the value BuildTimedOut with no spaces. Over a week the rule shows zero invocations and no error appears anywhere. A manager says this proves no builds timed out. What is the best next step?
choices: Add a second rule that matches every event from every source so nothing is missed.
Compare the pattern to a real sample event from the producer and correct the spelling so the rule can match.
Increase the number of targets on the rule so that more events can reach it.
Accept the manager's conclusion, because a rule with zero invocations means no event matched a real problem.
questions.why: A pattern that never matches fails silently, so the only reliable check is to test it against a real sample event and fix any mismatch in field names or values.

questions.prompt: A rule on a deployment event bus has this pattern: source must be com.acme.ci, and detail result must be one of FAILED or TIMED_OUT. Four events arrive, all from com.acme.ci. Which one causes the rule to deliver to its target?
choices: An event with result SUCCEEDED, because the rule only checks that the source is correct.
An event with result timed_out in lowercase, because letter case does not affect matching.
An event with result TIMED_OUT, because it is one of the listed values in the array.
An event with no result field at all, because a missing field counts as a match.
questions.why: An array in a pattern matches any one of its values, so TIMED_OUT satisfies the result check while SUCCEEDED does not, and lowercase or missing fields do not match.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how an event pattern decides which events a rule delivers, and name one limit or tradeoff of writing a pattern that is very broad versus very narrow.
lessons.modelAnswer: A rule compares each incoming event with its pattern. Every field listed in the pattern must be present in the event and must equal one of the values listed for it, and fields the pattern leaves out are not checked at all. So the pattern is a filter that only selects on the parts you name. The tradeoff is breadth. A very broad pattern, such as matching only the source service, catches everything from that service, so the team gets flooded and real failures get buried. A very narrow pattern, with many exact fields, can silently miss events when a value is spelled differently or the producer changes its format, and the rule then shows zero matches with no error. The practical approach is to match on the fields that identify the failure you care about, then test the rule against a real sample event so you know it fires when it should and stays quiet otherwise.
rubricPoints: An event pattern matches only when every listed field is present in the event and matches a listed value.
Fields left out of the pattern are ignored, so the pattern is a loose filter.
A broad pattern floods the team with noise, while a narrow one can silently miss events.
A misspelled field or value fails silently, so the rule should be tested against a real sample event.

suggested.rationale: Writing and testing event patterns against sample events is best practised in the planned messaging and events engine rather than read about.

lessons.plain: A server rented from a cloud provider is a virtual machine, and by default the provider only shows you a few numbers about it, such as how busy its processor is and how much network traffic passes through. Some useful facts stay hidden, like how full its disk is or how much memory is in use. An agent is a small helper program installed on the server to collect those hidden facts and report them to a central place. Think of it as a meter you fit inside the building, because the outside meter cannot see what is happening in every room. This lesson covers two such helpers and the setup they need before they can report anything.
lessons.guessPrompt: A virtual server's processor graph looks calm, yet users say it has stopped accepting writes. Why might the default graphs miss this, and what would you need to put on the server to see the problem?
lessons.teach:
An agent is a small program that runs on a server and does work for a central service. Two agents matter for EC2 instances, which are virtual servers you rent by the hour. The SSM Agent, part of AWS Systems Manager, lets the central service reach into the instance to run commands, open a remote shell, apply patches, or report inventory, without you logging in by hand. The CloudWatch agent collects what the platform cannot see from outside: memory use, disk space used on each mount point, and the contents of chosen log files. It then sends those readings to CloudWatch, the metrics and logs store.

Why this is needed: the hardware host under the virtual server measures processor, network and disk input and output, but it cannot see inside the operating system. Memory and disk fullness are only known inside the guest, so something there must measure them and push them out. The CloudWatch agent reads a configuration file listing which measurements to take, how often, and which log files to ship. The instance also needs an identity with permission to write metrics and logs. Without that permission the agent runs happily while its data is refused.

Worked example: a batch host's root disk fills. Step 1: the default processor graph shows five percent and looks healthy. Step 2: the CloudWatch agent is installed, and its configuration asks for disk used percent on the root path every 60 seconds. Step 3: the agent reads the disk usage and sends it as a data point under a named namespace with dimensions identifying the host and disk. Step 4: an alarm watches that value and fires when it stays above 90 percent for three consecutive periods, notifying a topic. Step 5: the team is warned before writes start failing.

Common mistake: assuming installing the agent is enough. If the configuration omits the metric, or the instance identity lacks permission, the alarm reports no data indefinitely. Consequence: the gap is silent. Monitoring looks fine while the disk fills, and the first sign of trouble is a failed write in production.

Treat the agent configuration as reviewed, versioned infrastructure, because one wrong path or missing metric is a blind spot that no default graph will reveal.

questions.prompt: A team runs a fleet of image-resizing workers on EC2 virtual servers. Their default processor graph shows 30 percent CPU and looks healthy, so they install the CloudWatch agent. Its configuration asks for memory used percent on each worker every 60 seconds, and the agent reads that value and sends it as a data point under a named namespace, with dimensions identifying the instance. Step 4 is missing: nothing yet watches that memory value. Step 5 is that the on-call engineer is paged before the workers start swapping heavily. Which choice correctly fills the missing Step 4?
choices: Restart each worker so the operating system reports its memory total at boot
Create an alarm on the memory used percent metric that fires when it stays above a threshold for several consecutive periods and notifies a topic
Enable detailed monitoring on the processor graph so CPU is sampled every minute
Create a separate log group and ship the resizing job output to it
questions.why: An alarm is the piece that watches a stored metric against a threshold over consecutive periods and sends a notification, which is what turns the sent memory reading into a warning before swapping starts.

questions.prompt: Which measurement is the CloudWatch agent specifically needed to collect on an EC2 instance, rather than relying on the hardware host's own readings?
choices: Memory used percent inside the operating system
Disk read and write operations at the host level
Processor utilisation seen from the hypervisor
Network packets sent and received per second
questions.why: Memory and per-mount disk fullness are known only inside the guest operating system, so an agent running there must measure and push them, while the host already sees network and processor activity.

questions.prompt: A payments API team installed the CloudWatch agent on several instances and the configuration lists the correct metrics and log files. Their alarm on one instance has shown no data for three weeks while the agent process is running. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The SSM Agent is a different version from the CloudWatch agent
The instance's identity lacks permission to write metrics and logs, so the data is refused
The processor graph is disabled, which stops the agent from starting
The alarm threshold is set too high to ever be crossed
questions.why: A running agent whose instance identity lacks permission to write metrics and logs has its data refused silently, which produces an alarm with no data even though the agent appears to be working.

questions.prompt: An operations group must run a security patch command across 40 EC2 instances without logging into each one by hand. Which agent makes this possible, and why?
choices: The CloudWatch agent, because it sends log files and metrics to the central store
An alarm on the processor graph, because alarms can apply patches when a threshold is crossed
The SSM Agent, because it lets the central service run commands and apply patches on the instance
The hypervisor host under each instance, because it updates guest operating systems automatically
questions.why: The SSM Agent is the agent that lets the central Systems Manager service reach into an instance to run commands and apply patches, whereas the CloudWatch agent handles measurements and logs and cannot apply patches.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate asks why we cannot rely on the default EC2 graphs for a server that keeps running out of disk space. Explain what the SSM Agent and the CloudWatch agent each do, why the defaults miss the problem, and name one limit or tradeoff of depending on agents.
lessons.modelAnswer: The default graphs come from the hypervisor under the virtual machine, so they show processor, network and disk input and output, but not what is inside the operating system. Disk space used and memory used are only visible from inside the guest. The CloudWatch agent runs there, reads those values on a schedule as set in its configuration file, and sends them to CloudWatch, where an alarm can watch disk used percent and notify us before writes fail. The SSM Agent is different: it lets the management service run commands and report status on the instance, which helps with patching and checks. The tradeoff is that the agent is another moving part. It needs installing on every instance, a configuration that names the right disk and metrics, and an identity with permission to publish. If any of those is missing, the alarm shows no data rather than an error, so we should monitor for missing data too.
rubricPoints: The default EC2 metrics come from outside the operating system and miss in-guest values like disk space and memory.
The CloudWatch agent collects those in-guest values according to a configuration and publishes them.
The SSM Agent lets a management service run commands and check status on the instance.
An agent needs correct configuration and permission, and a failure there shows up as missing data, not as an obvious error.

suggested.rationale: This objective is mostly product setup and console facts about two agents, which a clear reading with the one worked example covers better than any listed mission.

lessons.plain: AWS Config keeps a record of how your cloud resources are set up and checks them against rules you choose, such as 'storage must not be open to the public'. A remediation is a pre-written fix attached to a rule, so when a resource breaks the rule, the system can correct it either after a person approves or automatically. Think of a building inspector who not only writes up a violation but can also send a repair crew, and who may be allowed to fix small problems on the spot while asking first for big ones.
lessons.guessPrompt: A storage bucket is found to be open to the whole internet. Should a rule that notices this fix it immediately with no human involved, and what could go wrong if it did?
lessons.teach: AWS Config is the AWS service that records the configuration of your resources over time. Each recorded snapshot of one resource is a configuration item. A Config rule is a check that compares those configuration items against a desired state and marks each resource compliant or non-compliant. Some rules are managed by AWS, and others are custom rules you write yourself. An evaluation is one run of a rule, triggered either by a configuration change or on a schedule. A remediation action is the fix attached to a rule. It usually points at an AWS Systems Manager Automation document, which is a runbook of steps the system performs. Remediation parameters are the inputs the runbook needs, and one of them is typically filled with the ID of the non-compliant resource. The execution role is an IAM role, a set of permissions, that the runbook assumes when it makes changes. You can start remediation manually, or switch on automatic remediation, which can retry a failed fix a set number of times with a wait between attempts. Worked example: a rule checks that each bucket blocks public access. Bucket B fails, so the rule is non-compliant. The attached runbook receives B's ID as its bucket parameter, assumes the execution role, and turns on the block-public-access settings. The next evaluation marks B compliant. The common mistake is attaching a remediation without an execution role that has the needed permissions, so every attempt fails and retries quietly. Another is enabling automatic fixes for a rule where the change could break a running service. Removing a firewall rule that a live dispatcher depends on can cut its traffic within seconds. Automatic remediation is therefore safe only for changes you can reverse and that no live workload relies on being in the wrong state.

questions.prompt: A team writes a Config rule that checks each SQS queue has a dead-letter queue attached, so messages that keep failing are moved aside instead of being retried forever. Queue 'invoice-jobs' fails the check and is marked non-compliant. The attached runbook receives 'invoice-jobs' as its queue-name parameter. Step 1: the runbook assumes the execution role. Step 2: [missing step]. Step 3: the next evaluation runs and marks 'invoice-jobs' compliant. Which step 2 completes the process?
choices: The runbook attaches a dead-letter queue to 'invoice-jobs' using the permissions the execution role grants.
The runbook disables the Config rule so that 'invoice-jobs' is no longer evaluated against it.
The runbook sends a page to the on-call engineer and waits for a human to attach the dead-letter queue.
The runbook deletes 'invoice-jobs' and recreates it with the same name, so the queue starts empty.
questions.why: The runbook makes the change itself, using the permissions from the execution role it assumed, and that change is what lets the next evaluation mark the queue compliant.

questions.prompt: In AWS Config, what is a configuration item?
choices: A rule that decides whether a resource is compliant or non-compliant.
The IAM role that a runbook assumes when it makes changes.
A recorded snapshot of one resource's configuration at a point in time.
A scheduled run of a rule that checks many resources at once.
questions.why: The teaching text defines a configuration item as one recorded snapshot of one resource, and the other options describe rules, execution roles, or evaluations.

questions.prompt: A Config rule checks that each EC2 instance in a staging account carries a cost-center tag. The team attaches a tagging runbook to the rule but does not give it an execution role. Instance 'stg-batch-14' is non-compliant. With automatic remediation enabled with 3 retries, what is the most likely outcome?
choices: AWS Config deletes the instance because it cannot be fixed.
The runbook tags the instance on the first attempt and the rule is never evaluated again.
The rule is automatically switched to manual mode and the runbook runs with the account's administrator permissions.
Each attempt fails for lack of permissions, the retries run with waits between them, and the instance stays non-compliant.
questions.why: Without an execution role that carries the needed permissions, every attempt fails, and the configured retries simply repeat that failure while the resource remains non-compliant.

questions.prompt: A Config rule flags that a route table entry in a production network points to a deprecated NAT gateway. A live payment service depends on that route for its outbound traffic. Which remediation setup is safest?
choices: Leave the route unchanged and disable the rule so the payment service is never flagged again.
Keep the remediation manual, so an engineer reviews the change before it runs, since the change could cut live traffic and may not be easy to reverse.
Turn on automatic remediation with 5 retries so the route is corrected even if the first attempt breaks traffic.
Attach a runbook that deletes the route and enable automatic remediation so it runs at once on every evaluation.
questions.why: Automatic remediation is only appropriate for changes that are reversible and that no live workload depends on being in the wrong state, and this route fails both tests, so a human should review it first.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate when you would let an AWS Config rule remediate a problem automatically and when you would require a person to start the fix, naming one limit or tradeoff of automatic remediation.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would let a Config rule fix things automatically when the fix is small, well tested, and easy to undo, such as turning on a setting that should never be off. I would require a person when the fix could interrupt a running service, like removing a network rule that some live system uses. The main limit is that remediation only corrects the resource's configuration. It does not explain why the resource drifted, so the same problem can return if the cause is a deployment script or a manual change. The execution role also has to have the right permissions, or the fix fails and retries without anyone noticing unless we watch the failure counts. So before turning on automatic remediation, I check the runbook, its role, and the blast radius of the change.
rubricPoints: Explains that remediation is a runbook attached to a Config rule that runs against a non-compliant resource
Distinguishes automatic remediation from manually started remediation and when each suits the change
Names a real tradeoff such as service disruption or a fix that hides the root cause
Mentions the execution role or permissions needed for the fix to succeed

suggested.rationale: Choosing between automatic and manual remediation for a given rule is an exam-style judgement that is best practised through a scenario, and no listed mission covers it directly.

lessons.plain: A health check is a regular, automatic test that asks a server or endpoint 'are you working?' and records the answer. In AWS, two services run these checks for you. A load balancer, the traffic director that spreads visitors across several servers, uses health checks to stop sending visitors to any server that fails the test. Route 53, the AWS DNS service that tells the internet where a website lives, uses health checks to stop handing out the address of a site that is down and send people to a backup instead. The skill is choosing what the test asks, how often it asks, and how many failures count as broken, because a test that is too strict or checks too much can take healthy things out of service.
lessons.guessPrompt: A load balancer runs a check on each of its servers every 30 seconds. One server fails a single check because of a brief network blip. Should the load balancer stop sending traffic to that server right away, and why or why not?
lessons.teach:
Definitions. A target group is the set of servers, called targets, that an Application Load Balancer (ALB) sends requests to. A health check is the test the ALB runs against each target. It sends a request to a path, such as /health, on a port, and expects a success code, such as 200. The interval is the time between checks. The timeout is how long the ALB waits for an answer. The healthy threshold is how many passes in a row make a target healthy again. The unhealthy threshold is how many failures in a row make a target unhealthy. Route 53 health checks work in a similar way, but they run from several checker locations around the world, and they can watch an endpoint, a calculated combination of other checks, or the state of a CloudWatch alarm.

Why it works. The ALB only sends new requests to targets in the healthy state. The thresholds exist so that one slow answer does not remove a server, while a server that is truly down is removed after a small, bounded delay.

Worked example. A target group uses the path /health, an interval of 30 seconds, a timeout of 5 seconds and an unhealthy threshold of 2. A server stops responding at time zero. Its check at 30 seconds times out, which is the first failure. The check at 60 seconds fails again, which is the second consecutive failure, so the target becomes unhealthy around 60 seconds. From then on, no new requests go to it. The checks keep running, and the target returns to service only after it passes the healthy threshold number of checks in a row.

Common mistake. Pointing the health check at a page that calls the database. If the database fails, every target fails the check at the same moment. The ALB then has no healthy targets, and the whole site returns errors, even though the servers could still answer simple requests. A shallow check that only confirms the application process is responding usually fits the load balancer better. Deeper checks belong in monitoring and alarms.

Consequence. A strict, deep health check can turn a partial dependency failure into a total outage.

questions.prompt: A payments team has a target group whose health check uses the path /status, an interval of 15 seconds, a timeout of 4 seconds, an unhealthy threshold of 3 and a healthy threshold of 2. One server stops answering at time zero. The check at 15 seconds times out, which is the first consecutive failure. The check at 30 seconds returns a 500 error, which is the second consecutive failure. The check at 45 seconds also fails, which is the third consecutive failure, so the target becomes unhealthy at 45 seconds and receives no new requests. The team repairs the server at 50 seconds. The check at 60 seconds passes, which is the first consecutive pass. The check at 75 seconds passes, which is the second consecutive pass. The trace stops here. The missing step is the moment the target returns to service and why that moment is correct.
choices: It returns to service at 90 seconds, after three passes, because the unhealthy threshold is reused for recovery.
It returns to service at 50 seconds, the moment the repair is finished, because the checks only confirm failures.
It returns to service at 60 seconds, after one pass, because a single pass is enough once the server is repaired.
It returns to service at 75 seconds, after two passes in a row, because that is the healthy threshold.
questions.why: The healthy threshold of 2 means the target needs two passes in a row, and the second pass at 75 seconds is the point where it returns to service.

questions.prompt: How does a Route 53 health check differ from an ALB target health check?
choices: Route 53 checks remove targets from a load balancer directly, while ALB checks only send alerts to an operator.
Route 53 checks only run from the same region as the target, so they are less accurate than ALB checks.
Route 53 checks accept only a 200 response, whereas ALB checks accept any response below 500.
Route 53 checks run from several locations around the world and can watch a calculated combination of checks or a CloudWatch alarm, not only one endpoint.
questions.why: Route 53 checks run from several checker locations and can also watch calculated checks or alarm state, which is the difference described in the teaching text.

questions.prompt: A web team points its ALB health check at a page that queries a cache and an external payment provider. The provider has a 10-minute outage, while the web servers themselves keep running. What happens to the load balancer?
choices: Only the targets that call the payment provider are removed, and the others keep serving requests normally.
The ALB keeps every target healthy, because the web process is still running and can answer requests.
Nothing changes, because the ALB ignores failed health checks when the failing dependency is outside the company.
Every target fails the same check, so the ALB has no healthy targets to send requests to and the site returns errors.
questions.why: A deep check that depends on a shared outside service fails on every target at once, leaving the ALB with no healthy targets even though the servers could answer simple requests.

questions.prompt: A target group has an unhealthy threshold of 5 and an interval of 10 seconds. A single slow answer happens once, and then every later check passes. Does the target become unhealthy?
choices: Yes, immediately, because any single failed check marks the target unhealthy.
No, because health checks mark a target unhealthy only when its process has stopped completely.
No, because the unhealthy threshold counts consecutive failures, and one failure followed by passes never reaches five.
Yes, after 50 seconds, because five intervals of 10 seconds must pass before any change takes effect.
questions.why: The unhealthy threshold counts failures in a row, so one failure followed by passes resets the count and the target stays healthy.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how an ALB health check decides that a target is unhealthy, and name one tradeoff in how deep the health check path should be.
lessons.modelAnswer: The load balancer sends a request to each target on a set path and port every interval seconds. If the answer is not one of the success codes, or it does not arrive within the timeout, that counts as a failure. After as many consecutive failures as the unhealthy threshold, the target is marked unhealthy and receives no new requests. It is marked healthy again after enough consecutive passes to meet the healthy threshold. The tradeoff is depth versus blast radius. A check that only confirms the process answers rarely removes servers by mistake, but it will not notice a broken feature. A check that calls the database or a third party catches more problems, yet if that dependency fails, every target fails together and the whole site goes dark. So I would keep the load balancer check shallow and put deeper checks in alarms and Route 53 failover policies, where a partial failure can be handled more gently.
rubricPoints: Explains that a target is marked unhealthy only after consecutive failures reach the unhealthy threshold
Describes what a failure is: a wrong status code or no answer within the timeout
Names the tradeoff between a shallow check and a deep check that tests dependencies
Notes that a deep check can remove every target at once during a dependency outage

suggested.rationale: Choosing health check settings for a fleet is best learned by reasoning through a partial outage scenario and predicting what each setting does.

lessons.plain: When something happens in a cloud account, such as a server being retired, a deployment failing, or someone changing a security setting, that happening is an event. This objective covers three services that create those events, carry them to a place where they can be routed, and keep a record of who did what. Think of them as the cloud's notice board, mail room, and logbook. Once you know which event happened, a program can react to it instead of a person noticing hours later. Learning how these three pieces fit together is the first step toward an automatic response.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose a production database is deleted at 2 a.m. Which kind of record would tell you who deleted it and when, and what would a program need in order to start a response on its own without waiting for a person?
lessons.teach:
An event is a record that something happened: a resource was created, a deployment finished, a platform notice was published. An event source is the service that produces events. Three sources matter here. AWS Health publishes notices about the health of the platform and about your own resources, such as a scheduled maintenance affecting a host you run. AWS CloudTrail records API calls, which are the requests made to change or read resources, including who made the request, from where, and whether it succeeded. Amazon EventBridge is an event router: it receives events on an event bus, checks each one against rules, and passes matches to targets such as a function or a notification topic.

Why it works: producers do not need to know who listens. A rule contains an event pattern, a description of the fields an event must have, such as a source service and an action name. Only matching events are delivered, and each target receives its own copy.

Worked example: someone edits a firewall rule so that a database port is open to the whole internet. Step 1: the edit is an API call, so CloudTrail records it with the caller identity and the action name. Step 2: that record reaches the default event bus in the same account and region. Step 3: a rule whose pattern names that action matches the event. Step 4: the rule delivers the event to a target that alerts the on-call team or starts a response.

Common mistake: assuming a rule will catch events from another region or another account. Event buses are scoped to one account and one region, so a rule in the wrong place never sees the event, and the response silently never runs.

The consequence is that a missed event produces no error that anyone sees; the protection simply does not happen. Event routing is only as reliable as the rule placement and the pattern you wrote.

questions.prompt: A logistics company, account 5530 in ap-southeast-2, has a platform team that wants an alert whenever someone opens a security group to the internet. Here is the chain they are building, with one step left blank. Step 1: an engineer changes a security group ingress rule, which is an API call, so CloudTrail (the service that records API calls, including the caller and whether the call succeeded) writes a record naming the caller and the action. Step 2: that record arrives on the default event bus (the bus in one account and one region that receives that account's events) in account 5530, ap-southeast-2. Step 3: [blank]. Step 4: the matching rule's target, a notification topic, sends an alert to the security channel. Which statement correctly fills the blank?
choices: CloudTrail copies the record into a storage bucket in every region so that any rule in any region can read it.
The health service publishes a maintenance notice for the security group, which the rule then forwards to the topic.
The event bus forwards the record to the rule in us-east-1, which is the default region for all accounts.
