A rule whose event pattern names that action matches the record, and only the matching copy is delivered to the target.
questions.why: Step 3 is where a rule's event pattern is checked against the event, and a match causes delivery to the target, which is the only option that describes that routing behaviour without adding a service or cross-region step the setup does not have.

questions.prompt: A junior engineer asks which service would let a security reviewer check, after the fact, that a particular IAM user made a failed attempt to delete a snapshot from a particular IP address. Which service should the reviewer look at?
choices: Amazon EventBridge, because it stores every event and lets you search it by caller.
The event bus itself, because every event passes through it and is kept there.
AWS Health, because it publishes notices about your own resources and the platform.
AWS CloudTrail, because it records API calls with the caller identity, source address, and whether the call succeeded.
questions.why: CloudTrail is the source that records who made an API call, from where, and whether it succeeded, while the other options either publish notices, route events without keeping a history, or are not a separate log source at all.

questions.prompt: A team in account 710, running in eu-west-3, created a rule in account 710 in us-east-1 to respond when a storage bucket is deleted. A different team, account 884 in eu-west-3, deletes a bucket and nothing happens. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The event pattern should have used a wildcard, because bucket names are never exact matches.
The notification topic cannot receive events from storage buckets, only from functions.
CloudTrail does not record delete actions, only read actions, so nothing was ever produced.
The rule lives in a different account and region from where the deletion happened, so it never sees that event.
questions.why: Event buses are scoped to one account and one region, so a rule placed elsewhere cannot receive the deletion event and the response silently never runs, which is why the last option is the cause rather than a pattern or target problem.

questions.prompt: An operations lead has one event, a notice that a host in her fleet will be retired, and wants both a ticket created and a paging alert sent. She has one rule on the event bus matching that event, and two targets attached to that rule. Which statement correctly describes what happens?
choices: Each target receives its own copy of the matching event, so both the ticket and the page are triggered.
The event is saved to a queue, and each target must poll the queue to find out whether it has work to do.
The rule splits the event so each target receives half of its fields, which together make up the whole event.
The event is delivered to the first target only, and the second target is used if the first one fails.
questions.why: A rule passes matching events to every attached target and each target gets its own copy, so both actions run, which is the fan-out behaviour the other three options misdescribe as failover, splitting, or polling.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would make sure a security group change made by hand in production is noticed automatically. Name which service produces the record, which one routes it, and one limit or tradeoff of relying on this setup.
lessons.modelAnswer: CloudTrail is the record: every API call that changes a security group is logged with the caller, the action and the time. EventBridge is the router: I would write a rule on the default event bus in the same account and region whose pattern matches that action, with a target such as a notification topic that pages the on-call engineer. AWS Health is different, because it reports platform and resource notices, such as a scheduled host retirement, so it would not show a manual firewall edit. One tradeoff is that the rule only sees events in its own account and region, so a change in another account needs its own rule or a forwarding setup. Also, CloudTrail's built-in event history keeps only recent management events, so for longer retention I would configure a trail that delivers logs to storage. The alert tells someone about the change; it does not undo the change by itself.
rubricPoints: CloudTrail records API calls with the caller identity, action, and time, and is the source of the change record.
EventBridge routes events by matching rule patterns to targets on an event bus.
Rules and event buses are scoped to one account and one region, which limits where a response can see changes.
Alerting notifies people but does not by itself reverse the change, and log retention needs a trail for longer periods.

suggested.rationale: Matching events against rules and delivering them to targets is the core skill the planned messaging and events engine would exercise.

lessons.plain: Event-driven design means components communicate by announcing that something happened, instead of calling each other directly. The announcement is called an event. There are three common shapes. Fan-out sends one announcement to many listeners at once, so each listener gets its own copy. A queue holds work in a line until a worker takes it, which lets a fast producer and a slower consumer work at different speeds. Event streaming keeps an ordered, replayable record that many readers can read at their own pace. Think of a newspaper delivered to many houses, a ticket line at a bakery, and a ship's logbook that anyone can read from any page.
lessons.guessPrompt: A payment service must tell the email service, the analytics service, and the fraud service that a payment succeeded. Should the payment service call all three directly, or publish one message that all three receive? Which choice makes adding a fourth listener easier, and why?
lessons.teach:
An event is a record that something already happened, such as an order being placed. A producer is the component that publishes an event. A consumer is a component that reacts to it. In event-driven design the producer announces facts and does not need to know who listens, so you can add or remove consumers without changing the producer.

Three patterns cover most cases. Fan-out means one published message is copied to several subscribers, each getting its own copy, usually through a topic (a named channel that subscribers attach to). A queue holds messages until a worker takes one, processes it, and deletes it. Several workers can share the load, and the queue absorbs bursts so producer and consumer run at different speeds. Event streaming writes events to an ordered log kept for a set retention period. Each reader tracks its own position, called an offset, and can read again from an earlier point, which helps when you need to replay history after a bug fix.

Worked example: an order-placed event is published once. Step 1: the topic copies it to three subscriptions. Step 2: the billing subscription's queue holds its copy. Step 3: a billing worker takes the message, which makes it invisible to other workers for 30 seconds, and charges the card. Step 4: the worker deletes the message after success. If the worker crashes before deleting, the message becomes visible again after 30 seconds and another worker picks it up.

Common mistake: assuming each message is processed exactly once. Most managed queues deliver at least once, so the same message can arrive twice. The handler must be idempotent, meaning running it twice has the same effect as running it once, typically by recording the order ID before charging the card.

Consequence in a running system: if workers stop draining the billing queue, its depth grows without limit. Messages that repeatedly fail can be moved to a dead-letter queue, a holding queue for inspection, so they are not lost silently.

questions.prompt: A photo app publishes an upload-received event once for each image. Trace it through the pattern. Step 1: the topic copies the event to two subscriptions, one for thumbnails and one for content moderation. Step 2: the thumbnail subscription's queue holds its copy. Step 3: a thumbnail worker takes the message, which hides it from other workers for 60 seconds, then generates three image sizes and saves them. Step 4 is missing. Which action completes the sequence so the same message does not come back to another worker?
choices: The worker deletes the message from the thumbnail queue after the sizes are saved.
The worker shortens the hidden period to zero so the message is visible to everyone at once.
The topic removes the copy it made for the moderation subscription.
The worker publishes a new upload-received event so that moderation runs again.
questions.why: A worker that finishes successfully must delete its message; otherwise the message becomes visible again when the hidden period ends and another worker picks it up.

questions.prompt: A video transcoding team keeps its events in an ordered log with 7-day retention. Their analytics reader has read up to position 4120. What does that position identify?
choices: The number of workers currently attached to the log.
The reader's own place in the ordered log, from which it can read again or move back.
The total number of events ever published to the log.
The number of seconds since the last event was published.
questions.why: In event streaming each reader tracks its own offset, which marks its position in the log and lets it re-read earlier events.

questions.prompt: A label-printing service has a worker that prints a shipping label, then crashes before deleting its queue message. The handler keeps no record of which shipment IDs it has already handled. Once the hidden period ends, what is the likely result, and which fix matches the teaching text?
choices: The queue ends the subscription, so the topic must resend every event from the start.
The message is lost for good, so the team should switch to a larger queue.
The message is deleted automatically on a crash, so a second label cannot be printed.
The message may be processed a second time, so the handler should record shipment IDs and skip repeats, making it idempotent.
questions.why: Queues often deliver at least once, so a redelivered message can run twice; recording the ID before acting makes repeat runs harmless.

questions.prompt: A billing queue has 40 workers stopped over a long weekend while producers keep publishing. Which outcome does the teaching text predict, and how are the messages that cannot be processed kept from being lost silently?
choices: Messages are dropped once the queue passes ten items, so nothing needs inspecting afterwards.
Queue depth grows without limit while the workers are stopped, and messages that repeatedly fail can be moved to a dead-letter queue for inspection.
Each worker's offset resets to zero, so the backlog is processed twice when the workers restart.
Queue depth stays flat because the topic stops copying new events while no worker is running.
questions.why: With no workers draining the queue its depth keeps growing, and a dead-letter queue is the holding place for messages that keep failing so they are not silently lost.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate when you would choose a queue over fan-out to a topic, and name one cost or limit of the choice you make.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would use a queue when one kind of work should be done once by one of several workers, such as charging a card, and I want a burst of requests to wait instead of overwhelming the worker. Fan-out to a topic is better when several independent consumers each need the same event, like email, analytics, and fraud checks. The limit of a queue is that delivery is usually at least once, so a message can arrive twice after a timeout or crash, and the worker has to be idempotent, for example by recording the order ID before acting. The cost of fan-out is that every subscriber gets its own copy, so more subscribers means more processing and more places a failure can hide. I would also watch queue depth and set a dead-letter queue so repeatedly failing messages are visible rather than lost.
rubricPoints: A queue gives one message to one worker and smooths bursts of load
Fan-out copies one event to many independent subscribers
Delivery is usually at least once, so handlers must be idempotent
Queue depth and dead-letter queues are how failures become visible

suggested.rationale: The messaging engine would let the learner wire fan-out, queues and streams and watch what happens when a consumer stops, which is the core skill of this objective.

lessons.plain: When something happens in a cloud account, such as a server failing, a deployment finishing, or a setting being changed, the platform can announce it as a short message called an event. Integrating event sources means connecting those announcements to a chain of steps that reacts on its own: someone is paged, a fix runs, or a record is written. The goal is that a problem gets handled while people sleep, and that the reaction is predictable and safe to repeat. Think of it as a mailroom that reads each incoming notice and sends it to the right desk.
lessons.guessPrompt: A database fails over at 3 a.m. and the on-call engineer is asleep. What would you want to happen automatically, and what could go wrong if the automatic reaction runs twice?
lessons.teach:
An event source is anything that emits an event, meaning a record that something happened, with a timestamp and details. Common sources in AWS include AWS Health (notices about platform events affecting your resources), AWS CloudTrail (a log of API calls, such as someone changing a firewall rule), and CloudWatch alarms (a measured value crossing a threshold). An event bus is a central router that receives events and forwards them. A rule is a filter on that bus: it matches events by pattern, such as source service and event name, and sends matches to a target. A target is whatever does the work, such as a queue, a function, a workflow, or a notification topic.

Why it works: the source does not need to know who reacts. You can add a second reaction later without changing the source, and the router ensures the response logic only sees events it cares about.

Worked example: a CloudTrail record shows that an inbound rule was opened to port 22 from anywhere. Step 1: CloudTrail records the API call and the event bus receives it. Step 2: a rule matches authorization changes to security groups. Step 3: the rule sends the event to a workflow that checks the change against an approved list, then either reverts it or opens a ticket for a human. Step 4: the workflow records what it did and why.

Common mistake: assuming each event is delivered exactly once. Most event delivery is at-least-once, so the same event can arrive twice. A remediation that is not idempotent (safe to repeat, producing the same end state each time) may act twice and cause harm.

Consequence: if a rule is too broad, a revert loop can start, where the fix itself emits an event that triggers the fix again.

Every reaction must be idempotent and must stop itself from re-triggering, because an unattended loop can do more damage than the original drift.

questions.prompt: A payments team has a CloudWatch alarm that enters the ALARM state when a work queue's oldest message is older than 900 seconds. The response is wired like this. Step 1: the alarm changes state and the event bus receives the state-change event. Step 2: a rule matches alarm state changes whose alarm name starts with payments-queue and sends them to a function. Step 3: [blank]. Step 4: the function writes what it did and why to a log table. Which step 3 completes the design so that a duplicate delivery of the same event cannot cause a second scale-out?
choices: The rule forwards every event on the bus to the function, with no pattern filter, so that no alarm is ever missed by the response logic.
The alarm is deleted after it fires, so it cannot emit a second state-change event and cause a repeat.
The function checks for an in-progress scale-out for that queue and exits if one exists, so a duplicate event changes nothing.
The function raises the consumer fleet to 500 instances straight away, without reading the current size or any prior action, so the queue clears quickly.
questions.why: Because events can arrive more than once, the function must check whether the work is already in progress and do nothing on a repeat, which keeps the reaction idempotent.

questions.prompt: In the teaching text's sense, what is an event bus?
choices: A central router that receives events and forwards them to matching targets.
A threshold on a measured value that causes a notification when it is crossed.
A log file that records every API call made in an account so auditors can review it later.
A queue that stores events until a worker picks each one up and removes it from storage.
questions.why: The teaching text defines an event bus as a central router that receives events and forwards them, which is different from a queue, a log, or an alarm.

questions.prompt: A fintech team wants to be told whenever AWS Health posts a scheduled change affecting its accounts, and wants to be able to add a second reaction later without editing the Health source. Which design fits the teaching text?
choices: Edit the Health service configuration so it calls the team's script directly whenever a notice appears.
Send every event on the bus to one function that checks the event type inside its own code.
A rule on the bus matching the Health source and event name, sending to a notification topic.
Have engineers read the CloudTrail log each morning and search it for maintenance wording by hand.
questions.why: A rule filters by source and event name and sends matches to a target, so the source needs no changes and the response logic only sees events it cares about.

questions.prompt: An automated workflow adds a missing cost-center tag to a storage volume. The tag change itself emits a configuration event that matches the same rule, which runs the tagger again. What is the risk, and what must the reaction do?
choices: The bus disables the rule after its first match, so the loop cannot form and no guard is needed.
A revert or tag loop can start, so the reaction must be safe to repeat and must stop its own re-triggering.
Nothing happens, because the bus delivers each event exactly once, so the tag-change event is never sent a second time.
The loop cannot form because the configuration service only records changes made by human users, not by automated workflows.
questions.why: The fix emits an event that matches its own rule, so without idempotency and a guard against self-triggering, the workflow can repeat indefinitely and do more harm than the original problem.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would connect a security-change event to an automatic response, and name one limit or tradeoff of automating that response.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start with the source: CloudTrail records the authorization call, and the event bus receives it. A rule filters for that specific kind of change to a security group, so unrelated events never reach the response. The rule targets a workflow that checks the change against an approved list, then either reverts it or raises a ticket for a person. The main tradeoff is that an automatic revert can break something a team changed on purpose, so the approved list and a clear escalation path matter as much as the code. I would also make the revert idempotent and tag it, so the revert's own event does not trigger another revert.
rubricPoints: Names the event source and how the event reaches a router or rule.
Explains that a rule filters events so only relevant ones trigger a response.
Describes the target and what the response does, including a human escalation path.
States a real limit, such as false positives, at-least-once delivery, or the risk of a re-trigger loop.

suggested.rationale: Routing events through filtered rules to targets is a messaging skill that the planned messaging engine would let the learner practise directly.

lessons.plain: Event processing workflows are the chains of automatic steps a cloud system runs when something happens, such as a server failing a health check or a deployment breaking. Instead of a person noticing and acting, the event is passed along a path. It may be held in a waiting line, copied to several listeners, or recorded in an ordered stream, and small programs react to it. A workflow manager can then track a multi-step recipe, including retries and what to do when a step fails. The skill is choosing the right piece for each job and making sure no event is lost, harmfully repeated, or silently stuck. Think of a restaurant kitchen: tickets go on a rail, several cooks see the same order, and an expediter tracks each dish through its steps.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose a payment event arrives and the program that handles it crashes halfway through. What do you think should happen to that event, and how would a team find out later that it was lost?
lessons.teach:
An event is a record that something happened, such as a deployment finishing or a server going unhealthy. A producer publishes events, and a consumer reacts to them. Four building blocks cover most designs. A queue (Amazon SQS, a managed message queue) holds messages until a consumer takes each one, which smooths bursts and lets work wait. A topic (Amazon SNS, a publish and subscribe service) pushes one message to many subscribers at once; this copying to several receivers is called fan-out. A stream (Amazon Kinesis) keeps an ordered, replayable log that several readers can consume at their own pace. A function (AWS Lambda) runs a small piece of code each time it is triggered. A state machine (AWS Step Functions) coordinates several steps, with retries and branches, as one tracked workflow.

Why it works: each piece decouples the producer from the consumer, so a slow or broken consumer does not stop the producer, and messages wait instead of being dropped.

Worked example: a failed deployment publishes one event to a topic. Three subscribers receive it: a queue feeding a notifier, a function that opens a ticket, and a state machine that starts a rollback. The rollback step fails twice. The state machine waits and retries, then routes the run to an error branch that alerts an engineer. Each step is visible in the run history.

Common mistake: assuming each message is delivered exactly once. Queues and topics usually deliver at least once, so a message can arrive twice after a timeout. If the handler charges a card or sends an email on every arrival, the customer is charged twice. The fix is an idempotent handler, one that records the message ID and skips work it has already done.

Consequence: a message that always fails gets retried forever and clogs its queue, delaying every message behind it. Systems send such messages to a dead-letter queue, a holding line for messages that failed too many times, so someone can inspect them.

questions.prompt: A furniture company's warehouse sends scanner events into a queue. A label worker takes each message, prints a shipping label, and deletes the message when printing succeeds. One message names a label template that does not exist, so the worker fails on it every time it is taken. Step 1: the failed message becomes available again and is taken by the worker a second time. Step 2: [missing step]. Step 3: the scanner messages queued behind the bad one are printed normally. Which choice correctly fills in step 2?
choices: The message is retried indefinitely, and the scanner stops sending new events until someone fixes the template
The worker prints a blank label and deletes the message so the queue stays clean
The queue copies the message into a topic that emails every subscriber about the failure
After repeated failures the message is moved to a dead-letter queue, a holding line where someone can inspect it
questions.why: A dead-letter queue is the holding line that receives messages after they fail too many times, which stops the bad message from blocking those behind it.

questions.prompt: A cloud team wants one 'instance became unhealthy' event delivered at the same moment to a paging subscriber, a log archiver, and a chat notifier. Which building block is the best fit?
choices: A stream, because it keeps an ordered log that only one reader reads
A function, because it runs code each time it is triggered
A queue, because each message is held until one consumer takes it
A topic, because it pushes one message to many subscribers at once
questions.why: A topic (Amazon SNS) performs fan-out, copying one published message to several subscribers, whereas a queue hands each message to a single consumer.

questions.prompt: A payment confirmation consumer reads from a queue. After a timeout, the same confirmation message arrives twice, and the handler charges the customer each time. Which change prevents the double charge?
choices: Make the handler record each message ID and skip any message ID it has already processed
Remove the queue and call the payment code directly from the producer
Add more consumers so each copy is processed faster and the charge completes sooner
Enable exactly-once delivery so that the queue never sends a second copy
questions.why: Queues and topics usually deliver at least once, so the handler must be idempotent, meaning it records the message ID and skips work it has already done.

questions.prompt: A logistics company needs several independent analytics readers to each read the full ordered history of vehicle location events, at their own pace, and to replay older events if a reader needs to reprocess them. Which building block fits?
choices: A stream (Amazon Kinesis), which keeps an ordered, replayable log that each reader consumes at its own pace
A topic (Amazon SNS), which pushes each event to subscribers and does not keep a history for replay
A queue (Amazon SQS), where each message is removed once a single consumer takes it
A function (AWS Lambda), which runs a piece of code each time an event arrives
questions.why: A stream keeps an ordered log that multiple readers can consume independently and replay, which a queue (messages removed after being taken) and a topic (pushed, not stored for replay) do not provide.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between a queue, a topic, and a stream for a new event, and name one tradeoff or limit of the choice you make.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start with who needs the event and whether it must be kept for replay. If one group of workers should take each job once, a queue fits: work waits there until a consumer picks it up, which absorbs bursts. If several independent systems all need the same event, I would publish to a topic so each subscriber gets its own copy, which is fan-out. If many readers need an ordered history they can re-read or replay from a chosen point, I would use a stream. The tradeoff is that queues and topics generally deliver at least once, so the handler must be idempotent, meaning a repeat does no harm. Streams keep order within a partition but add operational work to track each reader's position. Whatever I pick, I would attach a dead-letter queue so poison messages, meaning messages that always fail, stop blocking the line and can be inspected.
rubricPoints: Matches the pattern to the need: a queue for one group of workers, a topic for many subscribers, a stream for ordered replayable history.
Names at-least-once delivery and the need for idempotent handlers.
Explains that a dead-letter queue or failure path keeps poison messages from blocking other work.
States a real tradeoff such as ordering scope, replay cost, or operational overhead.

suggested.rationale: That mission makes you trace a queue backed up by messages that keep failing, which is the failure-handling half of this objective.

lessons.plain: Fleet management means keeping many servers in a known, healthy state without logging into each one by hand. AWS Systems Manager is a toolbox for that job: it runs a command across a group of machines, applies patches on a schedule, and checks that settings still match a template you define. AWS Auto Scaling is the part that adds or removes servers automatically so the group matches the load. Think of a staffing agency that both checks that every worker is trained and hires extra people when the queue gets long.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose 40 servers should all have the same security patch, and one server has quietly stopped answering while two others are running an older configuration. Without logging into each machine, how would you find which servers are out of step and bring them back without disturbing the healthy ones? What would you need to know about each server before deciding what to change?
lessons.teach: A managed instance is a server registered with Systems Manager, usually through an agent program plus an instance role that grants it permission to report in. Run Command sends a predefined action, called a document, to a set of targets selected by tags, and it reports a result for each target. State Manager holds an association, which is a rule that applies a desired configuration and re-checks it on a schedule. Patch Manager uses a patch baseline, a list of rules saying which updates are approved. Auto Scaling works on an Auto Scaling group, which has a minimum, maximum and desired capacity, a launch template describing the machine image and settings for new instances, and a scaling policy that decides when the desired count changes. A target tracking policy keeps one chosen metric near a target value.  Worked example: a group has minimum 2, maximum 10, desired 4, and a target tracking policy on average CPU of 50 percent. Step 1: load rises and average CPU reaches 80 percent. Step 2: the policy compares actual to target, a ratio of 80 to 50, or 1.6. Step 3: 4 times 1.6 is 6.4, rounded up to 7. Step 4: the group launches 3 instances from the launch template, and once they pass health checks, load spreads across 7 machines.  Common mistake: assuming new instances match the rest of the fleet. If the launch template points at an old machine image, every scale-out brings back unpatched servers, so a patch applied only with Run Command is undone the next time the group grows. The fix is to update the image or template and let State Manager keep checking the running machines.  Consequence: during an incident, a group that scales out quickly can spread an outdated configuration faster than anyone notices, so the launch template is part of the release, not an afterthought.

questions.prompt: A batch-processing team runs an Auto Scaling group with minimum 1, maximum 6, and desired 5. Its scaling policy is target tracking on average CPU with a target of 60 percent. Step 1: a nightly job pushes average CPU to 100 percent. Step 2: the policy compares actual to target, a ratio of 100 to 60, or about 1.67. Step 3: 5 times 1.67 is 8.33, which rounds up to 9. Step 4 is missing. The group's maximum is 6, and the desired count can never go above the maximum. What is the correct step 4?
choices: The group launches 4 instances so that the total reaches 9, because the policy result is always applied exactly.
The group sets desired to 9 and waits for a person to approve the change before launching anything.
The group terminates 3 instances so that average CPU falls back to the 60 percent target.
The group launches 1 instance from the launch template, because the desired count is capped at the maximum of 6.
questions.why: A target tracking result is limited by the group's maximum, so desired becomes 6 and the group launches the one missing instance from the launch template.

questions.prompt: A small team has 40 Linux servers tagged env=staging. They want a specific security setting checked and re-applied every week without anyone starting it by hand. Which Systems Manager feature fits this need?
choices: Patch Manager with a patch baseline, because it lists which updates are approved.
A State Manager association, because it holds a desired configuration and re-checks it on a schedule.
Run Command, because it sends an action to tagged servers and reports the result once.
An Auto Scaling scaling policy, because it changes the number of servers when load changes.
questions.why: State Manager associations apply a desired configuration and re-check it on a schedule, which is the recurring check the team needs, while Run Command is a one-off action.

questions.prompt: A web tier runs in an Auto Scaling group whose launch template points at a machine image built three months ago. A security fix was pushed to the running servers with Run Command last week. Today a traffic spike causes the group to scale out by 4 instances. What is the most likely problem?
choices: The scale-out will fail, because Run Command and Auto Scaling cannot operate on the same group.
The four new instances will lack the security fix, because they are built from the old image and the template was not updated.
The four new instances will be patched automatically because the target tracking policy applies all past Run Command actions.
Nothing is wrong, because the fix on the running servers is copied to new instances at launch.
questions.why: New instances come from the launch template's image, so a fix applied only to running machines is missing from every scale-out until the image or template is updated.

questions.prompt: An Auto Scaling group has minimum 3, maximum 12, and desired 6. Its target tracking policy keeps requests per target near 200. Current load gives 350 requests per target. Using the same logic as the standard approach of comparing actual to target, what happens next?
choices: The desired count stays at 6, because scale-out only happens at fixed times of day.
The desired count becomes 12, the maximum, because any breach of the target jumps straight to the maximum.
The desired count becomes 11, so the group launches 5 more instances from its launch template.
The desired count becomes 10, because the ratio is rounded down.
questions.why: The ratio is 350 to 200, or 1.75, so 6 times 1.75 is 10.5, which rounds up to 11, and the group launches 5 instances to go from 6 to 11.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how Systems Manager and Auto Scaling differ in what they do for a fleet of servers, and name one limit or tradeoff of relying on them to keep servers in a good state.
lessons.modelAnswer: Systems Manager works on machines that already exist. It runs commands on tagged targets, applies patches from an approved baseline, and uses State Manager to re-check that settings still match what you defined. Auto Scaling changes how many machines exist. It keeps a group between a minimum and maximum size and adds or removes instances based on a policy such as target tracking on CPU. The two cooperate, but they do different jobs. The main tradeoff is that Systems Manager only reaches instances it can contact, so a server with a broken agent or missing instance role can look fine in Auto Scaling while drifting out of date. Auto Scaling also creates new machines from a launch template, so any fix that lives only on running servers will be lost when the group scales out. The template and the Systems Manager rules both have to be kept current.
rubricPoints: Systems Manager acts on existing managed instances through commands, patching and desired-state checks
Auto Scaling changes the number of instances within a minimum and maximum based on a policy
New instances come from a launch template, so fixes must be in the template or image
Systems Manager cannot manage a server whose agent or instance role is broken

suggested.rationale: Choosing and reasoning about scaling policies is best practised by a planned autoscale engine that changes capacity against a simulated load.

lessons.plain: Applying a configuration change to a system means changing a setting on a running machine or service, such as a timeout, a log level, or a file path, without rebuilding it from scratch. When many machines need the same change, doing it by hand over remote sessions is slow and error-prone. Instead you describe the change once, aim it at a chosen group of machines, run it, check the result, and keep a record of what changed. In an incident, this is how a fix reaches every affected server in minutes rather than one at a time.
lessons.guessPrompt: Forty web servers each read a timeout setting from a local file, and you need it raised from 5 to 10 seconds right now. What would you worry about before changing all forty at once, and why?
lessons.teach:
A configuration is the set of settings a program reads when it starts or while it runs: timeouts, file paths, feature flags, log levels. Applying a configuration change means writing a new value into that setting on one or more live systems and making the running software pick it up, usually by reloading or restarting it. The key idea is that the change is described once and applied the same way everywhere, so the fleet ends up in a known state.

Three terms matter here. A fleet is the group of machines that serve the same role. A runbook, sometimes called a document, is a stored set of steps that a fleet-management tool runs against its targets. Idempotent means running a change twice leaves the system in the same state as running it once; a good change checks the current value before writing, so a retry is safe. Blast radius is how many systems a bad change could harm if it goes wrong.

Why it works: a central tool runs the same steps over an agreed group, records which targets succeeded, and lets you stop when something goes wrong. Selecting targets by tag, such as only servers tagged as the API tier, keeps the blast radius small.

Worked example: the timeout is 5 seconds on 40 hosts. Step 1: select the hosts tagged api-tier in production. Step 2: apply the change to 2 hosts first. Step 3: watch their error rate and latency for ten minutes. Step 4: if healthy, apply to the next batch of 10, then the rest, pausing between batches. Step 5: write the old and new values to your change log.

Common mistake: applying the change to everything at once, then discovering the new value breaks a dependency, with no clear record of what was changed first. The fix is staged batches and a recorded previous value so you can roll back.

Consequence: a host whose settings no longer match the intended ones, which is called configuration drift, may have been edited by hand. It will behave differently under load, and the next automated run can silently overwrite that edit or fail on it. A configuration change is only as safe as its verification step and its rollback plan.

questions.prompt: A logistics company changes the connection pool size from 10 to 30 on a fleet of 12 warehouse-reporting servers, using a stored procedure that its fleet-management tool runs against the targets. The steps they ran were: (1) read the current pool size on each host and skip any host already at 30, so a retry is harmless; (2) write 30 into the config file on the first 2 hosts; (3) [missing step]; (4) confirm the running process now reports a pool size of 30. Which step fills the gap?
choices: Run the write against all 12 hosts at once so the fleet ends up in the same state.
Double the pool size to 60 so the hosts have headroom for the next busy period.
Reload or restart the service so the running process reads the new value from the file.
Delete the old config file so only one copy of the settings remains on disk.
questions.why: Writing a new value to a file does not change a program that already loaded its settings, so the process must be reloaded or restarted to pick it up, and the check in step 4 only passes after that.

questions.prompt: Which term describes a change that leaves a system in the same state whether it is run once or run several times, so a retry is safe?
choices: Blast radius
Idempotent
Configuration drift
Fleet
questions.why: Idempotent is the term for a change that checks the current value before writing, so repeating it produces the same final state as running it once.

questions.prompt: A team must change a retry limit on the payment-gateway hosts tagged tier=checkout, but only in one region, and wants to keep the blast radius small. Which approach best fits that goal?
choices: Pick a random half of all hosts across regions and apply the change to them.
Apply the change to every host in every region at once to save time.
Edit each host by hand through a remote terminal, one at a time, without recording values.
Select hosts by the checkout tag in the one region, start with two hosts, watch them, then widen in batches.
questions.why: Selecting by tag limits the targets, and starting small with staged batches and a watch period lets you stop before a bad value reaches many systems.

questions.prompt: An engineer manually edited a timeout setting on one of 30 hosts last week. Today the automated change to that setting fails on only that host. What is the most accurate explanation, and what does it imply?
choices: The blast radius of the change has grown to include that host, so the change must be cancelled everywhere.
The host has drifted from the intended configuration, so the automated run can fail on it or overwrite the manual edit.
The fleet is healthy and the failure is a brief network blip that will clear on its own.
The runbook has become corrupt and must be rewritten before any further change can run.
questions.why: A setting edited by hand that no longer matches the intended value is configuration drift, and it causes exactly this failure or silent overwrite on the next automated run.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would push a new setting to a fleet of servers in response to an alert, and name one limit or tradeoff of doing it automatically rather than by hand.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would describe the change once as a stored, repeatable step, target it by a tag so only the intended servers receive it, and run it in batches: two canary hosts first, then the rest. Between batches I check the metric the change was meant to fix, such as error rate or latency, and I stop if things get worse. I record the previous value so rollback is the same procedure with the old value. The tradeoff is that automation makes a wrong change reach many machines fast, so the blast radius has to be kept small through batching, and the tool only does exactly the steps I gave it. If a host was edited by hand, the automated run may overwrite that edit or fail on it, so I check for drift before running. Automation speeds up the fix, but it does not replace verification.
rubricPoints: Describes the change once as a repeatable, targeted step rather than manual edits on each host.
Applies the change in small batches with a check between batches to limit blast radius.
Records the previous value so the change can be rolled back quickly.
Names a limit such as configuration drift, a wrong value spreading fast, or the tool doing only what it was told.

suggested.rationale: Applying a setting in staged batches with checks between them is the core of a staged fleet rollout, which this engine would practise.

lessons.plain: When something in a running system changes in a way nobody intended, software can notice the change and correct it automatically, instead of waiting for a person to read an alert. This objective is about designing that response. A signal arrives, a rule decides whether it matters, and an action changes the configuration back toward what was intended. A good response is quick, narrow, and safe to repeat. A poor one can undo legitimate work or fight with another automation, so the design choices matter as much as the change itself.
lessons.guessPrompt: At 3 a.m., someone edits a server's firewall by hand and opens a port to all addresses, and nobody is watching. What would you want an automated system to do about it, and what could go wrong if it reacted too aggressively?
lessons.teach: A configuration is the set of settings that decides how a resource behaves, such as which network ports are open or how many copies of a service run. A desired state is the configuration your team intended, usually written down in code. Drift is what happens when the real resource no longer matches the desired state, often because someone changed it by hand. A remediation is an automatic action that moves the resource back toward the desired state. The usual chain has three parts. An event source emits a signal that something changed. A rule matches that signal and selects a target. The target, often a small function or a managed automation document, makes the correction. Why it works: the rule runs within seconds, so the window of exposure is short, and the same action runs every time, so the result is predictable. Worked example: a firewall entry opening port 22 to all addresses is created. The change event is emitted. The rule matches changes to firewall entries where the port is 22 and the source is everywhere. The target removes only that one entry, leaves everything else alone, and writes a log line naming the change and the time. Running it a second time changes nothing, which is what idempotent means. Common mistake: making the action too broad, such as resetting the whole firewall to a template. That also removes approved entries and can cut off a service. A second mistake is having no exemption path, so an intentional change gets reverted every time. Consequence: if another automation reapplies the old value, the two can keep flipping the setting back and forth, and the system never settles. Every response should be narrow, idempotent, and logged so a person can see what changed and why.

questions.prompt: A logistics company runs a fleet of parcel-label workers in a second cloud account. The code says the desired count is 6. During a peak-season test, an engineer raises the live count to 20 and tags the fleet with exemption set to peak-test. The response chain is: 1) The count change event is emitted. 2) A rule matches count changes above 6 on the label-workers fleet. 3) [missing step]. 4) The target writes a log line naming the fleet, the old and new counts, and the time. Which choice completes step 3?
choices: The target sets the count back to 6 for every fleet in the account, including fleets that carry tags.
The rule is disabled so the count change event is never emitted again.
The target reads the exemption tag; if the tag is present, it leaves the count at 20 and logs that it skipped the change.
The target deletes the whole fleet and recreates it from the template so the count resets cleanly.
questions.why: The exemption check must happen inside the target before any correction, so an intentional change is not reverted, while the other choices are too broad or remove the signal entirely.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what is drift in a response chain?
choices: An automatic action that moves a resource back to its intended settings.
The real resource no longer matching the intended configuration, often after someone changes it by hand.
The short delay between a change happening and a rule running.
A rule that matches the wrong kind of event signal.
questions.why: Drift is defined as the situation where the real resource no longer matches the desired state, often because of a manual change.

questions.prompt: A target resets an entire security group to its template every time one port is opened. Which pair of problems does this design create?
choices: It removes approved entries and can cut off a service, and intentional changes get reverted with no exemption path.
It only works on Linux hosts, so Windows hosts are left unprotected.
It writes too much log data and fills the storage volume.
It runs too slowly and the events arrive out of order.
questions.why: The teaching text names both problems: a too-broad reset removes approved entries, and having no exemption path reverts intentional changes every time.

questions.prompt: Two automations each set the size of a worker pool. One sets it to 4 every hour, and the other sets it to 10 on each deploy. What is the likely consequence, and which design principle helps prevent it?
choices: The pool size is cached and the two values are averaged.
The pool scales up faster, but nothing else changes.
The two settings can keep flipping the value back and forth so the system never settles; narrow, idempotent, logged responses help prevent this.
The pool stays at the first value because the second is ignored by default.
questions.why: The teaching text warns that competing automations reapplying different values can flip a setting back and forth indefinitely, and that every response should be narrow, idempotent, and logged.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would make a running system automatically correct a configuration change that was made outside the normal process. Name one limit or tradeoff of doing that.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would have the system emit a change event whenever a monitored setting is modified, then use a rule to match only the specific setting we care about. The target would be a small, idempotent action that restores that one value to the version in our code, so running it twice does no harm. I would log the change and the correction so someone can review it. The main tradeoff is that automatic correction can undo a change someone made on purpose during an incident, so we need an exemption mechanism, such as a tag, and a clear owner for each rule. Without that, the automation can make a manual fix harder to make.
rubricPoints: Defines drift as the live state diverging from the intended state in code
Describes the chain of event, rule, and target, and keeps the correction narrow
Explains idempotency or safe repetition of the correction
Names a real limit, such as undoing intentional changes or conflicting automations, and a way to handle it

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through a drift event and choosing a narrow, safe correction is best practised as an exam-style scenario, since no listed mission covers it directly.

lessons.plain: A desired state is the setup you have decided a system should have: a port is closed, a server runs the right software version, a disk has room to spare. Over time things drift away from that setup, often because someone made a quick manual change or a process failed halfway. Remediating a non-desired state means noticing the gap and bringing the system back to the setup you chose, ideally without a person having to act. Think of a thermostat: you set the target, it measures the room, and it switches the heater on or off to close the gap. The skill is building that loop safely, so the fix is correct, repeatable, and never causes a bigger outage than the drift it corrects.
lessons.guessPrompt: A teammate manually opens a port on a production server to debug something and forgets to close it. Without anyone checking, how could your team make the system notice and close it again, and what could go wrong with that automatic fix?
lessons.teach: Desired state is the configuration you declare as correct, usually written as code or stored as a compliance rule. Drift is any difference between that declared state and what is actually running. Non-compliant means a resource currently breaks one of your rules. Remediation is the action that brings it back in line. The loop has three parts: detect, decide, act. A detector evaluates resources against rules, either on a schedule or when a change event arrives. A rule engine such as AWS Config records each resource's configuration and marks it compliant or not. An automated action then runs, often an AWS Systems Manager Automation runbook, which is a stored list of steps executed against the resource. Routing the detection through an event bus such as Amazon EventBridge lets the fix start within seconds of the change. The fix is written once and applied the same way every time, so it is repeatable and auditable instead of depending on a tired engineer at 3 a.m. Worked example. Rule: no security group may allow port 22 from 0.0.0.0/0. Step 1: someone adds that ingress entry by hand. Step 2: the configuration recorder captures the new state. Step 3: the rule evaluates it and marks it non-compliant. Step 4: the runbook removes only that one ingress entry. Step 5: the rule re-evaluates and reports compliant. The change, what triggered it, and the before and after states are all recorded. Common mistake: fixing the symptom without asking why the drift happened, or scoping the action too broadly. If the deployment pipeline reapplies the old template on its next run, the manual fix and the pipeline fight each other and the drift returns. Consequence: a remediation that deletes a resource a running service depends on can cause the very outage it was meant to prevent, so remediations need narrow scope, a dry run where possible, and a guard against repeating endlessly in a loop. Automatic correction is only as safe as the rule and the scope behind it.

questions.prompt: A data team at a ticketing company finds that deletion protection keeps switching off on their database instances. Their rule flags each change within a minute, and a runbook turns the protection back on each time. Yet the same drift returns every night. Here is the sequence. Step 1: a nightly pipeline applies an older template that sets deletion protection to off. Step 2: the rule marks the instance non-compliant. Step 3: the runbook re-enables deletion protection on that one instance. Step 4 is missing. Step 5: the next night, the pipeline runs again and the cycle repeats. The missing Step 4 is the one that stops the cycle at its source.
choices: Delete and recreate the instance each night so the flag starts clean
Update the stored template in source control so it sets deletion protection on, matching what the runbook enforces
Turn off the rule so the nightly drift stops being reported
Have the runbook run every few minutes indefinitely so it always wins the race
questions.why: The pipeline reapplies whatever the template says, so the template must match the desired state or the manual fix and the pipeline will keep fighting each other.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best describes drift in the sense used for remediation?
choices: A resource that currently breaks one of your compliance rules
The schedule on which a detector evaluates resources against rules
Any difference between the declared desired state and what is actually running
The stored runbook that brings a resource back into line
questions.why: Drift is the gap between what you declared as correct and what is really running, while non-compliance is a narrower idea about breaking a specific rule.

questions.prompt: A rule flags one shared database snapshot as publicly readable. The team writes a runbook that makes every snapshot in the account private in one pass. What is the main risk of this runbook?
choices: It may break other services that legitimately depend on snapshots that were never flagged, because the action is wider than the non-compliant resource
The drift will be recorded twice in the audit history
The rule will stop evaluating snapshots once the runbook has run
It will finish faster than a runbook that changes one snapshot at a time
questions.why: A remediation that touches resources beyond the one that failed can cause an outage, so its scope must be narrow to the flagged resource.

questions.prompt: A runbook corrects a setting on a load balancer. A pipeline reverts that setting every two minutes, so the runbook fires again and again. Which safeguard best addresses this?
choices: Ignore any change event that arrives within ten minutes of the first one, and do nothing else
Remove the tags from the rule so the runbook no longer matches the resource
Run the runbook every second so the setting is always corrected first
Cap how many times the runbook may fire within a time window, and alert a person once the cap is hit
questions.why: A loop guard stops endless repetition and brings a human in when automation cannot settle the conflict on its own, which fits the pipeline-versus-fix tug-of-war described here.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would make a production system automatically correct a drifted setting, and name one limit or tradeoff of doing that automatically.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would first write the desired setting as an explicit rule, for example that no security group may allow SSH from anywhere. A detector such as AWS Config checks resources against that rule and records anything that breaks it. When a violation appears, an event on Amazon EventBridge triggers a remediation runbook in AWS Systems Manager that removes only the offending entry. Then the rule is re-checked to confirm the resource is compliant. The main tradeoff is that automatic fixes can undo changes that were made on purpose, or conflict with the deployment pipeline, which reapplies the old template and brings the drift back. So I would scope the action narrowly, log every change, require approval for risky fixes, and correct the source template so the drift cannot recur.
rubricPoints: Defines the desired state as an explicit rule that can be checked.
Describes detection, then an automated action, then re-evaluation to confirm the fix.
Names a limit: automatic changes can undo intentional work or conflict with the deployment pipeline.
Mentions scoping the fix narrowly and recording the change for audit.

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through a drifted-setting incident and choosing the detect, decide and act steps adds more than reading facts about rules.

lessons.plain: When something breaks, the job is to find out why, not just that it broke. Root cause analysis means working backwards from a symptom, such as a slow page, to the earlier change or condition that set it off. Three kinds of evidence help. Numbers recorded over time show what changed and when. Written records from the software show what it reported at that moment. A third kind follows a single request across several helpers and shows which step took the time. Used together, these let you point at the real trigger and fix that, instead of the loudest symptom.
lessons.guessPrompt: Latency and the error count both jumped on a checkout service at 14:05. What would you check first to tell which one started the problem, and what would that check tell you?
lessons.teach:
A metric is a number recorded over time, such as request count, error count, or the latency of each call. A monitoring service stores metrics as time series, grouped into fixed periods such as one-minute buckets. A log is a timestamped line of text that an application or service writes when something happens. A trace is the record of one request as it travels through several services. Each service that handles the request writes a span, which X-Ray calls a segment, with a start time, a duration and an outcome. All spans for one request share a trace ID, so they can be stitched back together. The p99 latency is the value that the slowest one percent of requests fall under.

Root cause analysis moves from symptom to earliest cause using the three signals in order. Metrics show that something changed and roughly when. Logs show what the component said at that moment. Traces show which hop in a multi-service request spent the time or failed. Each signal answers a different question at a different resolution: metrics are cheap and cover everything but average away detail, logs are detailed but noisy, and traces connect one slow request across service boundaries.

Worked example. At 09:02 a dashboard shows the p99 latency of the positions API jumping from 80 ms to 2.4 seconds. Step 1: check the deployment marker, which lines up with a release at 09:00. Step 2: filter the API logs for the window and count cache-miss messages; they rise about fortyfold after 09:00. Step 3: open a slow trace; its cache segment takes 20 ms but its database segment takes 2.1 seconds, so the database is where the time goes. Step 4: the release removed a cache key, so every request now reads the database at once.

Common mistake: stopping at the first correlated graph, such as blaming the service with the most errors, without checking whether the spike began before the suspected change.

Consequence: a wrong root cause means the fix treats a symptom, and the slowdown returns after the next release.

questions.prompt: A concert-ticket company runs a seat-hold API, the service that reserves a seat for a buyer while they pay. Its 5xx error rate (server-side failure responses) rose from 0.2% to 9% starting at 18:27. A deployment marker shows a release at 18:31. Step 1: the error-rate metric began climbing at 18:27, four minutes before the release, so the release cannot be the first trigger. Step 2: filtering the seat-hold logs for that window shows 'lock wait timeout' messages rising from almost none to about 40 per minute after 18:26. Step 3: [missing step]. Step 4: a batch job started at 18:25 held row locks on the seats table, so each hold request waited until it timed out.
choices: Open a slow or failed trace and read which span carries the time or the error
Average the error rate over a full day so the spike is smoothed out
Roll back the 18:31 release immediately, since it is the most recent change
Add more instances to the seat-hold service to absorb the failed requests
questions.why: A trace links the spans of one request across services, so it identifies which hop, here the seats-table call, spent the time or failed, which is the step between logs and the root cause.

questions.prompt: A video-upload service reports a p99 latency of 1.1 seconds for a five-minute window. Which statement describes what that number means?
choices: 99 of every 100 uploads in the window finished in 1.1 seconds or less, and the slowest 1% took longer
Each upload was retried at most once, adding 1.1 seconds
The single slowest upload in the window took 1.1 seconds
The average upload took 1.1 seconds, with a few outliers
questions.why: The p99 is the value that the slowest one percent of requests fall under, so 99 percent finished at or below it and only the slowest one percent went beyond it.

questions.prompt: A food-delivery team changed a courier-location service's configuration at 07:45 and now sees intermittent slowness. They want to know whether the slowdown started before the change. Which signal should they check first, and why?
choices: A single trace captured after 07:45, because traces show the request path
Logs filtered for the word 'error' from the current hour only, because logs are the most detailed
The latency metric for the hours before and after 07:45, because metrics show that something changed and roughly when
The change log entry, because it tells you what caused the spike
questions.why: Metrics are the first signal in root cause analysis and show whether the time series moved before the change, which is the test for whether the change could be the trigger.

questions.prompt: A payments team sees that its service has the most 5xx errors and ships a fix to that service. Their latency graph shows that a fraud-check service's p99 began rising six minutes before the payments errors did. What is the most likely outcome of the fix, according to the root cause reasoning in the teaching text?
choices: Nothing will change, because percentile metrics always lag behind error counts
The payments service must be restarted, and the fraud-check service needs no investigation
The fix is sound, since the service with the most errors is always the root cause
The slowdown is likely to return after the next release, because the fix treated a symptom rather than the earliest cause
questions.why: The teaching text warns that blaming the service with the most errors without checking whether the spike began earlier leads to a fix that treats a symptom, so the slowdown returns.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would go from a sudden slowdown in an AWS-hosted API to a probable root cause, using CloudWatch metrics, CloudWatch Logs and X-Ray traces. Name one limit of this approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start with the latency metric on the API in CloudWatch and find the minute it moved, then line that up with deployment and configuration timestamps to get a candidate change. Next I would query the application logs for that window in CloudWatch Logs, looking for a jump in a particular message or error type that points at one component. Then I would open a few X-Ray traces from the slow period. A trace shows the segment for each service a request touched, so whichever segment holds most of the duration is where I look next. Once I have a component and a change, I test the explanation: does the timing line up, and does rolling back the change bring the metric back? The main limit is that traces are usually sampled, so the slow requests I see may not be typical, and metrics only show correlation. I only treat the cause as confirmed when reverting or fixing it reproduces the recovery.
rubricPoints: Starts from a metric to find when the change happened
Uses logs in the same time window to identify the component or message involved
Uses traces to see which service or call holds the time or failure
States a limit such as sampling, correlation versus cause, or missing data
Confirms the cause by testing a rollback or fix

suggested.rationale: That mission makes you trace a post-deploy slowdown back to its cause from metrics and logs, which is the core skill of this objective.

lessons.plain: When something goes wrong with your systems, you need to learn about it quickly and from the right source. Some problems come from the cloud provider itself, such as an outage in one data centre region or a degraded service that many customers share. Others come from your own workloads, like a server running out of memory or an error rate climbing after a change. Service health tools cover both sides. One kind tells you about provider-side problems that affect your resources. Another watches measurements from your own systems and raises alarms when they cross a line. A third collects those findings into a work queue your team can act on. Knowing which tool speaks to which kind of problem is the first step in any response.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose your application suddenly slows down at 3 a.m. and no code changed. Should you check first for a notice from the cloud provider about its own infrastructure, or for a change in your own server measurements, and why?
lessons.teach: A health event is a notice that the cloud provider publishes when it knows of an issue that may affect resources in your account. The AWS Health service is where these notices appear. Some are specific to resources in your account, and others describe broader problems in a region or service. Amazon CloudWatch is the metrics and alarms service. It stores numbers such as CPU use, error counts, and latency, and an alarm watches one metric against a threshold and changes state, for example to ALARM, when the threshold is crossed. Systems Manager OpsCenter is a work queue in which findings become OpsItems, which are tracked operational tickets that people, alarms, or events can create, and that the team then assigns, investigates, and resolves. The reasoning behind this split is that provider-side problems are invisible in your own measurements until they hurt you, so you subscribe to health notices for them; your own faults show up in your own metrics, so you alarm on those; and OpsCenter gathers both so that nothing sits unread in an inbox. Worked example: a checkout service's latency alarm enters ALARM at 14:02. Step 1, the alarm notifies the team and creates an OpsItem that carries the alarm name. Step 2, the responder checks the health notices for the region and finds nothing for the account. Step 3, they read the service's error and CPU metrics, which show that error counts rose at 14:00, the same time a deployment finished. Step 4, the OpsItem records that cause, and the rollback is linked to it. A common mistake is treating the health page as the only signal, which misses every fault that is yours, or building alarms with no owner so that OpsItems pile up unread. If no alarm feeds OpsCenter, a degraded service can run for hours before anyone responsible sees it.

questions.prompt: A media company runs a thumbnail service in one region. At 10:20 an alarm on its image-processing queue age moves to ALARM, and the alarm notifies the on-call engineer and creates an OpsItem that carries the alarm name. At 10:22 the engineer opens AWS Health and finds a notice, posted at 10:05, that describes a networking problem affecting a storage service in that same region. Step 3 is missing from the investigation. Step 4 is that the OpsItem records the cause and links the mitigation. What should Step 3 be?
choices: Create a second alarm on the queue depth so that the next occurrence creates a second OpsItem.
Delete the alarm, since a provider-side problem cannot be caused by anything in the company's own account.
Close the OpsItem as resolved because the provider has already posted a notice about the problem.
Read the thumbnail service's own error and latency metrics to see whether they rose at the time the notice describes and whether they match the affected storage service.
questions.why: Checking the service's own metrics against the timing and scope of the provider notice is the step that shows whether the fault is provider-side or the company's own, which is what the rest of the investigation depends on.

questions.prompt: Which AWS tool is the place where notices about provider-side issues that may affect resources in your account appear?
choices: AWS Health
Amazon CloudWatch alarms
A metric stored in CloudWatch with no alarm attached
Systems Manager OpsCenter
questions.why: The teaching text says AWS Health is where provider notices appear, including those that describe region- or service-wide problems.

questions.prompt: A team has many CloudWatch alarms that all notify a shared inbox, but no person or team is named as the owner of any alarm. What is the most likely consequence for a running service?
choices: The provider automatically assigns each alarm to a responder.
OpsItems and notices pile up unread, so a degraded service can run for hours before a responsible person sees it.
Faults are fixed faster because the inbox is shared by everyone.
AWS Health stops sending notices about the account.
questions.why: The teaching text warns that alarms with no owner let OpsItems pile up unread, and that a degraded service may then run for hours unseen.

questions.prompt: A disk-usage metric on one of your own servers crosses its threshold and an alarm enters ALARM. Which signal is this, and where should the team look first?
choices: A fault in your own resources, shown in your own metrics, so the team should look at that server's metrics and the alarm.
A deployment failure, which only Systems Manager can detect.
A provider health notice, so the team should check AWS Health for the region.
A provider health notice, so the team should wait for AWS to publish a fix.
questions.why: The teaching text says your own faults show up in your own metrics and are alarmed on, so the investigation starts with those metrics rather than the provider's health notices.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would tell whether a slow service has a provider-side cause or a cause in our own systems, and name one limit of relying on provider health notices.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start with two sources. The provider health feed shows whether a published event affects our account or our region, which would point to a cause outside our code. Our own metrics in CloudWatch show whether CPU, error rate, or latency moved, and when it moved. If the metrics changed at the time of a deployment, the cause is probably ours, and I check that release first. If nothing is published and the metrics show a dependency timing out, I escalate with that evidence. The limit is that the provider feed only covers problems the provider has noticed and chosen to publish. A quiet feed does not prove the provider is healthy, because notices can lag behind a real outage or describe only part of it. So I never close an investigation based on a clean health page alone.
rubricPoints: Uses the provider health notices to check for provider-side causes affecting the account or region
Uses our own metrics and their timing to check for causes in our systems, such as a recent deployment
Names a real limit: provider notices may be late, partial, or absent, so a quiet feed is not proof of health
Does not conclude from one source alone and records the evidence in the work item

suggested.rationale: This objective is mostly about which service covers which kind of signal and how they connect, which a clear reading of the service roles teaches directly before any hands-on work.

lessons.plain: When an automated release fails partway through, the team has to work out which step broke, why it broke, and what state the live system is in now. This objective is about reading the trail each delivery tool leaves behind. You start with the outer view of the whole pipeline run, then move inward to the build, the deployment, the infrastructure change, and finally the check that tests whether the site still works for a user. Think of a detective reconstructing a relay race where the baton was dropped: first you read the overall timing sheet, then you go to the exact lap where it fell, then you read that runner's notes.
lessons.guessPrompt: A release pipeline has four stages: build, test, deploy to servers, then a check that the website answers. The overview shows the deploy stage is red, yet the website still serves the old version and users are not seeing errors. What would you look at first to find out why the deploy failed, and why might the site still be working?
lessons.teach:
A pipeline is an automated sequence of stages that moves a change from source code to a running environment. Each stage holds one or more actions, and one run is one full pass through them. Each managed tool in the chain keeps its own record. CodeBuild runs a build job and writes an output log. CodeDeploy pushes a new version to a set of instances, called a deployment group, and tracks each instance through lifecycle event hooks, which are named scripts that run at fixed points such as installing or starting the new version. CloudFormation applies infrastructure changes as a stack, and its stack events list the status of each resource. A CloudWatch Synthetics canary is a scheduled script that behaves like a user, calls an endpoint, and records pass or fail.

Why this works: a failure starts in the innermost tool, and the outer tools only report it. So you read outward to inward. Start at the pipeline to find the failing stage, then open the tool that stage called, then read that tool's log for the exact failing step.

Worked example. At 09:04 the Deploy stage turns red. The CodeDeploy deployment shows Failed, with one of four instances failing its ApplicationStart hook. That instance's hook log shows the start script could not read a required settings file. The deployment group had automatic rollback enabled, so the instances returned to the previous revision. A canary check at 09:05 passed, which confirms users were served the old version.

Common mistake: stopping at the name of the red stage and calling it a pipeline problem, or assuming that rollback fixed the cause. Rollback restores service. The cause still has to be found and fixed before the next release.

Consequence in a running system: with rollback disabled, the fleet can be split between old and new code. A CloudFormation stack whose rollback fails ends in UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED and needs manual recovery before any further change can be applied safely.

questions.prompt: A company's release pipeline turns red at its Infrastructure stage while deploying a new reporting service. That stage calls CloudFormation. Step 1: the pipeline shows the Infrastructure stage as the failing stage. Step 2: open the reporting service's stack and read its stack events. Step 3: (missing). Step 4: correct the resource definition in the template and run the pipeline again. Which choice correctly fills the missing step 3?
choices: Roll back the pipeline and mark the Infrastructure stage as fixed so the next release can start.
Read the CodeBuild log for the template linter, because the failure always starts in the build tool.
Find the first resource in the stack events whose status shows a failure, and read its status reason for the exact failing step.
Check the most recent canary result, since a passing canary proves the stack is healthy.
questions.why: The method reads outward to inward, so after the stack events identify the failing resource, its status reason gives the exact failing step that must be fixed.

questions.prompt: A CodeDeploy deployment reports Succeeded on every instance, but ten minutes later a CloudWatch Synthetics canary that calls a checkout endpoint starts recording failures. What does the canary result tell you?
choices: The deployment record is wrong, so the canary result can be ignored until the next release.
The deploy succeeded, so the canary script must contain a bug and should be deleted from the account.
The canary is a scripted user check with its own schedule and pass or fail record, so users may be affected even though the deploy reported success.
Canaries only run during a pipeline execution, so this failure belongs to an earlier run and is already closed.
questions.why: A canary acts like a user on its own schedule and records its own pass or fail, so it can show a problem that the deployment record does not show.

questions.prompt: A team's pipeline Deploy stage turned red. An automatic rollback restored the previous version, and the team then closed the incident and scheduled the next release. Which statement best describes the gap in their response?
choices: They never checked whether the CodeBuild artifact was signed and stored in the right bucket before closing the incident.
They rolled back without first pausing the source stage, which may have pulled in extra changes during the rollback.
Rollback restored service, but the root cause was never traced, so the next release could hit the same failure.
They should have disabled rollback so that the fleet stayed on the new code while they investigated the failure.
questions.why: Rollback restores service but does not fix the cause, which must be traced in the tool's log and fixed before the next release.

questions.prompt: A CloudFormation stack update fails, and the automatic rollback also fails, leaving the stack in UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED. What should the team do before applying any further change to that stack?
choices: Delete the stack immediately, since a broken rollback means the stack cannot be repaired.
Start a new stack update right away, since CloudFormation will reconcile the stack on its own.
Recover the stack manually first, because further changes are unsafe until it is returned to a known state.
Rerun the pipeline's Deploy stage, which retries the failed rollback automatically.
questions.why: A stack in UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED needs manual recovery before any further change can be applied safely.
