lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would work out why a release failed when the pipeline view only shows one red stage. Name one limit of this approach, such as what a canary check can and cannot tell you.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start at the pipeline view to find which stage went red and when. Then I would open the tool that stage called, such as the CodeDeploy deployment or the CloudFormation stack events, because those list which step, instance, or resource failed. From there I would read that step's log, which usually holds the actual error. I would also check whether automatic rollback ran and confirm what version users are seeing now. The limit is that a canary only checks what its script tests. If it passes, that does not prove the release is correct, only that the scripted path worked. Rollback also restores the old version without fixing the cause, so the root cause still needs a code or configuration change and a new run before anything ships again.
rubricPoints: Read from the pipeline stage inward to the tool and then to the specific failing step or log
Identify the failing instance, resource, or hook using the tool's own event or status records
Confirm the current live state, including whether rollback ran
Explain that rollback restores service but does not remove the root cause
Name a limit of synthetic checks: they only verify the paths they script

suggested.rationale: That mission already has the learner roll back a bad release and then trace the failure to its cause, which matches analyzing failed deployments.

lessons.plain: When a system that is supposed to grow, restart, or run containers breaks, someone has to work out which step failed and why. Think of a fleet of delivery vans where the dispatcher keeps adding vans but some never leave the depot. The job is to read the record of what the system tried, find the first thing that went wrong, and follow the chain from there to the real cause. This objective covers three places where that happens on AWS: groups of virtual servers that scale up and down, and two services that run containers, called ECS and EKS. Each keeps a record of its decisions and failures, and reading those records in the right order is most of the work.
lessons.guessPrompt: A group of servers is set to keep between 2 and 6 servers running, and it is supposed to add servers when load rises. Load has risen, but the server count has stayed at 2 for ten minutes. Without any more information, list two places you would look first and say why.
lessons.teach:
An Auto Scaling group is a set of virtual servers, called instances, kept between a minimum and a maximum count. It launches new instances from a launch template, which is a saved recipe of machine settings such as the machine image and instance type. The scaling activity history is the group's log of every launch and termination attempt, including the failure message when one fails. Health checks decide whether an instance is working; an unhealthy instance is terminated and replaced. A lifecycle hook pauses an instance during launch or termination so that something can run first, and it has a timeout after which the group moves on.

Amazon ECS (Elastic Container Service) runs containers. A task definition is the blueprint for a container, and a task is one running copy of it. A service keeps a desired number of tasks running and writes service events when it cannot place a task or a health check fails. Stopped tasks carry a stop reason and an exit code. Amazon EKS (Elastic Kubernetes Service) is managed Kubernetes. A pod is the smallest unit, and its events show why it is pending or restarting; a pod stuck in CrashLoopBackOff starts, exits, and restarts over and over.

Worked example: an Auto Scaling group with a maximum of 6 receives a traffic rise and tries to add 2 instances. The activity history shows the first launch failing with a message that the referenced machine image does not exist. The launch template points to an image that was deleted. Every retry fails the same way, so the count stays at 2. Trace order: the alarm fired, the scale-out activity started, the launch failed, the failure message names the missing image, and the template is the root cause. Raising the maximum would change nothing.

Common mistake: stopping at the most recent error and fixing that symptom. An instance that fails its health check may be healthy but judged by a wrong health check path, so check the check before blaming the application.

Consequence: a launch loop that never succeeds holds the group at a reduced count during a surge, so latency rises while the dashboard suggests the system is merely busy.

questions.prompt: A payments team runs an ECS service with a desired count of 5 but only 3 tasks running. Its task definition reserves 3072 MB of memory per task, and the service events say it cannot place a task. Trace it: (1) The service writes a placement failure event. (2) That event names memory as the reason, meaning no container instance has enough free memory for the reservation. (3) [missing step]. (4) The team lowers the reservation to fit the instances and the count returns to 5. Which choice correctly fills step 3?
choices: Compare the reservation with free memory on each container instance to confirm none can fit it
Restart the stopped tasks to clear their stop reasons
Raise the desired count to 8 so that more placement attempts happen
Check the health check path, since the running tasks are probably fine
questions.why: Step 3 must test the cause named in step 2 by comparing the task's memory reservation against the free memory on each instance, which shows whether any instance could ever accept the task.

questions.prompt: A pod in an EKS cluster at a logistics company shows the status CrashLoopBackOff. Which description fits this status?
choices: The container starts, exits, and restarts over and over
The pod is running normally but its readiness check has not passed yet
The pod was deleted and its controller is building a replacement on another node
The pod is waiting for a node with free capacity before it can be scheduled
questions.why: CrashLoopBackOff means the container repeatedly starts, exits, and restarts, which is different from a pod waiting to be scheduled or one that is running but not ready.

questions.prompt: An ECS service at a retail company keeps stopping its tasks with the stop reason that the tasks failed the load balancer health check. The application logs show it answering requests on its root path with success. The load balancer's health check is set to call a path called slash healthz, which returns a not found response. What should the team check first?
choices: Whether the container image was deleted from the registry
Whether the health check path configured on the load balancer matches a path the application actually serves
Whether the task definition's memory reservation is larger than the instance memory
Whether the desired count is high enough for the traffic
questions.why: The tasks are judged unhealthy by a check that calls the wrong path, so the health check configuration should be verified before blaming the application, which is working on its root path.

questions.prompt: An Auto Scaling group at a media company has a termination lifecycle hook with a timeout of 300 seconds. The drain script attached to the hook needs 420 seconds to finish. What happens when the script runs?
choices: The group skips the hook entirely and terminates the instance immediately at the start
The group proceeds once the timeout passes, so the script is cut short and its work may be incomplete
The group keeps waiting until the script finishes, because the hook never expires on its own
The group cancels the termination and keeps the instance running until the script is fixed
questions.why: A lifecycle hook has a timeout after which the group moves on, so a script longer than the timeout is interrupted rather than allowed to finish.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would find the root cause when an ECS service or EKS deployment keeps replacing tasks or pods during a load spike. Name one limit of the first place you would look.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start with the service's own event record, not the application logs. For ECS, the service events and the stopped task reasons tell me whether tasks failed to place, failed a health check, or exited. For EKS, the pod events and restart counts tell me whether pods are pending for lack of capacity or crashing on start. Then I follow the chain back: if tasks are placed and then exit, I read the container logs for the exit reason; if they never place, I check capacity and the task definition. The limit of the service event record is that it is short and it only shows what the service itself observed. It does not show why an application crashed, so I still need container logs and metrics to confirm the cause before changing anything.
rubricPoints: Starts from the orchestrator's own events and stop reasons before application logs
Distinguishes placement or capacity failures from crashes on start
Traces the chain back to the first failure rather than the latest symptom
Names a real limit of the event record and what fills the gap

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through an exam-style failure scenario across scaling and container services teaches the trace-back skill more than reading alone.

lessons.plain: Every action in a cloud account is taken by someone or something, and the account must know who is asking and what they are allowed to do. IAM, identity and access management, is the part of the cloud provider that handles this. People and programs are both called identities. A user is a long-lived login for one person or one machine. A group is a bundle of users that share the same rules. A role is a temporary identity that an allowed person or program can step into for a while, like a visitor badge. Policies are the written rules that say what is allowed or denied. This lesson covers these pieces and how they fit together, so a build server can get exactly the access it needs and nothing more.
lessons.guessPrompt: If an automated pipeline needs to upload files to one storage bucket and nothing else, would you give it a long-lived login key with full account access, or a temporary identity limited to that bucket? Say why.
lessons.teach:
A principal is whoever makes a request: a person, a program, or a service. IAM decides whether a principal may do something. A user is a long-lived identity with its own password or access key. A group is a named collection of users, used to attach rules to many people at once; a group does not log in itself. A role is an identity with no permanent key. A principal assumes the role and receives temporary credentials that expire. An identity provider is an outside system, such as a corporate directory, that vouches for people so they can use roles without a separate user being created for each.

A policy is a JSON document made of statements, each saying allow or deny, for which actions, on which resources, and under which conditions. An identity-based policy is attached to a user, group, or role and says what that identity may do. A resource-based policy is attached to the resource itself, such as a bucket or a queue, and says who may touch it. A session policy is passed when a role is assumed. It only narrows what that one session can do; it never grants anything the role lacks. A role also has a trust policy that names who may assume it.

Worked example. A build job runs as a role called deployer. Step 1: the job asks to assume deployer, and the trust policy confirms the build service is allowed to do so. Step 2: the service issues temporary credentials valid for one hour, with a session policy limiting them to the prefix prod-artifacts. Step 3: the job uploads to prod-artifacts/app-42. The role's identity policy and the session policy both allow this, so it succeeds. Step 4: the job tries to write to logs-tmp. The role's own policy might allow it, but the session policy does not, so the request is denied.

Common mistake: treating a session policy as a way to grant access, or giving a pipeline a long-lived user key. Such keys end up in config files and keep working until someone rotates them.

Consequence in a running system: a leaked long-lived key gives an attacker standing access until it is found and replaced, while a leaked temporary role credential expires within the hour.

questions.prompt: A partner firm's auditor uses a role called audit-read in our AWS account. Step 1: The auditor signs in through the partner's identity provider, which vouches for her, so no separate user is created in our account. Step 2: She assumes audit-read, and the trust policy confirms the partner's identity provider may assume it. Step 3: The session receives temporary credentials valid for 45 minutes, with a session policy limiting them to the prefix tax-reports/2023. Step 4: She reads tax-reports/2023/q2.pdf. The role's identity policy and the session policy both allow this, so it succeeds. Step 5: She then requests tax-reports/2024/q1.pdf, which the role's identity policy does allow. Which completion correctly explains the outcome?
choices: the role's identity policy must also list the 2024 prefix before it can be used at all
a read request is always allowed once the session has started, whatever the prefix
the session policy does not include tax-reports/2024, and a session policy only narrows access
the identity provider must first create a separate user account for her in our account
questions.why: The session policy limits this one session to the 2023 prefix, so a 2024 request is denied even though the role's identity policy would allow it.

questions.prompt: A nightly report script in a company that runs two AWS accounts needs to read one storage bucket. Which setup best follows the principle that machines should receive temporary credentials rather than long-lived keys?
choices: A long-lived user with an access key stored in the script's config file
A role the script assumes, which issues credentials that expire after a set time
A group that contains the script, with a shared password for the group
A resource-based policy attached to the script itself
questions.why: A role gives the script temporary credentials that expire, whereas a stored user key keeps working until someone rotates it.

questions.prompt: A team attaches a session policy to a contractor's role. The role's own policy only allows reading reports, and the team's session policy tries to allow writing to a bucket the role cannot write to. What happens when the contractor tries to write?
choices: The write is denied until the trust policy is edited to allow writing
The write is denied, because a session policy can only narrow what the role already allows
The write succeeds, because session policies add permissions to the role
The write succeeds, because the credentials are long-lived enough to override the role
questions.why: A session policy never grants anything the role lacks, so the write stays denied regardless of what the session policy says.

questions.prompt: A build server's long-lived access key is found in a public code repository. Which statement best describes the consequence for the running system?
choices: The key expires automatically within an hour, so no action is needed
The key keeps working until someone finds and replaces it, giving standing access
The key only works from the original build server's network address
The key is harmless because only the pipeline's trust policy can use it
questions.why: A long-lived key has no built-in expiry, so it stays usable until someone rotates it, which is why leaked long-lived keys are dangerous.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why a build pipeline should assume a role instead of using a long-lived user access key, and name one limit or tradeoff of the role approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: A user access key is permanent until someone rotates it, so if it leaks, anyone holding it has standing access and the leak may go unnoticed. A role gives the pipeline temporary credentials, typically valid for an hour, so a leaked credential expires on its own. The pipeline also has nothing stored in its configuration that needs to be guarded for months. A session policy can narrow those credentials further for one job. The tradeoff is that roles add setup: the trust policy must name the right caller, the role's permissions must be right, and a job running longer than the credential lifetime must refresh its credentials. Misconfigured trust can also let the wrong principal assume the role, so the trust policy needs as much review as the permissions.
rubricPoints: A long-lived user key stays valid until rotated, so a leak gives lasting access.
A role issues temporary credentials that expire, limiting the damage of a leak.
A session policy can narrow permissions for one session but cannot grant more.
A tradeoff: roles need correct trust policies and credential refresh for long jobs.

suggested.rationale: The planned authorization policy evaluator would let the learner trace allow and deny decisions across identity, resource, and session policies, which is the core skill here.

lessons.plain: Federation means letting people sign in to cloud accounts using the login system their company already runs, instead of creating a separate username and password for each person in the cloud. Think of a building where a receptionist checks your company badge at the door and hands you a visitor pass for only the floors you are allowed on. The company login system is the trusted badge office, and the cloud account accepts its word. When someone leaves the company, disabling their one login in the company system cuts off their cloud access too, with no separate cleanup. This lesson covers how that trust is set up and what goes wrong when it is set up too loosely.
lessons.guessPrompt: If 40 engineers each need access to five cloud accounts, would you rather create 200 separate cloud logins with long-lived passwords, or let one company login system vouch for them? What breaks first when someone leaves the company under each approach?
lessons.teach:
Federation is a trust arrangement in which one system, the identity provider (IdP), proves who a person is, and another system, the service provider, accepts that proof and grants access without storing that person's password. The IdP is the company's directory or sign-in service, such as a corporate directory or a hosted OpenID Connect (OIDC) provider. The proof travels as a signed statement. In SAML 2.0 it is an XML assertion. In OIDC it is a signed token containing claims, which are facts such as the user's email address or group names.

AWS offers two main routes. The first is an IAM identity provider: you register an external SAML or OIDC provider in an account, then create a role whose trust policy says identities from that provider may assume it, optionally only when specific claims match. The second is AWS IAM Identity Center, a service that gives you one place to assign people and groups to many accounts. It draws identities from its own directory, from Active Directory, or from an external IdP. You attach a permission set, which is a template for a role, to a group and an account. When a person signs in, Identity Center creates a role session in each target account.

Why it works: nobody holds a long-lived cloud secret. Each sign-in produces short-lived credentials for a role, and disabling a person in the source directory stops new sign-ins at once.

Worked example. The group payments-devs in the corporate directory is assigned a read-only permission set on the staging account and a deploy permission set on the dev account. Step 1: Ana authenticates to the IdP. Step 2: the IdP sends a signed assertion listing her group memberships. Step 3: Identity Center checks that payments-devs has an assignment for each account. Step 4: she receives temporary credentials for each role, valid for a limited time. Step 5: when Ana leaves, her directory account is disabled, and her next sign-in fails while existing sessions expire on their own timer.

Common mistake: an OIDC trust policy that checks only the audience and not the subject claim. Then any identity from that provider, including identities from other repositories or tenants, can assume the role. The fix is to add condition keys that pin the subject or group claim to exactly what you intend to allow.

In a running system this matters most for CI pipelines. A loose trust policy can let a pull request from a forked repository assume a production deploy role, so the trust condition is part of the deployment's security, not an optional detail.

The safe default is to federate every human and pipeline identity and to pin each trust to the specific claims you intend to allow.

questions.prompt: Northwind Logistics runs a CI pipeline from the repository northwind-logistics/ledger-api. The account registers that CI service's hosted OIDC provider and creates a role called ledger-deploy. Its trust policy pins the subject claim to the main branch of that one repository. Here is the sign-in traced step by step. Step 1: the pipeline job asks the OIDC provider for a token. Step 2: the provider signs a token whose claims include the subject for the main branch. Step 3: a step is missing here. Step 4: AWS compares the audience and subject claims with the conditions in the trust policy. Step 5: AWS returns temporary credentials for ledger-deploy, valid for one hour. Which sentence correctly fills the missing Step 3?
choices: Step 3: The pipeline copies the token into a repository variable so it can be reused on later runs.
Step 3: AWS checks the token's signature against the public keys of the OIDC provider that was registered in the account.
Step 3: AWS checks that ledger-deploy's permission policy allows writes to the release bucket.
Step 3: Identity Center creates a role session in every account that the pipeline's group is assigned to.
questions.why: Before AWS can trust any claim in the token, it must confirm that the token was signed by the provider registered in the account, which is the signature check that comes before the trust policy comparison in Step 4.

questions.prompt: In a SAML 2.0 federation, what does the service provider receive from the identity provider to decide whether to grant access?
choices: A signed assertion that lists facts such as group memberships, so the service provider never needs the password
A full copy of the user's directory record, which the service provider stores for later sign-ins
The user's plaintext password, which it checks against a local copy of the directory
A permanent access key that is tied to the user's account and never expires
questions.why: In federation the identity provider sends a signed statement (an assertion in SAML) containing claims, and the service provider accepts that proof without ever receiving or storing the password.

questions.prompt: A team at Kestrel Labs created an OIDC role whose trust policy checks only the audience claim and not the subject claim. A workflow in an unrelated company's repository, which the same OIDC provider also signs tokens for, starts a job. What is the main risk?
choices: The job is blocked because the audience claim does not match the repository name
Only pushes made by the Kestrel Labs repository owner can assume the role, because the audience is fixed
The role stops working for forks, because forks always produce a different audience value
Any identity the provider signs for, including the unrelated repository, can assume the role, because the subject was never pinned
questions.why: Without a subject condition, any token the trusted provider signs passes the audience check, so identities from other repositories or tenants can assume the role, which is the common mistake described in the teaching text.

questions.prompt: Priya, a contractor at Vantage Health, has access through IAM Identity Center to two accounts. Her directory account is disabled at 09:00. At 09:20 she tries to sign in again. She had signed in at 08:30, and her temporary role credentials last one hour. Which outcome is correct?
choices: Her new sign-in fails, and her existing role credentials keep working until they expire on their own timer, around 09:30
Both the console and her command-line access continue until the next directory sync, because they use long-lived keys
Her new sign-in succeeds, because permission sets are cached and remain valid for the full day
Her existing session ends at 09:00 because disabling the account revokes all credentials instantly
questions.why: Disabling the person in the source directory blocks new sign-ins at once, while credentials already issued are short-lived and expire on their own timer rather than being revoked immediately.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has been creating IAM users with access keys for each engineer why federation through IAM Identity Center or an IAM identity provider is preferable, and name one limit or tradeoff of federating.
lessons.modelAnswer: Instead of making an IAM user with a password and access keys for each engineer, we let the company's identity provider prove who they are and let AWS hand out short-lived credentials for a role. Access follows the directory: adding someone to a group grants access to the accounts assigned to that group, and removing them stops new sign-ins immediately, with no keys to hunt down. IAM Identity Center gives us one place to assign permission sets across accounts. The tradeoff is dependency. If the identity provider is down, nobody can sign in, so we keep a documented break-glass path. We also have to get the trust conditions right, because a loose trust policy lets outsiders assume the role. Sessions last only as long as their configured duration, so long-running jobs need their own credential design.
rubricPoints: Federation lets an external identity provider vouch for people so AWS issues short-lived credentials instead of storing long-lived keys.
Access follows directory group membership, so removing someone from the source directory revokes new sign-ins quickly.
IAM Identity Center or an IAM identity provider with a role trust policy are the two routes, with permission sets or role trust defining what access is granted.
A tradeoff or limit: dependence on the IdP's availability, and the need to pin trust conditions so the wrong identities cannot assume the role.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine practises federation trust or Identity Center assignments, so this is mainly concepts and console configuration best learned by reading.

lessons.plain: Imagine a building manager who lets a team lead hire helpers and hand them keys. The manager does not want any helper to get keys to rooms the manager itself would never open. A permissions boundary is a ceiling placed on one user or role in Amazon Web Services. It states the most that identity can ever be allowed to do, no matter what other permissions are handed out later. A ceiling gives no power by itself; it only limits what other grants can reach. This lets a central team let others manage permissions safely without giving them full control.
lessons.guessPrompt: A developer's role has a policy that allows deleting any S3 bucket, and a permissions boundary that allows only reading S3 objects. Can the developer delete a bucket, and why?
lessons.teach:
A permissions boundary is a managed policy attached to an IAM user or role. IAM is the identity and access management system that decides which people or machines may call which cloud actions. A boundary is the maximum set of actions that identity can ever be effectively allowed. It grants nothing on its own. The effective permission is the overlap: an action works only if the identity's own policies allow it and the boundary also allows it. An explicit deny anywhere still wins.

Why it works: delegation. A central administrator lets a team create roles for their own services. The administrator writes a rule that such roles may only be created if they carry the approved boundary, and that the boundary cannot be removed or replaced by the delegated team. The team can now grant more permissions only inside the ceiling.

Worked example. The boundary app-ceiling allows S3 actions and logging actions, and nothing for IAM or EC2. A team creates a role called deploy-bot with that boundary attached, and an identity policy allowing s3:GetObject and ec2:RunInstances. Step 1: reading an object is in both sets, so it succeeds. Step 2: launching an instance is in the identity policy but not in the boundary, so it is denied. Step 3: the team adds iam:CreateUser to the identity policy. This changes nothing, because the boundary still excludes it.

Common mistake: assuming a boundary is a grant. A role with a boundary and no identity policy can do nothing at all.

Consequence in a running system: a pipeline that works in a test account can fail with access denied in production when the production boundary is stricter. The failure shows up in logs as a denial, not as a code error.

The ceiling, not the individual policy, sets the limit for delegated roles.

questions.prompt: Harbor Labs has a boundary named report-ceiling that allows dynamodb:PutItem and s3:GetObject and nothing else. A role called tally-job has report-ceiling attached, and its identity policy allows dynamodb:PutItem, sqs:SendMessage and s3:GetObject. Step 1: dynamodb:PutItem is in the identity policy and in the boundary, so the call succeeds. Step 2: the job calls sqs:SendMessage. Step 3: the team adds s3:DeleteObject to the identity policy, and it is still denied because the boundary does not allow it. Fill in step 2.
choices: Allowed, since a boundary only blocks actions that a deny names explicitly
Allowed, because the identity policy grants it
Denied, because the boundary leaves it out
Denied only when the role has no identity policy at all
questions.why: A boundary is a ceiling, so an action must be allowed by both the identity policy and the boundary, and sqs:SendMessage is missing from the boundary.

questions.prompt: A role has a boundary that allows ec2:DescribeInstances. Its identity policy allows ec2:DescribeInstances and ec2:StopInstances. Which statement is true?
choices: The role can do both, because a boundary adds permissions to the identity policy
The role can do neither until an explicit deny is removed
The role can stop instances, because the identity policy names the action
The role can describe instances but cannot stop them
questions.why: The effective permission is the overlap, and StopInstances is outside the boundary, so only describing works.

questions.prompt: A pipeline role in account 9082 has an identity policy allowing cloudwatch:PutMetricData and kms:Decrypt. The production boundary allows only kms:Decrypt. The deploy log shows AccessDenied for PutMetricData, while the code is otherwise unchanged. What is the most likely cause?
choices: AWS retries denied calls automatically, so the denial is temporary
The metric code has a syntax error that the log reports as a denial
The identity policy is missing kms:Decrypt
The production boundary excludes cloudwatch:PutMetricData, so the overlap blocks it
questions.why: A denial for an action that the identity policy allows points to a boundary that excludes it, and the log shows that as an access denial rather than a code error.

questions.prompt: A role named ci-artifact has a boundary allowing only ecr:BatchGetImage. Its identity policy allows ecr:GetAuthorizationToken, ecr:BatchGetImage and sns:Publish. Which call succeeds?
choices: sns:Publish, because the identity policy names it
ecr:BatchGetImage, because both layers allow it
ecr:GetAuthorizationToken, because the identity policy names it
Both ecr actions, because a role with a boundary inherits every identity grant
questions.why: Only ecr:BatchGetImage appears in both the identity policy and the boundary, and a boundary never grants anything by itself.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what a permissions boundary does when a team lead lets developers create their own roles. Name one limit of this approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: A permissions boundary is a ceiling attached to a role or user. It does not give any access. A role can only use an action if its own policies allow it and the boundary also allows it, so the boundary caps what the role can ever do. For delegation, the lead can require that every role a developer creates carries the approved boundary, and block developers from removing or changing that boundary. Developers then write their own policies, but only up to the ceiling. One limit is that a boundary only restricts identity-based permissions. It does not stop access granted through other mechanisms, such as resource policies or organization-level controls, so the lead still has to review what the ceiling allows and check those other controls too.
rubricPoints: A permissions boundary is a maximum limit on permissions, not a grant.
Effective permission is the overlap of the identity's own policies and the boundary.
Delegation works by requiring the boundary on created roles and protecting it from removal.
A limit: boundaries only constrain identity-based permissions, so other controls must still be reviewed.

suggested.rationale: Tracing which requests pass or fail when a policy and a boundary overlap is best practised in the planned authorization policy evaluator.

lessons.plain: A service control policy is a rule set that a central manager places over a group of cloud accounts to set the outer limit of what those accounts may do. Think of a building with many offices: the building rules decide which kinds of work are ever permitted in any office, and each office's staff can only use tools inside those rules, even if their own manager has handed them a key to more. These rules never hand out new powers by themselves. They only remove options. A central team can use them to stop everyone, including account administrators, from switching off security logging or using places the company never approved.
lessons.guessPrompt: An account administrator has full permissions inside their own cloud account, but a rule attached above that account allows work in only one region. Can the administrator still launch a server in a different region? Give your guess and your reason.
lessons.teach:
A service control policy, usually called an SCP, is a policy attached to a node in AWS Organizations, the service that groups many cloud accounts into one tree. An account is an isolated container for resources and billing. The tree has a root at the top, optional organizational units (OUs) that act as folders of accounts, and the accounts themselves. You can attach an SCP to the root, to an OU, or to a single account.

Why it works: an SCP never grants access. It sets a ceiling. For any action in an account, the action is allowed only if every SCP on the path from the root down to that account allows it, and an identity policy in the account (a rule attached to a user or a role) also allows it. An explicit deny in any SCP blocks the action regardless of anything else. The management account, the account that created the organization, is not limited by SCPs.

Worked example: the root has an SCP that allows everything. An OU named Sandbox has an SCP that denies any action unless the requested region is one approved region. An account inside Sandbox has an administrator role that allows all actions. Step 1: the administrator role asks to launch a server in a region the Sandbox SCP does not approve. Step 2: the root SCP allows it. Step 3: the Sandbox SCP does not allow it. Step 4: the request is denied, even though the administrator role would allow it. The account administrator cannot change this from inside the account.

Common mistake: treating an SCP as a way to grant permissions, then wondering why an account still cannot act after an allow was added. Another is attaching a broad deny to an OU without checking which running services depend on that action. A deployment role that calls a blocked action will then fail on the next pipeline run in every account under that OU.

An SCP is a ceiling that every account below it must stay under, so a deny placed high in the tree takes effect everywhere beneath it at once.

questions.prompt: Lumen Health uses AWS Organizations. The root has an SCP that allows every action. An OU named Analytics has an SCP that explicitly denies s3:DeleteBucket. An account named data-prod sits inside Analytics, and its role has an identity policy that allows all actions. Trace a request by a data-prod role to delete a bucket. Step 1: the role asks to call s3:DeleteBucket. Step 2: the root SCP allows it. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: the request is denied, even though the role's identity policy allows it. What belongs in step 3?
choices: The data-prod account's identity policy allows the action, so the request continues to Step 4 as allowed.
The Analytics OU SCP has an explicit deny for that action, which blocks the request regardless of the other policies.
The management account exemption applies because the role is an administrator role, so the deny is skipped.
The root SCP's allow overrides lower-level denies, so the Analytics OU SCP has no effect on this request.
questions.why: An explicit deny in any SCP on the path blocks the action no matter what else allows it, so the Analytics OU deny is the step that produces the denial.

questions.prompt: A retail company attaches an SCP to its account web-shop that allows ec2:RunInstances and nothing else changes. The deployment role in web-shop still gets an error when it tries to launch an instance. Which explanation is correct?
choices: The SCP is only a ceiling, and the role's own identity policy must also allow the action, which it does not here.
The management account exemption applies to deployment roles, so the SCP does not reach them.
SCPs only apply to human users, so the allow in the SCP has no effect on a role.
The SCP is a grant, so the role should now succeed and the error must be a temporary caching delay.
questions.why: An action needs every SCP on the path and the identity policy in the account to allow it, and an SCP alone never grants access.

questions.prompt: A logistics company puts an OU named Staging over 12 accounts and attaches an SCP to that OU that explicitly denies cloudwatch:PutMetricData. Their deployment jobs in those accounts call that action on every run. What should the team expect?
choices: Only the accounts where the SCP was attached directly will fail, since OU policies do not flow down to member accounts.
Jobs in all 12 accounts that call that action fail, since the deny sits above each account and applies to everything beneath the OU.
Only the management account jobs fail, because member accounts are exempt from OU-level denies.
Nothing fails, because an allow in each account's identity policy overrides an SCP deny.
questions.why: An SCP deny on an OU applies to every account beneath it at once, and the account administrator cannot override it from inside the account.

questions.prompt: Vance Freight created its AWS Organization several years ago, and its management account holds the billing setup. An engineer attaches a root SCP that denies every action except sts:AssumeRole across all accounts in the organization. Which account is still not restricted by that SCP?
choices: A member account sitting directly under the root with no OU
The management account
A member account inside an OU
A sandbox account with an SCP attached directly to it
questions.why: The management account, which created the organization, is not limited by SCPs, so the root deny does not apply to it.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a service control policy differs from an identity policy that grants access, and name one limit or risk of attaching an SCP to a whole organizational unit.
lessons.modelAnswer: An identity policy says what a particular user or role may do, and it adds permissions. A service control policy works one level higher. It sets the maximum set of actions any identity in the affected accounts can ever use, and it never grants anything by itself. So an action succeeds only when the SCPs on the path from the root to the account allow it and the identity policy also allows it. An explicit deny in an SCP wins over everything else. The main limit is that SCPs do not apply to the management account, so sensitive work there needs other controls. The main risk of attaching one to a whole OU is that a broad deny can silently break a running deployment role or a monitoring agent in every account beneath it. I would test the SCP in a small OU first and check which actions the running services call before widening it.
rubricPoints: An SCP sets a maximum boundary and does not grant permissions on its own
An action needs both the SCP path and the identity policy to allow it, and an explicit deny always wins
SCPs do not restrict the management account
Attaching a broad deny to a large OU can break running services in every account below it, so test first

suggested.rationale: The planned authorization policy evaluator would let the learner trace how layered allow and deny rules combine to a final decision, which is the core skill here.

lessons.plain: Least privilege means giving a person or a machine only the permissions it needs to do its job, and nothing more. In AWS, permissions are written as policies: documents that say who may perform which actions on which resources, and under what conditions. Designing a least-privilege policy means starting from the real work, granting specific actions on specific resources, and adding conditions where they help. Think of a hotel key card that opens your room and the gym, but not every door in the building, and only during your stay.
lessons.guessPrompt: A deploy job needs to read one configuration file stored in one storage location. Would you grant it read access to just that file, to the whole storage location, or to every storage location in the company? Say why.
lessons.teach:
A policy is a JSON document attached to an identity, such as a user, group or role, or attached to a resource. Each statement in it has an Effect, either Allow or Deny; an Action, which is one API operation such as reading an object from storage; a Resource, which names the specific thing the action applies to using an Amazon Resource Name, a unique identifier string; and optionally a Condition, an extra check such as the network a request comes from or a tag on the resource. Least privilege means the Allow statements list only the actions and resources a job truly needs.

It works because access is denied by default. A request succeeds only if some Allow statement matches it and no explicit Deny blocks it. So the safe method is to start with nothing and add exactly what a task requires, instead of starting broad and trying to subtract. Every wildcard, such as an action of star or a resource of star, widens what a leaked credential can do.

Worked example: a deploy role must upload build files to the bucket releases-prod, under the folder builds/. Step 1: the only action needed is upload, so allow only the write-object action. Step 2: scope the resource to releases-prod/builds/* rather than the whole bucket. Step 3: add a condition that the request comes from the CI runner's network range. The result: the role can add new builds to one folder, and it cannot read other buckets or delete anything. A broad grant of every action on every resource would let a leaked key erase the whole account's storage.

Common mistake: adding star to a policy because a request failed with access denied. The denial message names the missing action; read it and add only that action, then retest.

Consequence in a running system: an over-broad pipeline role can be used by any compromised build step to change production, so the damage is limited only by the account's boundaries. Narrow policies keep a single failure from becoming a full outage or a data breach.

questions.prompt: A nightly reconciliation job at a dental clinic group needs to read daily ledger files stored in the bucket ledger-archive, inside the folder daily/. It must never write or delete anything. Step 1: allow only the read-object action, because reading is the only thing the job does. Step 2: scope the resource to ledger-archive/daily/* so nothing outside that folder is readable. Step 3 is missing: the team also wants the read to succeed only when the request comes from the job's private network range, 10.40.0.0/16. Which completion of Step 3 keeps the policy least privilege?
choices: Add a Condition that the request must originate from the network range 10.40.0.0/16.
Add a second Allow statement for delete-object, so the job can clean up old copies.
Add a Deny statement for read-object, so the network range check is enforced by the explicit block.
Add an Allow statement with Action star on the whole bucket, so the job never hits an access denied error again.
questions.why: A Condition is the extra check the teaching text describes for limiting a statement by network origin, and it narrows the existing read grant without adding any new action or resource.

questions.prompt: In a policy statement, what does the Resource field do?
choices: It names the specific thing the action applies to, identified by a unique Amazon Resource Name string.
It sets how many minutes a temporary credential stays valid.
It lists the people who are allowed to sign in to the account.
It lists every region in which the account is permitted to run services.
questions.why: The Resource field identifies the particular object or service an action targets, using an Amazon Resource Name, which is a unique identifier string.

questions.prompt: A service role at a logistics firm is refused when it tries to receive messages from a managed message queue. The error message names the single action ReceiveMessage. What is the least-privilege fix?
choices: Add only the named ReceiveMessage action, scoped to that one queue's identifier, then retest.
Attach a policy with Action star on all resources so that no future denial can occur.
Remove every Condition from the role, because conditions are the usual cause of denials.
Create a Deny statement covering all actions on the queue, then retest the request.
questions.why: The denial message names the missing action, so the right move is to add only that action and limit it to the specific queue, rather than broadening access.

questions.prompt: A role at a bakery chain has exactly one Allow statement, permitting read-object on the bucket shop-photos. Nothing in the policy mentions a Deny. The role then tries to delete an object in a different bucket, invoices-2024. What happens?
choices: The request is allowed, because no Deny statement blocks it.
The request is denied only if a Deny statement is added later for that bucket.
The request is allowed, because delete actions are permitted by default on every bucket.
The request is denied, because no Allow statement matches a delete on that bucket.
questions.why: Access is denied by default, so a request succeeds only when some Allow statement matches it, and here none covers deleting from invoices-2024.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who is writing their first AWS policy for a deploy job why we start from the smallest set of permissions, and how we would know the policy is right. Name one limit or tradeoff of this approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: We start small because AWS denies anything not explicitly allowed, so the policy should list only the actions and resources the job really uses. For a deploy job that uploads builds to one folder, that means allowing only the write action, on only that folder path, and perhaps only from the CI runner's network. To check we have it right, we run the job and confirm it succeeds, then look at any access denied messages, which name the exact missing action, and add only that. The tradeoff is time: writing narrow policies takes iteration, and a task that starts failing after a new feature is added needs its policy revisited. Teams often accept that cost because a broad role is much harder to audit and much more damaging if its credentials leak.
rubricPoints: Defines least privilege as granting only the actions and resources a task needs
Explains that access is denied by default, so narrow allows are safer to start from
Describes using denial messages to add only the missing action, not broad wildcards
Names a real tradeoff such as iteration time or maintenance when the job changes

suggested.rationale: The planned authorization policy evaluator would let the learner test whether narrowed statements allow and deny the right requests.

lessons.plain: Access control is deciding who may do what to which thing. Two common patterns exist. Role-based access control (RBAC) groups permissions into named roles, such as deployer or auditor, and gives people or machines the role that matches their job. Attribute-based access control (ABAC) instead decides from labels, called attributes or tags, attached to both the person and the thing they touch: an engineer tagged for the payments team may act on resources tagged for payments and nothing else. RBAC is easy to reason about, while ABAC scales across many teams without a new rule for each one. Real systems often use both together.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company has 40 teams and 2,000 storage buckets. Would you rather write one rule for each team-and-bucket pair, or one rule that says a person may touch a bucket when their team label matches the bucket's team label? Why?
lessons.teach:
A role is a named set of permissions that an identity can take on for a period of time. In AWS IAM, a role is assumed by a user, a service, or another account, which then receives temporary credentials. Role-based access control (RBAC) means you attach permissions to roles that match job functions, then grant people membership in those roles. It works well when the number of job functions is small and stable.

Attribute-based access control (ABAC) moves the decision into conditions. A tag is a key-value label, such as team=payments, attached to a principal (the identity making the request) or to a resource (the thing being acted on). A policy condition compares values, for example: allow the action only when the principal's team tag equals the resource's team tag. The policy is written once and covers every new resource carrying the matching tag. Anything not explicitly allowed is denied by default.

Worked example. A deployer role has an allow statement with the condition that the resource's team tag equals the principal's team tag. Step 1: Asha assumes the deployer role, and her session carries team=payments from her identity. Step 2: she requests an update to a configuration entry tagged team=payments. Step 3: the evaluator compares the two values, finds them equal, and allows the call. Step 4: she requests an update to an entry tagged team=billing; the values differ, no allow applies, and the request is denied.

Common mistake: letting people edit their own tags. If an engineer can change the team tag on their own identity, the condition protects nothing. Restrict tag-writing permissions as tightly as the access they unlock.

Consequence in a running system: one unguarded tag-edit permission can let a member of one team read or change another team's data. The audit log records the tag change, but nothing blocks it unless someone has deliberately restricted that permission. Treat tag-writing permission as part of the access decision itself.

questions.prompt: Dimitri works at a logistics firm. The company has a reader role with one allow statement: the action is allowed only when the principal's region tag equals the resource's region tag. Step 1: Dimitri assumes the reader role, and his session carries region=eu-west from his identity. Step 2: he requests to read a shipment manifest stored in a resource tagged region=us-east. Step 3: [missing step]. Step 4: the request is denied because no allow statement applies.
choices: The evaluator copies region=us-east onto Dimitri's session, so the two values now match and the read is allowed.
The evaluator checks whether Dimitri has a separate reader role for the us-east region and grants access if he does.
The evaluator skips the tag comparison because the reader role is a role rather than a user, and allows the read by default.
The evaluator compares the two region values, finds them different, and no allow applies, so the default deny takes effect.
questions.why: The condition compares the two tag values, and when they differ no allow matches, so anything not explicitly allowed is denied by default.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what does attribute-based access control (ABAC) decide access on?
choices: Conditions that compare labels on the requesting identity with labels on the target resource.
Whether the identity has ever previously accessed the same resource.
A fixed list of job titles that each person has been assigned to.
The time of day at which an identity first signed in to the account.
questions.why: ABAC uses conditions comparing tags (key-value labels) on the principal and the resource, so the decision follows those attribute values rather than a fixed job-title list.

questions.prompt: A platform team uses a policy that allows an action only when the principal's cost-center tag equals the resource's cost-center tag. One engineer is permitted to change the cost-center tag on their own identity. What is the main risk?
choices: The policy automatically denies all requests, because tags on identities are never compared to tags on resources.
The engineer can set their own tag to match any resource and then pass the condition, so the check protects nothing.
The engineer can no longer assume any role, because changing a tag invalidates temporary credentials.
The engineer's change is blocked by default, because tag edits always require a second approver in AWS IAM.
questions.why: If the identity can edit its own tag, the condition compares attributes the user controls, so the tag check no longer restricts anything; tag-writing permission must be restricted as tightly as the access it unlocks.

questions.prompt: A company has three stable job functions, but it launches a new project every week, and each project's data is tagged with its project name. Which approach fits best, and why?
choices: Use ABAC with project tags on principals and resources, because one policy covers every new resource carrying the matching tag.
Use RBAC for everything, because roles alone can match resources by their tag values without a condition.
Give everyone administrator access, because tags cannot be used in access decisions.
Create a new role for every project, because RBAC handles a growing number of job functions best.
questions.why: RBAC suits a small, stable set of job functions, while ABAC writes the rule once in conditions so that new weekly resources with matching tags are covered without new policies.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between RBAC and ABAC, and name one limit or tradeoff of using tags for ABAC.
lessons.modelAnswer: RBAC gives each job function a role with a fixed set of permissions, and people get the role they need. It is simple to review, because you can list who holds the deployer role. Its weakness is growth: with many teams and many resources you end up with a role per team per function, and new resources often need new rules. ABAC writes one rule with conditions that compare attributes, usually tags, on the caller and on the resource, so a new bucket tagged for the payments team is covered automatically. The tradeoff is that security now depends on the tags being correct and protected. If someone can change a tag on themselves or on a resource, they can change which rules apply to them. So in practice I would use roles as the outer boundary, put tag-based conditions inside it, and tightly control who can write tags.
rubricPoints: RBAC grants permissions through roles matched to job functions.
ABAC decides access with conditions that compare tags on the caller and the resource.
ABAC scales to new resources without new rules, provided tags are applied consistently.
The main limit is that tags must be trustworthy, so tag-writing permissions must be restricted.

suggested.rationale: The planned authorization policy evaluator would let the learner test role and tag-condition requests against allow and deny outcomes, which is the core skill here.

lessons.plain: Machine identities are the logins that programs use to talk to each other and to databases, rather than the logins people type. Each one has a password or key, and if that secret stays the same for years, a leaked copy stays dangerous for years. Credential rotation means replacing the secret on a schedule, without anyone changing it by hand. AWS Secrets Manager is a managed vault that stores these secrets, can change them automatically, and lets programs fetch the current value when they need it. The core idea is that the secret changes often and programs always ask the vault for the latest value instead of keeping a private copy forever.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a database password changes every 30 days, what would have to be true about the application that uses it so that users never see a login failure on the day it changes?
lessons.teach:
A secret is any value that proves identity, such as a database password or an API key. Rotation is the act of replacing that value with a new one. Automated rotation means a scheduled process does this without a person. AWS Secrets Manager is a managed service that stores secrets encrypted, keeps a history of versions, and runs rotation on a schedule you set in days.

Versions carry labels. The label AWSCURRENT marks the value applications should use now. AWSPENDING marks a candidate during a change. AWSPREVIOUS marks the last value that worked, so you can step back. Rotation is carried out by a rotation function, a small piece of code that the service invokes in four steps: create a new candidate, set it on the target system such as the database, test that it works, and finish by moving the current label to the new version.

Worked example: a payments service connects to a database using a secret named orders-db. Day 30 arrives. Step one creates a new password and labels it pending. Step two changes the database user's password to match. Step three logs in with the pending value to confirm it works. Step four moves the current label to the pending version. The application fetches the current value at runtime, through the SDK or a caching client, so it picks up the new password when its cache refreshes.

Common mistake: copying the secret value into an environment variable or a config file at deploy time. After the first rotation that copy is stale, and every login fails until someone redeploys. The fix is to fetch at runtime and let the cache expire, so the application follows the label.

Consequence: if the test step fails, the rotation stops before the finish step, so the current label still points at the old working value. A failed rotation still needs an alarm, because a stuck rotation can leave a secret half-changed and nobody will notice unless something reports it.

questions.prompt: A bakery chain's order-sync service connects to a reporting database using a secret named bakery-reports. It is rotated every 14 days by a rotation function. On day 14 the rotation runs as follows. Step one creates a new password and labels it AWSPENDING. Step two sets that password on the reporting database user. Step three is missing from this trace. Step four moves the AWSCURRENT label to the pending version. Which step belongs in the gap, and why must it come before step four?
choices: Set the AWSPREVIOUS label on the new version so the rotation can be rolled back later.
Delete the previous version so only one password exists at a time, because stale versions are a security risk.
Copy the new password into the order-sync service's config file so the service restarts with it.
Test that the AWSPENDING password successfully logs in to the reporting database before the label moves.
questions.why: The test step must confirm the candidate works on the target before the finish step moves AWSCURRENT, so a failed test leaves the old working value in place.

questions.prompt: In AWS Secrets Manager, which version label marks the last value that worked, so an operator can step back to it?
choices: AWSCURRENT
AWSPREVIOUS
AWSDRAFT
AWSPENDING
questions.why: AWSPREVIOUS is the label reserved for the last value that worked, giving operators a way to return to it, while AWSCURRENT is the value applications should use now.

questions.prompt: A rotation function for a read-only ledger credential named ledger-readonly creates a new candidate and sets it on the database. The test step then fails because the login is refused. What state does the secret remain in?
choices: The old value is deleted automatically, so no login is possible until someone creates a new one.
The candidate is promoted to AWSCURRENT after a timeout, so the failure resolves itself.
AWSCURRENT still points at the old working value because the finish step never ran, and an alarm should report the stuck rotation.
AWSCURRENT has moved to the new candidate, so applications are now failing to log in.
questions.why: Because the test failed, the rotation stops before the finish step, so AWSCURRENT keeps the old working value and only an alarm will reveal the half-finished change.

questions.prompt: A team's order-sync service reads its database password at container build time and bakes it into the image. The rotation runs every 14 days. Two weeks after a rotation, the service starts failing logins. Which change fixes the root cause?
choices: Increase the rotation interval to 365 days so the baked-in password is rarely stale.
Have the service fetch the current value from Secrets Manager at runtime through the SDK or a caching client, so it follows the AWSCURRENT label.
Rebuild the image every two weeks by hand so it always contains the newest password.
Store the password in a second secret and point the image at that copy instead.
questions.why: A value baked into an image is frozen at build time and goes stale after the first rotation, while fetching at runtime lets the service follow the current label.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a rotated database password reaches a running service without an outage, and name one limit or tradeoff of this approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: The secret lives in Secrets Manager, not in the code or the deploy config. A rotation function creates a new password, changes it on the database, tests the new login, and then moves the current label to that version. The service calls GetSecretValue for the current value and caches it for a short time, so once the cache expires it uses the new password without a redeploy. The tradeoff is that the old value may still be cached somewhere until the cache lifetime ends, so the database has to accept both values during that overlap. Rotation also depends on the rotation function's own permissions and tests. If the test fails, promotion never happens and the old password keeps working, but someone still has to notice, which is why failed rotations should raise an alarm.
rubricPoints: Secrets are stored in Secrets Manager and fetched at runtime, not copied into code or config.
Rotation runs as a function through create, set, test and finish steps, and the new value is promoted only after a successful test.
Services use a short-lived cache, so they pick up the new value without a redeploy, and the old value may linger during the overlap.
Failed rotations must be detected and alarmed, since a stuck rotation can leave a half-changed secret.

suggested.rationale: That mission has the learner wire a deploy's secret into place without exposing it, which is the runtime-fetch habit this rotation depends on.

lessons.plain: Access to cloud accounts should prove who you are strongly, and should hand out permission for a limited time. Multi-factor authentication asks for a second proof, such as a code from a phone, on top of a password. A security token service issues short-lived passes instead of permanent keys, and an instance profile lets a server borrow such a pass automatically. Together these mean fewer long-lived secrets lying around, so a stolen password or a copied key does far less damage. This objective is about setting that up with automation rather than clicking through screens.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose a developer's laptop is stolen, and it held a file with a permanent access key for the cloud account. Which would limit the damage more: a key that never expires, or a key that stops working after one hour? Why?
lessons.teach:
Multi-factor authentication (MFA) means a login needs two or more kinds of proof: something you know, such as a password, and something you have, such as a one-time code from a device. In AWS, an identity that makes requests can be a user, a role, or a service. A role is a named set of permissions that an identity can temporarily take on instead of owning them permanently. AWS Security Token Service (STS) is the service that issues temporary credentials: an access key ID, a secret, and a session token, all with an expiry time. Asking STS for a role's credentials is called AssumeRole. An instance profile is a container that attaches a role to a virtual server, so software running on that server receives temporary credentials automatically and gets them refreshed before they expire, with no stored keys.

Why it works: a credential that expires limits how long a leaked copy is useful. A role's trust policy, which says who may assume the role, can also require MFA, using a condition that checks whether the caller authenticated with MFA.

Worked example: Priya signs in with her password and an MFA code. She calls AssumeRole for a deploy role. STS checks the trust policy, sees that MFA was present, and returns credentials valid for one hour. She runs the deploy with them. Two hours later the same commands fail with an expired-token error, and she must assume the role again.

Common mistake: believing that MFA on the console protects every action. Calls made with long-term access keys skip the console login, so the MFA check never runs for them unless a policy requires it.

Consequence: a pipeline that uses a session expiring mid-job will fail halfway through, so long jobs need a session duration that covers them or a step that refreshes the role. Temporary credentials shrink the window in which a stolen key can be used.

questions.prompt: Dana works in audit at a regional bank. Her steps so far: 1) She signs in with her password and an MFA code. 2) She calls AssumeRole for the audit role. STS checks the role's trust policy, sees that MFA was present, and returns credentials valid for 15 minutes. 3) She starts a reconciliation job that takes 40 minutes, using those credentials. The job will fail at about minute 15 unless one more step is added between step 2 and step 3. Which step fixes it?
choices: Remove the MFA condition from the role's trust policy so the session lasts longer
Request the AssumeRole call with a session duration long enough to cover the 40-minute job
Copy the access key ID and secret into the job's config file so they never expire
Sign in again with only a password before starting the job
questions.why: The job outlasts the 15-minute credentials, so the fix is to request a session duration that covers the whole job, since a session expiring mid-job is what causes the failure.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what does an instance profile do?
choices: It attaches a role to a virtual server so software there receives temporary credentials that are refreshed automatically
It records every login to a server so auditors can see who used MFA
It sets the password policy for the users who log in to a server
It stores a long-term access key on a server so software never has to ask for credentials
questions.why: An instance profile is the container that attaches a role to a server, and software on that server then gets temporary credentials that are refreshed before they expire, with no stored keys.

questions.prompt: A build script on a server uses long-term access keys to call AWS directly. The role it could assume has a trust policy that requires MFA. Does that MFA condition protect the script's calls?
choices: Yes, because STS checks the trust policy for every request, whatever credentials are used
No, because MFA only ever applies to human users, never to scripts or roles
No, because calls made with long-term access keys skip the console login, so the MFA check does not run unless a policy requires it
Yes, because the server sends a device code with each call
questions.why: Calls made with long-term access keys bypass the console sign-in where MFA is checked, so a trust policy MFA condition does not guard them unless some policy separately requires MFA.

questions.prompt: A release job takes 90 minutes. The role it assumes issues credentials valid for 45 minutes. Which approach keeps the job from failing halfway through?
choices: Keep the 45-minute session and hope the job finishes early
Request a session duration that covers the full 90 minutes, or add a step that refreshes the role before the credentials expire
Delete the session token so the credentials stop expiring
Run the job twice in a row so the second run reuses the first run's credentials
questions.why: A session that expires mid-job makes the job fail, so the job needs either a session duration covering its full length or a step that assumes the role again before expiry.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, why a server should get temporary credentials from an instance profile rather than from a stored access key, and name one limit or tradeoff of temporary credentials.
lessons.modelAnswer: A stored access key is a permanent secret. If it is copied from the server, whoever holds it can keep using it until someone notices and revokes it. An instance profile instead attaches a role to the server, and software there receives short-lived credentials that STS issued and that refresh on their own. Nothing secret sits in a config file, and a copied pass expires soon. The tradeoff is that temporary credentials need refreshing. If a process runs longer than the session allows, or the refresh logic breaks, calls start failing with expired-token errors. So the team must size session duration to the longest job and monitor refresh failures. Human access works similarly: MFA on the role's trust policy confirms a person is present before issuing a pass.
rubricPoints: Temporary credentials expire, so a leaked copy has a short useful life.
An instance profile supplies and refreshes role credentials without stored keys.
Tradeoff: sessions must outlast the work or refresh correctly, or calls fail.
MFA is checked at the point of assuming a role, and can be required by policy.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine covers MFA, STS sessions, or instance profiles, so reasoning through an exam-style scenario is the best fit.

lessons.plain: Network security components are the gates and filters that decide which network traffic may reach your servers and applications, and from where. Think of a building with several checkpoints: a lock on each room, a guard at the lobby, a doorman who reads each visitor's request, and a crowd-control team for floods. Each one works at a different point and checks different things. Some allow or deny by address and port, some read the content of a web request, and some absorb huge floods of traffic. Knowing which checkpoint sees which traffic lets you stop the right thing without blocking the wrong thing.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your web server should accept HTTPS from anyone on the internet, but SSH only from your office address. Which network component would you reach for first to enforce that, and why might you need a second component as well?
lessons.teach:
A security group is a stateful virtual firewall attached to a network interface, so it guards one server or one load balancer. It holds only allow rules. It is stateful, meaning that once a connection is allowed in, the reply is allowed back out without a separate rule. A network ACL is a stateless filter attached to a whole subnet, which is a range of addresses inside a larger network. It holds numbered allow and deny rules, checked from the lowest number upward, and the first match wins. Because it is stateless, it judges each direction separately, so reply traffic needs its own rule. A route table is a list of destinations and where to send traffic for each. A subnet is reachable from the internet only if its route table points at an internet gateway, the component that connects a network to the internet. A packet with no matching route is dropped. AWS Network Firewall is a managed inspection device you place in a subnet and steer traffic through using routes. It applies stateful rules, including rules about domain names. AWS WAF, a web application firewall, reads HTTP and HTTPS requests at the front door of a service such as a load balancer or CloudFront, matching on paths, headers and request rates. AWS Shield defends against distributed denial-of-service floods, with a basic tier that is always on and an advanced tier that adds protection and access to a response team.

Worked example: a web server in a private subnet accepts HTTPS only from a load balancer. A customer request arrives at the load balancer, which sits in a public subnet whose route table sends internet traffic to the internet gateway. The subnet network ACL allows inbound port 443 and also the outbound high port range used for replies. The server's security group allows port 443 from the load balancer's security group. The reply leaves, and the security group lets it out automatically because it is stateful. Each layer checks one thing, and all of them must agree.

Common mistake: opening port 443 in the security group and assuming the job is done, while the network ACL silently blocks replies on high ports. Connections then hang, and the site looks broken even though the group rules look right.

In a running system, a single missing rule at any layer makes the service unreachable, so when a connection fails you check the routes, then the network ACL, then the security group, in that order.

questions.prompt: A team at Harrow Dental runs a reporting server in a public subnet. An administrator at 203.0.113.40 connects over SSH on port 22. The subnet route table has a route sending internet traffic to the internet gateway, the component that connects a network to the internet. The subnet network ACL, a stateless numbered filter for the whole subnet, has inbound rule 100 allowing TCP 22 from 203.0.113.0/24. The server's security group, a stateful firewall on the single instance, allows TCP 22 from 203.0.113.40/32. The server sends its reply. The security group lets that reply out automatically because it is stateful. Step missing from the trace: the network ACL needs an outbound rule allowing the reply, and the trace is incomplete until that rule is named. Which outbound rule completes it?
choices: Add an outbound network ACL rule allowing TCP ports 1024-65535 to 203.0.113.0/24, because the network ACL is stateless and judges replies separately
Add a network ACL inbound deny rule for ports 1024-65535, so that high ports are filtered before the security group sees them
Add a route from the subnet to the internet gateway, because the route table is what decides whether replies can leave
Add an outbound security group rule allowing TCP 22 to 203.0.113.40/32, since the group must approve every reply
questions.why: Because a network ACL is stateless, the reply on high ports needs its own outbound allow rule, while the security group needs nothing extra for replies.

questions.prompt: Which description best fits a security group as the teaching text defines it?
choices: A managed inspection device placed in a subnet that matches domain names in outbound traffic
A stateful virtual firewall attached to a network interface that holds only allow rules, with replies allowed back automatically
A stateless numbered filter attached to a whole subnet, where the lowest matching number decides the outcome
A request filter at the edge of a service that reads HTTP paths and headers before they reach the application
questions.why: A security group is a stateful firewall attached to a network interface that holds only allow rules, so replies to an allowed connection need no separate rule.

questions.prompt: A subnet's network ACL has rule 100 denying TCP port 22 from 198.51.100.0/24 and rule 200 allowing TCP port 22 from 0.0.0.0/0. An engineer at 198.51.100.7 tries to SSH to an instance in that subnet, and the instance's security group allows port 22 from anywhere. What happens to the connection?
choices: It is blocked only if the security group is also changed, since the group decides final access
It succeeds, because the security group allows port 22 and is checked after the network ACL
It is blocked, because the network ACL checks rules from the lowest number upward and rule 100 matches first
It succeeds, because rule 200 is a broader allow and wins over the narrower deny
questions.why: The network ACL evaluates rules from the lowest number and the first match wins, so rule 100 denies the engineer before rule 200 is reached.

questions.prompt: A team wants to block any request to the /admin path that carries a specific User-Agent header, at the load balancer that fronts their web application. Which component should they use, and why not AWS Shield?
choices: AWS Shield, because it inspects HTTP paths and headers at the load balancer and blocks matching requests
A network ACL on the subnet, because it is stateless and can match HTTP header values
AWS WAF attached to the load balancer, because it reads HTTP requests and matches on paths and headers, while Shield defends against denial-of-service floods
AWS Network Firewall, because it matches URL paths and headers inside any subnet it is routed through
questions.why: AWS WAF reads HTTP requests at the front door and matches on paths and headers, while AWS Shield is aimed at distributed denial-of-service floods rather than request contents.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says we should put every block rule in the network ACL because it is the stronger layer. Explain to them how security groups and network ACLs differ, and name one limit or tradeoff of relying on either one alone.
lessons.modelAnswer: Security groups attach to individual instances or network interfaces, are stateful, and only have allow rules, so a reply to an allowed connection is automatically permitted. Network ACLs attach to whole subnets, are stateless, support both allow and deny rules, and check numbered rules in order, so reply traffic and high ports must be allowed explicitly. Putting everything in the network ACL would make each change affect a whole subnet and would be easy to break by forgetting return ports. Relying only on security groups means you cannot explicitly deny a known bad address across a subnet.
