Analysis means reading them, or better, having software count and watch them so a pattern stands out. Metrics are numbers summarised over time, such as failed logins per minute. Security findings are a security service's own verdicts that something looks wrong, such as a server contacting a known bad address. This lesson covers making sure the right notes are recorded, that something is watching them, and that a violation produces a signal while it is still happening.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose an application writes a line every time someone types a wrong password, but nobody reads those lines. What would you need to add so that a burst of failures alerts a person within minutes?
lessons.teach:
A log is a timestamped record of one event. A metric is a number sampled over time, such as failed logins per minute. A finding is a verdict from a security service that some behaviour looks suspicious, usually with a severity. The chain that matters is: record the event, keep the record somewhere it survives, turn it into a number or a match, then alarm on that number.

On AWS, the audit trail of account activity (which API was called, by whom, from where, and when) is recorded by AWS CloudTrail. Application and system logs are sent to Amazon CloudWatch Logs, organised into log groups and streams. Logs may be kept indefinitely by default, which costs money, so you set a retention period on purpose. VPC Flow Logs record metadata about network connections, not their contents. A metric filter scans incoming log lines for a pattern and increments a custom metric each time it matches. An alarm watches that metric and notifies someone when it crosses a threshold for a set number of periods. Amazon GuardDuty analyses logs and other data sources and produces findings. AWS Security Hub collects findings from several services into one place.

Worked example: an app writes 'login failed for user X' on each bad password. A metric filter matching that text counts 40 matches in one 5-minute period. An alarm set to fire at 20 or more matches per period sends a notification within minutes.

Common mistake: enabling logs but never alarming on them or reviewing them, so the evidence exists and nobody sees it. Another mistake is writing secrets or full card numbers into log lines, which then spreads them to everyone with log read access.

Consequence: if an instance writes logs only to its local disk and is terminated during an incident, the evidence is lost with it, so logs must leave the machine as they are written. The value of any detection depends on how short the gap is between the violation and the alert.

questions.prompt: A ticketing service runs on three EC2 instances and writes the line 'refresh token rejected for client ID' to a local file on each instance. Step 1: the application writes one line for each rejected token. Step 2 is blank: [missing step]. Step 3: a metric filter matches 15 lines in one 10-minute period and increments a custom metric. Step 4: an alarm set to fire at 10 or more matches per period notifies the on-call engineer. After an instance was replaced during an incident, the team found no rejection lines from it. Which choice correctly fills the missing Step 2?
choices: A log agent ships each line to a CloudWatch Logs log group as it is written, so the record survives if the instance is terminated.
A VPC Flow Log is turned on for the subnet so that rejected token lines are copied into it.
The application restarts itself after every 10 rejected tokens so the counter resets.
The team deletes the local log files each night to keep disk usage low.
questions.why: The logs must leave the machine as they are written, so a shipping step to CloudWatch Logs is what lets the evidence survive instance replacement and lets the metric filter see the lines at all.

questions.prompt: In the sense used for monitoring, which of these is a metric?
choices: A count of HTTP 503 responses per hour, recorded as a number over successive time periods.
A single log line that records one HTTP 503 response with its exact timestamp.
A VPC Flow Log entry showing the packet contents of one network connection.
A GuardDuty finding that rates a port scan as high severity.
questions.why: A metric is a number sampled over time, such as a count per period, whereas a single log line is one event and a finding is a verdict from a security service.

questions.prompt: A team logs the full request body during debugging, and one body contains a complete card number. What is the main risk the teaching text warns about?
choices: CloudWatch Logs hides card numbers automatically, so the risk is only a slower metric filter.
The card number is stored as a metric, which makes it visible on dashboards only.
Only the server that wrote the line can read it, so the risk is limited to that server.
The card number spreads to everyone with log read access, widening exposure well beyond the application.
questions.why: Secrets or full card numbers written into log lines are readable by anyone who can read those logs, which is the exposure the teaching text names as a common mistake.

questions.prompt: A metric filter records 9 matches in each of three consecutive 1-minute periods. The alarm fires when a period has 8 or more matches, and it must breach for 3 consecutive periods before notifying. Does the alarm notify?
choices: No, because 9 is not a multiple of 8.
No, because the alarm only evaluates once per hour regardless of the period length.
Yes, immediately after the first period, because 9 is above the threshold of 8.
Yes, after the third period, because each of the three periods reached 8 or more matches.
questions.why: An alarm notifies only when the metric crosses its threshold for the set number of consecutive periods, and here all three periods meet the threshold of 8 or more.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, how a burst of failed logins on a server becomes an alert, and name one limit of this chain that could let a real violation go unnoticed.
lessons.modelAnswer: The app writes a line for every failed login, and that line is shipped off the server into a central log group so it survives if the server is replaced. A metric filter matches the failure text and turns each match into a count, so ten minutes of attacks becomes a number on a graph. An alarm watches that count and notifies the team when it stays above a threshold for a set number of periods. The main limit is that the chain only sees what was written down. If the app never logs failed logins, or the filter matches a slightly different phrase after a code change, the count stays at zero and the alarm never fires. Threshold choice is another limit: set it too high and a slow, patient attack under the line goes unnoticed. Security findings from GuardDuty can also need tuning before they are trusted.
rubricPoints: Distinguishes a log (one event record), a metric (a number over time), and a finding (a service's verdict).
Describes the path: record the event, ship it off the machine, match or count it, then alarm on a threshold.
Says where account-level activity is recorded (CloudTrail) versus application and network logs.
States a real limit, such as missing or changed log text, a threshold set too high, unset retention, or findings that need tuning.

suggested.rationale: Investigating failed SSH logins in a real log file practises reading and counting security events the way this objective expects.

scenarios.title: Harbourline Freight: building the first automated path from commit to production
scenarios.scenario: Harbourline Freight is a fictional logistics company. Its customer-tracking web service runs on Amazon EC2 virtual servers behind a load balancer, which is a component that spreads incoming web traffic across several servers. Releases are currently copied to the servers by hand. Last month a bad release broke the database connection, and the tracking page stayed down for forty minutes because nobody noticed until customers called. Your team lead asks you to design the first automated path that takes a commit to production. Some terms you will need: a pipeline is an automated sequence of stages, where each stage must pass before the next one runs. A build is the step that turns source code into a runnable package. An artifact is a packaged output of a build, such as a zip file, that later stages deploy. Amazon CodeBuild is a managed build service that runs your build commands in a clean, temporary container and saves the output as artifacts. A pull request is a request to merge a proposed change into the main branch, and running checks on a pull request means problems are found before the code is merged. Amazon CodeDeploy is a deployment service that depends on a small program called the CodeDeploy agent, installed on each server, which runs named lifecycle hooks (steps such as stop, install, start and validate) defined in a file in the package. Blue/green deployment means building a new set of servers beside the old set and moving traffic across once the new set is healthy. In-place deployment means stopping and replacing the application on the existing servers. Answer the following three sub-tasks. 1. For each test type (unit tests, integration tests, security scans, and user interface acceptance tests), state at which pipeline stage it belongs and what it would catch that the others would not. Say which of these should also run on every pull request, and why. 2. Harbourline must choose between in-place and blue/green deployment for the tracking service. Choose one, justify it against the forty-minute outage, and explain what happens when a validate hook fails and what customers see as a result. 3. The build needs a database password. Explain where the password should be stored (AWS Secrets Manager or AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store), how CodeBuild gets it at run time, and the one mistake a team is most likely to make here.
subParts: Test types, pipeline stages and pull request checks
Choosing a deployment strategy and explaining rollback
Storing and retrieving the database password
modelAnswer: Unit tests check one small piece of code in isolation, so they belong in the earliest stage right after the build, and they run fast enough to run on every pull request. They catch logic errors inside a function that integration tests would bury under many moving parts. Integration tests check that components work together, for example the service talking to a real or test database, so they belong after the build and before any deployment, and they are usually run on merges to the main branch rather than every pull request because they are slower. Security scans look for known vulnerabilities in dependencies and risky patterns in code, so they belong early, ideally on pull requests, and again on the built artifact before deployment; they catch problems that no functional test checks. User interface acceptance tests drive the real page in a browser to confirm a user can complete a task, so they belong after deployment to a staging environment that resembles production, and they catch broken pages that pass every server-side test. Unit tests and security scans should run on pull requests; integration tests can run on merges; acceptance tests run in staging on each release candidate.

Blue/green is the better choice for the tracking service. In-place deployment stops the running application on the same servers, so a failed release means customers see errors until someone fixes or reverts it. Blue/green builds the new version on fresh servers beside the current ones, so the old set keeps serving customers until the new set passes its checks, and traffic can be moved back quickly. In CodeDeploy, each lifecycle hook is a script; the agent runs it and reads its exit code, which is the number a program returns when it finishes, where zero means success and any other value means failure. If the validate hook, which might request the tracking page and check for a healthy response, exits with a non-zero code, CodeDeploy marks the deployment as failed and, if automatic rollback is configured, moves traffic back to the old servers. Customers see at most a brief period of errors during the switch rather than an open-ended outage, provided the health check is meaningful and the old servers are kept until validation passes.

The password should live in AWS Secrets Manager, a managed service for storing and rotating secrets, or in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store, a service for storing configuration values including encrypted ones. Secrets Manager is the usual choice for a database password because it can rotate the value automatically. CodeBuild is given an IAM role, which is a set of permissions attached to the build, that allows reading that one secret. The buildspec file, which describes the build steps, references the secret by name, and CodeBuild fetches it into the environment only while the build runs, so the password never appears in the source repository. The most likely mistake is hard-coding the password in the buildspec file or an environment variable typed into the project settings, where it is then stored in the repository history or shown in build logs; a good answer also notes that secret values should never be printed by a build step.

scenarios.title: Governed from birth: a new analytics account at Harbor Lantern Logistics
scenarios.scenario: Harbor Lantern Logistics is a fictional freight company opening a new AWS account for its regional analytics team. The platform lead wants the account governed from its first minute: a standard baseline of networking and logging, guardrails that stop risky settings before they happen, a way to push the same baseline into other accounts and Regions, and scheduled patching of its servers. Nobody should click through the console to set it up. Infrastructure as code (IaC) means describing resources in a text template that a tool builds for you, so the result is repeatable and reviewable. Drift means the live resources no longer match the template, usually because someone changed them by hand. Read the situation and answer the three tasks below. 1. The team must choose how to write the baseline template. Explain in one or two sentences each the difference between a plain CloudFormation template, an AWS SAM template, and an AWS CDK app, then recommend one for a baseline made mostly of plain resources (a VPC, a logging bucket, and an IAM role) and justify your choice. 2. Harbor Lantern has four other accounts and wants the same baseline stack in all of them across two Regions, managed from one administrator account. Explain what a CloudFormation StackSet does. Then explain how a service control policy (SCP), an AWS Config rule, and a drift check each contribute to governance, and state which of these prevents a change and which only reports it. 3. Servers in the new account must be patched on a schedule and kept in a desired software state. Explain the difference between AWS Systems Manager State Manager and AWS Config, state which service applies the patch schedule and which records whether the servers still comply, and name one common mistake a team makes here.
subParts: Choosing the template technology and justifying it for a mostly plain baseline
Explaining StackSets and which governance control prevents versus reports
Separating the job of applying patch schedules from the job of checking compliance
modelAnswer: A plain CloudFormation template is a YAML or JSON file that lists resources and their settings, and CloudFormation builds them directly. AWS SAM is an extension on top of CloudFormation with shorthand for serverless pieces such as functions and APIs. The AWS CDK is a framework where you write the infrastructure in a general programming language and it generates a CloudFormation template from that code. For a baseline of a VPC, a logging bucket, and a role, a plain CloudFormation template is the best fit: it has no build step, every reviewer can read exactly what will be created, and the baseline has no serverless or complex logic that would benefit from SAM shorthand or CDK abstraction. A common mistake is choosing the CDK because it looks more modern, which adds a code build step and makes the final template harder for reviewers to verify.

A StackSet is a CloudFormation feature that deploys one template as stack instances across many accounts and Regions from a single administrator account, using the account structure in AWS Organizations to choose targets. An SCP is an Organizations policy that sets the maximum permissions accounts may use, so it blocks a forbidden action before it happens, for example denying anyone the right to switch off logging. An AWS Config rule evaluates a resource's settings against a desired condition and reports whether it is compliant, optionally with a fix attached, so it detects rather than prevents. A drift check compares the live stack resources with the template and reports the differences, but does not revert them. Only the SCP prevents a change; the Config rule and the drift check report. A common mistake is assuming Config stops a risky change. The consequence is that a publicly readable bucket can stay public until someone acts on the report.

State Manager is a Systems Manager feature that keeps managed instances in a defined state by running associations on a schedule, such as applying a patch baseline or installing an agent, and repeating them. AWS Config records the configuration history of resources and evaluates them against rules, reporting compliance, but it does not change anything on its own. So State Manager applies the patch schedule, and AWS Config, using a Systems Manager patch compliance rule, checks whether the servers still meet the patch state. A common mistake is treating AWS Config as the thing that patches servers. The consequence is that non-compliance gets noticed in a report while the servers stay unpatched.

scenarios.title: Lumen Tickets checkout resilience review
scenarios.scenario: Lumen Tickets is a fictional ticket-sales company that runs its checkout service on AWS. The web tier runs on Amazon EC2 instances, which are virtual servers, behind an Application Load Balancer, a managed service that spreads incoming web requests across healthy servers. The bookings database is an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL instance, a managed relational database. Today the web servers and the database all sit in a single Availability Zone, which is one isolated data center inside a Region, a geographic area that contains several such zones. The business has set three requirements. First, checkout must be available 99.9 percent of the time each month. Second, if the database is lost, the recovery time objective (RTO, the longest the service may be down) is 30 minutes, and the recovery point objective (RPO, the most recent data the business can afford to lose) is 5 minutes. Third, the company must survive a full outage of the whole Region. Complete the following. 1. Translate the 99.9 percent availability target into a monthly downtime allowance, then redesign the web tier and the database so that losing one Availability Zone does not stop checkout. 2. Choose a disaster recovery strategy for a whole-Region outage, either pilot light or warm standby, explain which one can meet the 30-minute RTO and 5-minute RPO, and name the cross-Region capability you would use for the database and for switching customer traffic. 3. Describe how you would test the failover so you know it works rather than assuming it does, and name one thing that a passing test does not prove.
subParts: Pilot light or warm standby choice with cross-Region features
modelAnswer: A 99.9 percent target over a 30-day month (43,200 minutes) allows 0.1 percent of that time to be down, which is about 43 minutes of downtime per month. Availability simply means the share of time the service correctly answers requests. The redesign should run at least two EC2 web servers in two different Availability Zones, managed by an Auto Scaling group, which is a set of servers that a policy adds or removes automatically when needed. The Application Load Balancer should be enabled across both zones, so its health checks stop sending traffic to servers in a zone that has failed. For the database, enable the RDS Multi-AZ deployment option, which keeps a synchronous standby copy of the database in a second zone and lets RDS switch the database name to that standby if the primary fails. Worked example: at 14:00 the zone holding the primary database and one web server fails. The load balancer's health checks mark the failed targets unhealthy within a few check intervals, and all traffic goes to the web server in the surviving zone. RDS promotes the standby in the other zone and the application reconnects using the same database endpoint name. Common mistake: running both web servers in one zone, or assuming the Multi-AZ standby can serve read queries, which it cannot in that deployment option. Consequence: if both web servers sit in one zone, a single zone outage takes checkout fully down for as long as the zone is out, which can use up the 43-minute monthly allowance in one incident.

Disaster recovery means the plan for getting a service running again after a major failure. Pilot light keeps only the core, such as a database copy, running in a second Region, while the web servers are defined in code but switched off until needed. Warm standby keeps a full but smaller copy of the whole stack running in the second Region and scales it up on failover. For a 30-minute RTO, pilot light is risky because creating and starting web servers, warming caches, and passing health checks can take longer than 30 minutes. Warm standby is the better choice because the servers already run and only need to scale up, which fits inside the window. For the database, use an Amazon RDS cross-Region read replica, which is a copy in another Region that updates asynchronously. Asynchronous means the copy trails the primary by a small delay called replication lag, and that lag decides the data-loss exposure, so the team should watch the lag metric and keep it well under 5 minutes. Worked example: normal lag is about 1 second, and at 10:00 the primary Region fails when the lag is 3 seconds, so at most about 3 seconds of recent bookings can be lost, within the 5-minute RPO. The team then promotes the replica to a standalone database, which takes minutes. For traffic, use Amazon Route 53, a DNS service that answers name lookups, with failover routing and health checks that point the primary record at the main Region and the secondary record at the warm standby. Use S3 cross-Region replication for ticket PDFs stored in S3, an object storage service. Common mistake: assuming a Multi-AZ setting protects against Region loss, or setting a very long DNS cache time, so customers keep resolving the dead Region. Consequence: a one-hour DNS cache means many clients keep failing well past the 30-minute RTO even after the standby is healthy.

Testing failover means deliberately causing a failure in a controlled way and measuring what happens, instead of relying on the console showing a standby exists. Run a planned game day, either in a copy of the environment or in production with notice to the business. Stop one web server and confirm the Auto Scaling group replaces it while checkout keeps working. Simulate losing an Availability Zone by removing one zone's targets from the load balancer and checking that requests still succeed. Trigger a Multi-AZ database failover on purpose and time how long until checkout succeeds again. For the Region case, promote the replica in a rehearsal, cut DNS over, and record the actual elapsed time as your measured RTO. Measure data loss by comparing the timestamp of the last committed booking before the failure with the last booking present after recovery, which gives your measured RPO. Common mistake: testing only the happy path, with no live traffic, or confirming that a standby exists without ever switching to it. Consequence: a passing test shows that the mechanism worked in that run, not that it will work in a real disaster. One thing a passing test does not prove is that the standby Region currently has the same application version, IAM permissions, certificates, and machine images as production, so the test should include a check of those as well.

scenarios.title: Checkout errors go unnoticed for 40 minutes
scenarios.scenario:
Harbor Bloom Grocers is a fictional online grocery company. Its order API runs on EC2 instances (virtual servers that AWS rents to you) behind an Application Load Balancer, which is a managed service that spreads incoming web requests across a set of servers. The servers write application logs to a CloudWatch Logs log group, which is a named container in Amazon CloudWatch Logs holding the log streams from one source. Last month a bug made some checkout requests fail with HTTP 500 errors, and nobody noticed for 40 minutes because no alarm existed. Your lead asks you to fix the monitoring. Answer the three sub-tasks below.

1. The load balancer already publishes a metric that counts 5XX responses for each target group. Name the CloudWatch namespace, the metric name and the dimensions you would use to watch the checkout target group, and explain what period (resolution) you would choose so the alarm reacts within a few minutes.

2. Failed payments are written to the checkout log group with the text PAYMENT_DECLINED. Describe how you would create a metric filter (a rule that scans log events and turns matches into a number in CloudWatch) that counts these lines. Then state where you would set the log group's retention to 90 days and its encryption with a customer managed AWS KMS key (a key you create and control in AWS Key Management Service).

3. Describe the alarm action that notifies the on-call engineer without anyone watching a dashboard. Then explain what you would set for the missing data treatment, which decides what the alarm does when no metric data arrives at all, and why that choice matters if the logging pipeline itself breaks.
subParts: Pick the 5XX metric, dimensions and period
Alarm action and missing data treatment
modelAnswer: Use the namespace AWS/ApplicationELB, which is the namespace (a container that groups related metrics) for Application Load Balancer metrics. The metric is HTTPCode_Target_5XX_Count, which counts 5XX responses from the targets. A metric is the measured quantity itself. Dimensions are name and value pairs that narrow a metric to one resource, so you would set LoadBalancer to the checkout load balancer's name and TargetGroup to the checkout target group's identifier. Without both dimensions the alarm would mix in traffic from other services. Standard load balancer metrics arrive at a resolution (the length of each datapoint) of 60 seconds, so set the alarm period to 60 seconds and require several consecutive breaching datapoints, for example 3 out of 3, so one brief spike does not page anyone while a real outage still fires within a few minutes. High-resolution one-second data is available only for custom metrics you publish yourself, not for this built-in one.

Create a metric filter on the checkout log group. Its filter pattern is the text PAYMENT_DECLINED, so each matching log event counts. Set the metric namespace to a name you own, such as HarborBloom/Checkout, and the metric name to DeclinedPayments, with a metric value of 1 for each match. Then CloudWatch publishes a count per period. A metric filter only counts events that arrive after it is created; it does not look back at old logs. For retention, set the log group's retention setting to 90 days. Retention on a log group controls how long events are kept, and the default is never expire, which keeps storage costs growing indefinitely, so a common mistake is leaving that default on groups that do not need it. For encryption, associate the log group with your customer managed KMS key. The key's policy must allow the CloudWatch Logs service to use it. If that key is disabled or its policy blocks CloudWatch Logs, the group cannot encrypt or decrypt its data, and new log events can be rejected.

Create an Amazon SNS topic, which is a managed messaging service that delivers a notification to every subscriber, and subscribe the on-call paging tool or an on-call distribution endpoint to it. Attach the topic as the alarm action for both the ALARM state and, if you want, the recovery to OK state. The alarm then notifies people without a dashboard being watched. The missing data treatment decides the alarm's state when no datapoints arrive in an evaluation window. Options are missing, notBreaching, breaching and ignore. If you choose notBreaching or ignore, a broken logging or metrics pipeline looks healthy, so the alarm stays quiet while checkouts may be failing. Choosing breaching makes absent data count as a failure, so the alarm fires and pages when the pipeline goes silent. The trade-off is possible false pages during genuinely quiet periods, such as very low overnight traffic, so the choice should match how the checkout metric behaves.

scenarios.title: Harbor Lantern Logistics: a failed deployment, a retiring host, and a drifted firewall rule
scenarios.scenario: Harbor Lantern Logistics is a fictional parcel-tracking company. Its customer tracking API runs as containers managed by Amazon ECS (a service that starts, stops, and replaces containers across a pool of servers) behind a load balancer. At 02:10 last night, a rollout through AWS CodeDeploy (a service that moves a new application version onto servers or containers in controlled steps) changed from in progress to failed, and the service rolled back to the previous version. Two hours later, AWS Health (the service that publishes notices about problems and planned maintenance affecting your own resources) posted a scheduled notice that one underlying host in the production region is due for retirement. A security auditor also flagged that a production security group, which is a set of network allow rules attached to a resource, now accepts traffic from a wider address range than the runbook permits. You are the on-call engineer. Your team wants automated handling for these kinds of events and a clear explanation of the failed rollout. Complete these tasks: 1. Describe how an AWS Health event and a CloudTrail record (an audit log of API calls made in your account) can reach an automated response. Name the service that matches events against patterns and routes them to targets, the buffering layer you would place between that router and the work, and explain why you would add the buffer. 2. The rollout failed. Explain which records you would check and in what order to find the root cause, and how you would tell a bad application version apart from an environment problem. 3. For the security group change, explain how you would detect that it no longer matches the desired state and how you would restore it automatically, and state the role AWS Systems Manager (a fleet management service that runs commands and automation documents on instances and resources) plays in that restore.
subParts: Root cause of the failed rollout
Detecting and restoring the security group
modelAnswer: Amazon EventBridge is the event router in AWS. It receives events from AWS services, including AWS Health and CloudTrail, and checks each event against a pattern you write, such as source equal to the health service and an event category of scheduled change. When an event matches, the rule sends a copy to one or more targets. For the host retirement notice, the target could be an AWS Lambda function (a small piece of code that runs on demand) or an AWS Step Functions state machine (a workflow that runs steps in order and records progress). Between the router and the work, you would put Amazon SQS, a managed queue that holds messages until a consumer reads them. The queue absorbs bursts, so a flood of events during a regional incident does not overwhelm the consumer, and messages survive if the consumer is briefly unavailable. The common mistake is to point the rule straight at a function with no queue and no retry plan, so a burst or a downstream outage silently loses events. In this scenario, the retirement notice should trigger a workflow that drains the affected host's tasks onto healthy capacity before the retirement date, and the queue ensures that notice is not lost if the workflow is busy.

Start with the deployment record in CodeDeploy, which shows the deployment ID, the lifecycle event that failed, and the instance or task list involved. The lifecycle event name tells you which step broke, for example a script that ran before traffic was shifted. Next, read the logs written by that step on the affected container or instance, which hold the actual error text. Then check CloudTrail for API calls made by the deployment role in the same time window, because a denied permission or a changed parameter shows up there even when the application log is silent. Finally, look at CloudWatch metrics and logs for the service during the window, such as error rate and task restart counts, to see whether the new version was failing or the environment was. To separate the two, compare the failing hosts with a host that was not in the deployment, and check whether the same error appears on the old version. If only the new version fails everywhere, the cause is the application. If every version fails on one subnet or after a capacity change, the cause is the environment. The common mistake is to read only the final status and blame the code. The consequence is that you may ship a fix to the application when the real cause is a permission change, and the next rollout fails the same way.

Detect drift by comparing the live security group against the desired rule set in your runbook. Systems Manager State Manager can run a check on a schedule and report whether a resource matches its association, which is the desired configuration you define. When the check finds a rule that is wider than allowed, it can trigger a Systems Manager Automation document, which is a saved runbook of steps, to remove the non-compliant rule and reapply the approved one. Also route the CloudTrail record of the authorize call into your event pipeline from task 1, so the change is recorded with the caller's identity and time. The common mistake is to fix the rule by hand and not record the cause, so the same drift returns after the next manual edit. The consequence of an uncorrected rule in production is that traffic from addresses outside the policy can reach the service, which is a security exposure and an audit finding, and an automated restore closes that gap within the check interval instead of whenever someone next looks.
